title: Weekly Freight Report - June 12, 2026
excerpt: Market Pulse Truckload stayed firmly in a supply‑driven upcycle for the week of June 5–12, 2026, with record spot rates, tightening routing guides, and capacity exits pushing spot above contract across dry van, reefer, and flatbed, per NTG and C.H. R...
content:
Market Pulse

Truckload stayed firmly in a supply‑driven upcycle for the week of June 5–12, 2026, with record spot rates, tightening routing guides, and capacity exits pushing spot above contract across dry van, reefer, and flatbed, per NTG and C.H. Robinson updates.

According to NTG’s June 1–5 report, truckload spot rates are running about 40% higher year over year, a move they describe as structural, not a short‑term seasonal spike driven by holidays or DOT week timing. Capacity, not fuel, is identified as the primary driver of pricing, with elevated tender rejections and shrinking acceptable carrier pools forcing more freight into higher‑cost options.

DAT Trendlines confirm how tight the van market has become. For dry van, the load‑to‑truck ratio for the week of June 1–7 fell 23.0% week over week versus May 25–31, but May 2026 as a whole saw the van load‑to‑truck ratio up 48.4% month over month and a striking 92.0% year over year versus May 2025. That near‑doubling in a year underpins the rate strength brokers and carriers are feeling on the floor.

C.H. Robinson’s June 2026 outlook reports that U.S. truckload markets remain tight with spot rates now above contract, and that elevated spot pricing is hitting dry van, refrigerated, and flatbed alike. Flatbed is especially constrained, with one June macro‑freight brief highlighting flatbed spot rates at $4.32/mile and tender rejections above 38%, while broader truckload tender rejections have pushed up near 17%, a cycle high. That aligns with reports that routing‑guide depth is worsening and shippers are using backup carriers and spot more frequently.

On the volume side, 2026 is shaping up as a moderate‑growth year. ACT Research and other mid‑year outlooks describe freight volumes as stable to gradually improving, not booming, with truckload pressure coming mainly from constrained capacity. Manufacturing is carrying the load: May’s ISM Manufacturing PMI printed at 54.0, the highest since May 2022, and the Logistics Managers’ Index hit 69.5 with transportation prices at a record 96.0. Intermodal is participating in the upcycle as well. NTG notes international container rail volume up 8% year over year, domestic intermodal up 14% year over year, and drayage volumes roughly flat but with a constructive outlook tied to steady imports.

For brokers and carriers, the key takeaway this week: the downcycle is over. This is a tight‑capacity, price‑up environment where routing discipline and strategic carrier relationships matter more than chasing short‑term spot relief.

Regulation & Enforcement

Regulatory headlines were quiet during June 5–12, but several major changes are in force and shaping capacity, compliance burden, and fraud risk.

FMCSA’s rulemaking docket shows no new NPRMs or final rules dated June 5–12, 2026. The last notable Federal Register entries before this week were on May 6, 2026, including a notice on the availability of the new Motus registration system. The highly watched hours‑of‑service, broker transparency, CDL amendments, and safety fitness rules all remain in the pipeline without a June 5–12 publication.

Enforcement, not fresh rule text, is where the impact is landing. Earlier in 2026 FMCSA removed 12 ELD devices from its list of registered units for failure to meet technical requirements, including specific brands like Safe ELD and MYLOGS ELD. Carriers using revoked devices have 60 days to switch to a compliant ELD. During this week, no new revocations were announced, but the grace periods and replacement efforts are ongoing and still disrupting smaller fleets that waited to change over.

FMCSA also granted a temporary exemption on medical certification proof: interstate CDL and CLP drivers may rely on a paper medical examiner’s certificate for up to 60 days after issuance between April 11 and October 11, 2026. This is intended to smooth the transition to electronic medical record transmission but still requires brokers to verify that carriers are on top of their driver qualification files.

On the driver‑supply side, ACT Research notes that new enforcement around English‑language proficiency and non‑domiciled CDL programs is expected to remove about 25,000 drivers in the first year. Earlier in 2026, FMCSA also suspended more than 90,000 CDLs tied to non‑compliant non‑domiciled programs. That combination quietly tightens capacity beyond what rate charts alone show.

FMCSA continues to enforce the $75,000 broker bond requirement, and previous extensions put the key compliance date for certain broker and freight forwarder financial responsibility provisions at January 16, 2026. A second broker‑transparency NPRM is slated in the agenda, but no June 5–12 publication is recorded.

Finally, the new Motus DOT registration platform is live as of May, aimed squarely at reducing identity theft and carrier impersonation in the registration process. It is directly relevant to brokers vetting new carriers and trying to validate MC/DOT identities against a single authoritative system.

What this means for brokers

  • Expect ongoing small‑carrier disruption as ELD revocations and the Motus rollout shake out non‑compliant operators.
  • Assume tighter driver supply as ELP and non‑domiciled CDL enforcement works through 2026.
  • Keep your internal compliance checks aligned with the unchanged $75,000 bond and active FMCSA registration/insurance status; no relief is coming on those thresholds this week.

Broker Edge

This is a broker‑friendly pricing environment, but only for shops that can execute on carrier quality and routing‑guide performance.

With truckload spot rates roughly 40% higher year over year and van load‑to‑truck ratios up 92% year over year in May, per DAT and NTG, shippers are being forced into the market at elevated prices. Spot now sits above contract across many lanes as of mid‑June, according to major 3PLs. Yet ACT Research still expects contract rates to grow less than 2% in 2026, after similarly muted increases in 2025. That spread between fast‑moving spot and slow‑moving contract creates leverage for brokers who can price dynamically and sell capacity reliability.

Routing‑guide strain is the tell. NTG reports “elevated tender rejections and reduced acceptable capacity,” which translates to shippers leaning heavily on backup carriers and routing exceptions. If your brokerage can hold primary status and fill tenders with preferred carriers, you’ll be positioned to negotiate mid‑cycle contract adjustments while competing brokerages are stuck chasing one‑off spot loads.

Intermodal’s strength also opens arbitrage. International container rail volume is up 8% year over year, domestic intermodal up 14% year over year, and C.H. Robinson notes intermodal volumes are above historical averages as shippers react to high fuel and truck prices. Brokers with strong IMC relationships can offer truck‑to‑rail conversion on long‑haul lanes to defend shipper budgets while still capturing margin.

For American Lady Transportation and similar brokerages, the strategic plays this week are:

  • Re‑price expiring contracts using current spot levels (about 40% above a year ago) as your reference, not 2024 trough numbers.
  • Lean into quality carriers as “acceptable capacity” shrinks; shippers will pay to avoid fraud, missed appointments, and claims.
  • Sell modal flexibility—especially intermodal and LTL in select lanes—as a defense against truckload cost spikes.

Cross-Border Watchlist

Cross‑border trucking remains tight, with rising compliance and tariff risk on top of the same equipment and driver constraints seen domestically.

C.H. Robinson and other 3PLs report that Canada–U.S.–Mexico truckload markets are tightening, citing enforcement‑driven driver reductions, carrier exits, and currency pressure. Mexican diesel prices remain sharply higher than U.S. levels, squeezing Mexican carriers harder and reinforcing upward rate pressure on northbound moves even as U.S. diesel begins to ease.

Trade policy is the bigger wildcard. A Section 301 forced‑labor report from USTR identifies 60 economies as failing to adequately enforce bans on forced‑labor goods, with a proposal for 10% additional tariffs on countries taking partial steps and 12.5% on those that have not. A hearing is scheduled for July 7, 2026. At the same time, the Department of Justice is moving to block about $166 billion in tariff refunds, forcing importers to file individual actions to recover prior duties.

On June 3, 2026, a new executive order directed DHS and CBP to tighten importer‑of‑record rules, including:

  • Higher bonding requirements and a minimum domestic asset standard for importers.
  • A “good standing” requirement and stricter rules for foreign importers; informal entries limited to U.S. entities.
  • A penalty floor of at least 50% of duties with no mitigation for repeat offenders.
  • Expanded disclosure on beneficial ownership, supply chains, forced labor, and sanctions.
  • A 180‑day timeline for CBP to rebuild the importer registry using risk‑based tiering.

USMCA is also in the spotlight. Canada has formally requested that the U.S. and Mexico renew USMCA for another 16 years ahead of the July 1 review, with Mexico signaling support. If there is no agreement, the deal stays in place for 10 more years, but with annual reviews and an option for the U.S. to withdraw on six months’ notice.

For brokers managing cross‑border freight, the near‑term reality is continued strong demand and tight capacity, but the medium‑term risk is higher compliance cost and slower border processes as CBP tightens importer and broker vetting. Every new tariff, bond requirement, and importer rule ultimately feeds into landed cost and mode choice, especially for Texas border and Gulf gateways.

Fraud & Security

Freight fraud risk remains elevated even though there are no June 5–12‑specific enforcement headlines in the provided data.

Food Logistics reports that Q1 2026 freight fraud hit a record high, driven by four dominant patterns: direct theft by rogue carriers, compromised inboxes and communications, change‑of‑ownership schemes, and other digital attacks on the supply chain. FreightWaves’ 2026 Freight Fraud Symposium coverage adds that bad actors are using AI‑powered tools, forged identities, falsified documents, and more sophisticated phishing to defeat traditional vetting processes.

While not trucking‑specific, Safe Medicines’ March–April 2026 data show how fast illicit actors can adapt: semaglutide and tirzepatide shipments jumped 56.6% (from 474 to 837), and illicit attempts rose from 71 to 86, even as the illegitimate share fell from 14.98% to 10.27%. That pattern—volume growth alongside more targeted fraud—is relevant to high‑value pharma and healthcare freight under brokerage.

Cargo theft exposure is also drawing national attention. An industry coalition of more than 200 companies, including American Trucking Associations and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, is pushing the Senate to pass H.R. 2853 (Combating Organized Retail Crime Act). They cite trucking industry cargo‑theft losses of about $18 million per day and rail cargo theft of more than $200 million in 2025. The bill cleared the House with a 348–60 vote and sits with the Senate Judiciary Committee.

For brokers, the security posture that matches this risk profile includes:

  • Stricter identity verification for new carriers, aligned with FMCSA’s Motus system.
  • Multi‑factor authentication and segregation of duties on carrier setup and payment changes to combat inbox takeovers.
  • Heightened controls on high‑value and pharma loads, where attempted theft rates and regulatory scrutiny are both rising.

Equipment, Fuel & Ops

Fuel is easing off recent highs but remains a major cost line, while equipment decisions are being distorted by the approaching EPA‑27 standards.

EIA/FRED data show the national average diesel price at $5.210 per gallon for the week ending June 8, 2026, down from $5.350 the prior week and $5.523 two weeks earlier. That is a multi‑week decline but still well above the EIA May Short‑Term Energy Outlook full‑year 2026 average projection of $4.76/gal. The STEO calls for quarterly diesel averages of about $5.36 in Q2, $4.94 in Q3, and $4.73 in Q4, implying some relief later in the year if geopolitical risks stay contained.

Behind the pump price, crude is coming off conflict highs. Brent was quoted at $95.18/bbl on June 4, down 2.6% on news that the U.S. and Iran may move to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to tankers. WTI has fallen roughly $20/bbl over the last several trading sessions, taking some pressure off diesel even as domestic prices remain near historic peaks.

On the equipment side, NTG’s June 1–5 brief notes that fleets are bracing for higher new‑truck costs as pre‑buy activity ramps ahead of EPA‑27‑compliant vehicles. Many carriers are limiting capital to replacing older units rather than growing fleets, which, combined with ongoing carrier exits, keeps capacity tight. Cass and other 2026 outlooks suggest only moderate contract rate growth—on the order of 2%—but clearly higher asset and operating costs, reinforcing the case for disciplined network planning.

No specific June 5–12 data points were available on Class 8 order counts, used truck prices, or truck parking grants, but the directional story is consistent: higher cost to add or replace trucks, cautious fleet expansion, and ongoing operational friction from regulatory and security changes.

Action Checklist for Brokers

  • Re‑benchmark your pricing using current spot realities: truckload spot rates are about 40% higher year over year, and van load‑to‑truck ratios are up 92% versus May 2025. Make sure contract and mini‑bid offers reflect today’s tighter environment, not 2024 lows.
  • Prioritize carrier quality over lowest rate. NTG and C.H. Robinson both highlight shrinking “acceptable capacity” and elevated tender rejections. Double down on carriers with strong safety, on‑time performance, and clean fraud history.
  • Exploit modal options. With international intermodal up 8% YoY and domestic intermodal up 14% YoY, pitch rail and LTL conversions where they make sense to protect shipper budgets and margin.
  • Audit ELD and compliance status for every new carrier. Confirm they are not using one of the 12 revoked ELD devices and that their FMCSA registration is clean in Motus. Treat any mismatches as red flags.
  • Harden your anti‑fraud workflow. Q1 2026 marked a record in freight fraud. Require multi‑factor authentication on carrier setup, verify banking changes verbally through known contacts, and scrutinize documents for AI‑generated artifacts.
  • Adjust fuel strategies. With diesel at $5.210/gal but trending down, review FSC tables and be ready to re‑negotiate fuel schedules if crude keeps slipping toward EIA’s projected $4.76/gal 2026 average.
  • Prepare cross‑border customers for higher compliance cost. Brief them on the June 3 CBP executive order (higher bonds, stricter importer rules) and the potential 10–12.5% forced‑labor tariffs affecting sourcing and routing decisions into Texas and other ports of entry.
  • Target manufacturing‑heavy lanes. With ISM Manufacturing PMI at 54.0 and the LMI at 69.5 (transportation prices at 96.0), prioritize industrial, construction, and upstream supply‑chain accounts where freight demand is strongest and flatbed/van rates are most supportive.
  • Watch capacity exits and use them in your sales story. Carrier exits and a shrinking driver pool (including the expected removal of 25,000 drivers from new ELP enforcement) are real constraints. Use that data to justify higher rates and long‑term commitments rather than transaction‑only relationships.

title: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup - June 5, 2026
excerpt: Fleet & Market Trends Driver Shortage Tightens as Market Shifts to Supply-Driven Recovery The long-haul driver gap remains a structural headwind, with estimates still pointing to a six‑figure CDL driver shortfall despite softer freight in some lanes,...
content:
Fleet & Market Trends

Driver Shortage Tightens as Market Shifts to Supply-Driven Recovery

The long-haul driver gap remains a structural headwind, with estimates still pointing to a six‑figure CDL driver shortfall despite softer freight in some lanes, according to ATA updates and 2026 outlooks. ATA and multiple 2026 trend reports stress an aging, male‑dominated workforce and high turnover in long‑haul, non‑dedicated operations, keeping effective capacity constrained even as freight demand only modestly improves.[1][3][5][6] ACT Research now characterizes 2026 as a “supply‑driven recovery” where tightening driver availability, FMCSA enforcement, and below‑replacement tractor sales are pushing rates higher rather than a demand boom.[3] For brokers and carriers, this suggests sustained competition for experienced drivers and continued pressure to improve pay packages, home time, and route design over the next 3–12 months.[1][3][5][6]

LTL Remains Structurally Tighter Post-Yellow

The August 2023 Yellow liquidation removed roughly 10%+ of national LTL capacity, and remaining carriers have spent 2024–2025 absorbing freight and terminals while tightening networks. Analysts cited by NATSA note that LTLs are prioritizing yield management and dense, high‑margin freight over pure volume growth, with many focusing on network optimization rather than greenfield expansion.[3] That backdrop, combined with uneven industrial demand, points to firm LTL pricing and selective capacity through 2026, even as truckload spot markets recover more cyclically. Shippers will likely see less appetite for discounting on LTL base rates, pushing more volume toward regional TL and parcel where networks are still rebalancing.[1][2][3]

Carrier Exits Reshape Capacity Toward Larger Fleets

Expert Insights’ 2026 Freight Transport Report and multiple 2026 outlooks agree that undercapitalized carriers will continue to exit as fuel, insurance, maintenance, and equipment costs outpace rate gains.[1][3][4] Smaller firms—which represent about 90% of all carriers—are “hit the hardest,” and their failures are gradually tightening capacity and shifting freight to better‑capitalized mid‑size and large fleets.[4][6] C.H. Robinson links these exits to a forecast ~2% truckload price increase in 2026, with just over half driven by capacity tightening rather than pure inflation.[7] Brokers should expect more RFPs consolidating volume with larger, tech‑enabled carriers, while still nurturing reliable small‑fleet partners that survive this shakeout.[1][3][4][7]

Spot Rates Turning Up from Multi-Year Lows

Bergey’s 2026 outlook and ACT Research both describe a market in “cautious stabilization,” with spot truckload rates projected to rise 4–6% year‑over‑year in 2026 and contract rates moving up more modestly.[1][3] ACT notes that the industry has moved away from the oversupply that crushed margins in the last cycle; today’s rate gains are driven largely by capacity contraction, tighter driver availability, and regulatory pressure rather than a freight boom.[3][4] Ryder’s early‑2026 commentary adds that TL capacity exits and spot rates creeping above contract levels are classic early‑upcycle signals.[6] For brokers and carriers, this points to a 3–12 month window where disciplined pricing and carefully managed commitments can rebuild margins before the next capacity build‑out.[1][3][4][6]

Equipment Strategy: Replacement-Only and Used-Heavy

Across NATSA and Bergey’s 2026 outlooks, fleets are largely in a “replacement‑only” posture, refreshing tractors and trailers to maintain reliability while avoiding net capacity growth.[1][3] High capital costs, uncertainty around EPA 2027 engine rules, and only modest freight growth are pushing fleets toward used equipment and extended maintenance cycles, particularly in Class 8.[1][3][4] Dry van trailer demand remains soft and OEMs are keeping order boards tight, while flatbed demand is steadier due to infrastructure and utility projects, providing a firmer floor under that segment.[1][3] This cautious capex stance supports the broader supply‑driven tightening story and suggests limited “surprise” capacity additions over the next year.[1][3][4]

Fuel & Cost Pressures

Diesel Shock Replays 2022 Dynamics

FTR reports that national on‑highway diesel saw a record 96.2¢/gal one‑week jump to $4.859/gal in early March, the largest weekly increase on record and above the prior 74.5¢ spike during the 2022 Russia‑Ukraine shock.[1][2] The surge is tied to crude volatility from fresh Middle East tensions, with WTI briefly above $119/bbl before settling in the mid‑$90s, according to FTR and RSM.[1][2] FTR notes that this diesel shock pushed overall spot truckload rates up 4.3¢, with flatbed spot pricing at its highest since October 2022 and carrier conditions tightening.[1][2] For small carriers and owner‑operators without strong fuel surcharge programs or hedging, this kind of volatility can rapidly turn marginal lanes unprofitable, accelerating carrier exits.[1][2][4]

Fuel Surcharges Under Scrutiny in Volatile Markets

Legal and consulting analyses continue to highlight friction around diesel index choice and lag in fuel surcharge (FSC) formulas, especially when prices move as violently as they did in early 2026.[1][2] Shippers and brokers are re‑examining whether DOE national vs. regional indices, weekly lags, and outdated baseline MPG assumptions fairly reflect carriers’ actual fuel costs.[2][4] NACFE’s Fleet Fuel Study shows modern long‑haul diesels can reach 8.0–9.5 MPG and sometimes 10 MPG, making many legacy FSC tables—built on 5.5–6.0 MPG—misaligned with current equipment economics.[4] Over the next year, expect more contracts to migrate toward banded, mileage‑based FSC structures with updated MPG baselines to reduce windfall gains or losses during fuel spikes.[1][2][4]

Insurance, Nuclear Verdicts, and Safety Tech Investments

NATSA and Expert Insights both flag insurance as one of the fastest‑rising operating costs, with carriers lacking strong safety records facing outsized premium hikes that push them toward exit.[3][4] The backdrop is a still‑plaintiff‑friendly litigation environment with recurring $50–$100+ million “nuclear verdicts” in trucking accidents, which has driven higher excess liability pricing and tighter underwriting.[3][4] In response, many fleets are raising deductibles and investing in telematics, inward/outward‑facing cameras, and documented safety coaching to both prevent accidents and defend claims.[3][4] With FMCSA preparing changes to its Safety Measurement System and potential new Safety Fitness Determination rules, safety data will be more visible, making robust safety programs a pricing lever in both insurance and shipper procurement.[3][4]

Taxes and Structural Fuel Burden on Trucking

According to ATA, commercial trucks paid $30.26 billion in combined federal and state fuel taxes in 2023, with a federal diesel tax of 24.4¢/gal and average state diesel tax of 31.8¢/gal.[6] Several large freight states index their diesel excise taxes to inflation or budget formulas, creating a slow but steady upward drift in per‑mile tax burden regardless of commodity price movements.[6] These tax dynamics, layered on top of volatile rack prices and surcharges, make lane‑by‑lane fuel cost modeling increasingly important for brokers and carriers. Over the next year, expect more attention to route selection and cross‑state tax arbitrage, especially on long‑haul corridors where diesel taxes vary widely.[2][3][6]

Alternative and Renewable Fuels Stay Niche but Strategic

NACFE’s fuel studies and industry TCO models continue to find that diesel remains dominant in long‑haul given its range, fueling network, and residual values, while alt fuels grow in targeted niches.[4] CNG and LNG show cost advantages in high‑mileage, return‑to‑base operations with dedicated fueling, and battery‑electric tractors are gaining traction in short‑haul and drayage where incentives and low off‑peak power rates exist.[4] Renewable diesel capacity has expanded, particularly in LCFS states, offering 50–80% GHG reductions as a drop‑in fuel, but feedstock limits mean it often carries a price premium outside heavily subsidized markets.[4] Over the 3–12 month horizon, alt fuels are less about broad cost relief and more about meeting shipper ESG requirements and positioning for future emissions rules.[3][4]

Fraud & Security Watch

Congress Moves on SAFER in Transport Act

The SAFER in Transport Act, introduced in the House on April 14, 2026, would give DOT and FMCSA broader powers to combat freight fraud and cargo theft, according to Land Line.[3] The bill aims to enhance federal coordination, modernize fraud detection, and allow FMCSA to withhold or revoke registrations tied to certain felonies or nondisclosures at the application stage.[3] It directly responds to testimony that cargo theft and fraud cost supply chains up to $35 billion annually and demands for a Federal Supply Chain Crime Coordination Center, per Trucking Dive.[1][3] For brokers and carriers, passage would likely mean more aggressive authority inactivations and higher onboarding standards for new partners over the next 12–18 months.[1][3]

Cargo Theft at Record Levels, with Double Brokering at the Center

ATA and Trucking Dive both describe an “explosive rise” in cargo theft, fictitious pickups, and fraud, with about 65,000 cargo theft incidents in 2024, roughly a 40% jump over 2023.[1][7] FreightWaves and MOTOR identify double brokering and carrier identity theft—criminals using legitimate MC/USDOT numbers to steal freight—as primary vectors.[2][5] A local Ohio case highlighted by WNWO shows a single incident cost one business about $150,000, illustrating the scale of individual‑case exposure.[8] Expectations for 2026 include another double‑digit rise in cargo theft incidents unless verification, enforcement, and technology adoption accelerate.[1][2][5][7][8]

FMCSA Tightens Identity Verification and Authority Scrutiny

FreightWaves reports that starting in April 2024, FMCSA began working with Idemia to implement mandatory facial recognition and government ID checks for all new carrier applicants, aimed at blocking fraudulent entities from easily securing new DOT numbers.[5] FMCSA’s fraud guidance also urges brokers and shippers to verify counterparties through SAFER, avoid blind loads, and treat requests to pose as another carrier or accept “too‑good” rates as red flags.[6] A 2026 Cass/FTR roundup notes that FMCSA is now aggressively inactivating USDOT numbers and revoking authorities tied to unauthorized sales, rentals, or leases, which will remove some chameleon carriers from the system.[2][6] This enforcement push, combined with SAFER in Transport Act tools if enacted, should raise the bar for carrier onboarding and ongoing due diligence across the market.[2][3][5][6]

AI-Driven Fraud Detection and Dockside ID Checks Gain Traction

FreightWaves highlights partnerships like FreightValidate and AU10TIX that deliver real‑time identity verification for carriers, drivers, and brokers using facial recognition and ID scans that can be completed in under 90 seconds at the dock.[5] These tools are being paired with AI‑driven anomaly detection in load boards and TMS platforms that scan for unusual lane patterns, email domains, authority histories, and insurance changes to flag likely double brokering.[2][5] MOTOR’s guidance reinforces the need for digital verification of MC/USDOT data and careful inspection of documents to catch cloned websites, spoofed emails, and falsified insurance certificates.[2] Over the next 3–12 months, brokers that operationalize these tools into their onboarding and dispatch workflows will have a tangible advantage in reducing fraud losses and protecting shipper relationships.[2][5][6]

Telematics, GPS Data, and Cyber Hygiene as Core Security Tools

Industry security panels recommend preserving ELD and GPS histories whenever fraud occurs, both to reconstruct events and to support law enforcement, underscoring telematics as evidence, not just an operations tool.[4] FMCSA guidance stresses matching tractor/trailer identifiers to contracted carrier data and using geofencing and route‑deviation alerts (common in modern telematics) as practical defenses against load diversion and possible GPS spoofing.[4][6] Cyber‑enabled fraud—phishing, cloned domains, credential theft—is now central to cargo crime, with ATA‑cited data showing freight fraud up roughly 1500% in the 2020s, per a 2024 panel discussion.[4] Brokers and carriers that harden email domains, enforce MFA on TMS and load‑board logins, and route all verification calls through FMCSA‑listed contact numbers, not email signatures, will be better positioned as attackers continue to target the sector.[2][4][6]

Technology & Policy

FMCSA Invests Over $300 Million in Truck Parking and Digital Driver Support

A May 2026 USDOT release notes that FMCSA has invested more than $300 million in truck parking grants since April 2025, funding both new capacity and smarter parking information systems.[1] The same update highlights an upgraded DataQs platform (launched April 2026) to give drivers and carriers a more “fair, impartial, and timely” way to correct safety records, along with a modernized National Consumer Complaint Database that now captures non‑compliant brokers and training providers.[1] FMCSA also rolled out a refreshed mobile‑friendly driver resources portal, framing these changes as part of a broader push to support professional drivers and cut red tape.[1][5] For fleets, these investments should gradually ease parking constraints on key corridors and make it more practical to contest bad data before it impacts insurance, procurement, or enforcement decisions.[1][5]

Hours-of-Service Flexibility Pilots Could Reshape Scheduling

FMCSA is running two HOS pilot programs—the Flexible Sleeper Berth Pilot and the Split Duty Periods Pilot—using ELD data to see whether giving drivers more control over their rest breaks improves safety.[1] The Split Duty pilot, for example, allows pausing the 14‑hour on‑duty window for 30 minutes to 3 hours, while the Sleeper Berth pilot tests more flexible splits of the 10‑hour off‑duty period.[1] If data show safety benefits, these changes could eventually allow more nuanced scheduling around dock delays, congestion windows, and parking availability. Brokers and carriers should track these pilots closely, as future rule changes could open new options for designing service windows and driver home‑time commitments.[1][5]

CDL Integrity, English Proficiency, and Foreign Driver Rules Tighten

USDOT and FMCSA have launched a nationwide audit of state CDL programs and finalized a February 2026 rule aimed at blocking “unqualified foreign drivers” from obtaining non‑domiciled CDLs, per DOT announcements.[1] A White House action in 2025 directed full enforcement of long‑standing English‑language requirements for interstate CDL holders, with FMCSA moving to English‑only CDL testing and states like California formally enforcing English Language Proficiency beginning in January 2026.[1][3] These moves come alongside crackdowns on non‑domiciled CDL mills and fraudulent licensing schemes, which Expert Insights says could remove “tens of thousands” of drivers from the roads.[4] In the near term, fleets relying heavily on foreign or non‑English‑proficient drivers may face onboarding friction, but the broader effect is a smaller, more scrutinized driver pool and higher stakes for compliance.[1][3][4]

Digital TMS, Visibility, and AI Forecasting Become Table Stakes

Transport Topics and C.H. Robinson’s 2026 market updates both emphasize rapid consolidation and integration of TMS, visibility, and brokerage platforms, with shippers expecting real‑time tracking and API‑based connectivity as standard.[4][8] AI‑driven ETA prediction and automated exception management are being embedded into TMS workflows, helping carriers and brokers manage detention, re‑power decisions, and mode shifts more proactively.[4][8] Post‑COVID research on trucking operations underscores the value of digital dock scheduling and contactless processes in cutting delays and improving driver experience, reinforcing these tech investments.[5] Over the next year, brokers that can surface accurate ETAs, exception alerts, and lane‑level performance metrics in shipper portals will be better positioned as procurement teams prioritize service stability over marginal rate savings.[4][6][8]

EPA 2027 Engine Rules Drive Pre-Buy Planning and Alt-Fuel Pilots

Industry analyses of the EPA’s 2027 heavy‑duty engine standards forecast higher upfront truck prices, longer warranty and durability requirements, and more complex aftertreatment systems relative to pre‑2027 models.[3][4] This is already feeding into the “replacement‑only” capex posture many fleets are taking in 2026, as they evaluate whether to pre‑buy pre‑2027 trucks or delay major expansions until after costs and reliability data settle.[1][3][4] The same regulatory pressure is accelerating pilots of battery‑electric and hydrogen fuel‑cell trucks in short‑haul and drayage, even as diesel remains the dominant long‑haul solution for the foreseeable future.[3][4] For brokers and asset‑light carriers, understanding which fleets are pre‑buying versus delaying will be important when assessing which partners can sustain service through the next emissions transition.[1][3][4]

Autonomous Trucks Advance Slowly on Southern Corridors

Policy debates anchored by UC Berkeley’s Labor Center report and AV industry advocacy stress that full driverless long‑haul trucking is still years away, but Level 4 pilot corridors in states like Texas and Arizona are expanding.[6][7] These operations remain highly supervised and corridor‑specific, with regulatory frameworks built from state AV laws, FMCSA waivers, and NHTSA defect authority rather than a comprehensive federal AV statute.[6][7] For the next 3–5 years, the practical impact is incremental: autonomous tractors may begin to handle specific long‑haul legs while human drivers focus on first/last mile, drop‑and‑hook, and customer service functions.[5][6][7] Brokers should view autonomy less as an imminent capacity shock and more as a developing service option on select lanes that could influence transit times and trailer pooling strategies down the road.[5][6][7]

Bottom Line

Capacity is finally tightening after years of oversupply, but this is a supply‑driven recovery, not a freight boom: driver shortages, carrier exits, replacement‑only capex, and stricter FMCSA and EPA rules are all constraining the available truck and driver pool.[1][3][4][6] At the same time, diesel volatility, insurance inflation, and nuclear‑verdict risk are raising the cost floor, while fraud and cargo theft are forcing brokers and carriers to harden onboarding, identity checks, and cyber defenses.[1][2][3][4][5][7] Technology and policy responses—from truck parking grants and HOS pilots to AI‑driven TMS, visibility, and fraud tools—are becoming essential, not optional, for maintaining margins and service quality. Over the next 3–12 months, brokers and carriers that price for rising costs, invest in safety and verification tech, and deepen relationships with stable, compliant fleets will be best positioned as rates grind higher and weaker competitors exit the market.[1][2][3][4][6][7]

title: Weekly Freight Report - June 5, 2026
excerpt: Market Pulse Truckload is moving into a tighter but still transitional phase for the week of May 29–June 5, 2026. Spot demand is elevated, pressure is building under contract rates, and capacity is quietly exiting in key regions instead of in headlin...
content:
Market Pulse

Truckload is moving into a tighter but still transitional phase for the week of May 29–June 5, 2026. Spot demand is elevated, pressure is building under contract rates, and capacity is quietly exiting in key regions instead of in headline bankruptcies.

NTG’s late‑May update shows that truckload spot activity remained elevated heading into the June–July shipping stretch, driven by seasonal and project freight, with tightness most obvious in dry van and reefer lanes tied to produce and retail restocking, especially in the Southeast and Texas (NTG, May 25–29 report). Spot pricing in those regions was already above early‑Q2 levels, and that pattern is carrying into early June.

Ryder’s 2026 outlook, using DAT Truckload Volume Index and rate data, reports that spot prices have moved above contract rates in several regions as carrier exits stack up, with volatility strongest in the Southeast, Midwest, and Texas markets. It characterizes 2026 as a market where “contract rates are flat, but spot market volatility is increasing”, and spot remains the main pressure point for shippers and brokers.

On the rate cycle, ACT/FTR’s Avery Vise projects that total truckload rates will end 2026 up less than 2% year‑over‑year, with spot leading contract. That puts this week squarely in an early‑upswing phase: spot is tightening first, contract indices are still mostly flat on paper, but every rebid is facing upward pressure where routing guides are breaking.

By segment:

  • Dry van: Elevated spot demand into June on retail and project freight, especially out of the Southeast, Texas, and the Midwest, with spot repeatedly popping above contract whenever local capacity tightens, per DAT‑based commentary in Ryder’s outlook and NTG’s late‑May snapshot.
  • Reefer: Strong seasonal demand off produce and food/beverage freight is driving firm reefer spot rates in the major produce corridors (California, Texas, Southeast), with NTG calling out these flows as a major reason the overall spot market is “elevated” heading into June.
  • Flatbed: No week‑specific national averages are published, but 2026 outlooks cite construction and industrial freight as steady‑to‑improving, and RXO and others point to gradual tightening in industrial/flatbed capacity during 2026. Expect at least stable to slightly firmer flatbed pricing into summer on construction, energy, and manufacturing projects.

DAT has not yet published public load‑to‑truck ratios for this exact week, but the pattern is clear from the regional commentary: Ryder cites carrier exits tightening capacity in the Southeast, Texas, the Mountain West, and parts of the Midwest, driving “sudden congestion and routing‑guide disruption.” Combined with NTG’s report of elevated volumes and tighter capacity heading into June, that implies rising loads‑per‑truck in those hot markets versus earlier in 2026.

On the demand side, the ATA Truck Tonnage Index rose 2.6% in February 2026 and another 0.3% in March 2026, signaling a slow firming of underlying freight after 2025’s soft patch. Ryder labels current freight demand as “stable, but not surging”: aggregate volumes are modest, but seasonal and project freight is enough to tighten capacity where truck counts have already thinned.

Net result for the week: expect firm to rising spot rates in seasonal and exit‑heavy regions, particularly for dry van and reefer, with more lane‑by‑lane spread in pricing. Contract rates are mostly unchanged in index terms, but real‑world bids in tight markets are getting pulled higher as shippers chase service and try to pull freight off the spot board.

Regulation & Enforcement

Between May 29 and June 4, 2026, federal rulemaking activity was light but the enforcement environment remains tougher, especially around CDL status, English proficiency, and medical and registration compliance.

FMCSA notices and paperwork changes

  • June 3, 2026: FMCSA published a notice titled “Parts and Accessories Necessary for Safe Operation; Application for Exemption From Truck‑Lite Co. LLC”. This opens public comment on a parts/accessories exemption request but does not change any safety rules yet.
  • June 2, 2026: FMCSA posted a notice for a Commercial Driver’s License exemption application for a specific driver (Jenifer Sanchez Vilchis). This is an individual petition, not a system‑wide CDL change.
  • June 1, 2026: FMCSA issued an information‑collection notice titled “Commercial Motor Vehicle Marking Requirements”, seeking approval for a new information collection under 49 CFR Part 390. This affects paperwork burden and data tracking around USDOT number and carrier identification marks, but does not change the underlying marking rules.

CDL tightening and state enforcement

The big regulatory lever in force this week is the non‑domiciled CDL final rule, effective March 16, 2026. Under this rule, only drivers lawfully present in H‑2A, H‑2B, or E‑2 status can hold non‑domiciled CLPs/CDLs; licenses are capped at the I‑94 “Admit Until” date and at a maximum of one year, with mandatory DHS SAVE checks and in‑person issuance and renewal.

Industry estimates indicate this framework will disqualify roughly 97% of about 200,000 existing non‑domiciled CDL holders from renewal, a meaningful hit to labor supply for carriers relying heavily on that population.

FMCSA is actively enforcing this in California via funding pressure. Compliance briefings report that FMCSA has withheld roughly $160 million in federal highway safety funding from California over delays in canceling non‑domiciled CDLs that no longer meet federal standards; California had reportedly committed to cancel about 13,000 non‑domiciled CDLs but has lagged, triggering the funding action. This is a clear signal that state‑level laggards will face financial leverage until their CDL databases match federal rules.

HOS, medical certificates, English proficiency

  • Hours of Service: No new HOS rules, waivers, or broad emergency exemptions were posted between May 29 and June 4. The operative framework remains the September 29, 2020 HOS rule set (short‑haul expansion, adverse‑conditions extension, 30‑minute break changes, and flexible sleeper‑berth splits).
  • HOS research: FMCSA is recruiting 18 drivers for six‑week HOS research tests during spring/summer 2026. That is research only, but signals that future HOS tweaks remain on the table.
  • Medical certification: Because multiple states are still not fully integrated into the National Registry II electronic medical system, FMCSA has a nationwide temporary exemption in place from April 11–October 11, 2026, allowing CDL/CLP holders and carriers to rely on a paper medical examiner’s certificate for up to 60 days after issuance.
  • English Language Proficiency: FMCSA’s policy making English proficiency an out‑of‑service condition (effective May 2025) remains active and is a major theme in 2026 enforcement, with Iowa’s SF 2426 bill positioning to push English standards even beyond federal requirements if enacted.

ELDs, broker rules, Clearinghouse

  • ELDs: No specific devices were removed from the ELD registry in this window, but post‑Roadcheck commentary says FMCSA intends to tighten ELD self‑certification and is exploring third‑party testing requirements for ELD manufacturers under 49 CFR Part 395.
  • Clearinghouse: No new Clearinghouse rulemaking in this exact week, but the critical rule in force is that states must automatically downgrade CDLs for certain Clearinghouse violations, reinstating only after Return‑to‑Duty is complete.
  • Broker bond: No changes to the $75,000 broker bond or 49 CFR Part 371 in this window. Broker financial‑responsibility rules and double‑brokering crackdowns are still in the “planned/under discussion” bucket, not yet final.

Broker Edge

This week favors brokers who can move fast on spot and manage risk tightly.

  • Lean into regional spot where spot > contract: With spot pricing above contract in parts of the Southeast, Texas, Midwest, and Mountain West, lock in dependable carriers there now. Use short‑term routing‑guide builds and mini‑bids to capture mid‑cycle contract upticks before indices catch up.
  • Exploit seasonal reefer and van demand: Produce, food/beverage, and retail replenishment are driving the elevated spot market. Prioritize California–Texas–Southeast reefer and Texas/Southeast dry van lanes where NTG and Ryder both flag tightness. Build carrier rosters specifically for these seasonal corridors and secure repeat commitments rather than one‑off spot.
  • Prepare shippers for rate drift: Use the <2% full‑year contract rate growth forecast and the existing spot > contract inversion to reset expectations: “contract indices look flat, but your lanes in X/Y/Z regions are already repricing higher.” Back that with examples of routing‑guide failures tied to carrier exits.
  • Treat compliance as a sales asset: The non‑domiciled CDL rule, English OOS enforcement, and Clearinghouse downgrades are thinning the driver pool. Build talking points around vetting carriers for valid CDL status, medicals, and English proficiency. Position your brokerage as a filter that keeps shippers out of those enforcement crosshairs.
  • Watch small carrier exits as opportunity, not just risk: Industry outlooks emphasize continued smaller‑carrier exits and consolidation instead of big bankruptcies. Proactively target those carriers early, offer them consistent freight and faster pay, and bring them into your network before they fail—or take over freight when their shippers are scrambling for coverage.

Cross-Border Watchlist

Cross‑border remains structurally important this week even without a new headline event.

  • USMCA 2026 review is approaching: Policy analysis from CSIS notes that the mandatory 2026 USMCA joint review is driving positioning around energy, automotive rules of origin, and agricultural market access. For cross‑border truckers, that means rising medium‑term risk on autos, parts, and ag commodities traffic between the U.S., Mexico, and Canada.
  • Agricultural disputes: CSIS highlights ongoing disputes over Mexico’s treatment of U.S. corn and biotech crops. Carriers moving corn, meat, and fresh produce should assume that rule changes, inspections, or tariff shifts could hit with short notice as the review date nears.
  • Non‑domiciled CDL rule impact: The March 16, 2026 non‑domiciled CDL rule is particularly sensitive for cross‑border operations. With an estimated 97% of ~200,000 non‑domiciled CDL holders likely ineligible at renewal, expect continued tightening in cross‑border driver supply, especially in California and other high‑immigrant‑driver states.

No specific new US‑Mexico or US‑Canada border policy, tariff, or CBP change dated May 29–June 5 appeared in the available data, so the focus this week is on structural risk and driver supply constraints rather than a fresh regulatory shock.

Fraud & Security

Fraud risk continues to rise faster than freight volumes, and Q1 2026 numbers set the tone for how brokers and carriers should operate in June.

  • Highway’s Q1 2026 Freight Fraud Index recorded 527,940 blocked fraudulent inbound emails, a 49.9% year‑over‑year increase, plus 71,801 spoofed phone calls and 2,256 reported identity‑theft instances. Freight fraud is at an all‑time high.
  • Ownership‑change fraud is exploding: the index reported 169.6% growth in this category with 399 ownership changes flagged in Q1. Roughly 50% of theft incidents involved carriers with previously “clean” operating histories.
  • Highway also logged 551 international access attempts into broker networks, most frequently from India, Pakistan, and Serbia, underscoring the scale of global, organized probing against TMS and email systems.
  • FreightWaves coverage emphasizes that attackers are using AI‑powered tools, phishing, forged identities, and falsified documents, and that legal and regulatory scrutiny of brokers’ controls is increasing.
  • On the driver side, an Idaho case saw a CDL applicant plead guilty to federal program bribery for offering a $500 bribe to a CDL examiner in exchange for a passing skills score without taking the test, with exposure of up to 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine. Expect regulators to keep tightening on CDL fraud.
  • Legislatively, the SAFER Transport Act has been introduced in the U.S. House as a companion to a prior Senate bill, targeting freight fraud and cargo theft with stronger enforcement tools.

Operationally, treat every new carrier and ownership change as suspect until verified; the data show that “clean history” alone is no longer a reliable safety signal.

Equipment, Fuel & Ops

Fuel is the main operational shock this week; other equipment metrics are thin, but diesel alone is enough to move the P&L.

  • The EIA/DOE U.S. average on‑highway diesel price for the week of June 1, 2026 is $5.350 per gallon, down from $5.523/gal the prior week and $5.596/gal on May 18. YCharts confirms this $5.35/gal national average, noting a 3.13% week‑over‑week drop but a 53.43% increase versus $3.487/gal one year earlier.
  • Regional averages for June 1, 2026:
  • East Coast: $5.237/gal
  • New England: $5.731/gal
  • Central Atlantic: $5.694/gal
  • Lower Atlantic: $5.016/gal
  • Midwest: $5.392/gal
  • Gulf Coast: $4.900/gal
  • Rocky Mountain: $5.331/gal
  • West Coast: $6.398/gal
  • California: $7.051/gal

Work Truck Online, summarizing EIA data, reported that as of May 25, 2026 the national average diesel price was $5.52/gal, more than $2.03 higher than 2025 and $1.76 higher than 2024 at the same time, with regional averages like East Coast $5.39, Midwest $5.62, Gulf Coast $5.04, Rocky Mountain $5.49, West Coast $6.50. California was noted at $7.38/gal and Oklahoma at $4.94/gal in that late‑May dataset.

Trendline: diesel climbed from $3.897/gal on March 2 to $5.643/gal on April 6, then eased slightly into late May and early June. Fuel surcharges built off DOE’s national index should be updated aggressively; carriers with weak fuel programs are under heavy margin pressure, and brokers should expect more active fuel‑based repricing mid‑contract.

No specific Class 8 new‑order or used‑truck price data are available in this week’s sources, but 2026 outlooks stress that high acquisition and maintenance costs, combined with fuel and insurance, are driving cautious replacement and continued capacity attrition. That reinforces the broader theme: fewer marginal trucks, more sensitivity to rate and fuel movements.

Action Checklist for Brokers

  • Re‑price hot regional lanes weekly: For Southeast, Texas, Midwest, and Mountain West lanes, assume spot > contract. Refresh buy‑side and sell‑side pricing every week and push for short‑term, higher‑paying mini‑bids with shippers.
  • Prioritize seasonal reefer and van freight: Build dedicated carrier pools for California–Texas–Southeast produce and food/beverage moves. Offer carriers consistent volume through the season to secure capacity before peak weekends.
  • Audit your carrier base for CDL and medical compliance: Confirm that carriers operating in California and other high‑risk states understand the non‑domiciled CDL rule, the NRII paper‑certificate waiver window, and English OOS exposure. Remove any carrier that cannot show current medical cards and valid CDL status.
  • Adjust fuel schedules now: With DOE diesel at $5.350/gal and California over $7.00/gal, review all shipper fuel tables. Where possible, move to indexed surcharges that reset weekly and explicitly reference DOE averages.
  • Lock in strong small carriers before they exit: Use internal scorecards to identify small, high‑service carriers in tight regions. Offer faster pay and committed freight to keep them in your orbit and avoid losing capacity to quiet market exits.
  • Implement hard anti‑fraud gates: Require multi‑factor authentication for all internal systems; verify every carrier’s identity with multiple data points (MC, phone, email domain, bank details, insurance) and treat any recent ownership change as a red‑flag event needing extra verification.
  • Train staff on social‑engineering threats: Use the Q1 data—527,940 blocked fraudulent emails, 71,801 spoofed calls, 2,256 identity theft cases—as a training anchor. Run short weekly drills: spotting spoofed domains, urgent payment requests, and forged rate confirmations.
  • Use compliance and security as sales ammo: When talking to shippers, lead with your screening around CDL status, English proficiency, Clearinghouse checks, and fraud controls. In a rising‑fraud, tightening‑capacity market, risk management is a tangible differentiator.
  • Monitor cross‑border lanes for policy risk: For automotive and ag freight tied to USMCA and Mexico disputes, price in volatility and build alternate routings or carrier options. Flag these accounts internally as “policy‑sensitive” ahead of the 2026 USMCA review.

title: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup - May 29, 2026
excerpt: Fleet & Market Trends Freight Recession Bottoming Out, But Recovery Stays Shallow The 2026 truckload market is moving from contraction to a slow, uneven stabilization, with analysts calling it a “structural transition year” rather than the start of a...
content:
Fleet & Market Trends

Freight Recession Bottoming Out, But Recovery Stays Shallow

The 2026 truckload market is moving from contraction to a slow, uneven stabilization, with analysts calling it a “structural transition year” rather than the start of a true upcycle, according to recent freight outlooks and NATSA’s 2026 report. Spot rates are improving in select lanes and ATA economists report the strongest truckload demand since late 2024, but volumes remain below prior peaks and manufacturing demand is still soft.[4][5] For brokers and carriers, this points to a fragile recovery where pricing power will come more from capacity attrition than from robust demand growth over the next 6–12 months.[4][5]

Capacity Tightening Driven by Small-Carrier Exits

Multiple 2026 outlooks highlight ongoing carrier attrition—especially among fleets with ≤20 trucks—as high operating costs and stubbornly low rates force weaker players out, gradually tightening effective capacity.[3][4][5] Recent data show truck postings at a 10-year low and early‑2026 load postings up roughly 6%, with van and reefer spot rates reportedly 20%+ higher year over year, indicating that fewer available trucks, not booming freight, are driving rate firming.[5] This environment favors well-capitalized carriers and disciplined brokers who can secure reliable capacity as the spot market becomes more capacity‑driven than demand‑driven through 1H27.[3][4][5]

Driver Shortage to Re-Emerge as Binding Constraint

The ATA’s latest driver shortage update says the shortfall narrowed during the downturn but could return to the 70,000–80,000 driver range as freight recovers, with the average long‑haul TL driver now around 46–47 years old and a large cohort over 55.[8] NATSA and FTR both stress that even with freight growth under 2% annually, structural driver constraints—turnover, lifestyle, and regulatory disqualifications—will cap how quickly capacity can rebound.[1][4] Carriers are responding with higher pay and more regional/dedicated routes to improve home time, but brokers should assume driver availability will again tighten lanes once volumes pick up in late 2026.[1][2][4][8]

LTL Post-Yellow Capacity Discipline Reshapes Freight Mix

ATA’s “Trends” recap notes that the 2023 Yellow shutdown displaced roughly 30,000+ employees and significant LTL volume, which surviving carriers absorbed while maintaining strong yield discipline.[8] Analysts describe a more concentrated LTL market, with unionized LTL jobs still below pre‑2023 levels and many experienced drivers shifting into parcel, dedicated TL, and private fleets.[8] For the next 6–12 months, expect LTL pricing to remain structurally firmer than TL, with limited willingness by large LTLs to chase marginal freight on price.

Fleets Pivot from Growth to Asset Renewal

NATSA’s 2026 outlook and SSUI’s transport report both describe fleets prioritizing replacement of aging tractors over net growth, amid deferred trade cycles, weak new orders, and uncertainty around EPA 2027 and ZEV mandates.[1][3] A December spike in Class 8 orders is viewed as an anomaly rather than the start of a broad expansion, with overall freight demand growth expected at roughly 2% or less and contract rate growth below 2% through 2026.[1][3][4] Brokers should plan for an older but gradually refreshed fleet profile, with capacity shifts driven more by exits and utilization than by new iron coming into the market.

Fuel & Cost Pressures

Diesel Price Shock Resets 2026 Cost Baselines

Following recent volatility, the U.S. Energy Information Administration revised its 2026 diesel outlook higher, lifting the expected annual average from about $3.43 to roughly $4.12 per gallon after a historic early‑March spike where national diesel jumped nearly $1 in a week.[5] Bloomberg Intelligence previously showed that at $5 diesel, U.S. heavy diesel users were on track to spend around $6.1 billion in a single week, underscoring how quickly fuel shocks can compress margins for carriers that cannot fully recover via surcharges.[1] For the next 3–12 months, brokers should assume structurally higher fuel baselines and continued volatility tied to geopolitics and refining constraints, with small fleets most exposed.[1][2][4][5]

Refinery Constraints Keep Diesel Spreads Volatile

EIA’s distillate analyses emphasize that diesel availability hinges on refinery utilization, configuration, and distillate inventories; when utilization is tight and stocks sit below five‑year norms, diesel crack spreads can widen sharply relative to crude.[4] Limited incremental U.S. refining capacity and seasonal maintenance increase the risk that any crude‑market disruption translates into outsized diesel moves, a pattern seen in mid‑2022 and again in 2024.[1][2][4] Carriers should continue treating fuel as a strategic variable—using hedging, MPG improvements, and optimized routing—rather than assuming gradual, predictable price paths.

Fuel Surcharges Under Scrutiny in a Changing Fuel Mix

Most contracts still index to DOE/EIA on‑highway diesel averages, but industry discussion is intensifying around whether national benchmarks, weekly resets, and legacy tables accurately reflect lane‑level costs and modern fuel efficiency.[4] As some fleets deploy CNG/LNG, battery‑electric, and renewable diesel in specific corridors, analysts note that traditional diesel‑linked surcharges can over‑ or under‑recover costs when applied to non‑diesel energy profiles.[2] Over the next year, large shippers and sophisticated carriers are expected to experiment more with “energy cost” indices that better account for alternative fuels and regional tax differentials, which brokers will need to model into pricing.

Insurance, Legal, and Tariff Costs Squeeze Margins

NATSA identifies insurance alongside fuel, maintenance, and equipment as a core driver of operating cost inflation, especially for small fleets lacking scale or strong safety records.[1] In high‑risk states like Florida, insurance commentary points to a capacity crunch with fewer carriers willing to write new trucking risks and higher deductibles, reflecting elevated nuclear‑verdict exposure.[5] At the same time, freight outlooks note that tariffs and supply‑chain‑driven parts inflation continue to pressure opex, leaving little room for carriers to absorb further shocks without pushing for rate increases over the next 6–12 months.[1][3][5]

Diesel Taxes and Policy Keep Floor Under Fuel Costs

ATA data show commercial trucks paid about $30.26 billion in federal and state fuel taxes in 2023, with a federal diesel tax of 24.4 cents per gallon as of early 2024.[3] Several states continue to ratchet diesel excise rates to fund infrastructure and are exploring road‑usage charges for alternative‑fuel trucks, moves that can offset savings from efficiency gains and complicate surcharge modeling for interstate carriers.[3] Brokers should be mindful of state‑by‑state diesel tax spreads when evaluating linehaul bids and routing options in high‑tax corridors.

Fraud & Security Watch

Strategic Cargo Theft Surges 1,500%, Shifting Risk Profile

ATA’s cargo theft materials and multiple investigations report that “strategic theft”—identity fraud, broker/carrier cloning, and load interception—has risen roughly 1,500% since 2021, making it the dominant cargo‑crime mode.[2][3][5] A recent congressional hearing cited federal estimates that cargo theft and broker fraud now cost supply chains up to $35 billion annually, with about 65,000 thefts in 2024 and a 40% year‑over‑year increase.[1] For brokers, the key shift over the next year is that the biggest losses are now cyber‑ and identity‑driven, not just trailer break‑ins, requiring tight controls on onboarding, credentials, and data access.[1][2][3][5]

Double-Brokering and MC Hijacking at the Center of Losses

ATA and WFAA’s 2025 investigation detail how criminals acquire or hijack MC numbers, spoof legitimate brokers’ branding, and re‑broker loads to legitimate carriers while diverting freight or payments.[2][3][5] Congress heard testimony that MC numbers can be bought and sold with minimal oversight, enabling “chameleon carriers” to reincarnate after safety or fraud issues and continue operating under apparently clean identities.[1][2] Expect FMCSA and potential SAFER‑style legislation to focus heavily on MC/DOT transfer rules and real‑time verification, and brokers should not wait—tighten policies around who can be onboarded, how often records are re‑checked, and how payment instructions are vetted.

AI Fraud Analytics and Identity Verification Become Standard Controls

As strategic theft accelerates, ATA and security partners are pushing data‑driven monitoring and AI risk scoring as essential, not optional, tools.[3][5] Modern platforms now score carriers and brokers in real time on factors like MC/DOT history, inspection trends, IP/email fingerprints, document forensics, and sudden behavior shifts, flagging high‑risk entities before tenders are awarded.[3][5] Over the next 12 months, brokers who cannot demonstrate robust AI‑assisted vetting and multi‑factor identity proofing will face higher loss risk, tougher insurance terms, and increasing pushback from risk‑sensitive shippers.

GPS Spoofing and Telematics Tampering Push Need for Multi-Layer Tracking

Security briefings from 2023–2025 describe organized rings using GPS spoofing and jamming to make assets appear on‑route while diverting loads, undermining single‑signal tracking.[1][3][5] In response, best practice is shifting toward multi‑signal verification—cross‑checking GPS against cell, Wi‑Fi, and engine data—plus covert secondary trackers on high‑value freight and encrypted telematics devices with tamper detection.[1][3][5] Brokers managing critical or high‑value loads should increasingly require multi‑layer location security and anomaly‑detection alerts as part of their carrier requirements.

CDL Mills and Licensing Fraud Intersect with Cargo Crime

Federal and state investigations since 2023 have repeatedly exposed “CDL mills” issuing licenses without proper training or testing, sometimes tied to broader fraud schemes.[3] Enforcement agencies are now cross‑referencing CDL fraud data with chameleon carriers and shell entities, recognizing that straw drivers with fraudulent credentials are often used to obscure responsibility in cargo theft cases.[3] For risk‑sensitive freight, brokers and fleets should tighten verification around driver identity, licensing source, and training history, not just carrier‑level metrics.

Cyberattacks Target TMS, Load Boards, and Factoring Platforms

ATA’s security discussions and TruckingDive’s hearing coverage note a growing wave of cyber incidents—ransomware, credential theft, and business‑email compromise—aimed at brokers, fleets, and logistics tech vendors.[1][3][5] Attackers commonly hijack TMS or load‑board credentials to reroute loads, change payment instructions, and harvest data for later fraud, making MFA and least‑privilege access table stakes for logistics operations.[1][3][5] Over the next year, shippers are likely to factor cyber hygiene into their RFPs, so brokers should treat security controls and staff training as a core commercial capability, not just an IT concern.

Technology & Policy

Autonomous Trucking Moves from Pilot to Limited Commercial Use

Transport Topics reports that Aurora plans to launch commercial driverless freight operations on I‑45 between Dallas and Houston in 2025, targeting about 20 driverless trucks by late 2025 and 100+ by 2026 in partnership with large carriers.[7] Kodiak, Torc, and others are expanding Level 4 hub‑to‑hub pilots in Texas and the Southeast, while FMCSA continues its rulemaking on safe integration of automated trucks.[1][7] For the next 3–5 years, adoption will remain corridor‑specific, but brokers in Texas and adjacent states should begin planning how AV capacity may enter their networks for middle‑mile moves.

TMS and Visibility Platforms Shift From Track-and-Trace to Decision Engines

Transport Topics and TruckingDive highlight how major TMS vendors and visibility platforms are embedding AI-based load matching, dynamic pricing, and predictive ETAs as standard features.[1][7] Visibility systems are evolving into workflow tools that handle detention analytics, appointment management, and carrier scorecards, reducing manual check calls and supporting more granular service commitments.[1][7] Brokers and carriers who fully integrate ELD/GPS feeds and customer data into these tools will be better positioned to differentiate on reliability and cost in an otherwise tight but low‑margin market.[1][7]

FMCSA Safety Fitness and Broker Transparency Rules on the Horizon

NATSA’s 2026 outlook flags two regulatory moves with direct implications for brokers and carriers: a Safety Fitness Procedures rulemaking that would overhaul how carrier safety is rated, and a Broker Transparency rule that will expand recordkeeping and disclosure obligations.[1] Both are expected to lean heavily on safety and operational data—crashes, out‑of‑service rates, and transaction records—raising the stakes for accurate reporting and clean compliance histories.[1] Over the next 12 months, brokers should prepare for more stringent documentation expectations from both regulators and shipper customers, while carriers should shore up SMS metrics before ratings become more consequential in real time.

EPA 2027 Engine Rules Driving Pre-Buy Talk and Capital Caution

Transport Topics regulatory coverage indicates that EPA’s 2027 heavy‑duty GHG and NOx standards will add tens of thousands of dollars per tractor in upfront cost, while also introducing new maintenance complexity.[7] ATA and other industry groups argue that aggressive timelines could distort replacement cycles and hit small carriers hardest, prompting expectations of a pre‑buy wave in 2025–2026 as fleets pull forward orders of pre‑2027 trucks.[2][7] For brokers, this means watching for short‑term equipment demand spikes—even as fleets overall remain cautious—followed by a tighter new‑truck market and potentially stronger used‑tractor pricing heading into 2027.

Infrastructure Law Brings More Work Zones Before Capacity Gains

IIJA funding is now translating into active highway projects on key freight corridors like I‑70, I‑80, I‑95, and I‑5, per Transport Topics and congressional hearing testimony.[6][7] While these investments will eventually improve freight flow and bridge capacity, the near‑term effect is more congestion and work-zone exposure, raising transit‑time variability and accident risk for carriers.[6][7] Brokers should factor work‑zone delays into routing and appointment planning, and use visibility tools to manage ETA expectations with shippers.

Truck Parking Investments Lag Behind Need but Are Gaining Traction

Transport Topics reports that IIJA and related grant programs are funding new or expanded truck parking facilities, while states test real‑time parking information systems and private truck stops scale reservation programs.[1][7] Despite these efforts, federal safety data still show a structural shortfall of legal parking spaces, which contributes to driver fatigue, HOS challenges, and safety risk.[1][7] Over the coming year, carriers that leverage reservation systems and integrate parking planning into dispatch—and brokers that recognize the cost and schedule impact of parking constraints—will have an operational edge on service reliability.

Conferences Emphasize Cost Discipline, Tech Adoption, and Workforce Strain

Coverage of ATA MCE, TMC, and freight‑tech events shows a consistent message: 2026 is about cost control, targeted tech investment, and workforce retention, not big expansion bets.[1][7] Sessions focus on the maintenance implications of next‑gen emissions systems, technician training, AV timelines, and AI‑enabled pricing and dispatch, alongside persistent concerns about driver recruiting and retention even in a soft market.[1][4][7] Brokers should expect shippers to ask sharper questions about how technology and safety programs translate into dependable service and risk management.

Bottom Line

The next 3–12 months in domestic trucking will be defined by a slowly tightening market where capacity exits, fuel and insurance inflation, and regulatory uncertainty outweigh only modest demand growth. Structural constraints—aging drivers, cautious fleet capital spending, and high legal/insurance costs—point to gradual rate firming with thin margins rather than a robust upcycle. At the same time, strategic freight fraud and cyber‑enabled cargo theft are forcing brokers and carriers to harden onboarding, identity, and telematics controls as a cost of doing business. For brokers and carriers that are well‑capitalized, data‑driven, and disciplined on safety and security, this environment offers an opportunity to gain share and lock in durable relationships as the market grinds off the bottom.

title: Weekly Freight Report - May 29, 2026
excerpt: Market Pulse Truckload spot conditions stayed tight this week as seasonal demand, inspections, and produce flows overlapped. C.H. Robinson’s May 2026 Freight Market Update reports that truckload capacity is already tight, with Mother’s Day, Roadcheck...
content:
Market Pulse

Truckload spot conditions stayed tight this week as seasonal demand, inspections, and produce flows overlapped. C.H. Robinson’s May 2026 Freight Market Update reports that truckload capacity is already tight, with Mother’s Day, Roadcheck Week, and the ramping produce season expected to push rates higher and increase service risk into early summer (per C.H. Robinson). Intermodal is gaining share as shippers react to capacity and fuel costs, which adds competitive pressure on long‑haul truckload lanes (C.H. Robinson).

NTG’s weekly view for May 25–29, 2026 confirms that truckload remains elevated heading into the June–July shipping stretch, with no meaningful pullback in demand so far (NTG Freight). For brokers, the key takeaway is that May’s overlapping events are behaving like a mini‑peak, not a typical shoulder month.

On the LTL side, C.H. Robinson notes that LTL demand has edged up off Q1 2026 lows, with carriers reporting stronger shipment trends, firm pricing discipline, and ongoing network investment. That signals limited room for discounting; LTL carriers are more likely to protect yield than chase marginal tonnage right now.

Structurally, NATA’s 2026 trucking outlook still describes a market where freight demand softened but is expected to gradually stabilize, with dry van and reefer spot rates projected to move modestly higher through 2026 (NATA). On the supply side, NATA expects overcapacity to correct slowly as fleets pull back on growth and focus on replacing aging equipment rather than expanding aggressively, keeping a lid on capacity additions (NATA).

Cost pressure remains the swing factor. NATA flags fuel, insurance, maintenance, and equipment costs as still elevated and compressing carrier margins when rates lag (NATA). That combination—tightening capacity, modestly improving demand, and high input costs—supports a firm to rising rate bias into June, especially in produce‑heavy and inspection‑sensitive corridors.

Regulation & Enforcement

Regulatory activity during May 22–29, 2026 was light, but several items matter for carrier qualification and cost structure. FMCSA’s rulemaking docket shows no new NPRMs or final rules in this week affecting hours of service, ELD rules, broker regulations, or CDL standards (FMCSA Federal Register index). Compliance expectations are status‑quo, but several open actions are moving in the background.

On May 28, FMCSA published a notice titled “Qualification of Drivers; Exemption Applications; Epilepsy and Seizure Disorders”, continuing its practice of case‑by‑case medical exemptions under 49 CFR 391.41 rather than broad rule changes (FMCSA). For fleets, that means medical qualification is still highly individualized; don’t assume expanded blanket eligibility.

The most direct cost lever in play is the May 18, 2026 proposed rule on Commercial Driver’s License Information System (CDLIS) fees, which remained open during this week (FMCSA). The NPRM would update the CDLIS user fees paid by states and other participants; higher backend costs at the state level often feed through to licensing fees and administrative friction for carriers and drivers over time.

There were no new ELD revocations or suspensions posted between May 22–29, and FMCSA took no HOS‑related NPRMs, interim rules, or final rules to the Federal Register in this window (FMCSA). Planned rulemakings for 2026—ELD technical revisions, Clearinghouse updates, safety fitness procedures, ADS truck operations, and CDL testing flexibility—remain on the horizon but did not move materially this week (DOT regulatory agenda).

On the broker side, DOT’s regulatory agenda continues to list a second broker‑transparency NPRM aimed at pricing and disclosure issues with a projected date in 2026, but no broker‑related NPRM or final rule published May 22–29, and the $75,000 broker bond minimum under 49 U.S.C. 13906 remains unchanged (DOT agenda; FMCSA index).

States were quiet as well: there were no new Texas trucking statutes or TxDOT trucking rules adopted in this week, and no Congressional trucking‑specific bills advanced out of committee, including anything on HOS, ELDs, or broker bonds (legislative trackers). Enforcement energy remains focused on earlier initiatives, especially non‑domiciled CDL cleanup, English‑language compliance, and ELDT provider purges—FMCSA has already removed 9,000+ training providers from the registry and withheld over $140 million in highway safety funds from California tied to CDL issues (FMCSA/DOJ coverage).

What this means for brokers

  • Assume no immediate rule changes, but build 2026 planning scenarios around higher CDLIS‑related costs and tighter ELD and Clearinghouse rules.
  • Treat driver qualification and training documentation as an active risk area; regulators are clearly willing to pull funding and revoke credentials where states fall short.

Broker Edge

In this market, brokers win by tightening execution around capacity, cost, and fraud. On capacity, both C.H. Robinson and NTG describe an environment where truckload capacity is tight and spot conditions are elevated heading into June (C.H. Robinson; NTG Freight). That favors brokers who can pre‑secure power and align mode choices ahead of surges.

Intermodal is “gaining momentum” as high diesel prices, new regulations, and truckload constraints push freight to rail (C.H. Robinson). With the national average retail diesel around $5.596/gal the week of May 18 and easing only to about $5.523/gal for the week of May 25—a roughly 1.3% week‑over‑week decline according to YCharts’ EIA‑based series—shippers are looking for structural fuel savings, not just spot wins (EIA; YCharts). Brokers who can put hard numbers on truck vs. intermodal fuel exposure have an edge in RFPs.

LTL’s modest rebound and “firm pricing discipline” mean customers will see fewer easy concessions from carriers (C.H. Robinson). Brokers can add value by consolidating multi‑stop truckload into optimized LTL and partials, and by using regional carriers to work around national network congestion.

Tactical plays for late May–June

  • Lock in primary carriers on key lanes through early July, especially produce and holiday‑sensitive corridors, using short‑term mini‑bids instead of pure day‑to‑day spot.
  • Model mode shift scenarios: where lane transit allows, build optionality between truckload and intermodal for high‑volume shippers to hedge diesel and capacity risk.
  • Re‑price stale contract freight where you’re underwater on fuel—diesel is up roughly $2.00/gal year‑over‑year versus the ~$3.50 range a year earlier (YCharts/EIA), and many 2025 fuel tables don’t reflect that shock.
  • Lean into service risk management: Roadcheck Week is behind you, but inspection‑risk behavior persists; build slightly wider scheduling windows and push strict tender lead times.

Cross-Border Watchlist

The available data show no major US–Mexico or US–Canada border policy changes, USMCA decisions, or tariff moves specifically dated May 22–29, 2026 (CBP/trade sources survey). Port hours, inspection regimes, and cross‑border truck policies appear stable for this window.

However, cross‑border freight is squarely in the sights of anti‑theft legislation. The House recently passed the Combating Organized Retail Crime (CORCA) Act, H.R. 2853, on a 348–60 vote “last week” relative to a mid‑May Talking Logistics report (Talking Logistics). CORCA expands federal enforcement against organized retail and supply‑chain crime, explicitly covering:

  • Interstate transportation of stolen property
  • Sale or receipt of stolen goods
  • Theft from interstate or foreign shipments tied to an organization

The bill also allows prosecutors to aggregate the value of stolen items over a 12‑month period for offenses involving interstate transportation or sale/receipt of stolen goods (Talking Logistics). For cross‑border carriers and brokers, that means multi‑incident schemes spanning U.S. and foreign segments are more likely to trigger high‑value federal cases.

Given that NMFTA’s analysis shows California, Texas, and Illinois account for about 46% of U.S. cargo‑theft incidents and that theft from foreign shipments is explicitly referenced, brokers moving freight through South Texas ports and southern California should assume heightened investigative interest even without a formal rule change (NMFTA).

Fraud & Security

Fraud and cargo theft remain the fastest‑rising threats to brokerage margins in 2026. Highway’s Q1 2026 Freight Fraud Index, summarized by Talking Logistics in mid‑May, reports that fraud volume hit an all‑time high, with every major indicator accelerating year over year (Talking Logistics/Highway). Key metrics heading into late May:

  • Highway blocked over 527,000 fraudulent email attempts in Q1 2026, a 49.9% increase versus Q1 2025.
  • The platform generated 2,256 identity alerts in Q1, an 89.6% year‑over‑year increase.
  • Change‑of‑ownership reports linked to MC transfers climbed 169.6% year over year, highlighting how fraud rings weaponize authority transfers.
