NMFTA’s May 14 Freight Fraud Prevention Hub webinar describes industrial‑scale schemes where rings sell “packages of MC numbers by the hundreds” and blast phishing emails to enable identity‑based double‑brokering (NMFTA webinar). Panelists said freight fraud “blew up” in 2025 and is now dominated by cyber‑enabled attacks rather than purely physical theft (NMFTA webinar).

On the theft side, NMFTA cites NICB, Overhaul, and other data showing that annualized cargo‑theft cost to U.S. transportation is up to $6.6 billion, or more than $18 million per day (NMFTA). NICB reports cargo‑theft losses up 27% in 2024 with a further 22% increase expected in 2025, while Overhaul recorded 2,217 cargo‑theft events in 2024, about a 49% jump over the prior comparable period (NMFTA). Overhaul also logged 525 thefts in Q2 2025, up 33% year over year (NMFTA). For logistics providers specifically, average annual cargo‑theft losses are estimated at $1.84 million (NMFTA).

The American Trucking Associations, citing ATRI and CargoNet, underscores the scale by noting that cargo theft costs trucking over $18 million per day and that strategic theft using cyber‑fraud and identity manipulation has surged 1,500% since 2021 (ATA/CargoNet). ATA backs the SAFER Transport Act as a direct response to high‑tech freight fraud and overseas‑originated scams (ATA).

Brokers are responding by upgrading their tech stack. Freight360’s May 22, 2026 piece on “Preventing Freight Fraud with Quikskope” highlights active deployment of identity‑verification and behavioral analytics tools in brokerage operations (Freight360). That aligns with the risk profile: the most effective controls now are data‑driven (email/domain validation, MC‑history scoring, behavioral monitoring) rather than purely manual vetting.

Equipment, Fuel & Ops

Fuel is the dominant operational story this week. EIA’s national on‑highway diesel series shows:

  • May 4, 2026: $5.640/gal
  • May 11, 2026: $5.639/gal
  • May 18, 2026: $5.596/gal

(EIA). YCharts, which tracks the same EIA data, reports a U.S. retail diesel price of $5.523/gal for the week of May 25, 2026, down from $5.596/gal the prior week and up from $3.536/gal a year earlier—a week‑over‑week drop of about 1.3% but a year‑over‑year increase of nearly $2.00/gal (YCharts/EIA). That combination—slight easing but historically extreme levels—keeps fuel as a top line‑item risk for carriers and pricing pressure point for shippers.

No Class 8 order or used‑truck pricing reports were published in the May 22–29 window in the accessible data, but NATA notes that fleets are shifting from growth to replacement of aged assets due to high equipment costs and soft but stabilizing freight (NATA). Elevated interest rates and uncertain demand continue to suppress aggressive fleet expansion.

There were also no documented driver pay changes, parking‑capacity announcements, or electric truck launches specifically dated in this week across the sources. Zero‑emission truck regulations (like California’s ACF rule) and OEM EV programs remain important but did not generate new late‑May datapoints in this dataset.

Action Checklist for Brokers

  • Re‑price fuel tables now. With diesel around $5.523–$5.596/gal versus roughly $3.536/gal a year ago, audit all major customers’ fuel schedules and renegotiate where you’re exposed to under‑recovered surcharges (EIA; YCharts).
  • Secure capacity through July. Use short‑term agreements or mini‑bids on top lanes where C.H. Robinson and NTG both signal tight capacity and elevated truckload conditions.
  • Push intermodal options. Where transit allows, present rail‑plus‑dray solutions to high‑volume, fuel‑sensitive customers as intermodal gains momentum under high diesel and constrained truckload capacity (C.H. Robinson).
  • Harden fraud defenses. Implement or upgrade carrier and shipper identity‑verification tools. Aim to detect patterns similar to Highway’s Q1 findings—MC ownership changes, mismatched emails, and identity alerts that are up 89.6%–169.6% year over year (Highway/ Talking Logistics).
  • Build a theft‑risk map by lane. Flag loads touching California, Texas, and Illinois—states that together drive about 46% of theft incidents—for higher scrutiny, additional insurance checks, and secure parking instructions (NMFTA).
  • Update carrier contracts for CORCA and SAFER. Add explicit language on organized theft, identity fraud, and cooperation with law enforcement as CORCA and the SAFER Transport Act move forward, raising stakes on organized crime (Talking Logistics; ATA).
  • Tighten qualification workflows. Even without new rules this week, FMCSA’s exemption notices, non‑domiciled CDL crackdowns, and ELDT registry cleanup mean brokers should require current CDL and medical certification documentation from carriers and maintain auditable files.
  • Leverage LTL where networks are strengthening. With LTL shipments recovering from Q1 lows and carriers holding pricing discipline, convert appropriate truckload and multi‑stop freight into optimized LTL to improve service and margin (C.H. Robinson).
  • Communicate proactively on service risk. Explain to shippers that seasonal events and tight capacity increase volatility; set realistic transit and tender‑lead expectations now rather than absorbing avoidable penalties and accessorials later.

content:
Fleet & Market Trends

Marginless Recovery: Capacity Shakeout Meets Slow Freight Rebound

The truckload market is moving into what FTR’s Avery Vise calls a “marginless recovery,” where freight demand inches higher while carriers still operate on thin margins. FTR expects a steady but not robust recovery starting in spring 2026, even as more fleets exit the market, according to Commercial Carrier Journal’s late‑2025 outlook. For brokers and carriers, that means more bid activity and higher utilization, but limited pricing power unless you’re in a constrained lane or service niche. Expect continued pressure on costs and careful scrutiny of contract commitments as routing guides are re‑built around a smaller carrier base.

Trucking Conditions Index Flashes Strongest Reading Since 2022

FTR’s Trucking Conditions Index reached 9.3 in January 2026, the best reading since February 2022, as rates and utilization improved, Fleet Equipment reports. This reflects a market where capacity attrition and modest demand are finally re‑balancing after the “freight recession” years. While not a boom, it signals that the worst of the downcycle is likely behind the industry. Brokers should anticipate more upward rate pressure into peak seasons, especially where carrier rosters have thinned.

Industry Outlook: Moderate Growth, No Boom

NASTA’s 2026 outlook describes trucking entering a phase of “moderate growth” and stabilization after several years of volatility. Freight volumes are expected to gradually improve or at least hold steady, with spot rates edging up where capacity tightens, per mynatsa.org. This aligns with ACT Research’s April 2026 view that the industry is in a healthier position than a year ago but not yet in full expansion. Strategic takeaway: plan for slow, uneven volume gains, not a demand surge, and build contracts that can flex to lane‑by‑lane tightness.

Spot vs. Contract: Signs of a Turning Cycle

Multiple market guides point to spot rates firming against contract rates as capacity exits. RXO’s Q2 2026 truckload forecast expects spot rates to remain above contract rates near‑term, signaling that shippers underbid during the downturn and are now paying a premium when routing guides fail. C.H. Robinson’s January 2026 update similarly raised its 2026 truckload spot rate outlook to about +8% year‑over‑year, citing tighter‑than‑expected capacity. Brokers should prepare for more mini‑bid activity and tactical repricing as shippers adjust under‑market contracts.

Capacity Bleed: Carrier Exits Redraw Regional Maps

Ryder’s 2026 freight trend report notes that freight tonnage kept falling through 2025, yet regional capacity in areas like the Southeast, Texas, the Mountain West, and parts of the Midwest has quietly tightened as small carriers shut down. TrueNorth highlights high‑profile closures such as 10 Roads Express exiting in early 2026 after a 70% revenue drop, which has already caused localized congestion and tighter supply. Expect more routing‑guide failures, especially on low‑volume or secondary lanes where niche carriers disappeared. Brokers can gain share by backfilling these gaps with reliable small fleets and creative multi‑stop solutions.

LTL Capacity Remains Concentrated Post‑Yellow

Yellow’s 2023 bankruptcy removed roughly 10% of U.S. LTL capacity and 30,000 employees, and follow‑up coverage in the Journal of Commerce shows that consolidation is now baked into the network. Major carriers like XPO, FedEx Freight, Estes, and Old Dominion have absorbed freight while maintaining disciplined growth and yield-focused strategies. Analyst notes from late 2024–2025 point to high‑single‑ to low‑double‑digit LTL contract rate hikes in the aftermath, with carriers still shedding marginal freight. Shippers will continue to see firm LTL pricing and tighter freight profiles, pushing some volume toward multi‑stop TL and pool distribution in 2026–27.

Driver Availability: Short‑Term Relief, Long‑Term Constraint

ATA data show total truck driver employment slipped 0.8% in 2024 to 3.58 million, even as trucks moved 72.7% of U.S. freight by weight, underscoring structural limits on labor supply. ATA’s 2024 shortage report estimated an 82,000‑driver gap, which could exceed 160,000 by 2034 without changes. ACT Research and TrueNorth both note that driver availability feels “near neutral” right now due to soft demand and fleet right‑sizing, but demographics and FMCSA enforcement (including language proficiency and medical standards) will tighten qualified supply once volumes accelerate. Carriers that invest now in retention, training, and better schedules will be positioned to capture share when the next upcycle arrives.

Cross‑Border Corridors: Nearshoring Keeps Pressure On

ProTrans’ 2026 outlook highlights U.S.–Mexico lanes (Laredo, El Paso, Nogales) as structural demand drivers as nearshoring accelerates in autos, electronics, and industrials. At the same time, FMCSA is tightening enforcement on cross‑border driver standards and English proficiency, creating a shortage of qualified cross‑border drivers. This is already translating into premium pricing and service bottlenecks on key corridors. Brokers and carriers with compliant, bilingual driver pools and strong Mexico partners will command outsized margins over the next 12 months.

Fuel & Cost Pressures

Diesel Shock Underscores Cash‑Flow Risk

FTR’s March 9, 2026 Trucking Market Update flagged an unprecedented diesel spike: the U.S. on‑highway average jumped 96.2 cents in a single week to $4.859/gal, the largest one‑week increase on record. Driven by crude swings and Middle East tensions, the spike hit small and spot‑exposed carriers hardest before fuel surcharges could adjust. FTR warns that similar shocks can rapidly accelerate capacity exits as cash‑constrained fleets see margins erased. Brokers and shippers should revisit fuel surcharge lag and index choices now, before the next spike.

Structurally Tight Diesel: Refining Capacity as a Ceiling

EIA’s “This Week in Petroleum” and refinery capacity reports note that U.S. operable refining capacity sits around 18.1 million barrels per day, below pre‑COVID highs after multiple closures and conversions. Distillate fuels account for roughly 30% of refinery output, and inventories repeatedly run below five‑year averages whenever Gulf Coast utilization slips into the mid‑80% range. The International Energy Agency adds that much new refining capacity is overseas, increasing U.S. exposure to global diesel spreads. Taken together, these factors point to a structurally tight diesel market where geopolitical shocks can translate quickly into sustained high pump prices for trucking.

Fuel Surcharges Under the Microscope

Journal of Commerce reports that diesel volatility has put traditional surcharge formulas under pressure, especially those built around the national DOE/EIA index with a 1–2 week lag. Carriers argue that this lag under‑recovers costs during spikes, and some large fleets are pushing for regional indices or even rack‑based benchmarks (OPIS, Platts) for more precise recovery. ATRI’s cost analysis shows fuel at roughly $0.64 per mile in 2022, and fleets with robust surcharge programs weathered volatility better than those without. Expect renewed negotiation around FSC structures in 2026 contracts, with more frequent adjustments and explicit line‑haul vs. fuel splits.

Insurance Costs: Persistent Double‑Digit Pressure

AM Best and Marsh Specialty’s 2024–25 market reports show commercial auto liability remains a “challenged” line, with combined ratios consistently above 100 and mid‑single‑ to low‑double‑digit annual premium increases for trucking. Nuclear verdict data from ATRI—where average verdicts above $1 million rose nearly 1,000% to $22.3 million—continues to drive insurer caution. Underwriters are tightening terms with higher deductibles, mandatory telematics, and strict scrutiny of driver files and CSA scores. Smaller fleets without strong safety documentation or technology will face the steepest increases, accelerating consolidation into larger, better‑capitalized operators.

State Fuel Taxes Deepen Regional Cost Gaps

ATA and API tax data underscore wide diesel tax disparities: states like Pennsylvania and California impose total diesel burdens above 70¢/gal, while low‑tax states such as Missouri and Mississippi sit near 20–25¢/gal. Recent CPI‑linked increases in Illinois, New Jersey, and California add incremental cents per gallon each year. These gaps now exceed 50¢/gal in some corridors, materially impacting delivered cost per mile. Carriers and brokers should account for tax geography in network design and fueling strategies, especially on multi‑state regional freight.

Equipment Strategy: Replace, Don’t Grow

NASTA’s 2026 outlook notes that soft freight and regulatory uncertainty around emissions are pushing fleets to defer major expansion and focus on replacing aging assets. ACT Research data shows Class 8 net orders hovering in the 20,000–30,000 units per month range—well below 2021–22 peaks but still enough to support several‑month OEM backlogs. Fleets are extending trade cycles, which can increase maintenance risk and roadside failures, but they are wary of committing to large ZEV or post‑2027 diesel purchases until policy is clearer. Expect a sharp order upturn—and potential backlog crunch—once demand clearly improves or final engine rules are settled.

Diesel Still Dominant as Alternative Fuels Stay Niche

NREL’s market trends report estimates only 60,000–70,000 natural gas Class 7–8 trucks in operation and just a few thousand battery‑electric heavy‑duty units, mainly in refuse, transit, and short‑haul delivery. ATRI’s 2022 ZEV study projects that fully electrifying long‑haul would require massive grid upgrades and thousands of megawatt‑scale charging sites, with hydrogen still costlier per mile absent subsidies. EIA adds that U.S. renewable diesel capacity has surpassed 3 billion gallons per year, offering a drop‑in low‑carbon option but also tightening conventional diesel supply as refineries convert. Over the next 3–5 years, diesel remains the baseline energy source, with alt‑fuels confined to defined regional and urban niches.

Fraud & Security Watch

Freight Fraud Volume Hits All‑Time High

Talking Logistics reports that Highway’s Freight Fraud Index shows record fraud volume in Q1 2026, with double‑digit quarter‑over‑quarter growth in attempts. Identity‑based scams—fake carriers, impersonated brokers, and domain spoofing—now dominate incident reports. ATA’s “Freight Under Fire” article describes an “explosive rise” in organized cargo theft, often leveraging VPNs and spoofed domains to mask origin. Brokers and carriers need to treat identity verification and data security as core operational disciplines, not back‑office tasks.

Broker Identity Hijacking Surges 1,500%

Investigative reporting by WFAA in Texas highlights a specific pattern: criminals impersonate legitimate brokers using stolen MC numbers, spoofed domains, and real trucking companies to disappear with loads. The station cites law‑enforcement data showing a 1,500% rise in broker identity hijacking over three years, with average losses above $200,000 per incident. FMCSA confirms it does not regulate the sale of MC numbers, leaving a loophole for shell entities. Shippers and brokers should hard‑gate onboarding and verify email domains, phone numbers, and banking details against official FMCSA and insurance records.

Double Brokering and Cargo Theft Draw Federal Scrutiny

OOIDA’s 2025 comments to DOT label double brokering and carrier identity theft as among the most significant cargo theft risks, particularly harming small carriers. The group calls the National Consumer Complaint Database “ineffective” and urges a more robust, centralized federal repository plus tougher new‑entrant screening. Related legislation like the Household Goods Shipping Consumer Protection Act would give FMCSA clearer authority to penalize unregistered shippers and fraudulent entities and to shut down double‑brokering rings, according to a 2025 Talking Logistics panel. While broad anti‑fraud bills (including SAFER‑branded proposals) are still pending, the policy direction is plainly toward higher compliance expectations and more aggressive enforcement.

FMCSA Targets Chameleon Carriers, CDL Mills, and Fraudulent ELDs

At a March 2026 freight fraud panel covered by Overdrive, FMCSA officials outlined active investigations into chameleon carriers, registration fraud, CDL training “mills,” and bogus ELD devices marketed to help cheat hours‑of‑service rules. Since September 2025, the agency has blocked about 280 ELD registrations using a new vetting process that flags re‑registrations of revoked devices. FMCSA is also conducting in‑person audits of CDL schools and publicizing enforcement actions against reincarnated carriers. Brokers and shippers should expect more authority revocations and should continuously monitor carrier safety and registration status—not just at onboarding.

Cargo Theft Goes “Inside the Truck”

FreightWaves reports a shift from trailer‑yard theft toward “Trojan driver” schemes, where criminals pose as legitimate drivers or collude with insiders to steal freight. These attacks often combine cyber intrusion—compromised portals, spoofed load confirmations—with GPS spoofing to mask real truck locations. Recommended defenses include multi‑signal location verification, geo‑fenced alerts for route deviations and high‑risk parking, and stronger in‑cab identity checks. For high‑value and high‑theft commodities, shippers should require real‑time tracking and explicit pickup identity protocols as a condition of tender.

AI‑Driven Fraud Detection Becomes Standard Practice

Talking Logistics’ May 2026 coverage notes that platforms like Highway are now using machine learning to analyze MC history, authority changes, inspection records, domain age, IP addresses, and behavioral patterns to flag suspicious carriers and transactions. These tools can spot red flags such as recently activated MC numbers tied to known fraud clusters or sudden bank‑detail changes. By 2026, fraud‑specialist advisors describe “know your carrier” (KYC) workflows and automated identity checks as standard practice for sophisticated brokers and shippers. Smaller players that still rely on manual checks and email alone will remain prime targets for fraud rings.

Practical Reporting Guidance for Small Carriers

Overdrive’s summary of the FMCSA/OOIDA panel emphasizes that small carriers should not try to “self‑investigate” complex fraud, which can take 1,000–2,000 hours for law enforcement to unravel. Instead, fleets are urged to secure a local police report, then upload documentation to FMCSA’s complaint system and engage trade groups like OOIDA for help. Panelists also stress basics like ensuring the carrier’s legal name appears correctly on the bill of lading—correcting it if needed—to preserve a clean liability and claims trail. Solid documentation is increasingly a precondition for any recovery effort or insurer support.

Technology & Policy

Market Outlook: Cautious Stabilization with Rising Rates

ACT Research’s April 2026 outlook describes the industry entering the year in a stronger position than 2025, thanks to excess capacity leaving the system and firmer spot and contract rates. Freight demand remains uneven across sectors, but tightening driver availability and improving supply‑demand balance are creating a healthier backdrop for fleets, lenders, and dealers. TrueNorth characterizes the environment as a “slowly tightening, still‑fragile market” where capacity is shrinking faster than demand is growing. American Lady Transportation and its partners should plan around modest rate inflation driven more by supply constraints than by robust freight growth.

FMCSA Broker Transparency and Safety Fitness Rules on Deck

NASTA’s 2026 outlook highlights two important FMCSA rulemakings: a revised Broker Transparency Rule under 49 CFR Part 371 and a Safety Fitness Procedures NPRM scheduled around May 2026. The transparency rule is expected to tighten recordkeeping and access to transaction data, while the safety fitness update would put more weight on crash history, out‑of‑service rates, and critical violations in determining a carrier’s fitness. OOIDA is pushing for stronger broker transparency to combat fraud and double brokering, as noted in Land Line coverage. Brokers should prepare for more rigorous documentation requirements and potential changes in how carrier safety is evaluated in procurement.

Autonomous Trucking: Pilots Expand, Policy Still Patchwork

Aurora, Kodiak, and Gatik continue to expand autonomous trucking pilots on Texas and regional lanes, with Aurora targeting driverless operations on the Dallas–Houston I‑45 corridor using 20–50 trucks in its initial commercial service, per Transport Topics. Gatik is already running driverless box‑truck routes for major retailers in Arkansas, while Torc Robotics and OEMs push controlled pilots in the Southwest. However, FMCSA’s proposed rule on “Safe Integration of ADS‑Equipped CMVs” has been delayed and may be reshaped under current political leadership, according to FreightWaves. For the next 3–5 years, autonomy will stay in pilot or limited‑lane deployment; brokers should watch specific corridors like I‑45 rather than expect broad national impact.

Emissions Rules, 2027 Engines, and Policy Recalibration

EPA’s heavy‑duty NOx rule and Phase 3 GHG standards, finalized in 2022 and 2024, call for up to 80–90% NOx reductions and stricter CO₂ limits for model years 2027–2032. Industry groups warn these rules could add $20,000–$40,000 per new diesel truck, pushing fleets toward pre‑buys and longer trade cycles. FreightWaves expects the Trump–Vance administration to reset or delay these standards, emphasizing diesel efficiency and renewable diesel rather than rapid ZEV adoption. Until there is regulatory clarity, many fleets are likely to postpone major purchases, which could yield a compressed, more volatile replacement cycle later in the decade.

Digitalization: TMS, Visibility, and Telematics Converge

Gartner and industry press note that most new TMS deployments from providers like Oracle, Blue Yonder, McLeod, and MercuryGate are now cloud‑based and API‑first, integrating tightly with load boards and visibility platforms. Project44 reports tracking over 1 billion shipments annually, while FourKites connects more than 500,000 carriers, using machine learning to refine ETAs. Telematics vendors such as Samsara and Motive increasingly feed real‑time truck and trailer data into TMS and shipper control towers, with Samsara stating that over half its transportation customers use APIs for this purpose. For brokers and carriers, this convergence enables exception‑based dispatch, dynamic appointment scheduling, and more granular service metrics that can differentiate them in a tight market.

FMCSA’s English‑Language and Safety Tech Emphasis

A 2025 White House memo titled “Enforcing Commonsense Rules of the Road for America’s Truck Drivers” reaffirmed FMCSA’s English‑language proficiency requirement, signaling stricter enforcement at the roadside and during audits. This will particularly affect cross‑border operations and carriers with internationally recruited drivers, as highlighted by ProTrans’ 2026 trends piece. At the same time, FMCSA grants are encouraging adoption of ADAS, collision‑avoidance systems, and onboard monitoring, according to Transport Topics. Carriers that pair strong language compliance with safety tech will be best positioned for favorable inspections, insurance pricing, and access to premium freight.

Infrastructure and Truck Parking: Slow Relief, Ongoing Pain

Implementation of the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act is gradually improving key freight corridors, but Trucking Dive notes that construction zones are creating near‑term congestion and planning challenges. The chronic truck‑parking shortage remains severe, with FHWA’s Jason’s Law survey showing demand exceeds capacity by 30–50% during peak hours in many states. The proposed Truck Parking Safety Improvement Act would dedicate $755 million over three years to expand safe parking, and FreightWaves expects renewed momentum under current federal leadership. In the meantime, private apps like Trucker Path and expanding paid/reserved parking at truck stops are stopgaps carriers must integrate into route planning.

Bottom Line

Domestic trucking is exiting a deep downcycle into a slow, capacity‑driven recovery: freight volumes are only modestly improving, but carrier exits, driver demographics, insurance pressure, and fuel volatility are tightening supply and nudging rates higher. At the same time, fraud risk and regulatory scrutiny are both climbing, pushing brokers and carriers toward better identity controls, safety practices, and documentation. Technology—TMS, telematics, visibility, and AI‑based fraud detection—is becoming the differentiator between those who can manage margin in a “marginless recovery” and those who cannot. Over the next 3–12 months, the winners will be the fleets and brokers that get ahead of fuel and insurance cost structures, harden their fraud defenses, and selectively lean into high‑service lanes like LTL, cross‑border, and time‑sensitive truckload where capacity is already tight.

title: Weekly Freight Report - May 22, 2026
excerpt: Market Pulse U.S. truckload capacity tightened in the week of May 18–22, 2026 as seasonal and regulatory pressures stacked up. NTG reports that **“truckload tightens”** this week, citing produce season, Memorial Day positioning, and Roadcheck spillov...
content:
Market Pulse

U.S. truckload capacity tightened in the week of May 18–22, 2026 as seasonal and regulatory pressures stacked up. NTG reports that **“truckload tightens”** this week, citing produce season, Memorial Day positioning, and Roadcheck spillover as the main drivers.

On the demand side, multiple macro sources line up behind a “off the bottom but not booming” story. SSUI’s 2026 Freight Transport Report, summarizing FTR, TD Cowen/AFS, and ACT, describes 2026 truckload demand as **flat to “tepid before improving”**, with **freight and rate recovery expected to become “meaningful” in 2H‑2026** (per ACT Research). TD Cowen/AFS sees **truckload demand flat** and **LTL demand growth “limited”** in Q1‑2026, reinforcing that May’s tightness is heavily seasonal, not cycle‑peak.

Regionally, ATS flags classic May dislocations:

  • Reefer/dry van – Produce pulls trucks into Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, Texas, and California, tightening outbound capacity and pushing up both headhaul and backhaul costs from these states.
  • Flatbed/open deck – Construction and project freight has shippers “jostling for limited trailer space” in **North Dakota, Minnesota, Montana, and Iowa**, tightening open‑deck capacity “across the board.”

Spot markets are riding a higher base: SSUI, citing FreightWaves, notes that during the 2025 retail peak, **spot rates jumped 18.9% from mid‑November to late December 2025** and tender rejections hit a multi‑year high. From that higher Q4‑2025 level, FTR expects overall freight rates to increase only about 2% in 2026, while Morgan Stanley projects **mid‑single‑digit gains in truckload contract rates** as supply slowly tightens.

Bottom line for May 18–22: capacity is tighter vs early Q2, especially in produce and construction states; volumes are better than early‑year lows but still not in “boom” territory; and seasonal pressure is doing more work than underlying macro demand.

Regulation & Enforcement

Three concrete FMCSA actions hit the tape in the May 15–22 window, on top of broader 2026 enforcement initiatives:

  • May 18, 2026 – CDLIS fees proposed rule FMCSA published a **proposed rule on Commercial Driver’s License Information System (CDLIS) fees** (49 CFR Part 384 framework). The docket listing confirms a fee rulemaking but does not show specific dollar amounts in the index. Brokers and carriers should anticipate higher state CDLIS access costs ahead and watch for pass‑throughs in DMV and MVR fees.
  • May 20, 2026 – 12 ELDs revoked FMCSA announced it **removed 12 electronic logging devices** from the registered ELD list, shifting them to “Revoked Devices” for failure to meet **49 CFR Part 395, Appendix A** technical standards. Any carrier still running these units is now exposed to citation risk for non‑compliant logs.
  • May 22, 2026 – Driver hearing exemption notice FMCSA issued a Federal Register **notice of applications for exemptions** from hearing requirements under driver qualification rules (**49 CFR Part 391**). This does not change the core rule set but signals ongoing case‑by‑case medical/qualification scrutiny.

Several larger enforcement and integrity moves frame the rest of 2026:

  • NRII medical card transition – FMCSA’s temporary exemption, effective **April 11–October 11, 2026**, allows CDL/CLP holders and carriers to rely on a **paper medical certificate for up to 60 days** post‑exam while the National Registry II system stabilizes.
  • Anti‑fraud registration system (“Motus”) – FMCSA is rolling out **Motus: the U.S. DOT Registration System**, replacing “decades‑old” legacy systems described as “rife with fraud, waste, and abuse.” The goal is tighter identity and registration controls for carriers, school bus operators, and drivers.
  • $217 million enforcement and workforce funding – FMCSA and USDOT are investing **$217 million** into trucking safety enforcement and workforce programs, targeted at “rooting out bad actors,” strengthening supply chains, and expanding driver opportunities.
  • $73 million withheld from New York – USDOT is withholding **over $73 million** in highway safety funds from New York for failing to revoke illegally issued non‑domiciled CLPs/CDLs. Bobtail separately reports FMCSA previously withheld **over $140 million** from California over similar non‑domiciled and English proficiency issues, prompting mass license revocations and stepped‑up roadside enforcement.
  • Driver qualifications crackdown – FreightWaves notes that by **January 9, 2026**, FMCSA data showed **370 English language proficiency out‑of‑service orders** and a net loss of **17 carriers** early in the year, reinforcing a trend SSUI says will remove “tens of thousands” of marginal drivers through ELP and CDL crackdowns.

No new hours‑of‑service, broker bond, or Texas‑specific rule changes are on record for this week, but enforcement intensity around registration, ELD compliance, and CDL integrity is clearly rising.

Broker Edge

In this environment, the broker advantage is execution: understanding where capacity is genuinely tight versus where headline noise is overstated, and monetizing the spread.

  • Exploit seasonal imbalances – ATS warns that **“securing capacity away from [Southern produce regions] will typically cost a bit more in May.”** That means outbound from Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, Texas, and California is rate‑rich, while inbound and non‑produce markets are often mispriced. Build carrier routing guides that stitch high‑paying produce headhauls to discounted backhauls into softer regions.
  • Lean into “stagnant” annual rate growth with short terms – FTR projects only **~2% overall freight rate growth in 2026**, while Morgan Stanley expects **mid‑single‑digit contract increases**. Lock in short‑term (3–6 month) mini‑bids with shippers using today’s modestly higher but not inflated contracts, then capture upside as ACT’s expected **2H‑2026 rate recovery** materializes.
  • Sell risk control around regulations – Many shippers have no visibility into revoked ELDs, the Motus rollout, or NRII medical card rules. Turning regulatory complexity into a service—pre‑qualifying carriers’ ELD status, CDL standing, and medical compliance—justifies premium margins in a market that otherwise looks “flat” on paper.
  • Use intermodal as a hedge – C.H. Robinson reports **intermodal freight is gaining momentum** in 2026 as **high diesel prices** and capacity constraints push shippers to rail. With national diesel around **$5.60/gal** the week of May 18 (EIA/YCharts), brokers who can quickly quote and execute IMDL options on long‑haul freight gain a pricing edge.
  • Target carrier churn – SSUI warns that **undercapitalized carriers will exit** as operating costs outpace rate gains. With diesel up **~61% year‑over‑year** to **$5.596/gal** on May 18, 2026 (YCharts, EIA), many small carriers are underwater on one‑way spot loads. Use your network to consolidate volumes with the strongest small fleets and step into lanes where shippers just lost low‑cost incumbents.

Cross-Border Watchlist

Mid‑May did not bring fresh truck‑border volume data, but trade and customs policy shifts are building latent risk in cross‑border lanes, per Maersk’s North America Market Update and related advisories:

  • Supreme Court tariff ruling and refunds – After a **February 20, 2026 U.S. Supreme Court ruling** invalidated certain tariffs imposed under the **International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA)**, CBP opened a **refund‑claims portal on April 20, 2026**. Maersk says refund processing is expected to take **60–90 days**, which runs directly through the May–July window. Brokers moving import freight need to coordinate with customs brokers and shippers on whether refunds alter landed‑cost decisions in their networks.
  • Trade Fraud Task Force – Maersk reports that the U.S. DOJ has launched a **Trade Fraud Task Force** focused on transshipment and origin mis‑declaration. This is especially relevant for cross‑border truckers hauling commodities at risk of anti‑dumping or circumvention investigations.
  • Canada CARM go‑live – Canada’s CARM system became the **official system of record for all imports January 1, 2026**, tightening controls around origin, valuation, and data accuracy. For U.S.–Canada truck freight, documentation sloppiness now has a clearer enforcement endpoint.
  • Mexico aluminum “Automatic Import Notice” – Mexico’s Ministry of Economy now requires an **Automatic Import Notice for aluminum (Chapter 76)** to monitor origin and prevent trade circumvention, with direct impact on IMMEX and industrial shippers. That raises paperwork risk and potential border delays for flatbed and van hauling aluminum and downstream products.
  • Tariff and Section 301 noise – C.H. Robinson notes a **temporary 10% Section 122 tariff** in place after earlier rates were overturned and ongoing **Section 301 hearings** that could reset tariff structures and country‑specific deals. Expect episodic volatility in northbound and southbound volumes tied to short‑notice policy changes.

No specific USMCA changes, CBP seizure actions, or border wait‑time spikes are documented for May 15–22, but the regulatory backdrop is clearly tightening. Cross‑border brokers should be treating compliance and data accuracy as core offerings, not afterthoughts.

Fraud & Security

Fraud and cargo theft risk continued to escalate in mid‑May, with several industry signals converging:

  • Security focus from NMFTA – On **May 15, 2026**, Truckinginfo reported that **NMFTA is targeting freight fraud and telematics supply chain risks**, underscoring that telematics‑layer vulnerabilities are now a mainstream concern, not niche IT talk.
  • FreightWaves “Fraud Fighters Awards” – Also **May 15**, FreightWaves closed entries for awards recognizing FreightTech and Fintech firms combating freight fraud, showing how much capital and technology has shifted into this problem space.
  • Escalating fraud metrics – On **May 18**, Talking Logistics noted that **freight fraud and cargo theft are “escalating across the supply chain,”** citing 60 Minutes coverage and rising loss data as drivers of congressional attention.
  • Congressional bills aimed at freight fraud – C.H. Robinson’s May 2026 update highlights **proposed congressional bills** targeting freight fraud and cargo theft, emphasizing stronger enforcement and tougher penalties.
  • AI‑driven attacks – At FreightWaves’ Freight Fraud Symposium 2026, organizers described an **“exponential surge” in freight fraud**, with bad actors using **AI‑powered tools**, sophisticated phishing, forged identities, and falsified documents to execute digital supply‑chain attacks.

The common thread is scale, not isolated events: no single big theft story dominates the week, but every serious industry voice is treating fraud as systemic. For brokers and carriers, that means identity verification, document authentication, and payment controls are now core operational disciplines, not overhead.

Equipment, Fuel & Ops

Fuel is the dominant cost story this week. EIA and market data show diesel at levels that break a lot of small‑carrier math:

  • National diesel price – EIA/YCharts data show U.S. retail diesel at **$5.596/gal on May 18, 2026**, down from **$5.639/gal** a week earlier but up from **$3.476/gal** a year before. That’s a **–0.76% week‑over‑week move, but a +60.99% year‑over‑year jump**.
  • AAA and GasBuddy confirmation – AAA lists **$5.656/gal** on **May 21**, with the top 10% of stations averaging about **$6.45/gal** and the bottom 10% around **$4.78/gal**, per GasBuddy. GasBuddy notes a national average near **$5.618/gal**, with the most common pump price at **$4.99/gal**. Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi are in the **$4.96–$5.04/gal** band, while California sits around **$7.40/gal**, with Hawaii at **$7.21** and Washington at **$6.78/gal**.
  • EIA outlook – EIA’s May 12, 2026 Short‑Term Energy Outlook pegs the **2026 U.S. on‑highway diesel average at $4.76/gal**, slightly below a **2025 average of $4.80/gal** but still far above pre‑pandemic norms. Q2–Q4 2025 projections of **$5.36**, **$4.94**, and **$4.73/gal** show the path of softening from earlier highs.

On the equipment side, order and used‑truck markets continue to normalize:

  • Class 8 orders – ACT Research and FTR put **April 2026 North American Class 8 net orders in the high‑teens‑thousands (≈17,000–18,000 units)**, below typical replacement demand of **20,000–25,000/month**. That’s consistent with carriers shifting from growth to replacement mode, as NATSA and SSUI note.
  • Used trucks – Trade‑press commentary in early May points to continued **price pressure on 3‑ to 5‑year‑old sleepers**, with elevated inventories versus 2023. No new numeric mid‑May index was released, but the direction remains down.
  • Electric trucks – OEMs continue to talk 2026–27 ramp‑ups for battery‑electric Class 8 units (e.g., eCascadia, VNR Electric), but there were no major new purchase announcements or deployment numbers reported May 15–22. Zero‑emission commitments remain a planning issue, not a near‑term capacity swing factor.

Operationally, these numbers translate into sustained margin pressure for small fleets, especially in high‑diesel states. Brokers that understand individual carriers’ fuel exposure and can bundle fuel‑surcharge logic, backhaul pairing, and rate floors into their carrier programs will have an easier time keeping capacity solvent through the summer.

Action Checklist for Brokers

  • Reprice May lanes now – Treat NTG’s **“truckload tightens”** call as a trigger. Re‑review outbound rates from **FL, GA, SC, TX, CA** and open‑deck lanes in **ND, MN, MT, IA**; build temporary surcharges or seasonal adders into quotes through at least the week after Memorial Day.
  • Exploit diesel‑driven dislocation – With national diesel at **$5.596/gal** and up **~61% YoY**, assume small carriers are already in survival mode. Offer multi‑stop or round‑trip packages that guarantee fuel‑surcharge coverage and predictable reloads rather than chasing one‑off cheapest trucks.
  • Run an immediate ELD compliance audit – Cross‑check all in‑network carriers’ ELD brands against FMCSA’s current list and the **12 devices revoked May 20, 2026**. Suspend dispatch for any carrier using revoked units until they show proof of compliant hardware and data transfer capability.
  • Tighten carrier vetting around Motus and CDL integrity – As the **Motus registration system** and non‑domiciled CDL crackdowns roll forward, expect more sudden carrier suspensions. Verify USDOT status before each onboarding and periodically scrub your active carrier list against out‑of‑service and revocation data.
  • Build a fraud playbook – Based on NMFTA’s warnings and FreightWaves’ “exponential surge” narrative, deploy hard rules: independent call‑backs to known phone numbers, mandatory multi‑factor identity checks for new carriers, document watermarking, and strict payment changes only via validated channels.
  • Offer cross‑border compliance support – Use Maersk’s notes on CBP refund claims, the DOJ Trade Fraud Task Force, **CARM** in Canada, and Mexico’s aluminum import notice as a sales wedge. Package customs‑broker coordination, paperwork audits, and lane‑specific compliance guidance into your cross‑border service.
  • Lean into intermodal and mode‑shift options – With C.H. Robinson reporting **intermodal gaining momentum** on the back of high diesel and tight truckload capacity, quote IMDL on long‑haul lanes for cost‑sensitive shippers and keep it ready as a relief valve when spot TL blows out.
  • Time your contract talks to the cycle – Use FTR’s **~2% 2026 rate increase** outlook and ACT’s **2H‑2026 recovery** call to push shippers toward 3–6 month terms now, with language that allows you to re‑open rates as the market tightens late in the year.
  • Monitor regulatory dockets weekly – Track the **CDLIS fee proposed rule (May 18)** and FMCSA’s enforcement and grant activity. Rising CDLIS and compliance costs will eventually filter into carrier overhead; brokers who can explain these cost drivers to shippers will defend margin more effectively.

title: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup - May 15, 2026
excerpt: Fleet & Market Trends Driver Pool Tightens Even as Tonnage Stabilizes The driver workforce continues to shrink while freight volumes show early signs of recovery. LDP Logistics reports that trucking employment has fallen year-over-year for 33 consecu...
content:
Fleet & Market Trends

Driver Pool Tightens Even as Tonnage Stabilizes

The driver workforce continues to shrink while freight volumes show early signs of recovery. LDP Logistics reports that trucking employment has fallen year-over-year for 33 consecutive months, even as the ATA For-Hire Truck Tonnage Index rose +2.1% YoY in February 2026 to 116.2. Combined with SSUI’s forecast that enforcement will remove “tens of thousands” of non-compliant drivers, this points to structurally tighter capacity. For brokers and carriers, any modest demand uptick over the next year is likely to push rates higher faster than in past cycles.

Carrier Attrition Caps Supply Growth

The 2024–2025 freight recession has taken a lasting toll on capacity. LDP Logistics notes a net loss of 2,648 operating authorities in 2025, with 46% of those exits occurring in Q4 alone, mostly among 1–20 truck fleets that entered during the 2020–2022 boom. C.H. Robinson’s April 2026 market update characterizes the shift as structural, with a less elastic carrier base unable to flood the spot market when rates firm. Shippers should expect faster transitions from loose to tight conditions, especially on volatile lanes.

LTL Networks Lean Out but Hold Pricing Power

Long-distance LTL is slimming headcount while maintaining high pricing. According to LDP Logistics, the sector cut 5,000 jobs in January 2026, dropping to about 241,000 employees, described as network optimization amid soft demand. Yet LTL rates entered 2026 at all-time highs, up 5.2% YoY, with carriers focused on yield and density-based pricing rather than volume chasing. As truckload tightens, expect more spillover freight into LTL, reinforcing pricing discipline at major carriers.

Capital Discipline Limits Fleet Expansion

Fleets are prioritizing asset management over growth, which will curb capacity additions through 2026. ProTrans reports “limited fleet growth” as carriers manage replacement cycles and sweat existing tractors and trailers, while NATSA notes that rising insurance and equipment costs are squeezing margins. OEM order books have normalized from 2021–2023 peaks, but higher vehicle prices and financing costs are slowing new orders, particularly for small carriers. In practice, demand growth over the next 12 months will lean on existing equipment rather than a wave of new iron.

Insurance, Litigation, and Compliance Favor Scale Players

High insurance costs and nuclear verdict risk are reshaping who can stay in the game. NATSA highlights “rising insurance and equipment costs” as a key drag on TL and LTL margins, while Trucking Dive notes that carriers are “building resiliency” through tighter compliance in response to litigation risk and CDL enforcement. SSUI adds that undercapitalized carriers with weak safety records are being priced out by tougher underwriting, effectively pushing freight toward larger, better-capitalized fleets. For brokers, this means a more consolidated core carrier base but less slack capacity to tap when spot demand spikes.

Fuel & Cost Pressures

Diesel Remains Structurally Volatile on Refining Constraints

Refining bottlenecks keep diesel spreads elevated even when crude eases. EIA’s Today in Energy notes that U.S. distillate inventories have been running below five-year averages and that refinery capacity has been flat to down since 2019, with high utilization but limited new capacity additions. This environment, combined with tight crack spreads, supports periods where diesel jumps faster than crude benchmarks. For carriers, that means continued fuel surcharge sensitivity and the need to manage speed, routing, and purchasing strategies closely over the next 6–12 months.

Fuel Surcharges Still Don’t Fully Protect Smaller Carriers

Fuel surcharges remain contractual and uneven, leaving many small fleets exposed when diesel spikes. Supply Chain Management Review explains that most TL and LTL FSCs are pegged to the EIA diesel index with cents-per-mile formulas, but they are not regulated and are highly negotiable. ATA’s brief reinforces that surcharges rely on the DOE/EIA all-U.S. average, while FreightWaves data shows that in the spot market, some brokers and shippers adjust slowly or not at all, allowing intermediaries to capture part of the FSC as margin. For small carriers, this keeps fuel as a key failure risk during any new price surge.

High Fuel Costs Drove Past Exits and Still Threaten the Marginal Carrier

Extended periods of high diesel have already contributed to capacity rationalization. DAT research cited by China Daily found that 18% of surveyed U.S. trucking firms temporarily halted operations during 2022 fuel spikes, and a DAT white paper in 2022–2023 tied sustained high diesel directly to small-carrier exits and higher spot rates with a lag. ATRI’s 2023 “Operational Costs of Trucking” confirms fuel as one of the largest variable expenses in the cost-per-mile stack. Heading into the next rate upcycle, fuel volatility will again play a central role in which small carriers survive.

Alternative Fuels: CNG/RNG Lead Near-Term Diesel Substitution

CNG and renewable natural gas are emerging as the most commercially mature diesel alternatives for certain use cases. TruckingDive reports that industry groups see CNG/RNG as “the most mature alternative fuel technology currently in widespread commercial deployment,” especially in regional and LTL operations with predictable routes and station access. NACFE and ATRI studies show potential TCO advantages where CNG is priced competitively, offset by higher vehicle costs and infrastructure limits. For mid-sized regional fleets, 2026–2027 looks like the key window to test CNG/RNG on dedicated lanes while diesel remains volatile.

Zero-Emission Trucks: Niche-Competitive in Short-Haul, Not Yet a Diesel Replacement

Electric and hydrogen trucks are gaining traction in defined pockets but remain a complement, not a replacement, for long-haul diesel in the near term. ICCT and NACFE show that battery-electric trucks can be cost-competitive in urban delivery and short regional runs when diesel is above roughly $4–$4.50/gal and incentives are stacked, with several fleets proving the model in “Run on Less – Electric.” NREL’s hydrogen analysis suggests fuel-cell trucks are still more expensive per mile at current hydrogen prices but could converge by the 2030s in high-volume corridors. Over the next 3–5 years, diesel cost management remains central, with EVs and hydrogen playing targeted roles where policy and duty cycles align.

Fraud & Security Watch

Sophisticated Cargo Theft Rises Even as Overall Events Dip

Headline cargo crime volumes are down, but risk per load is rising. CargoNet data reported by Heavy Duty Trucking shows 767 supply chain crime events in Q1 2026, down 5.3% YoY, yet confirmed cargo thefts climbed to 596 cases and losses held at about $131.6 million. California incidents increased to 277, and New Jersey more than doubled to 59, with sharp growth in targeted thefts of seafood and personal care products. The trends point to organized rings focusing on higher-value, harder-to-detect crimes rather than opportunistic grabs.

Impersonation-Based Freight Fraud Hits Record Levels

Identity-driven fraud has become the dominant freight crime vector. Truckers News’ Freight Fraud Index report notes that freight fraud reached an all-time high in the most recent quarter, driven by double-brokering and carrier impersonation. CargoNet describes criminals harvesting credentials via phishing and malware to take over email, phones, and load board accounts, then accepting and diverting loads under trusted identities or through purchased operating authorities. For brokers, this raises the bar for carrier onboarding, payment controls, and continuous identity monitoring.

Trojan Drivers and CDL Mills Bring Risk Inside the Truck

The threat is increasingly coming from inside legitimate operations. FreightWaves details “Trojan driver” scams where fraudulent drivers secure employment or lease-on status and then steal freight after disabling telematics using GPS jammers or spoofers. Parallel FMCSA and state investigations into CDL “mills” have uncovered schools issuing credentials without proper training or using fake identities, feeding unqualified drivers into the system. Over the next year, carriers will need tighter hiring, document validation, and telematics tamper alerts to defend against internal theft.

AI-Powered Carrier Vetting Becomes a Core Control

Data and AI tools are moving to the front line of fraud prevention. FreightWaves and other outlets report that DAT, C.H. Robinson, Uber Freight, and factoring firms like Triumph now use machine learning to risk-score carriers and loads, flagging anomalous behavior, identity changes, and links to known bad actors. Platforms such as Highway, Carrier Assure, RMIS, and MyCarrierPackets are integrating fraud scoring, bank account verification, and cross-checks against FMCSA and CargoNet data. For brokers, investing in this tech stack is increasingly non-optional given heightened legal exposure and rising fraud sophistication.

Cyber Compromise of TMS and Load Boards Fuels Theft

Cybersecurity lapses are directly enabling cargo theft and payment fraud. Truckinginfo and FreightWaves highlight the growing role of phishing and business email compromise in gaining access to carrier and broker systems, allowing criminals to accept loads, alter payment instructions, and issue convincing but fraudulent documents. Concerns are also growing around potential exploitation of ELD and telematics systems to track and target high-value loads. Industry groups like ATA and TIA are pushing MFA, role-based access, and staff training as baseline defenses that brokers and carriers will need to standardize over the next 6–12 months.

Legal Exposure Grows for Brokers After Supreme Court Ruling

Brokers now face clearer liability for negligent carrier selection. Truckinginfo notes that the U.S. Supreme Court’s unanimous decision in Montgomery v. Caribe opened the door for state-law negligence claims against brokers that hire unsafe carriers, rejecting broad federal preemption arguments. This ruling, affecting an estimated 28,000+ freight brokers per FreightWaves coverage, effectively raises the standard of care around vetting and monitoring. Expect more civil suits after fraud or crash events and greater emphasis on documented due diligence in carrier selection.

SAFER in Transport Act Targets Fraud at the Registration and CDL Level

Congress is moving to harden the system against fraudulent entities and drivers. Land Line reports that Rep. Brad Knott’s House “SAFER in Transport Act,” introduced April 14, 2026, mirrors a Senate bill from Sen. Todd Young and would create a Freight Fraud and Theft Advisory Committee, mandate a DOT–DOJ information-sharing MOU, and give FMCSA explicit power to revoke or deny registrations for fraud. The bill would also phase out MC numbers within 5 years in favor of USDOT identifiers, require monthly CDL issuance and revocation reporting, and enable audits and removal of rogue training providers. If enacted, it will reshape onboarding, compliance, and identity checks for brokers and carriers over the next several years.

Technology & Policy

Autonomous Trucking Expands from Texas to California and the Midwest

Autonomous pilots are scaling across key freight corridors, signaling medium-term structural change. TruckingDive reports that California has removed restrictions on driverless heavy trucks, opening a major freight market to permitted Level 4 operations. In Texas, Aurora and McLane are expanding driverless food and grocery hauls between Dallas and Houston, while International, Ryder and PlusAI are piloting a daily 600-mile Laredo–Temple lane. Kodiak’s expansion to the I-70 corridor in the Midwest and Torc’s testing in Michigan show that AV activity is moving beyond the Southwest, with hub-to-hub commercialization targeted late this decade.

EPA 2027 Engine Rule Triggers Pre-Buy and Drives Tech Choices

The next emissions step-change is pushing fleets to front-load diesel purchases and reassess powertrain strategies. CCJ’s “Pushmi-Pullyus in freight” coverage highlights that EPA’s 2027 heavy-duty rule will require roughly 80–90% NOx reductions and longer useful-life and warranty periods, raising truck purchase prices and complexity. Many fleets are planning significant pre-buys in 2025–2026 to avoid early-generation 2027 engines, echoing behavior from past emissions cycles. This dynamic will affect used equipment pricing, OEM build slots, and maintenance planning for at least the next 3–4 years.

CNG/RNG and Early ZEV Adoption Align with Emissions and Cost Pressures

Regulation and economics are nudging more fleets toward lower-emission options where duty cycles allow. TruckingDive’s May 2026 analysis notes that CNG/RNG is now the most commercially mature diesel alternative in fleet use, especially in regional and LTL operations, and can be near carbon-neutral or negative under programs like California’s LCFS. ICCT and CARB briefs show that Advanced Clean Trucks and Advanced Clean Fleets rules will steadily ratchet ZEV adoption targets in states like California, pushing OEMs and fleets to integrate electric and hydrogen platforms. Over the next 3–12 months, expect more pilot deployments and RFPs that explicitly weigh emissions profiles alongside cost.

Telematics, Asset Tracking, and Starlink Connectivity Become Table Stakes

Visibility and connectivity investments are now core to both security and utilization. CCJ reports a surge in deployment of small asset trackers and trailer telematics with door sensors, environmental monitoring, and geofenced alerts, motivated by cargo theft and equipment cost inflation. Starlink for Fleets is enabling always-on ELDs, video, and cloud-based TMS access even in remote areas, while OEMs like Volvo are rolling out over-the-air updates and smart tractor–trailer connectors to feed richer data back into fleet systems. For brokers, integrating these feeds into TMS and customer portals will be a competitive differentiator in 2026–2027.

AI Enters Freight Procurement and Back-Office Workflow

AI is moving from buzzword to practical tool in procurement and operations. CCJ notes that project44 has launched an AI procurement agent to rationalize carrier bids using historical lane performance and live capacity data, signalling a more data-driven approach to annual and mini-bid events. AI-based invoicing tools are also automating freight bill audits, charge validation, and collections inside modern TMS platforms. Over the next year, brokers that embrace these tools can compress manual overhead and respond faster to rate shifts, particularly as TL spot markets firm.

Infrastructure Investments Add Friction Controls and Freight Flow Tools

IIJA-funded technology projects are gradually reshaping key corridors. TruckingDive reports that Caltrans is rolling out three freight tech projects with Quarterhill focused on traffic analytics and connected-vehicle infrastructure, while Massachusetts is adding 15 weigh-in-motion stations to enforce overweight limits and better manage pavement wear. Federal grants are also supporting truck parking expansions and real-time availability systems in multiple states. These investments won’t transform capacity overnight, but they will influence routing, compliance, and dwell on major lanes over the next 3–5 years.

Safety Tech and In-Cab Systems Shift Driver Expectations

Advanced safety features are quickly becoming standard equipment, changing both costs and driver experience. America Truck Driving notes that new tractors increasingly ship with ADAS suites—lane-keeping, adaptive cruise, collision mitigation, and blind-spot monitoring—while CCJ highlights Daimler’s exterior camera (digital mirror) systems and Volvo’s enhanced connectivity. These tools can support better safety outcomes and claim defense but require training and driver buy-in to avoid alert fatigue. As insurers incorporate ADAS data into underwriting, fleets that utilize and document these systems effectively may gain a cost and liability advantage.

Bottom Line

The domestic trucking market is entering a phase where supply-side constraints—driver availability, carrier attrition, insurance, and capital—matter more than demand swings, so even modest volume growth can drive sharper rate and service changes. Fuel and emissions trends are pushing fleets toward tighter fuel management and targeted alternative-fuel pilots while pre-buying newer diesel iron ahead of EPA 2027. At the same time, freight fraud and cyber-enabled cargo theft are forcing brokers and carriers to harden onboarding, identity verification, and telematics security, with AI tools increasingly central to that defense. Over the next 3–12 months, the most resilient players will be those that treat risk management, technology adoption, and carrier relationships as strategic levers—not just line items—while they position for a structurally tighter, more tech-intensive trucking landscape.

content:
Market Pulse

DAT spot conditions and contract behavior confirm that mid-May is a supply-driven market, not a demand boom.

  • Per Bison Transport’s May update, DAT spot rates are ~25% higher year-over-year in early–mid May 2026, even with “modest” demand. Carriers are pricing on tight capacity, not surging freight.
  • C.H. Robinson, citing DAT, reports the national load-to-truck ratio jumped in late April from 7.2:1 to 8.3:1, versus just 4.6:1 in the same week of 2025. That tighter backdrop is what you’re feeling on the boards this month.
  • Contract pricing is grinding higher too. FreightWaves’ May “State of the Industry” white paper pegs long-term contract rates up ~8% since fall 2025, with more increases likely as shippers lean on secondary capacity.
  • Bison notes the Cass Linehaul Index is up 1.8% year-over-year, confirming modest but real upward contract pressure.

Mode-level dynamics, per C.H. Robinson and ATS:

  • Dry van: Seasonal events plus Roadcheck are tightening capacity nationwide. Expect elevated spot and more calls on backup carriers through late May.
  • Reefer: Mother’s Day floral freight out of South Florida created a “sharp increase in demand” and a crush of outbound shipments. ATS adds that May produce pulls reefer and dry van drivers into Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, Texas, and California, draining capacity from the Midwest and Northeast.
  • Flatbed: C.H. Robinson reports “seasonally tight” conditions as construction ramps. ATS flags strong open-deck demand from Texas and the Southeast into northern markets like North Dakota, Minnesota, Montana, and Iowa, with cargo-securement focus during Roadcheck further constraining trucks.

Route-guide behavior is confirming the squeeze:

  • On C.H. Robinson’s managed freight, April 2026 route-guide depth was 1.49 for long hauls (>600 miles) vs 1.30 in April 2025, and 1.122 for short hauls (<400 miles) vs 1.15 in April 2025. More loads are falling past the primary carrier.
  • Bison reports its own route-guide depth at 1.41 overall and 1.71 for long-haul in May, with rising tender rejections and slipping service levels as evidence of tightening supply.

Carrier attrition is the core driver. Both C.H. Robinson and Bison report ongoing exits among smaller fleets, truck postings down, and driver availability tightening again. ACT Research adds that Class 8 orders are “well above prior-year levels” in early 2026 but largely replacement and pre-buy ahead of EPA 2027 – fleets are refreshing iron, not flooding the market with capacity.

Regulation & Enforcement

The enforcement climate in mid-May is as important as the freight itself.

  • International Roadcheck (May 12–14, 2026): C.V.S.A.’s 72‑hour blitz is in full effect this week. C.H. Robinson notes that driver inspections target ELD tampering and hours-of-service falsification/manipulation, while vehicle inspections focus on cargo securement, especially flatbed. Both C.H. Robinson and Bison warn that many small carriers simply park trucks to avoid inspections, cutting effective capacity and pushing up spot rates.
  • Non‑domiciled CDL crackdown: FMCSA’s final rule issued February 18 and effective March 16, 2026 tightens eligibility and state verification for non‑domiciled CDLs. States out of compliance must stop accepting transfers until they meet the standard. InTek Logistics estimates the broader CDL crackdown is touching ~200,000 CDLs and has removed or flagged roughly 7,000 schools.
  • Revoked ELD = out‑of‑service: As of February 7, 2026, enforcement can place a vehicle OOS immediately if it’s running a device on FMCSA’s revoked ELD list. TruckDispatchExperts notes there are no new ELDs being approved in recent months, so brokers and carriers need to keep a close eye on device status.
  • Broker financial responsibility: New broker/forwarder bond rules took effect January 16, 2026. TruckDispatchExperts advise carriers to verify broker bonds before hauling, and brokers should assume more carrier scrutiny on MC and surety details.
  • What’s coming next: FMCSA Administrator Courtney Barrs has roughly 10 rulemakings queued for NPRM by summer 2026, including codified English-language proficiency, English-only written CDL exams, ELDT updates, ELD revisions, URS modernization, and stricter new-entrant requirements (InTek Logistics).

Congressional activity

  • SAFER Transport Act (HR 8627 / S.2938): Highlighted in C.H. Robinson’s May 7 government update, this would expand FMCSA’s power to fight registration fraud and cargo theft, formalize data sharing between DOT, DOJ, and CBP, and create a Freight Fraud and Theft Advisory Committee.
  • Safety and Accountability in Freight Enforcement Act (HR 7539): Targets double brokering and identity manipulation via tighter registration and licensing rules.
  • “Delilah Law” proposal: As summarized by Bobtail, this bill would restrict CDL eligibility by immigration status, require English-only CDL testing, and impose $50,000 penalties on carriers employing ineligible drivers involved in crashes. Still a proposal, not law.

Broker Edge

In this environment, brokers who manage risk and timing are protecting margins while still covering freight.

  • Lean into supply-driven pricing: With spot up ~25% YoY (Bison) and contract up ~8% since fall (FreightWaves), treat May as a floor reset, not a temporary spike. Lock in strategic mini-bids now while capacity is tightening but not yet at full peak-season chaos.
  • Exploit the calendar: ATS and C.H. Robinson both advise shippers to avoid moving during Roadcheck. Push customers to ship either before May 12 or after May 14. Where they insist on those dates, quote surge pricing and tighten accessorials.
  • Route-guide intelligence: Depth at 1.41–1.71 (Bison) and 1.49 on Robinson’s long-haul book means primarys are missing more tenders. As a broker, monitor your own primary acceptance daily this week and pre-book core lanes 2–3 days out.
  • Carrier selection under enforcement pressure: With ELD revocation and non‑domiciled CDL rules active, push carriers for:
    • Proof their ELD model is not on the revoked list.
    • Clear driver qualification files, especially for cross-border or recent CDL holders.
    Build this into onboarding checklists.
  • Pricing play in tight reefer/flatbed: C.H. Robinson and ATS both show reefer and open-deck as the tightest modes right now. Use real data in your customer conversations: produce and floral out of South Florida; flatbed demand from Texas and the Southeast into the Upper Midwest. Quote dynamically by lane and time of week instead of using static seasonal tables.

Cross-Border Watchlist

Nearshoring and fraud-heavy cross-border flows demand closer attention, even without new tariffs this week.

  • C.H. Robinson’s May update underscores that Mexico’s manufacturing boom is increasing export volumes and squeezing cross-border trucking. High fuel and tighter driver enforcement on both sides of the border are lifting northbound rates.
  • No new USMCA or CBP rule changes were noted between May 8–15 in the sources provided, but the pending SAFER Transport Act would formalize data sharing between DOT, DOJ, and CBP and directly target cross-border registration fraud and double brokering (C.H. Robinson, May 7 regulatory update).
  • Reefer equipment into South Texas is tightening as Mexico produce season ramps, per C.H. Robinson. Expect scarcity on Laredo and McAllen origin loads and price accordingly.
  • Canadian port connectivity continues to erode. A Bank of Canada study cited in KESCO’s May 15 weekly report shows total deadweight tonnage through Canadian ports fell from 167 million metric tons in 2016 to 119 million in 2023 – a 28% decline. East Asia now holds 8 of the world’s 10 most-connected ports, up from 6. That shifts some transpacific freight patterns and could increase reliance on U.S. gateways, with downstream truckload impacts.

Fraud & Security

Fraud risk is accelerating faster than the freight market itself.

  • Q1 2026 fraud by the numbers (Highway):
    • 527,940 blocked email threats in Q1 2026.
    • 169.6% year-over-year increase in “ownership-change” fraud – think account takeovers and hijacked carrier profiles.
    • About 50% of fraud incidents involved carriers with “clean” safety profiles, meaning traditional vetting alone is not enough.
  • Losses and attack methods (TenTrucks):
    • Freight fraud cost U.S. trucking an estimated $725 million in the last year.
    • IDScan.net data cited by TenTrucks shows 213% growth in ID fraud attempts in cargo/logistics over two years.
    • Dominant scams: double brokering, carrier identity theft/chameleon carriers, fictitious pickups, and hostage loads; with a fifth bucket emerging – AI‑generated documents (fake rate cons, BOLs, COIs).
    • The “reroute scam” – mid-transit calls impersonating your team to redirect loads – is flagged as one of the fastest-growing variants.
  • Legislative push: As noted above, HR 8627, S.2938, and HR 7539 would give FMCSA more teeth against freight fraud and double brokering (C.H. Robinson, May 7 update). They are not law yet, but they signal the enforcement direction.
  • Industry response and events:
    • FreightWaves’ Freight Fraud Symposium 2026 in Cleveland this month brands freight fraud as an “existential threat,” highlighting AI‑powered phishing and document forgery. Freight brokers are flagged as having rising legal and fiduciary exposure.
    • The Fraud Fighters Awards entry deadline is May 15, with winners to be announced at the symposium on May 20.
    • NMFTA ran a Freight Fraud Prevention Hub webinar on May 14, pushing coordinated prevention strategies across shippers, brokers, and carriers.
  • Reporting and recourse (TenTrucks):
    • FMCSA National Consumer Complaint Database: nccdb.fmcsa.dot.gov.
    • FBI IC3: ic3.gov.
    • State attorneys general – Indiana, Illinois, and Texas are cited as having active freight-fraud task forces.
    • Factoring contracts often require 24–48 hour notification once fraud is discovered.
    • TenTrucks notes that in April 2026 alone, 12 small trucking companies filed bankruptcy, with many “two days from broke” if a $4,000–$8,000 invoice goes unpaid.

Equipment, Fuel & Ops

Fuel is back in the driver’s seat on operating costs.

  • Per EIA data compiled by YCharts and News‑Leader, the U.S. on‑highway diesel average for the week of May 11, 2026 is $5.639/gal, essentially flat week-over-week (down $0.001 from May 4) but up roughly $2.16/gal year-over-year.
  • Octagon AI notes that on May 4, diesel was $5.640/gal, up $0.289 from the prior week, with U.S. distillate inventories 11% below the 5‑year seasonal average and gasoline 4% below.
  • Politico reports diesel at $5.66/gal around May 6 – just $0.16 shy of the June 2022 record $5.82/gal. DAT’s Dean Croke told Politico that at roughly 900 truck stops, prices are already at or above that record level, and many small owner-operators are parking trucks because they cannot make money at current fuel prices.

On the equipment side:

  • ACT Research’s 2026 outlook says Class 8 orders in early 2026 are running well above prior-year levels, but driven by replacement and pre-buy ahead of EPA 2027 rather than aggressive growth. Capacity is being refreshed, not expanded.
  • FTR and ACT preliminary April 2026 Class 8 net order numbers (released in early May) are the latest benchmarks in play right now, but specific unit counts were not provided in the research set. The key takeaway: orders are consistent with a “constructive” market, not a glut of new trucks.

Operations and roadside risk:

  • Roadcheck 2026 (May 12–14) is imposing real utilization drag as drivers avoid scales and inspections. Bison states that “many smaller carriers pull trucks off the road,” lowering tender acceptance and causing short-term rate spikes.
  • TruckDispatchExperts and Smart‑Trucking highlight 2026 rule changes allowing electronic DVIRs in place of paper and removing requirements for liquid-burning flares and spare fuses, but these are relatively minor compared to diesel and Roadcheck in terms of day-to-day impact.

Action Checklist for Brokers

  • Price for a supply-driven market. Use Bison’s data – DAT spot up ~25% YoY, Cass linehaul up 1.8% YoY, contracts up ~8% since fall – when you reset customer expectations. Treat May pricing as the new base, not a blip.
  • Plan around Roadcheck. For loads May 12–14, pre-book capacity, add rate cushions, and warn shippers about increased dwell risk on inspection corridors. Where possible, shift pickup/delivery to outside the 72‑hour window.
  • Harden carrier vetting. Check that every carrier’s ELD is not on FMCSA’s revoked list; verify authority, insurance, and identity against recent fraud patterns (ownership changes, contact info shifts). Assume “clean” safety scores do not equal low fraud risk, per Highway’s finding that ~50% of incidents involve clean-profile carriers.
  • Lock in reefer and flatbed relationships. Mother’s Day floral, produce out of the South, and construction demand have reefer and open-deck in short supply. Offer dedicated or mini-bid volumes to your best carriers in South Florida, South Texas, California, and the Southeast to secure priority.
  • Adjust fuel programs. With diesel at roughly $5.64–5.66/gal and inventories 11% below normal, tighten your FSC formulas and shorten the time between fuel-index resets in contracts. Daily volatility justifies more frequent adjustments.
  • Update compliance paperwork. Make sure your carrier onboarding and SOPs reflect:
    • Non‑domiciled CDL rule effective March 16, 2026.
    • Broker bond/financial responsibility rule effective January 16, 2026.
    • Revoked ELD = immediate OOS authority (February 7, 2026).
    Include explicit questions on non‑domiciled CDL status and ELD model during vetting.
  • Build a fraud response playbook. Use TenTrucks’ guidance: define internal steps when a load goes bad (who to call, within how many hours), and standardize reporting to FMCSA NCCDB, FBI IC3, your surety, and your factoring partners.
  • Lean on data in customer talks. Show shippers concrete stats – 8.3:1 DAT load-to-truck ratio vs 4.6:1 last year, Roadcheck dates, and fraud loss estimates of $725M – to justify higher rates, more flexible appointment windows, and tighter tender lead times.

title: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup - May 8, 2026
