content:
Fleet & Market Trends

33 Consecutive Months of Employment Declines

Industry employment has fallen year-over-year for 33 straight months, signaling persistent workforce contraction and capacity tightening. LTL long-distance jobs dropped by 5,000 in January 2026 to 241,000 workers, the largest monthly decline in years, as carriers optimize networks amid weak demand. Brokers should anticipate reduced elasticity in truckload and LTL segments through H1 2026, per LDP Logistics Q1 analysis.

LTL Rates Hit All-Time Highs Amid Job Losses

LTL employment plunged 5,000 jobs in January, reflecting density-based pricing and network shifts, with tonnage expected slightly negative YoY through mid-2026. Yet rates reached all-time highs, up 5.2% YoY, as full truckload spillover tightens capacity. Carriers face consolidation pressures; brokers can leverage FTL rejects for LTL yield, according to LDP Logistics.

Net Exit of 2,648 Operating Authorities in 2025

A massive -2,648 net exit of operating authorities in 2025, with 46% in Q4, reversed truckload oversupply, pushing tender rejections to ~13% amid winter storms. Combined with carrier insolvencies, this sets up swift crunches as demand rebounds in 2026. ACT Research forecasts structural tightening supporting rates without major volume surges.

Carriers Shift to Aged Asset Replacement

Fleets are prioritizing replacement of aged assets over expansion, correcting overcapacity and supporting moderate volume growth. Equipment demand turns constructive as regulatory pressures slow new additions, aiding market rebalancing over the next 12 months. MyNATSA 2026 outlook advises brokers to plan for stabilizing but constrained trailer availability.

Fuel & Cost Pressures

Diesel Demand Remains Inelastic at 9.5M Barrels/Day

Trucking fuel consumption holds steady at ~9.5 million barrels per day despite price volatility, mirroring historical inelasticity from essential freight roles. Projections show 2024-2026 averages near $3.70/gallon amid geopolitical tensions, limiting operational cuts. Tank Transport analysis urges carriers to focus on empty mile reductions for cost control.

Refinery Constraints Drive Persistent Spikes

Post-COVID refinery capacity has not fully stabilized, with summer heat and external factors like OPEC causing diesel spikes of 57¢/gallon in recent patterns. Trucking remains vulnerable to these supply chain volatilities, inflating operating costs structurally. Commercial Carrier Journal highlights the need for fuel surcharge adjustments in contracts through 2026.

Geopolitical Tensions Spike Regional Diesel Costs

Iran-related conflicts and Ukraine war effects pushed Southeast Texas diesel over $5/gallon, hitting independents with $5-8 fill-ups and raising goods prices. These crude supply disruptors amplify insolvency risks for small fleets. Texas Trucking reports stress pass-through pricing strategies for brokers in high-risk lanes.

Fraud & Security Watch

Cargo Theft Shifts to Organized, Targeted Crimes

Q1 2026 saw 767 supply chain crimes, down 5.3% YoY, but confirmed cargo theft rose to 596 incidents (+41 YoY) with $131.58M losses. California (277 incidents, +8.6%) and New Jersey (+119%) lead hotspots; food/beverage tops targets. Verisk CargoNet via TruckingInfo warns of impersonation via credential theft on load boards.

Chameleon Carriers Buy Legit Authorities

Criminals acquire legitimate motor carriers online to operate under valid MC numbers, evading anti-fraud controls on tenders. They also infiltrate vetted fleets as drivers for coordinated thefts mimicking straight jobs. TruckingInfo recommends brokers verify authority changes and driver histories beyond basics.

SAFER Transport Act Targets Double-Brokering

Introduced April 14, 2026, the SAFER Act creates a DOT Freight Fraud Committee, phases out MC numbers for USDOT-only, and mandates fraud audits. It aims to close entry points like double-brokering via felony revocations and state CDL reporting. Landline Media notes no committee progress yet; carriers should prep for 2027 rollout.

Technology & Policy

California Lifts Driverless Truck Restrictions

California now permits heavy-duty autonomous trucks on public roads without safety drivers post-permit, easing deployment. This regulatory shift accelerates testing in high-volume corridors. Trucking Dive reports brokers monitor for capacity impacts in West Coast lanes over next 12 months.

FMCSA Overhauls ELD Vetting Categories

New ELD categories (e.g., Category 1 Approved, 4 Denied) block non-compliant devices pre-listing, cutting carrier replacement costs and boosting HOS compliance. FMCSA's December 2025 update enhances fatigue prevention amid driver shortages. Fleets gain actionable tools at eld.fmcsa.dot.gov/List for 2026 compliance.

EPA 2027 NOx Rules Reshape Engine Buys

Upcoming late-June NPRM on NOx standards prompts Volvo Trucks' D13 engine launch for 2027 compliance. This pressures fleets to accelerate purchases ahead of mandates, tightening near-term capacity. Transport Topics advises brokers to factor engine transition delays into Q3-Q4 planning.

Kodiak, Einride Advance Autonomous Corridors

Kodiak demos on I-70 (Ohio-Indiana); Einride builds 41-mile Texas Highway 130 corridor with rest stops. These pilots signal scaling autonomous freight by late 2026. Trucking Dive coverage highlights Midwest/Texas lanes for early broker adoption opportunities.

Bottom Line

Capacity tightens structurally from 33 months of job losses, carrier exits, and FMCSA rules, supporting elevated rates into 2026 despite soft demand. Fraud evolves to organized impersonation, countered by SAFER Act and verification tools, while autonomous pilots and ELD/NOx policies reshape operations. Brokers secure lanes now amid inelastic fuel costs and equipment shifts; carriers prioritize compliance for survival in a less elastic market.

title: Weekly Freight Report - May 8, 2026
excerpt: Market Pulse Spot rates climb as capacity tightens entering May. Long-haul dry van linehaul rates hit trough at $1.60 per mile by early May, per C.H. Robinson January forecast. Spot rates now exceed contract rates, trend holds through Q2 2026 accordi...
content:
Market Pulse

Spot rates climb as capacity tightens entering May. Long-haul dry van linehaul rates hit trough at $1.60 per mile by early May, per C.H. Robinson January forecast. Spot rates now exceed contract rates, trend holds through Q2 2026 according to DAT/Simplex Group analysis.

Reefer demand surges with southern produce season in Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, Texas, and California (ATS Inc.). Rates ease into these regions but spike outbound due to driver shortages. Flatbed market tightens nationwide from construction startup in northern states; capacity fights intensify in North Dakota, Minnesota, Montana, and Iowa (ATS Inc.).

Structural capacity shrinks from carrier exits, stalled fleet growth, and driver limits (ACT Research, April 2026). FMCSA rules push 194,000 drivers out via new employment authorizations (RXO). Q2 shapes as prime rate environment for small carriers amid constraints (DAT/Simplex Group).

Freight volumes stabilize unevenly across sectors with 8% year-over-year growth outlook (C.H. Robinson). Manufacturing PMI new orders rose in January, signaling volume gains (RXO). Prep for "Blitz Week" May 12-14: expect capacity crunch and rate spikes. Ship before or after; allow 24-72 hours lead time if needed (ATS Inc.). Memorial Day May 25 hikes costs from long weekend rush (ATS Inc.).

Regulation & Enforcement

No new FMCSA, DOT, or state rules hit May 1-8. Watch May finalizations: ADS Inspection Rule sets maintenance standards for Automated Driving System trucks (truckdispatchexperts.com, cnsprotects.com). ELD Rule Revisions NPRM targets technical specs and compliance (cnsprotects.com). Drug & Alcohol Clearinghouse eyes violation data expansion (cnsprotects.com).

Prior rules bite: Non-Domiciled CDL effective March 16 blocks new applicants (inteklogistics.com). Broker Financial Responsibility since January 16 demands bond checks (truckdispatchexperts.com). ELD enforcement since February 7 outsources revoked devices immediately (truckdispatchexperts.com).

  • Verify broker bonds weekly via FMCSA portal.
  • Audit carrier ELDs for revocation status before loads.
  • Track non-domiciled CDL impacts on foreign driver pools.

Broker Edge

Leverage tightening capacity: push spot loads into high-demand reefer outflows from produce states and flatbed lanes in northern construction zones. Book early for Blitz Week May 12-14 to sidestep spikes. Target small carriers thriving in Q2 rate uptick (DAT/Simplex Group).

Contract renewals favor shippers now but flip soon as spots lead. Secure Q2 deals at current levels before Memorial Day surge. Use 8% volume growth forecast to justify rate floors (C.H. Robinson). Monitor driver exodus of 194,000 for lane-specific squeezes (RXO).

Produce season tip: pair reefer with dry van backhauls from Florida/Georgia to balance loads. Flatbed: prioritize North Dakota/Minnesota hauls where competition heats (ATS Inc.).

Cross-Border Watchlist

No fresh US-Mexico/Canada data May 1-8. Nearshoring sustains northbound truckloads in automotive/appliances/electronics via Texas/Arizona/California (TrueNorth 2026 forecast). West Coast reefer tight through May from fuel/border delays, brief Pacific Northwest ease pre-cherry harvest late May (C.H. Robinson).

SAFER Transport Act (H.R. 8267) introduced April 20 expands FMCSA fraud powers, adds criminal penalties, forms Freight Fraud Advisory Committee, boosts DOJ/CBP data shares (C.H. Robinson May 7). Rep. Hageman's anti-double brokering bill tightens registrations to block identity scams (C.H. Robinson May 7).

  • Screen cross-border carriers via new SAFER tools once live.
  • Confirm Mexico loads avoid Blitz Week overlap with Roadcheck.
  • Lock intermodal shifts if diesel stays elevated.

Fraud & Security

Q1 2026 Freight Fraud Index logs 527,940 blocked email threats and 169.6% YoY surge in ownership-change scams; half hit clean-record carriers (Highway via GlobeNewswire, May 5). Freight Fraud Symposium in Cleveland May covers AI fraud, phishing, forgeries, supply chain attacks, broker scrutiny (FreightWaves).

NMFTA podcast from April TIA conference flags behavioral/digital/social engineering red flags (NMFTA). SAFER Act and anti-double brokering bills ramp penalties (C.H. Robinson May 7).

  • Implement Highway-style email blocks; scan for ownership shifts.
  • Attend Fraud Symposium for AI/phishing defenses.
  • Cross-check carrier MCs against FMCSA snapshots daily.

Equipment, Fuel & Ops

Diesel jumps: national average $5.64/gal week of May 4, up 5.40% from $5.351 prior week, 60.50% from $3.514 YoY (YCharts/EIA, May 5). Up $2.14/gal YoY (EIA via BobIsTheOilGuy, May 4). Regions: West Coast $6.530, East Coast $5.425, Midwest $5.131, Gulf Coast $5.012 (USA Today May 4). California hits $7.501 (Economic Times May 1).

Fuel surge accelerates carrier attrition, nudges shippers to intermodal (C.H. Robinson May update). Mother's Day floral shipments tighten East Coast reefer; Roadcheck May 12-14 cuts capacity (C.H. Robinson). No Class 8 orders, used truck, EV, pay, or parking updates this week.

  • Quote fuel surcharges at 60% YoY diesel hike.
  • Shift West Coast reefer to rail where possible.
  • Build 72-hour buffers for California/Gulf ops.

Action Checklist for Brokers

  • Book Blitz Week alternatives now: pre-May 12 or post-May 14 outbound produce/flatbed.
  • Raise spot bids 5-10% on reefer outloads from South, northern flatbeds.
  • Verify all carrier ELDs/bonds; flag 194,000-driver risks in tight lanes.
  • Deploy fraud screens: block suspicious emails, audit MC ownership weekly.
  • Adjust customer contracts for $5.64 diesel, Memorial Day premiums.
  • Target small carrier networks for Q2 capacity before Memorial Day rush.
  • Monitor SAFER Act progress for fraud enforcement boosts.
  • Pair reefer with dry van returns from Florida/Georgia/Texas.

title: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup - May 1, 2026

content:
Fleet & Market Trends

Moderate Growth Stabilizes After Volatility

The U.S. trucking industry enters moderate growth and stabilization in 2026, with carriers regaining pricing power as overcapacity corrects per NATSA analysis. Spot rates for dry van and refrigerated truckload freight edge upward modestly, while fleets shift to asset replacement over expansion. Brokers should prioritize reliable carriers in tightening regions like cross-border corridors for the next 6-12 months.

Driver Shortages Persist as Structural Hurdle

Driver availability remains constrained by FMCSA enforcement on visas, English proficiency, and out-of-state licensing, per Trucking Dive. High turnover in long-haul operations drives up training and downtime costs, pressuring owner-operators. Carriers must invest in retention strategies now to capture Q2 rate gains.

Fleet Consolidation Thins Smaller Operators

Prolonged downturns have exited many small carriers, leaving a leaner industry focused on efficiency and regional routes according to ProTrans. Remaining fleets emphasize strategic utilization amid low margins. Brokers gain leverage with consolidated networks but face capacity risks in fragmented lanes.

Nearshoring Boosts Cross-Border Demand

Mexico's manufacturing expansion in automotive and electronics drives sustained northbound dry van and flatbed volumes, per TrueNorth. C.H. Robinson added 450,000 sq. ft. of El Paso warehousing to handle growth. Secure long-term contracts on Laredo-El Paso lanes to lock in capacity through 2026.

Produce Season Tightens Southern Capacity

May 2026 produce harvest ramps dry van and reefer demand in Florida, Georgia, and Texas, pulling trucks south per ATS Inc. Outbound rates from these areas rise as drivers chase high-volume loads. Plan shipments 4-6 weeks ahead to avoid Memorial Day crunches on May 25.

Fuel & Cost Pressures

Middle East Conflict Spikes Diesel to $5.60+

U.S.-Israeli operations against Iran since February 2026 elevated national on-highway diesel above $5.60/gallon, with California at mid-$7, per DAT and fuel analyses. 18% of firms paused operations amid the spike. Carriers lean on fuel surcharges; brokers negotiate clauses reflecting real dwell and detention.

Distillate Stocks Create Price Floor

U.S. distillate inventories fell below five-year averages by mid-April 2026, sustaining high prices despite crude retreats, according to refinery data. West Coast constraints amplify pressures for California fleets. Smaller operators cut miles or park trucks—source alternatives via fuel cards for cash flow.

Fuel Costs Hit $6.1B Weekly at $5/Gallon

At $5/gallon diesel, industries spend $6.1 billion weekly on fuel—a 35% jump—without fixing carrier margins, per economic forecasts. Spot rates rise via surcharges, not base improvements. Lock contracts with volatility protections for H2 2026 stability.

Fraud & Security Watch

SAFER Act Targets FMCSA Loopholes

The SAFER Transport Act phases out MC numbers for USDOT, bolstering fraud detection and CDL oversight, backed by ATA per News-Insights. It addresses vulnerabilities like foreign dispatch exploits exposed in 2025 hearings. Implement USDOT vetting now to align with 2026 enforcement.

Double Brokering Hits 28% of Owner-Ops

28% of owner-operators faced double brokering with non-payment or ID theft, amid 750,000 fake posts yearly, per OverdriveOnline surveys. Fraud fuels 15% of cargo thefts. Brokers require photo verification and real-time tracking to mitigate risks over next quarters.

Strategic Fraud Surges 1,500% with Chameleon Tactics

Cargo theft shifted to strategic fraud up 1,500% since 2021, costing $18M daily via identity theft and GPS spoofing, per CargoNet and TruckingInfo. Cases like Tanager Logistics impersonation divert high-value loads. Deploy AI detection and email safeguards for mid-haul protection.

Trojan Driver Scams Infiltrate Legit Carriers

Trojan Driver tactics bypass fake entity checks by placing operatives in real fleets, per FreightWaves Fraud Symposium. International rings use VPNs for rerouting. Mandate carrier identity platforms and disable spoofable GPS for 2026 security.

Technology & Policy

Autonomous Pilots Build Momentum on Fixed Routes

Autonomous truck trials advance in middle-mile despite regulatory gaps, projecting $9B consumer savings by 2035 per industry outlooks. FMCSA evolves safety standards amid state patchwork. Carriers pilot urban drayage now for efficiency edges in tightening capacity.

TMS Adoption Rises to Combat Turnover

Fleets prioritize telematics and TMS at 19% adoption rate to optimize routes amid driver shortages, per NATSA. Platforms enable network resilience and M&A scale. Brokers integrate digital matching for Q2 bid seasons.

EPA 2027 Mandates Defer ZEV Purchases

EPA phased emissions standards from 2027 spur ZEV pilots in ports, offset by grants, but fleets defer buys amid costs per Trucking Dive. California's rules add pressure. Pursue tax credits for hydrogen/electric tests in next 12 months.

Highway Bill Eyes Fuel User Fee Shift

2026 highway bill proposes rebranding fuel tax to 52.9¢/gallon diesel user fee with low admin costs, per TCA outlook in TheTrucker. $275M truck parking grants prioritize infrastructure. Advocate for border-stable policies in contract renewals.

Bottom Line

Capacity tightens via attrition and nearshoring while fuel spikes above $5.60/gallon force surcharge reliance, reshaping H2 strategies for brokers. Fraud evolves to sophisticated infiltration, demanding tech vetting; policy shifts like SAFER Act and EPA mandates require compliance prep. Reliable carriers win in stabilizing markets—secure cross-border lanes and efficiency tools now for 3-12 month gains.

title: Weekly Freight Report - May 1, 2026
excerpt: Market Pulse Dry van spot rates held firm at a national average of $2.68 per mile through late April 2026, up 16¢ from the March average per DAT Trendlines data as of April 22. Linehaul rates excluding fuel reached $2.04 per mile, climbing $0.12 over...
content:
Market Pulse

Dry van spot rates held firm at a national average of $2.68 per mile through late April 2026, up 16¢ from the March average per DAT Trendlines data as of April 22. Linehaul rates excluding fuel reached $2.04 per mile, climbing $0.12 over two weeks and $0.07 in the last week alone, while Spot Inc. reported spot rates at $2.00 per mile, marking a 25% increase year-over-year and 22% above the five-year average. Keynnect Logistics noted all-in rates between $2.01 and $2.12 per mile, with DAT's top 50 dry van lanes averaging $2.40 per mile, up $0.11 weekly, and Midwest rates at $2.44 per mile across 13 states, up $0.08.

Reefer rates averaged $3.13 per mile nationally per DAT on April 22, up 9¢ from March, with Spot Inc. spotting $2.39 per mile (27% YoY gain) and Keynnect at $2.97 per mile, higher on TX/AZ lanes. Midwest reefer hit $3.37 per mile. Flatbed led the charge at $3.44 per mile national average (DAT, up 35¢ from March), the highest since August 2022 and up for 12 of 13 weeks per Keynnect, with a 15-week rally noted by Spot Inc. Spot flatbed stood at $2.58 per mile (21% YoY), Midwest at $3.52 per mile.

Load-to-truck ratios showed reefer at 12.39 nationally (DAT April 22, down from 13.4 in March but YTD 17.5 vs. 7.5 in 2025 per Spot Inc.), flatbed at 73.07 (down from 76.45 March, with C.H. Robinson reporting over 80:1 in Southeast/Midwest amid 30% MoM capacity drop and 100% decline since January), and dry van up 1.3% week-over-week but down 18% overall per DAT Trendlines. Flatbed ratios fell 0.8% WoW and 5.5% monthly.

Fuel prices pressed margins, with national diesel averaging $5.40 per gallon (up 33¢ MoM per YouTube Freight Update), $5.80 to $5.85 per gallon per DAT, and EIA reporting $5.351 per gallon for the week of April 27 (down 0.96% or $0.052 from April 20). Spot Inc. noted reefer surcharges up $0.22 per month and flatbed $0.24 per month. Contract rates for dry van sat at $2.72 per mile (Spot Inc.), with C.H. Robinson forecasting 17% YoY dry van cost increases and 16% for reefer in 2026, plus a 2% YoY reefer peak in Q4 per Arrive Logistics.

Broader signals included ISM Manufacturing PMI at 52.7% for March (up from 52.4% February, third month of expansion per DAT). FTR reported total spot rates hitting an all-time high for the week ended April 24, with flatbed up 17 straight weeks despite some van easing. ATA tonnage marked Q1 2026 as the best seasonally adjusted since Q3 2017, up 0.3% MoM. Spot load postings surged 68% YoY per Arrive Logistics, with FTR's total spot loads at 234.1 in week 12, highest since June 2022 and 35% above prior year. Produce harvests drove reefer demand along coasts and South, pulling dry van drivers to reefers and tightening enclosed capacity, while northern frost laws lingered into late April, easing spot rates up North but straining South per Kesco Logistics.

Regulation & Enforcement

FMCSA's DOT inspection rules changed effective March 23, 2026, with full enforcement from April 20: spare fuses and liquid flares are no longer required in vehicles, and electronic DVIRs are now legal under 49 CFR 396.11 and 396.13. FMCSA upgraded DataQs on April 14, adding firm deadlines and independent reviews to speed violation challenges and boost fairness.

Enforcement ramped up on existing rules like English proficiency and non-domiciled CDLs, with state partners applying them more strictly in 2026, though no new rulemakings emerged April 24-May 1. Broker transparency NPRM is slated for May 2026. CVSA Roadcheck Week looms May 12, historically sidelining 13,000 vehicles and 3,300 drivers last year, spiking dry van spots nearly 10% per Arrive Logistics—expect volatility in the 100 Days of Summer ahead.

Broker Edge

Brokers face tightening capacity into peak season, with carrier exits since May 2023 hitting roughly 20,000 fleets and truckload spot rates 20% higher YoY, pushing volumes to intermodal per Kesco. Total carrier operating costs reached $2.26 per mile in 2024 (non-fuel $1.779, driver wages $0.798, truck/trailer payments up to $0.390 from $0.279 in 2021 per KCH Transportation). Spot market activity thrives, load posts up 68% YoY as routing guides fail.

Contract rates lag spots but forecasts show dry van costs +17% YoY, reefer +16% in 2026. Midwest dry van at $2.88 per mile, reefer $3.37, flatbed $3.52. Nogales saw its first 2026 truck shortage, with reefer to Boston at $10,000-$10,600 and to Chicago $5,900-$6,200; South Texas out of McAllen ran 26% above last year per KCH. FTR spot loads peaked at 234.1. Position for Roadcheck and pre-Memorial Day crunches—rates won't dip to pre-disruption floors.

Cross-Border Watchlist

De minimis suspension holds firm per February executive order, requiring formal ACE entry, 10-digit HTSUS, origin declaration, and duties—including 10% global surcharge—on all shipments, with China/Hong Kong postal parcels at 54% tariff; 88 postal operators paused U.S. service at points per Kesco. Northbound U.S.-Canada capacity softens with growth, southbound/intra-Canada tight; parity emerging but U.S. peak risks reversal per Arrive Logistics and Loadlink.

Nogales reefer shortages drove premium rates. No USMCA updates, tariff shifts, or CBP actions reported April 24-May 1. Iran conflict reroutes ocean via Cape of Good Hope, up Far East-U.S. West Coast spots 29%, Europe/Med 30-31% since late February—watch for domestic ripple via intermodal rebound.

Fraud & Security

Freight fraud surges over 40% YoY, costing up to $35 billion annually; double brokering persists as top scam per industry estimates. SAFER in Transport Act, introduced April 14 by Rep. Brad Knott (House) with Sen. Todd Young Senate companion, phases out MC numbers for USDOT within 5 years, expands revocation for fraud/felonies, mandates automated detection, monthly CDL reports, 30-day ownership notices, and foreign dispatch broker registration.

Bill requires Unified Carrier Registration completion in one year and a DOT Freight Fraud and Theft Advisory Committee. CDL fraud case: Basnaw faces June 16 sentencing, up to 10 years for bribing tester to lift three restrictions sans exams. No specific thefts or enforcement actions April 24-May 1.

Equipment, Fuel & Ops

Diesel averaged $5.351/gallon week of April 27 (EIA, down $0.052 or 0.96% from $5.403 April 20; prior: $5.608 April 13, $5.643 April 6). Elevated but stabilizing post-Easter volatility per Arrive. Frost laws disrupted northern OD shipments into late April, returning capacity North while South tightened; produce peaks pulled drivers to reefers, hiking warmer-region costs.

No Class 8 orders, used truck, EV, driver pay, or parking updates for the week. Fuel surcharges: reefer +$0.22/mo, flatbed +$0.24/mo (Spot Inc.). Capacity leaner post-attrition, tender rejections near 14% per Kesco.

Action Checklist for Brokers

  • Lock contract rates now—dry van $2.72/mi, expect 17% YoY hikes; reefer 16%.
  • Prep for CVSA Roadcheck May 12: last year sidelined 13,000 vehicles/3,300 drivers, dry van spots +10%; build carrier buffers.
  • Monitor fuel: $5.35/gal avg, surcharges rising; pass through reefer/flatbed adds.
  • Target flatbed/reefer: national $3.44/$3.13/mi, Midwest peaks $3.52/$3.37; ratios tight at 73:1 flat, 12:39 reefer.
  • Scrutinize registrations amid SAFER push: flag MC/USDOT shifts, ownership changes.
  • Secure cross-border: formal entries mandatory, Nogales premiums to $10k+ reefer.
  • Watch fraud: 40%+ YoY rise, double brokering rampant—verify carriers rigorously.
  • Shift to intermodal if truck spots hit records (FTR all-time high week of Apr 24).
  • Route around northern frost remnants, Southern produce squeezes.
  • Update DataQs challenges with new deadlines; drop fuses/flares from inspections.

title: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup - April 24, 2026
excerpt: Fleet & Market Trends Driver Shortages to Remove 194,000 Trucks FMCSA's non-domiciled CDL rule effective March 16, 2026, mandates SAVE verification and visa restrictions, potentially sidelining 194,000 drivers—the biggest supply shock since 1980 dere...
content:
Fleet & Market Trends

Driver Shortages to Remove 194,000 Trucks

FMCSA's non-domiciled CDL rule effective March 16, 2026, mandates SAVE verification and visa restrictions, potentially sidelining 194,000 drivers—the biggest supply shock since 1980 deregulation, per RXO's Q1 forecast. Owner-operators face outsized hits from licensing hurdles and training shutdowns, tightening capacity unevenly with truckload normalizing by June 2026 faster in reefer and flatbed. Brokers should prioritize vetted carriers now to secure spots ahead of peak season demand from housing and Mexico manufacturing.

LTL Consolidation Accelerates via M&A

Analysts predict heavy 2026 M&A targeting regional LTL operators amid low demand and tech shifts, per Trucking Dive. Prolonged cost pressures thin carrier ranks, pushing firms toward efficiency-focused mergers over growth, according to C.H. Robinson and ProTrans. Carriers and brokers gain leverage by aligning with consolidating networks for stable backhauls through year-end.

Carrier Attrition Stabilizes but Fuel Risks Exit Spike

First-quarter authority revocations hit lowest since Q4 2021, yet rising diesel adds strain, accelerating small fleet and OO exits per Ryan Transportation. Fleets replace aged assets without expansion, gradually rebalancing overcapacity into mid-2026. Actionable: Lock in reliable partners before summer volatility from construction uptick.

Tender Rejections Signal Tight Capacity

Elevated rejection rates near 14% and spot rates at four-year highs reflect carriers chasing premium loads, per FreightWaves. Truckload costs project up 16-17% YoY from attrition and constraints, even in soft seasons, says C.H. Robinson. Shippers refine lane strategies to counter outbound strength entering produce peak.

Fuel & Cost Pressures

Diesel Averages $5.53-$5.60 Amid Iran Conflict

U.S.-Iran clashes since February spiked national on-highway diesel to $5.53-$5.60/gallon mid-April, with California at $7.53-$7.74 due to low distillate stocks and refinery limits, per Xinhua and EIA data. 18% of firms paused operations per DAT poll, as smaller operators reject loads or idle rigs. Brokers deploy dynamic surcharges tied to federal benchmarks to maintain carrier viability through Q2.

West Coast Refining Lags Crude Relief

Distillate inventories below five-year lows keep diesel firm despite crude drops, with California slowest to normalize above $7.50/gallon, per Tank Transport. Geopolitical surges burden 3.5 million drivers hauling 70% of freight, forcing higher bids. Carriers hedge via fuel cards; brokers stress-test regional routing for margin protection.

Fuel Volatility Inflates All-In Rates

March diesel jumped 37.3% YoY with record weekly gains, pushing spot rates to 2022 peaks and contract rates to 2023 levels, per Ryan Transportation. Rejection rates hold near early-2022 highs despite modest demand, signaling sustained pressure. Expect intermodal shifts for long-haul as truckload tightens further.

Fraud & Security Watch

SAFER Transport Act Targets Fraud Vectors

Senator Young's SAFER Transport Act, endorsed by ATA February 26, phases out MC numbers, blocks felons from registration, and mandates ownership notifications within 30 days, per FreightWaves. Cargo theft costs $18 million daily, with strategic cyber fraud up 1,500% since 2021 via CargoNet. Brokers verify USDOT-only carriers and BoL names to dodge reroutes like Tanager's six-figure energy drink scam.

FMCSA Cracks Down on ELD and Chameleon Schemes

FMCSA blocked 280 ELD registrations since September 2025 and probes Chicago's Extra Mile ELD cheating network plus chameleon carriers using fake decals, per Mid America Trucking Show disclosures. In-person CDL school audits and public investigations address identity theft at scale. Carriers reject unsigned BoLs per OOIDA to block fraud entry.

VIN Fraud Exploits Carrier Identities

A $287,000 VIN fraud scheme used false identities to infiltrate trucking, documented by FreightWaves. ATA pushes CDL mill shutdowns and foreign dispatch broker registration. Brokers implement automated SAFER flags for high-risk loads through 2026.

Technology & Policy

SELFDRIVE Act Enables Cabless Autonomy

Bipartisan 2026 SELFDRIVE Act introduced January 9 sets federal rules for autonomous cabless trucks, smoothing interstate ops beyond state patches, per policy trackers. Pilots target middle-mile highways, projecting $9 billion annual savings by 2035 via efficiency, per studies. Fleets test Southwest corridors; brokers eye cost drops in specialized hauls by late 2026.

AI and TMS Prioritized for Margins

Mid-sized fleets adopt AI-driven predictive maintenance, telematics, and TMS for turnover amid costs, with tech adoption up to 19%, per research. M&A favors automation platforms for regional scale, says Ryder. Carriers optimize routes now to build Q3-Q4 resiliency.

EPA 2027 Mandates Push ZEVs

Fleets prep for EPA 2027 and CARB rules driving zero-emission vehicles despite infrastructure gaps and high costs, per ProTrans. Policy uncertainty pairs with speed-limiter and ELD revision talks. Brokers target short-haul drayage for early ZEV synergies through 2026.

FMCSA Withholds Funds Over CDL Lapses

FMCSA docks New York $73.5 million for non-domiciled CDL failures, calling it a safety risk, per Trucking Dive. Interstate fees rise 20% via UCR. Expect gradual capacity hits; verify state compliance in carrier vetting.

Bottom Line

Capacity tightens structurally from 194,000-driver losses and attrition, amplified by diesel at $5.60+ squeezing small operators into Q3. Fraud crackdowns via SAFER Act and FMCSA probes demand rigorous BoL and USDOT checks, while SELFDRIVE and AI tools offer efficiency edges. Brokers secure premium lanes, dynamic surcharges, and tech-forward partners to navigate 16-17% cost hikes and peak-season volatility.

title: Weekly Freight Report - April 24, 2026
excerpt: Market Pulse Dry van spot rates held at $2.01-$2.12 per mile all-in per Keynnect Logistics April 2026 update, with national spot at $2.47 according to Dynamic Logistix March 2026 DAT Trendlines data, up 2.5% month-over-month and recovering +22% versu...
content:
Market Pulse

Dry van spot rates held at $2.01-$2.12 per mile all-in per Keynnect Logistics April 2026 update, with national spot at $2.47 according to Dynamic Logistix March 2026 DAT Trendlines data, up 2.5% month-over-month and recovering +22% versus November 2025. Reefer rates averaged $2.97 per mile in March per Keynnect Logistics, or $2.88 national spot via Dynamic Logistix DAT data, unchanged month-over-month but up +26% in South Texas corridors like McAllen. Flatbed rates hit the highest since August 2022, rising in 12 of the past 13 weeks per Keynnect Logistics, with national spot at $2.95, up 8.5% month-over-month per Dynamic Logistix.

Load-to-truck ratios tightened significantly for flatbed at over 80:1 nationally, up 30%+ month-over-month and nearly 100% since January per C.H. Robinson April 2026 data, with Southeast and Midwest lanes most constrained; DAT Trendlines showed flatbed ratios down 9.8% week-over-week but up 33.9% year-over-year. Dry van ratios fell 6.7% week-over-week and were flat +0.1% year-over-year per DAT, with capacity 93% tighter year-over-year per Dynamic Logistix. Reefer capacity tightened 120.1% year-over-year but loosened 4.7% month-over-month.

Contract rates in March outpaced spot: dry van up $0.16 per mile over spot, flatbed +$0.37 per mile, reefer +$0.13 per mile per Dynamic Logistix DAT Trendlines. Full-year 2026 forecasts rose to +17% year-over-year for dry van and +16% for reefer per C.H. Robinson. Spot rates trended higher overall, with flatbed up 20% in March versus January, fueled by construction gains and reefer lanes like Nogales-Boston at $10,000-$10,600 per load per Keynnect Logistics and C.H. Robinson. American Trucking Associations’ For-Hire Truck Tonnage Index dropped 3% to 128.6 in April 2026, the lowest in a year, though up 3.8% year-over-year, signaling softer GDP through June.

No bankruptcies, mergers, or layoffs hit major carriers this week. Capacity exit continues as rates hover near operating costs for small carriers, per industry forecasts, setting up potential tightening into late 2026 amid stabilizing demand.

Regulation & Enforcement

No new FMCSA, DOT, or state trucking regulations emerged April 17-24, including rulemakings, ELD enforcement, CDL changes, hours-of-service updates, drug clearinghouse actions, broker bonds, or Texas legislation. FMCSA Administrator Derek Barrs' March 17 announcement of 9 rulemakings for 2026 targeting CDL mills, chameleon carriers, and fraudulent ELDs remains on track.

Recent FMCSA actions carry over: a final rule effective week of March 17 restricts non-domiciled CDLs, poised to remove nearly 200,000 holders. February finalized 11 rules, including SMS/CSA overhaul reducing violations from 950+ to 116 types, 12-month lookback, utilization factor to 250K miles per power unit, and Driver Fitness threshold at 90%; plus non-domiciled CDL limits, ELD revisions, and National Registry II for medical certs. California revoked over 13,000 improperly issued non-domiciled CDLs after FMCSA withheld $140 million in funding, per March reports. Enhanced English language proficiency enforcement, with roadside out-of-service for violations, started late June 2025 and persists. A federal appeals court stay from November 2025 on non-domiciled CDL rules prompted FMCSA pushback.

Monitor ATA-endorsed SAFER Transport Act, introduced February 26 by Sen. Todd Young, phasing out MC numbers for USDOT, boosting CDL oversight, and hiking fraud penalties—no movement this week.

Broker Edge

Brokers face steady spot gains but watch contract premiums: March dry van contracts beat spot by $0.16/mi, flatbed $0.37/mi, reefer $0.13/mi per DAT Trendlines. Full-year 2026 revisions signal +17% dry van and +16% reefer growth per C.H. Robinson—lock in now before snapback. Flatbed ratios over 80:1 scream urgency in Southeast/Midwest; van capacity 93% tighter y/y, reefer 120.1% tighter.

C.H. Robinson waived fuel card and cash advance fees for April-May to counter diesel spikes from geopolitical risks—leverage if partnered. Transborder freight hit $130.8 billion in February, down 0.7% y/y, with U.S.-Mexico up 7.1% to $73.2 billion and trucks hauling $87.2 billion overall, up 0.7% per BTS. Tariffs reroute logistics: Asian import shifts boost North American trucking, per forecasts, as production moves to U.S./Mexico/Canada.

Tonnage down 3% to 128.6 in April per ATA—position for Q2 stabilization. Overcapacity corrects slowly; small carriers exit as rates pinch margins. Prioritize compliant carriers ahead of FMCSA's 9 rulemakings.

Cross-Border Watchlist

No US-Mexico or US-Canada developments reported April 17-24, including border crossings, USMCA updates, tariffs, or CBP actions. February transborder freight totaled $130.8 billion, down 0.7% y/y: U.S.-Canada $57.5 billion (-9.0%), U.S.-Mexico $73.2 billion (+7.1%); trucks moved $87.2 billion (+0.7%) per BTS.

Tariffs shift supply chains: new U.S. duties on Asian imports drive production to Mexico/Canada, hiking North American freight in 2026 per reports. Potential Trump-era tariffs could spike short-term U.S. imports from Mexico/Canada pre-inauguration, impacting truckers. Supreme Court struck IEEPA tariffs; new ones loom, with first-half 2026 container imports forecast down 2.5% to 12.21 million TEU. USTR's 2026 Trade Policy Agenda eyes America First shifts—no weekly updates. Reefer lanes like Nogales-Boston at $10,000-$10,600/load reflect Mexico produce strength.

Fraud & Security

No cargo theft, double-brokering, or fraud incidents reported April 17-24. Cargo theft costs $6.6 billion/year or $18 million/day per American Transportation Research Institute; CargoNet notes 1,500% surge in strategic theft since 2021.

FreightWaves Fraud Fighters Awards entries close May 15, winners at May 20 Cleveland symposium. April 24 Freight Gong Friday featured Mark Kummer (VNTR) and Mikhail Rasner (MiRUnited) on freight risk. ATA backs SAFER Transport Act for FMCSA registration overhaul, USDOT-only numbers, CDL crackdowns, and theft coordination. Tariffs spur cargo shifts to unfamiliar corridors, raising theft risks at ports/rail ramps.

FMCSA's 2026 rulemakings target CDL mills and fraudulent ELDs—vet carriers via SAFER.

Equipment, Fuel & Ops

U.S. on-highway diesel averaged $5.608/gallon week ending April 20 per EIA (released April 21); AAA pegged $5.593/gallon April 17, down from $5.614 prior day and $5.683 week prior. GasBuddy showed $5.617/gallon national, up 4.1 cents week-over-week. EIA April STEO forecasts diesel peak above $5.80/gallon this month, $5.61/gallon Q2, $5.00/gallon Q3, $4.59/gallon Q4; 2026 annual average raised to $4.80/gallon.

C.H. Robinson waived April-May fuel fees amid geopolitical diesel pressures. No Class 8 orders, used truck, EV, driver pay, or parking updates this week. High fuel squeezes small carriers; pair with rising flatbed rates (+$0.37/mi contract premium) for margin plays. Tariffs hit equipment costs via supply chains.

Action Checklist for Brokers

  • Lock 2026 contracts now: target dry van +17% y/y, reefer +16% per C.H. Robinson forecasts.
  • Prioritize flatbed lanes: ratios over 80:1, rates highest since 2022—Southeast/Midwest tightest.
  • Secure reefer capacity: 120.1% tighter y/y; book South Texas/Mexico corridors early.
  • Tap C.H. Robinson fuel waivers for April-May to offset $5.608/gal diesel.
  • Vet carriers for FMCSA rules: non-domiciled CDL cuts, SMS overhaul, 9 new rulemakings.
  • Monitor cross-border: Mexico freight up 7.1%; tariff shifts boost NA volumes.
  • Fortify fraud checks: cargo theft at $18M/day; use SAFER, enter Fraud Fighters by May 15.
  • Track tonnage: ATA index at 128.6 (-3% MoM)—brace for Q2 GDP softness.
  • Build tariff buffers: imports down 2.5% H1 2026; reroute via Mexico/Canada.
  • Push spot-to-contract: premiums at $0.37/mi flatbed—capture before capacity snapback.

title: Weekly Freight Report - April 17, 2026
excerpt: ```html Market Pulse Truckload, LTL, and parcel rates have reached their highest levels since early 2024, driven by diesel holding at $5.61 per gallon and persistent capacity constraints.[6] Spot market rates show mixed signals: dry van and refrigera...
content:
Market Pulse

Truckload, LTL, and parcel rates have reached their highest levels since early 2024, driven by diesel holding at $5.61 per gallon and persistent capacity constraints.[6] Spot market rates show mixed signals: dry van and refrigerated equipment declined week-over-week during the week ended April 10, marking the first retreat since fuel prices surged due to the Iran conflict, while flatbed spot rates rose for a 15th straight week to their highest level since July 2022.[2] Truckload markets are tightening faster than expected, with 2026 costs now projected up 16–17% year-over-year.[4] The freight market is hitting extremes not seen since COVID, creating significant uncertainty for carriers and brokers.[5]

Regulation & Enforcement

The FMCSA introduced new requirements for the DataQs system on April 14, 2026, including firm deadlines and independent review steps to improve fairness and speed of reviews, addressing long-standing complaints about inconsistent rulings and slow response times.[1] No additional rulemakings, ELD enforcement actions, or state-level trucking legislation changes were reported during this reporting period.

Broker Edge

Ocean freight conditions remain balanced but underlying disruptions are reducing network flexibility.[4] Spot rates have risen significantly, driven by emergency fuel surcharges and reduced space availability, with carriers shifting rate announcements to weekly amid increased volatility.[3] Capacity management remains aggressive, particularly across North China and inland origin points, with congestion persisting at major ports including Shanghai, Singapore, and Rotterdam.[3] MSC implemented changes across three Asia to U.S. West Coast services beginning in April to improve network efficiency and reduce congestion, including shortening the Orient service rotation and adding Qingdao as the first port of call.[3]

Air freight markets remain constrained, with elevated rates and limited capacity as airlines prioritize higher-yielding shipments.[3] A fresh wave of disruptions is hitting Asian air freight networks, with 58 flights canceled and at least 361 delayed across carriers including China Eastern, Batik Air, Korean Air, and Uzbekistan Airways.[1] Beijing sits at the center of the turbulence, with its dense mix of domestic and international routes leaving little recovery capacity when irregular operations hit.[1] Shippers relying on air freight through these hubs should expect delays and plan accordingly.

Cross-Border Watchlist

Cross-border markets are tightening as strong Mexico trade meets rising carrier costs and regulatory pressure.[4] Fuel, labor, insurance, and compliance changes are raising pricing risk and increasing execution complexity across key North American corridors.[4] Supply chain leaders with North American exposure need contingency plans now, as talks to renew the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement have begun between the U.S. and Mexico, with considerable uncertainty remaining about what happens in the weeks ahead leading up to July 1, 2026.[1] Under Article 34.7 of the USMCA, the three governments must decide by that date whether to extend the agreement for another 16 years.[1]

Fraud & Security

No freight fraud, cargo theft, or double-brokering incidents were reported during the April 10-17 reporting period. However, brokers should remain vigilant as the industry faces ongoing challenges with trade fraud and accounting tricks proliferating amid tariff increases.[1]

Equipment, Fuel & Ops

Diesel prices held steady at $5.61 per gallon during the week of April 13, 2026, down marginally from $5.643 the previous week.[6] Iran's disruption of the Strait of Hormuz has sent diesel prices surging to $5.40 per gallon, up nearly 39% since the conflict began, rewriting freight cost models for shippers on both spot and contract freight.[1] On contract freight, fuel surcharges are the primary impact, with carriers expecting current bids to come back higher across sectors starting in Q2.[1] Spot market carriers are taking the hit in real time.

Strong freight demand dictates the need for new trailers, particularly refrigerated equipment as produce harvest seasons begin along U.S. coasts and southern states, driving reefer trailer demand as dry van drivers pivot to refrigerated loads.[1] Frost laws remain active in northern U.S. regions into April 2026, restricting over-dimensional and heavy haul shipments to protect thawing roads, causing delays, rerouting needs, and potential fines for non-compliance.[1]

Action Checklist for Brokers

  • Lock in contract rates now: Carriers are expecting bids to come back higher across sectors starting in Q2 due to fuel surcharges. Secure Q2 and Q3 capacity before April 30.
  • Build USMCA contingency plans: With July 1, 2026 as the renewal deadline, develop alternative routing and sourcing strategies for Mexico and Canada trade lanes.
  • Adjust ocean freight strategies: De minimis exemptions have been stripped from many low-value imports and Southeast Asian transshipment rerouting enforcement has tightened. Shippers built around flexible routing assumptions need to start over.
  • Plan for air freight delays: With 58 flights canceled and 361 delayed across Asian hubs, add buffer time to air freight commitments and communicate delays to shippers proactively.
  • Monitor tariff impacts: Section 232 tariffs now apply to the full customs value of products, not just metal inputs, with a 50% rate on articles almost entirely composed of steel, aluminum, or copper. Review shipper contracts for tariff pass-through language.
  • Prioritize reefer capacity: Produce season is driving reefer demand higher. Secure refrigerated trailers for Q2 shipments before capacity tightens further.
  • Account for frost law restrictions: Northern regions still have active frost laws in April. Plan alternative routes or timing for heavy haul and over-dimensional loads.
  • Track DataQs updates: FMCSA's new DataQs system requirements took effect April 14. Ensure your compliance documentation meets new deadlines and independent review standards.

title: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup - April 17, 2026
excerpt: Fleet & Market Trends FMCSA Non-Domiciled CDL Rule Removes 194,000 Drivers Full enforcement of the FMCSA Final Rule on non-domiciled CDLs in 2026 will remove 194,000 drivers from the market, the largest supply-side change since 1980 deregulation, per...
content:
Fleet & Market Trends

FMCSA Non-Domiciled CDL Rule Removes 194,000 Drivers

Full enforcement of the FMCSA Final Rule on non-domiciled CDLs in 2026 will remove 194,000 drivers from the market, the largest supply-side change since 1980 deregulation, per RXO analysis. This accelerates carrier exits, tightening truckload capacity by H1 2026, especially temp-control and flatbed segments. Brokers should prioritize vetted carriers in cross-border corridors like Laredo to secure capacity amid uneven tightening.

Carrier Exits Reshape Capacity Entering 2026

Prolonged low demand and rising costs drive ongoing carrier attrition, with smaller operators exiting faster than during the 2017 ELD mandate, according to Ryder and ProTrans. FMCSA enforcement outpaces historical impacts, normalizing truckload by February-June. Carriers focused on asset management over expansion signal brokers to lock in reliable partners now for H2 rate leverage.

LTL Consolidation Targets Regional Operators

LTL anticipates modest rebound but tight margins from insurance and equipment costs, spurring M&A in regional operators and pharmaceutical carriers, per Trucking Dive. Economic uncertainty accelerates opportunistic deals shaping 2026 networks. Brokers can capitalize by aligning with consolidating players for stable regional coverage.

April Produce Harvest Tightens Reefer Capacity

Produce harvests drive reefer demand surges in warmer regions, with dry van drivers swapping trailers, per ATS Inc. Northern markets ease as trucks disperse south, lowering spot rates there while southern rates rise. Shippers need 24+ hour lead times around Easter (April 5) to avoid capacity crunches.

Fuel & Cost Pressures

Hormuz Closure Spikes Diesel to $5.37/Gallon

U.S.-Iran war closed the Strait of Hormuz since February 28, driving national diesel averages from $3.47 to $5.37/gallon by early April, adding $0.36/mile to costs where fuel is 21% of OpEx, per Brown University. Owner-operators park trucks and cut speeds to 65 mph, dropping DAT posts to 10-year lows. Brokers face spot rate climbs (dry van $2.01/mile) and should renegotiate surcharges lagging EIA baselines.

Diesel Relief as Hormuz Reopens

President Trump and Iran announced full Strait of Hormuz reopening April 17, with crude falling 10%, per Transport Topics. National diesel hit $5.64/gallon April 6 but could stabilize lower, though experts warn elevated costs as new normal per AFS Logistics. Carriers vulnerable to 30-day payments should hedge via contract adjustments for cash flow.

Insurance and Equipment Squeeze LTL Margins

Rising insurance and equipment costs pressure LTL rebound margins amid modest freight uptick, per industry analysts. Combined with diesel volatility, this favors scale via consolidation. Brokers monitor for rate pass-throughs in regional lanes over next 6 months.

Fraud & Security Watch

SAFER Transport Act Targets MC Number Loopholes

The SAFER Transport Act phases out outdated MC numbers for USDOT numbers, bolstering fraud detection amid 1,500% cargo theft surge since 2021 costing $18 million daily, per ATA. It closes foreign dispatch gaps exploited by thieves. Brokers verify carriers via updated SAFER System to mitigate risks in H1 enforcement.

FMCSA Cracks Down on Chameleon Carriers

FMCSA investigations block 280 fraudulent ELDs since September 2025 and shut chameleon carriers like Super Ego Holding accused of fraud by 800 drivers, per Overdriveonline and FOX 32. Tactics include fake decals and CDLs from mills under audit. Carriers contact OOIDA compliance for load checks to avoid double-brokering traps.

Double-Brokering Hits $140K Frozen Steaks Load

A $140K steaks fraud used hacked emails, fake identities, and five MC numbers, highlighting workflow gaps with annual losses at $750 million-$1 billion, per FreightWaves. FMCSA prioritizes complaints via National Database. Brokers match BOL names exactly and report overseas identity hijacks like Tanager Logistics case.

Technology & Policy

Autonomous Trucking Pilots Eye Middle-Mile Efficiency

Autonomous trials target highways and fixed routes to cut driver shortages, projecting $9 billion annual savings by 2035 via labor optimization, per FTR studies. Regulatory clarity lags but builds momentum for late-2020s adoption reversing capacity constraints. Brokers prepare for supplemented long-haul networks boosting manufacturing competitiveness.

EPA 2027 Mandate Delays ZEV Fleet Buys

EPA tailpipe standards and California rules push low/zero-emission shifts, but high costs and infrastructure gaps limit to urban pilots, per industry outlook. Federal grants aid drayage transitions over next 12 months. Carriers pursue incentives while TMS optimizes legacy assets amid turnover.

TMS Adoption Counters Turnover and Costs

Carriers ramp TMS, telematics, and route optimization for efficiency amid high turnover and cautious renewal, per 2026 outlook. M&A favors tech platforms for network scale. Brokers leverage digital matching for tighter capacity plays.

Bottom Line

Driver purges and carrier exits tighten capacity H1 2026, amplified by Hormuz diesel spikes now easing, pressuring small fleets most. Fraud crackdowns via SAFER Act and FMCSA actions demand rigorous verification workflows. Tech like autonomy and TMS offers brokers leverage for rate gains and efficiency in consolidating LTL/truckload markets over next 3-12 months.

title: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup - April 10, 2026
excerpt: Domestic trucking in early April 2026 is less about a sudden demand spike and more about a fragile supply base: a slow rate recovery, continuing carrier attrition, and structural workforce constraints that will matter as soon as volumes firm up.
content:
Fleet & Market Trends

Capacity Shakeout Continues as Smaller Fleets Struggle to Survive a “Marginless Recovery”

Industry economists continue to frame 2026 as a slow recovery where rates may not rise fast enough to offset cost inflation, keeping pressure on smaller fleets and accelerating carrier exits. For brokers, that means today’s loose market can tighten quickly once demand improves, because the surviving capacity base is more concentrated and more disciplined on price. Key data point: FTR’s forecast discussed by Commercial Carrier Journal suggested contract rate growth staying below ~2% through 2026—effectively flat after inflation—creating conditions for more fleet failures. (per Commercial Carrier Journal)

Bankruptcy Headlines Reinforce Ongoing Carrier Attrition Risk

Early-2026 bankruptcy filings across small and mid-size fleets underscore that liquidity—not load count alone—remains a key failure driver as debt service, insurance and maintenance costs stay elevated. The operational takeaway for shippers and brokers is to monitor carrier financial health more aggressively, especially on longer-haul lanes with thinner margins. Key data point: Standard Freight Logistics reported assets and liabilities in the $100,000–$1 million range in a February 2026 Subchapter V filing. (as reported by TheStreet)

Driver Workforce: Demographics Keep Tightening the Long-Term Labor Pipeline

Even with cyclical softness in some freight segments, the structural workforce challenge remains: trucking’s labor pool is aging, and participation from underrepresented groups is still low. Over the next 3–12 months, fleets that win will be those that can reduce churn (predictable home time, detention mitigation, better onboarding) rather than simply raising sign-on bonuses. Key data point: ATRI cited an average driver age around 47 and women comprising about 4.1% of truck drivers in its 2025 demographics research. (per American Transportation Research Institute)

LTL Pricing Power and Network Density Keep Steering the Market Toward Consolidation Strategies

Shippers are increasingly rethinking how they buy LTL capacity as carriers prioritize network density and yield management, a dynamic that tends to favor larger, well-capitalized providers and national networks. For brokerages, this supports more “managed LTL” playbooks: mode shift to zone-skips, consolidation, and dynamic tendering to reduce exposure to carrier accessorials and volatile surcharge tables. Key data point: 2026 planning cycles increasingly revolve around network density and pricing discipline rather than pure volume growth. (industry view highlighted in GoTrucking.news on LinkedIn)

Fuel & Cost Pressures

Diesel Prices Remain a Macro Wildcard, Keeping Procurement Teams Focused on Volatility Clauses

Government tracking showed diesel prices entering 2026 lower than late-2025, but carriers continue to push for fuel-risk protection as volatility can flip lane economics quickly. Over the next 3–12 months, expect more shipper scrutiny of baseline assumptions in fuel programs (MPG, baseline fuel price, and timing lag) and more negotiations over how quickly surcharges should adjust. Key data point: USDOT’s BTS reported the average diesel No. 2 price at $3.52 in January 2026 (down 2.5% from December 2025). (per Bureau of Transportation Statistics)

Energy Outlooks Point to Higher 2026 Diesel Averages, Raising the Stakes on Surcharge Design

Energy forecasts suggest diesel could average higher in 2026 than many shippers budgeted, which increases the importance of transparent, auditable surcharge tables and avoiding “double counting” where base rates already embed a fuel premium. Brokers should be ready to show customers the math on DOE-index-linked schedules and help normalize baselines across carrier bids. Key data point: EIA’s March Short-Term Energy Outlook cited in industry reporting projected U.S. on-highway diesel averaging about $4.12/gallon in 2026. (per Rigzone)

Insurance Inflation and “Nuclear Verdict” Exposure Continue to Reshape Carrier Cost Structures

Insurance remains one of the hardest-to-manage line items for small carriers, and litigation risk continues to spill into underwriting standards (driver screening, camera adoption, safety scoring). For the next few quarters, this cost pressure can accelerate carrier attrition and raise the true “floor” price required for sustainable service. Key data point: ATRI’s operational cost work is cited as putting insurance premiums at about $0.102 per mile in 2024—near 10% of total operating costs. (per AtoB)

Alternative Diesel Supply Is Growing—but Economics and Policy Still Drive Uncertainty

Renewable diesel capacity growth has been rapid, yet updated projections suggest capacity may plateau into 2026, keeping pricing and availability uneven by region. For fleets, that means near-term opportunities are more likely in dedicated geographies (West Coast, Gulf Coast) and specific customer programs, not broad long-haul conversion. Key data point: Updated estimates project 22 renewable diesel plants operating by the end of 2026 and total capacity remaining roughly flat in 2026 after reaching ~5.2 billion gallons in 2025. (per Farmdoc Daily (University of Illinois))

Fraud & Security Watch

SAFER Transport Act Puts Federal Attention on Freight Fraud, Registration Integrity, and Cargo Theft

New Senate legislation introduced in late February aims to harden FMCSA registration processes, improve interagency coordination, and expand mechanisms to detect and punish freight fraud and cargo theft. For the next 3–12 months, brokerages should expect customers to ask more pointed questions about carrier onboarding controls, identity verification, and how fraud signals are handled operationally. Key data point: ATRI calculated cargo theft costs the trucking industry more than $18 million per day, and CargoNet cited strategic theft surging 1,500% since 2021. (per American Trucking Associations)

SAFER Act Would Push Automated Suspicious-Activity Flagging and Registration Reforms

Beyond penalties, the bill’s direction toward automated systems to flag suspicious registration behavior is a signal that “trust but verify” will become embedded in federal processes, not only private platforms. If enacted or partially folded into other legislation, it could change how quickly bad actors can recycle identities and re-enter the market. Key data point: The SAFER Transport Act proposal includes requirements for FMCSA to develop automated systems to flag suspicious activity and phases out MC numbers within five years in favor of USDOT numbers. (per Overdrive)

Carrier Verification and AI-Led Fraud Tools Move from “Nice to Have” to Core Operating Control

As fraud tactics shift toward identity compromise and fictitious pickups, broker workflows are increasingly adopting layered verification (document checks, device intelligence, behavioral flags, and pickup validation). Over the next year, expect tighter shipper requirements for documented controls and wider use of dedicated fraud-monitoring products alongside traditional carrier packets. Key data point: Industry tools are explicitly marketing double-brokering detection and pickup identity verification as primary use cases. (per Overhaul FraudWatch)

Technology & Policy

FMCSA’s TechCelerate Now Pushes Faster Adoption of ADAS and Camera Systems

Fleet safety tech adoption continues to expand from core collision-mitigation to broader camera and vision systems, with more formal guidance emerging on calibration, cybersecurity, and driver training. For the next 3–12 months, brokers can expect more carrier differentiation based on technology posture—and potentially better insurability and service reliability from fleets that can prove safety ROI. Key data point: Transport Topics reported FMCSA launched TechCelerate Now in 2020 and renewed it in 2024 for a four-year second phase, with an updated ROI calculator for more system types. (per Transport Topics)

Autonomous Trucking Policy: “SELF DRIVE Act of 2026” Discussion Draft Signals a Federal Framework Push

A new discussion draft seeks to reduce regulatory friction by enabling limited commercial autonomous freight pilots while preempting conflicting state restrictions, a key step toward scaling beyond isolated tests. While widespread adoption is not imminent, the next year is likely to see more structured pilots on select corridors—particularly in the Sun Belt—plus more shipper conversations about lane eligibility and risk allocation. Key data point: The draft would require reporting of covered crashes and quarterly reporting of revenue-service miles traveled to build an autonomous safety record. (per FreightWaves)

Truck Parking Funding Becomes More Direct, with Federal Dollars Earmarked for Expansion

Truck parking constraints remain a daily operational bottleneck that affects HOS compliance, appointment reliability, and accident risk—making it a real capacity limiter when freight tightens. New federal funding signals that parking is increasingly being treated as a national freight-infrastructure priority, but buildout will take time, keeping near-term demand high for private capacity and reservation technology. Key data point: A 2026 federal spending bill included $200 million to expand public truck parking, and ATRI has estimated drivers spend about 56 minutes per day searching for parking. (per Trucking Dive)

Regulatory Whiplash Risk: Emissions and Enforcement Signals Keep Fleet-Planning Uncertain

Emissions policy remains a moving target, and fleets are watching closely because engine mandates influence equipment costs, residual values, and trade cycles. Uncertainty tends to delay new-truck purchases and can keep older equipment in service longer—raising maintenance risk and potentially tightening effective capacity when reliability issues spike. Key data point: Land Line reported EPA activity in early 2026 targeting truck emissions rule enforcement topics (including DEF-related issues and California programs), while the 2027 NOx standards remain a key milestone. (per Land Line Media)

Bottom Line

The domestic trucking outlook around April 10, 2026 is defined less by a sudden demand surge and more by a fragile supply base: a slow rate recovery, continuing carrier attrition, and structural workforce constraints that will matter as soon as volumes firm up. Cost inflation is shifting from “fuel-only” to a broader stack—insurance, litigation exposure, and compliance tech—making sustainable capacity more expensive than spot markets may imply. Meanwhile, freight fraud has moved into the policy spotlight, with the SAFER Transport Act and FMCSA modernization initiatives pushing more automated detection and tighter registration integrity. For the next 3–12 months, brokerages that win will be those that pair disciplined carrier sourcing with documented fraud controls and proactive cost transparency on fuel, safety, and service reliability.

title: Weekly Freight Report - April 10, 2026
excerpt: Market Pulse — spot/contract rates, load-to-truck ratios, capacity Spot rates moved higher into early April as fuel costs and tightening capacity pushed carriers to reprice. Spot rates for the week of March 29–April 4 rose across van, reefer, and flatbed.
content:
Market Pulse — spot/contract rates, load-to-truck ratios, capacity

Spot rates moved higher into early April as fuel costs and tightening capacity pushed carriers to reprice. For the week of March 29–April 4 (DAT Week 14), DAT reported national average broker-to-carrier spot rates of $2.40/mile dry van (up 7¢ week over week), $2.79/mile reefer (up 5¢), and $2.55/mile flatbed linehaul (up 11¢, the largest weekly increase in more than a decade). (The Trucker)

DAT’s load board activity for that same week showed a typical post-quarter reset in volume: total load posts fell to 3.58 million (down 12% week over week). (The Trucker)

Load-to-truck ratios (a proxy for spot-market tightness) eased slightly but remained elevated versus 2025 baselines: dry van 9.0 (down from 10.1), reefer 16.9 (down from 19.0), and flatbed 74.3 (down from 82.0). (The Trucker)

On the contract side, the key story for brokers is margin compression as the market moves toward parity: FreightWaves’ analysis of U.S. Bank Freight Payment Index data showed spot linehaul rising from $1.65/mile (Nov 2025) to $2.01/mile (Feb 2026), while contract linehaul rose from $1.99 to $2.12 in the same period. (FreightWaves)

That repricing has rapidly narrowed the contract premium: FreightWaves reported the contract-spot gap compressing from about 39¢/mile a year earlier to roughly 11¢/mile by March 2026, reducing the “buy-side cushion” brokers relied on during the downcycle. (FreightWaves)

Regulation & Enforcement — FMCSA/DOT rules, ELD, CDL, state regs

April’s compliance theme is identity, eligibility, and device integrity. FMCSA’s updated non-domiciled CDL final rule took effect March 16, 2026, with guidance instructing states unable to comply to pause issuance of non-domiciled CLPs/CDLs until they can meet the revised standards. (FMCSA)

For operational planning, the key risk is disruption in driver supply for carriers leaning on non-domiciled credentials, plus paperwork delays as states tighten verification and corrective actions. FMCSA also noted that credentials issued pre-effective date could be subject to revocation if found noncompliant during state program reviews. (FMCSA)

ELD enforcement also tightened: FMCSA removed the HERO ELD from the registered list on April 2, 2026 and provided a 60-day window to replace it (with enforcement consequences starting June 2, 2026 for continued use). (CDLLife)

In addition, the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance’s 2026 North American Standard Out-of-Service Criteria went into effect April 1, which matters for brokers because carriers operating with out-of-service defects will be more likely to miss pickups, require recovery capacity, or trigger claims exposure. (UCR Plan)

Broker Edge — what brokers need to know, competitive positioning

1) Reprice faster, quote tighter. With the contract premium compressing to about 11¢/mile by March, bid/award pricing based on “cheap spot” assumptions is increasingly risky. (FreightWaves)

2) Separate fuel-driven volatility from true demand. The week’s upward spot move coincided with sharply higher diesel (see ops section), meaning carriers will push for higher all-in even where demand is steady.

3) Treat flatbed as the early-warning market. DAT noted flatbed’s 11¢ weekly linehaul jump as an outsized move, and flatbed’s 74.3 load-to-truck ratio remains extremely high versus van/reefer—use it as a signal for broader capacity tightening. (The Trucker)

4) Update carrier qualification workflows. Between tighter non-domiciled CDL rules and continuing ELD removals, expect more “administrative capacity” loss: otherwise good carriers can become temporarily unusable because of documentation gaps, credential flags, or device compliance issues. (FMCSA) (CDLLife)

Cross-Border Watchlist — US-Mexico, US-Canada, USMCA, tariffs

Mexico remains the growth engine; Canada is softer. Using Bureau of Transportation Statistics data, Inside Logistics reported Canada–U.S. transborder freight down 18.4% year over year to $52.8 billion, while U.S.–Mexico freight totaled $74.1 billion (up 6.5%). (Inside Logistics)

For brokers, this mix matters because northbound Mexico capacity and customs compliance are becoming more valuable, while some Canada lanes may see more competitive pricing and looser capacity—depending on commodity and border crossing.

Watch the 2026 USMCA review runway. Cross-border stakeholders are positioning for the first formal USMCA joint review in July 2026, and several market updates frame it as a potential inflection point for documentation, inspections, and rules-of-origin scrutiny. (Yahoo Finance)

Separately, shippers should track tariff uncertainty and how it could affect industrial freight and equipment supply chains; Heavy Duty Trucking highlighted that USMCA-compliant goods remain at 0% tariff while non-USMCA compliant goods from Canada/Mexico face 25% tariffs under the White House framework described by ATA. (Heavy Duty Trucking)

Fraud & Security — cargo theft, double-brokering, CDL fraud

Fraud is increasingly operational, not just financial. FreightWaves warned that cargo theft can start with a carrier that appears legitimate and clears standard checks, underscoring the need for layered verification beyond “looks good on paper.” (FreightWaves)

Transport Topics reported on an alleged theft involving a $240,000 copper load that was rerouted to California instead of its intended destination, with the load ultimately recovered and a suspect charged with first-degree felony cargo theft in Texas. (Transport Topics)

Overdrive also reported an April 9 case involving an accused double-brokering cargo thief charged in court, with federal charges that can carry up to 10 years in prison for interstate transportation of stolen goods. (Overdrive)

Equipment, Fuel & Ops — diesel prices, truck orders, driver pay

Fuel is the week’s biggest cost shock. The EIA’s weekly on-highway diesel benchmark rose to $5.643/gal for the week of April 6, 2026, up from $5.401/gal the prior week. (YCharts)

Transport Topics’ DOE/EIA table likewise showed the U.S. average at $5.643 on 4/6 versus $5.401 on 3/30, with the West Coast (and especially California) running materially higher. (Transport Topics)

On equipment demand, Transport Topics reported preliminary North American Class 8 net orders of 37,200 units in March (up 126% year over year), with ACT noting orders were down sequentially from February’s 46,200 but still exceptionally strong for late “order season.” (Transport Topics)

Operationally, higher diesel plus tighter compliance enforcement (ELD removals and CDL rule changes) can produce “invisible capacity loss”: more carriers decline marginal loads, and more trucks lose utilization hours due to inspections, device swaps, or documentation fixes. (CDLLife) (FMCSA)

Action Checklist for Brokers

  • Refresh buy-rate assumptions weekly on core lanes; don’t rely on the historic contract premium now that the gap is ~11¢/mile. (FreightWaves)
  • Build fuel volatility into quotes (especially longer-haul) using the latest EIA diesel benchmark ($5.643/gal week of Apr 6). (YCharts)
  • Re-check ELD compliance in carrier onboarding/dispatch (e.g., HERO ELD revoked April 2; replacement deadline June 2). (CDLLife)
  • Increase identity verification steps for new carriers and “new email / new factoring / new phone” changes, given theft cases involving seemingly legitimate parties. (FreightWaves)
  • Prioritize flatbed capacity planning as an early indicator; Week 14 flatbed linehaul jumped 11¢ and LTR remained very high at 74.3. (The Trucker)
  • Cross-border: segment Canada vs Mexico playbooks (Canada-U.S. freight reported down 18.4% while U.S.-Mexico up 6.5%) and align pricing/coverage accordingly. (Inside Logistics)
  • Track Class 8 order momentum as a leading indicator for fleet expansion and future capacity; March orders were 37,200 units (+126% YoY). (Transport Topics)

title: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup - April 3, 2026
excerpt: The trucking market entering Q2 2026 faces simultaneous supply-side and cost shocks: diesel at $5.37/gallon from the Hormuz closure, spot rates up 18.7% year-over-year, and a carrier base contracted 11.4% since 2022. Texas-based freight brokers face an urgent window to...
content:
Fleet & Market Trends

Carrier Attrition Slows, But Mid-Sized Fleet Failures Are Climbing

After a historic purge that saw over 88,000 trucking authorities revoked in 2023 alone, the rate of carrier exits has finally begun to decelerate — but the nature of failures is shifting in ways that matter more to the market than raw counts. Per analysis published by IFA Commercial Factor, over 7,000 trucking businesses exited in a single spring month of 2025, and carriers older than three years now account for half of all exits, up from 37% in 2023 — a sign that the downturn is catching more established operators rather than just pandemic-era entrants. According to Trucking Dive's analysis of FMCSA revocations data, the for-hire carrier population ended 2025 essentially flat year-over-year — but with mid-sized fleets increasingly filing Chapter 11 rather than simply surrendering authority, the structural stress is becoming more visible in bankruptcy courts.

Key data point: From December 2022 through December 2025, FMCSA recorded an 11.4% decline in property carriers with active operating authority, per FTR Transportation Intelligence.

Driver Shortage Deepens — BLS Revision Exposes a Larger Hole

The American Trucking Associations puts the current driver shortage at roughly 60,000 positions, with projections reaching 160,000 by 2028 — but those figures were built on employment data that the Bureau of Labor Statistics quietly revised in February 2026, revealing that 122,000 trucking positions had effectively vanished from payrolls since October 2022, according to O Trucking. That revision means the real deficit may be significantly deeper than headline ATA estimates suggest. In Texas specifically, the combination of a booming freight corridor network, high border-crossing volume, and a March 2026 immigration-driven CDL restriction is creating acute near-term capacity stress for freight brokers and carriers operating in the Gulf Coast corridor.

Key data point: The industry must recruit 1.2 million new drivers over the next decade — roughly 120,000 per year — a pace it has never come close to achieving, per ATA data cited by O Trucking.

LTL Consolidation Reshapes the Carrier Map

Two and a half years after Yellow Corp.'s August 2023 bankruptcy, the redistribution of its 169-terminal network is substantially complete — and the LTL landscape has been fundamentally redrawn. By mid-2025, more than 210 former Yellow terminals had been sold for nearly $2.4 billion, according to Tank Transport Trader, with Saia (31 terminals), XPO ($870M for 28 centers), Estes, R+L Carriers, and others absorbing the capacity. The consolidation has reduced the number of true national LTL players while increasing network density for survivors — a dynamic that has supported firmer LTL pricing and is compressing shipper options for multi-region coverage over the next 12 months.

Key data point: XPO paid $870 million for 28 former Yellow service centers — the single largest terminal acquisition in the bankruptcy proceeding — per Tank Transport Trader.

Nuclear Verdicts and Insurance Inflation Are Permanently Repricing Freight

Trucking insurance premiums rose 10%–30% across the U.S. in 2025 depending on carrier profile, and 2026 renewals are tracking another 8%–15% upward for marginal operators, per Truckers National and Narvaez Insurance Services. The structural driver is social inflation: since 2012, jury verdicts exceeding $1 million in trucking-related cases have increased by more than 235%, according to Reliance Partners and FreightWaves data. At the ATA's Management Conference in October 2025, panelists reported per Transport Topics that claims are remaining open longer, plaintiff attorneys are bypassing pre-suit settlement talks, and ATRI now benchmarks insurance at $0.099 per mile — a cost level that is forcing smaller carriers out of the market and prompting larger fleets to treat legal defensibility as a procurement criterion rather than an afterthought.

Key data point: Nuclear verdicts exceeding $1 million have increased more than 235% since 2012, per Reliance Partners — restructuring how insurers evaluate commercial auto risk industry-wide.

Fuel & Cost Pressures

Hormuz Closure Blows Up Every 2026 Diesel Forecast

Every major forecaster entered 2026 expecting diesel to average $3.47–$3.50 per gallon, supported by U.S. crude production at record levels of 13.5 million barrels per day and global oversupply. That math collapsed when U.S.-Israeli military operations against Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping on February 28, 2026 — dropping vessel traffic from roughly 138 per day to just 20, per IRU ship-tracking data. As of late March, the national on-highway diesel average reached $5.37 per gallon per Tradlinx, representing the largest single-week diesel price increase ever recorded since EIA tracking began in 1994, per FTR analyst Avery Vise via Talking Logistics. For a typical long-haul trucking operation, the shock translates to approximately $0.36 per mile in additional operating cost.

Key data point: Diesel hit $5.37/gallon by late March 2026 — roughly $1.90/gallon above EIA's pre-war forecast — with the IEA warning that "April will be much worse than March" for global oil supply, per IRU.

Refinery Capacity Shortfall Compounds the Price Shock

Before the Hormuz disruption, the EIA had already flagged a structural inventory problem: two pending U.S. refinery closures, combined with rising consumption, were expected to push domestic inventories of motor gasoline, distillate, and jet fuel to their lowest levels since 2000 by end of 2026, per the EIA's February 2026 Short-Term Energy Outlook. That underlying tightness reduces the domestic buffer available to absorb a supply shock of this magnitude. Biodiesel and renewable diesel are forecast to comprise approximately 9% of U.S. distillate consumption in 2026, up from 5% in 2021, providing partial offset — but not at a volume sufficient to compensate for Hormuz-driven crude disruptions across a sustained conflict scenario.

Key data point: EIA projected U.S. petroleum product inventories would end 2026 at 375 million barrels — the lowest since 2000 — even before the Hormuz crisis removed additional global crude supply from the market.

Fuel Surcharge Mechanisms Lag the Spike — Contract Tension Is Building

Most carrier-shipper contracts include fuel surcharge tables indexed to the EIA's weekly on-highway diesel average, a mechanism designed for gradual price movement. The current environment — diesel up more than $1 per gallon within a single month — is exposing a structural lag that carriers absorb in the short term and recover through rate renegotiation or load selectivity, according to FreightWise. Talking Logistics reported that 45% of surveyed supply chain executives had no plans to modify their fuel surcharge programs despite the spike. DAT Freight & Analytics warned as of April 3 that "for shippers still operating on last year's pricing, the window to lock in favorable terms is probably closed, and that's before the fuel cost surge works its way into the numbers." Spot linehaul pricing increased over 23% from March 2025 through February 2026, while contract rates rose only 5%, per a U.S. Bank report cited by Trucking Dive.
