Key data point: The spot-to-contract rate gap compressed from $0.39/mile a year ago to just $0.11/mile by March 2026, per C.H. Robinson and DAT — signaling a market structure that increasingly favors carriers over shippers.

Fraud & Security Watch

SAFER Transport Act Targets the Registration Loopholes Behind Cargo Theft

U.S. Senator Todd Young (R-IN) introduced the Securing American Freight, Enforcement, and Reliability in Transport (SAFER) Act in late February 2026, backed by the ATA, OOIDA, and the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance, per Land Line Media. The bill targets specific FMCSA registration system weaknesses that sophisticated freight criminals have exploited to build "chameleon carrier" identities — including phasing out MC numbers in favor of USDOT numbers, requiring facial-selfie and government-ID verification for new registrants, and creating a Freight Fraud and Theft Advisory Committee within 60 days of passage. The ATA testified that ATRI calculated cargo theft costs the trucking industry over $18 million per day, and that strategic theft — using cyber fraud and identity manipulation to divert freight — has surged 1,500% since 2021 per CargoNet.

Key data point: Strategic cargo theft is up 1,500% since 2021 per CargoNet, cited in ATA Senate testimony — a threat that the SAFER Transport Act's registration reforms are designed to address at the FMCSA system level.

AI-Powered Fraud Is Outpacing Industry Defenses

Cargo theft losses reached $6.6 billion in 2025, with confirmed incidents rising 18% year-over-year and the average theft value per incident climbing 36% to nearly $274,000, according to a Geotab report released March 26, 2026 via Carrier Management. Criminals are now accessing fleet-tracking portals with stolen credentials, spoofing GPS signals to mask route diversions in real time, and using AI to automate phishing and voice cloning at scale — spinning up convincing fake broker identities with cloned websites, forged documents, and AI voices that can pass verbal verification calls, per FreightWaves analysis. The platform Highway reported blocking over 914,000 fraud attempts in a recent period; carrier vetting service Motive declined over $1.1 million in suspicious transactions. Freight Caviar polling shows double brokering is now brokers' top fraud concern heading into Q2.

Key data point: Cargo theft losses hit $6.6B in 2025 — with average theft value per incident up 36% to $274,000 — as criminals shift from physical theft to cyber-enabled identity fraud, per Geotab's 2026 supply chain security report via Carrier Management.

FMCSA's Double-Brokering Crackdown Takes Shape — and Teeth

The FMCSA received over 8,000 double-brokering complaints in 2025 — a fourfold increase since 2021 — and the Transportation Intermediaries Association estimates the scheme costs carriers $700 million to $1 billion annually, per Truck Dispatch Experts. The agency finalized three major rules in 2026: doubling the minimum broker surety bond from $75,000 to $150,000 (effective July 2026), requiring brokers to deploy load-tracking technology that verifies the actual executing carrier matches the contracted carrier (effective January 2027), and increasing civil penalties for double brokering from $16,000 to $50,000 per violation with mandatory authority revocation for repeat offenders. FMCSA is also eliminating MC numbers in favor of a single USDOT identifier, closing the loophole that allowed bad actors to reopen under a new MC number after shutdown, per Fast Forward TMS.

Key data point: FMCSA is hiring 150 additional investigators specifically for broker fraud — more than tripling the current enforcement team — with double-brokering penalties now reaching $50,000 per violation, per Truck Dispatch Experts.

CDL Mill Crackdown: 7,000 Training Providers Purged From Federal Registry

In the largest enforcement action against commercial driver training in FMCSA history, federal investigators have removed or flagged more than 7,000 CDL training providers from the Training Provider Registry since late 2025 — roughly one in five of all listed schools — per reporting from Jackim Woods & Co. and OneWayBIT. In February 2026, FMCSA deployed over 300 investigators to all 50 states in a five-day sting, conducting 1,426 on-site inspections and issuing 550 immediate noncompliance notices. Schools were removed for running two-day "express" programs, using unqualified instructors, and falsifying Entry-Level Driver Training records. Carriers that hired drivers trained at now-removed schools face immediate compliance exposure: those training certifications may be invalid, requiring retraining and retesting at the carrier's cost.

Key data point: FMCSA's February 2026 enforcement sting found a 47% out-of-service rate across 8,215 trucks inspected across 26 states — and 500 drivers failing English proficiency tests — illustrating how deeply non-compliance had spread through the active driver pool.

Technology & Policy

Aurora's Driverless Network Is Now a Commercial Reality on Texas Freight Lanes

Aurora Innovation has tripled its commercial driverless freight network to 10 active routes across the Sun Belt as of February 2026, validating a 1,000-mile lane between Fort Worth and Phoenix that exceeds what a single human driver can legally complete under HOS regulations, per Aurora's official press release. With over 250,000 driverless miles and zero Aurora Driver-attributed collisions, the company has its entire commercial truck capacity committed through Q3 2026 and is targeting 200-plus driverless trucks in operation by year-end. For Texas-based freight brokers, the near-term implication is capacity augmentation rather than displacement: Aurora's active routes — Dallas-Houston, Fort Worth-El Paso, Laredo-Dallas — are high-volume corridors where integrated autonomous capacity allows carrier partners like Hirschbach to achieve utilization levels impossible under single-driver HOS constraints.

Key data point: Aurora's Fort Worth-Phoenix autonomous lane cuts transit time nearly in half versus a single human driver under HOS rules — with 200-plus driverless trucks targeted by year-end 2026, per Aurora Innovation.

SELF DRIVE Act of 2026 Would Create the Federal Framework Autonomous Trucking Needs

The bipartisan SELF DRIVE Act of 2026, introduced by Reps. Bob Latta (R-OH) and Debbie Dingell (D-MI) in January, would establish the first federal statute advancing autonomous vehicle regulations for trucking, per FreightWaves. The draft bill preempts state-level restrictions on autonomous vehicles — eliminating the patchwork of state laws that has kept autonomous freight in perpetual testing status — while authorizing limited commercial operations during pilot evaluation. The bill also permits the design of cab-less trucks optimized for aerodynamics rather than human occupancy, and establishes a National Automated Vehicle Safety Data Repository to standardize crash reporting currently governed by NHTSA's Standing General Order. If enacted, the regulatory certainty it provides would compress the commercial scaling timelines of every major AV trucking platform operating today.

Key data point: The SELF DRIVE Act would preempt all state-level autonomous vehicle restrictions — resolving the single largest regulatory barrier to commercial AV trucking deployment at scale, per FreightWaves analysis.

EPA 2027 NOx Standards: The Pre-Buy Clock Is Running Out

Beginning with model year 2027, EPA heavy-duty NOx standards reduce allowable nitrogen oxide emissions by more than 80% compared to current benchmarks, with expanded requirements covering low-load, idle, and cold-start operating conditions, according to Tracey Road Equipment. New engines will require more sophisticated exhaust aftertreatment systems, additional sensors, longer-duration emissions warranties, and heavier-duty components — all expected to increase new truck prices materially above current levels. The window for fleets to spec compliant 2026 model-year equipment before the 2027 rules take effect is narrowing: ACT Research projects "considerable declines in equipment demand in 2026" as cash-strapped fleets extend asset life rather than absorb the price premium, making the current pre-buy cycle the last near-cost window before diesel truck economics are permanently repriced upward.

Key data point: EPA 2027 NOx standards cut allowable emissions by more than 80% versus current rules — with extended aftertreatment warranty and durability requirements that will increase new Class 8 truck prices regardless of fleet size, per Tracey Road Equipment and EPA final rule.

Congress Approves $200M for Truck Parking; One Space for Every 11 Drivers

The fiscal year 2026 federal funding package signed by President Trump on February 3 included $200 million for FHWA truck parking projects along freight and commuter corridors, per Transport Topics — a meaningful appropriation but modest against the documented shortage. The most recent national inventory under Jason's Law found approximately 313,000 truck parking spaces across the U.S., with ATRI and AASHTO calculating just one space for every 11 truck drivers nationally, per Parking & Mobility Magazine. The FHWA has designated the shortage a national safety concern. With freight activity projected to grow 50% by 2050 and autonomous trucking extending legal operating hours per asset, demand for secure staging and parking infrastructure will intensify significantly — a real-world bottleneck that limits efficiency gains from both driver capacity increases and AV deployment.

Key data point: The U.S. has approximately one truck parking space for every 11 truck drivers nationally, per ATRI/AASHTO data — a structural infrastructure gap that $200M in new federal funding addresses only partially, per Transport Topics.

Bottom Line

The trucking market entering Q2 2026 is operating under simultaneous supply-side and cost shocks with no clear near-term resolution: diesel at $5.37 per gallon due to the Hormuz closure, spot rates up 18.7% year-over-year per RXO and DAT, and a carrier base that has contracted 11.4% since 2022 — a combination that tilts pricing power decisively toward carriers who survived the Great Freight Recession. For American Lady Transportation and other Texas-based freight brokers, the strategic priority is locking in committed capacity relationships with vetted, financially stable carriers before the spot-contract rate inversion forces contract renegotiations across the industry. Freight fraud is evolving faster than enforcement can respond — the SAFER Transport Act, FMCSA double-brokering rules, and the CDL mill crackdown are all meaningful steps, but AI-powered identity fraud now requires every load tender to include multi-layer carrier verification as a baseline, not an option. The 3–12 month outlook is one of gradual rate escalation, persistent fuel cost elevation, and tightening capacity — brokers who build durable carrier relationships and invest in fraud-detection protocols today will outperform those chasing spot availability when the market turns fully in carriers' favor.

title: Weekly Freight Report - April 3, 2026
excerpt: The week of March 27–April 3 marked a decisive inflection point for U.S. trucking. Spot rates climbed across all three equipment types as carriers aggressively priced in surging fuel costs and routing guides began to crack...
content:
Market Pulse

The week of March 27–April 3 marked a decisive inflection point for U.S. trucking. Spot rates climbed across all three equipment types as carriers aggressively priced in surging fuel costs and routing guides began to crack under mounting tender rejections. Per DAT Freight & Analytics data for Week 14 (March 29–April 4), the national average broker-to-carrier spot rate for dry van reached $2.40 per mile, up 7 cents week over week, while reefer hit $2.79 per mile (up 5 cents) and flatbed surged to $2.92 per mile (up 11 cents). A separate DAT benchmark for the week of March 31 placed dry van at $2.47/mile, reefer at $2.88/mile, and flatbed at $2.95/mile — reflecting mid-week momentum gains that continued into the close of the reporting period.

Load-to-truck ratios tell the real capacity story. According to DAT data cited by iDispatchHub, the national van load-to-truck ratio for the week of March 31 sat at 7.73, reefer at 15.55, and flatbed at a commanding 73.75 — its highest reading since April 2025 per FleetOwner. Truck postings for dry van, reefer, and flatbed fell to their lowest Week 13 levels in at least ten years, per FTR Intelligence. Easter pulled total load postings down roughly 12% week over week, but available equipment contracted even faster, meaning net capacity tightened despite the holiday dip.

Tender rejections are now consistently flashing red. According to FreightWaves, rejection rates averaged below 5% for years but spiked into the mid-teens in early 2026. The FreightWaves April 2026 State of the Industry white paper confirmed tender rejections hovering near 14% — levels not seen since the post-COVID unwinding of 2022. The Keynnect Logistics April market update noted rejections approaching 14–15%, reinforcing that routing guides are failing for shippers on key lanes. Contract rates for dry van were quoted at $2.52 per mile per DAT benchmarks, meaning the spot-to-contract gap has now compressed to roughly $0.11 per mile — down from a $0.39 gap just one year ago — making contract freight unattractive for carriers who can easily find spot loads at near-parity. C.H. Robinson raised its full-year 2026 dry van rate forecast from +10% to +16–17% year over year, citing accelerating capacity constraints and carrier cost inflation.

The tractor count contraction continues to squeeze supply. Per Arrive Logistics' March 2026 market update, the total tractor population is down 3% year over year and is forecast to fall an additional 2.8% through year-end 2026. FTR's near-term outlook calls for truck utilization to exceed 97% by Q2 — a threshold historically associated with sustained rate escalation.

Regulation & Enforcement

FMCSA entered April 2026 with one of its most active enforcement calendars in years. Three overlapping rule changes are demanding immediate attention from brokers and carriers alike.

Non-Domiciled CDL Crackdown. Effective March 16, 2026, FMCSA's final rule restricts non-domiciled CDL eligibility to drivers holding H-2A, H-2B, or E-2 visas only — eliminating the prior pathway for Employment Authorization Document holders. The rule affects an estimated 200,000 current non-domiciled CDL holders, according to FMCSA figures cited by InTek Logistics. Several states, including Pennsylvania, have paused non-domiciled CDL issuance entirely while adapting verification systems. Carriers relying on this driver segment should audit qualification files immediately and prepare for potential workforce disruption as licenses reach expiration over the coming months.

ELD Enforcement Tightens. The CVSA released its 2026 North American Standard Out-of-Service Criteria on April 1, 2026, including updated conditions covering false records of duty status and ELD tampering. FMCSA has simultaneously continued removing non-compliant devices from the registered list — dozens were revoked in January and February alone per HOS247 — and is now requiring electronic data transfer at roadside inspections rather than accepting display-only reviews. Carriers using any recently revoked ELD face a 60-day replacement deadline before out-of-service orders begin. The 2026 International Roadcheck (scheduled for May 12–14) will specifically emphasize ELD falsification and cargo securement, per HDT reporting.

Drug & Alcohol Clearinghouse. FMCSA's 2026 Clearinghouse updates impose a 24-hour maximum reporting window for positive drug tests, alcohol violations, refusals, and Return-to-Duty completions. States are now required to automatically downgrade CDLs upon Clearinghouse violations, and state driver licensing agencies have real-time access to Clearinghouse data — impacting CDL renewals immediately. Civil penalties for failure to report a violation now reach up to $6,000 per incident, and hiring a driver with an unresolved violation carries penalties up to $7,500 per occurrence. FMCSA is also rolling out MOTUS, its new digital USDOT registration system, which will require identity verification and business validation checks in a phased deployment already underway.

Broker Edge

This week's market conditions favor brokers who act decisively. With spot rates rising 7–11 cents per mile week over week and tender rejections near 14%, shippers are scrambling for backup capacity — and willing to pay for it. The flatbed segment offers the most immediate opportunity: a load-to-truck ratio of 73.75, driven by strong construction and infrastructure demand heading into spring, puts flatbed carriers firmly in control of rate negotiations.

Reefer deserves particular attention. The convergence of Easter demand and the opening of spring produce season pushed reefer spot rates up more than 18 cents in a single week — the second-largest single-week gain of 2026 per FleetOwner data — and the reefer load-to-truck ratio of 15.55 confirms that specialized capacity is genuinely tight. Temperature-controlled lanes out of the Southeast and California produce corridors are where premium rates are being captured right now.

On the contractual side, brokers negotiating mid-year renewals should use current DAT benchmarks as leverage. The spot-to-contract compression to just $0.11/mile means carriers have little incentive to prioritize contract freight. Shippers who locked in low contract rates in 2024 and 2025 will face significant pushback at renewal — and brokers who can facilitate restructured agreements or spot-plus arrangements will be positioned as indispensable partners rather than commodity middlemen. C.H. Robinson's revised 2026 truckload cost forecast of +16–17% year over year gives brokers an authoritative benchmark when having these conversations.

Cross-Border Watchlist

The US-Mexico freight corridor remains the most dynamic and highest-risk cross-border lane heading into Q2. As of early April 2026, USMCA remains intact, but the mandatory joint review kicks off July 1, 2026, and trade policy uncertainty is already reshaping routing decisions. Per C.H. Robinson's April trade update, talks with Mexico are accelerating faster than with Canada ahead of that review date.

New Section 232 tariffs on metals are the immediate operational concern. Effective April 6, 2026, imports of aluminum, steel, and copper products face a flat 50% duty on their full value (or 25% for derivatives) — directly hitting auto and manufacturing inputs flowing from Mexican maquiladoras. The American Action Forum estimates these tariffs will cost U.S. businesses and consumers $30 billion annually. Meanwhile, the court-struck-down IEEPA reciprocal tariffs have been replaced by 10% Section 122 tariffs on all countries, currently in force through late July 2026. Per the Baker Botts Trump Tariff Tracker (April 1, 2026), medium- and heavy-duty truck imports face a 25% Section 232 duty effective since November 2025 — a factor adding approximately 9% to new Class 8 truck acquisition costs according to iDispatchHub analysts.

Cross-border truck volume data from the Bureau of Transportation Statistics showed Mexican freight up 14% in late 2025 while Canadian freight was down 7%, a divergence driven primarily by surging computer-related machinery imports from Mexico. That pattern faces pressure in 2026 as tariff structures shift incentive calculations for manufacturers. Brokers with active Mexico cross-border business should expect continued volatility in transit times, carrier pricing, and regulatory compliance requirements through at least Q3.

Fraud & Security

Cargo theft and freight fraud are operating at institutional scale in 2026. The American Transportation Research Institute estimates cargo theft now costs the industry approximately $6.6 billion annually — roughly $18 million per day, per a March 30 Fortune report citing ATRI data. Verisk CargoNet data shows an 18% increase in confirmed cargo theft incidents in 2025, with estimated losses surging 60% to nearly $725 million. Overhaul is forecasting an additional 13% increase in theft incidents throughout 2026.

The threat profile has fundamentally changed. Strategic theft — using identity fraud and cyber techniques to divert entire shipments — is up 1,500% since 2021, per ATRI data cited by Amundsen Davis LLC. Criminals are now hacking FMCSA's registration system to redirect carrier identity information, then using deepfakes to impersonate dispatchers over the phone. England Logistics reported that freight identity theft is up 36% year over year, with fraudsters able to execute convincing double-brokering schemes in minutes using AI tools.

On the legislative front, Sen. Todd Young (R-Ind.) introduced the SAFER Transport Act on February 26, 2026. The bill has been referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and carries broad industry support from ATA, OOIDA, TIA, and others. Key provisions include: phasing out MC numbers in favor of USDOT numbers within five years, establishing a Freight Fraud and Theft Advisory Committee, requiring FMCSA to implement automated systems to flag suspicious registration activity, requiring carriers and brokers to report ownership changes within 30 days, and strengthening CDL issuance standards. The bill would also mandate monthly state CDL issuance reports and formalize DOT-to-DOJ referral procedures for freight crimes.

For brokers: verification discipline must go beyond document collection. Confirm that the specific dispatcher calling you actually represents the carrier entity on the rate confirmation — contact information changes, new email paths, and rushed setup scenarios are the hallmarks of identity takeover fraud. Never release a load when the bill of lading carrier name differs from the rate confirmation, and treat any mid-load request to check in under a different MC number as an immediate fraud signal.

Equipment, Fuel & Ops

Diesel is the defining operational story of Q1 2026. The national average on-highway diesel price reached $5.375 per gallon for the week ending March 28, 2026, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration — the highest weekly national average since late 2022 and approximately 55% above pre-conflict EIA forecasts of $3.47/gallon. As of April 6, the DOE reported the national average had climbed further to $5.643 per gallon, up 24.2 cents in a single week, with California prices surpassing $7.567 per gallon. Samsara's preliminary Week 14 data showed diesel briefly exceeding $5.59/gallon — surpassing the prior 2022 record high of $5.50. The geopolitical trigger is the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz to most commercial traffic beginning February 28, 2026, which drove Brent crude above $100 per barrel with reported spikes as high as $119 in mid-March per Bramwith Consulting.

At $5.375/gallon, carriers averaging 6 miles per gallon are spending approximately 89 cents per mile on fuel alone, before touching any other operating expense. Every dollar increase in diesel per gallon adds 16–18 cents per mile in cost. Owner-operators — who cannot hedge fuel costs or negotiate bulk discounts — are most exposed. Many are parking trucks, reducing highway speed from 75 to 65 mph (saving roughly 8–9 cents per mile), and selectively declining unprofitable freight. ALG Worldwide reported that fuel increases are adding $0.15 or more per mile in carrier cost pressure industry-wide.

Class 8 ordering activity surged for a fourth consecutive month year over year. ACT Research preliminary data for March 2026 placed orders at 37,200 units, up 126% year over year, while FTR Transportation Intelligence estimated 38,200 units — a 137% year-over-year jump. The full 2026 order season (September 2025 through March 2026) is now up 15% year over year, per FTR senior analyst Dan Moyer, representing a clear departure from the double-digit declines of the prior cycle. Aging fleets, improving freight rates, tightening capacity, and front-running ahead of EPA 2027 NOx regulation cost increases are all cited as ordering drivers. However, Section 232 tariffs on medium- and heavy-duty trucks add approximately 25% to imported truck costs — a factor encouraging some fleets to accelerate domestic orders before tariff pass-throughs fully materialize. Class 8 orders are up 96% year-to-date in 2026 per FTR, suggesting genuine demand rather than purely speculative ordering.

On electric trucks: the global electric truck market is growing rapidly, but U.S. adoption remains in early stages. The U.S. electric truck market is projected at approximately $0.35 billion in 2026. Megawatt charging infrastructure is entering early corridor deployment, but grid connection timelines of 12–36 months remain a practical barrier for most fleets. For the near-term freight market, diesel-powered Class 8 trucks will continue to dominate capacity additions.

Action Checklist for Brokers

  • Re-price spot loads immediately. Dry van at $2.40–$2.47/mile, reefer at $2.79–$2.88/mile, and flatbed at $2.92–$2.95/mile are the current DAT baselines for the week ending April 4. Do not offer stale rate sheets — carriers are rejecting loads at a 14% rate and will walk.
  • Prioritize flatbed and reefer lane coverage. Load-to-truck ratios of 73.75 (flatbed) and 15.55 (reefer) signal that these are the tightest segments. Building carrier relationships in these equipment types now will pay dividends through summer.
  • Audit fuel surcharge mechanisms in all active contracts. At $5.375–$5.643/gallon diesel, standard FSC tables may be lagging pump reality by $0.20 or more per mile. Carriers absorbing that gap will either walk or demand renegotiation. Address it proactively.
  • Verify every carrier identity before releasing freight. With freight identity theft up 36% year over year and AI-powered deepfakes enabling phone impersonation, document verification alone is insufficient. Confirm dispatcher identity through known, verified contact channels — not numbers provided by a new contact.
  • Audit your carrier file for non-domiciled CDL holders. The FMCSA's March 16 rule change restricts non-domiciled CDLs to H-2A, H-2B, and E-2 visa holders. Carriers with affected drivers face potential capacity gaps as licenses expire. Know which carriers in your network may be impacted.
  • Update your Mexico cross-border carrier vetting ahead of USMCA review. The July 1, 2026 joint USMCA review is driving accelerated policy discussions. New Section 232 metal tariffs (effective April 6) are already disrupting maquiladora supply chains. Build contingency capacity on southern border lanes now.
  • Prepare shipper customers for sustained rate pressure through Q2. C.H. Robinson's revised 2026 forecast of +16–17% truckload costs YoY, combined with diesel above $5.40/gallon, means rate relief is not on the horizon before at least Q3. Shippers who hear this proactively from you will trust you more than those who get surprised at renewal.

title: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup - March 27, 2026
excerpt: After more than three years of depressed spot rates and brutal carrier attrition, the trucking industry enters Q2 2026 in a paradoxical state: capacity has been thinning from the bottom up, yet no demand surge has arrived to signal a clean recovery...
content:
Fleet & Market Trends

The Great Freight Recession Leaves Its Mark — And the Next Squeeze Is Loading

After more than three years of depressed spot rates and brutal carrier attrition, the trucking industry enters Q2 2026 in a paradoxical state: capacity has been thinning from the bottom up, yet no demand surge has arrived to signal a clean recovery. According to analysis by the International Factoring Association, carrier exits ran as high as 7,000 trucking businesses in a single spring month of 2025, and the proportion of mid-sized fleets filing Chapter 11 — rather than simply surrendering authority — has climbed noticeably as more structured operators reach their limits. ACT Research projects "considerable declines in equipment demand in 2026" with truckload margins still near historic lows, meaning the market is shedding capacity through financial exhaustion rather than an organic fleet upgrade cycle. For freight brokers like those operating in the Texas corridor, this slow-bleed environment means carrier network depth is quietly shrinking even when load boards still show apparent availability.

LTL Rates Hold Record Highs as FedEx Freight Prepares to Go It Alone

The less-than-truckload sector has been defying gravity for nine straight quarters. Per the TD Cowen/AFS Freight Index, LTL rates per pound stood 67.9% above their January 2018 baseline through Q4 2025, and analysts project the streak continues into 2026 even as demand remains soft — because LTL carriers operate on high fixed-cost terminal networks that don't deflate with volume. The biggest structural event reshaping the LTL landscape is the planned June 1, 2026 spin-off of FedEx Freight from its parent company, per the FedEx Newsroom. FedEx Freight, now North America's largest LTL carrier with $8.9 billion in fiscal 2025 revenue and 365 terminals serving 98% of U.S. zip codes, will trade publicly under ticker FDXF and has set a medium-term target of 4–6% annual revenue growth and over $1 billion in free cash flow. An independent FedEx Freight with its own dedicated salesforce and capital allocation flexibility could aggressively pursue verticals like healthcare, electronics, and AI infrastructure freight — intensifying competition across the LTL landscape over the next 12 months.

Driver Pool Tightening as CDL Crackdown Shrinks Hireable Supply

The driver shortage has a new pressure point that goes beyond demographics. The cost-per-hire for qualified drivers jumped 24% year-over-year in Q4 2025, per a joint report from The Professional Driver Agency and Conversion Interactive Agency, as federal crackdowns on non-domiciled CDLs, CDL mills, and English Language Proficiency requirements simultaneously reduced the hireable pool. Transport Topics reported that an estimated 90,000+ non-domiciled CDLs have been removed or are in jeopardy nationwide following FMCSA's emergency rule enforcement. The ATA projects the industry must hire 1.2 million new drivers over the next decade just to cover retirements and attrition — before accounting for demand growth. For carriers and brokers competing for capacity, the practical effect is that experienced, insurable, compliant drivers are increasingly scarce even in a soft freight environment, giving those drivers durable negotiating leverage when freight volumes firm up.

Nuclear Verdicts Are Repricing Trucking From the Inside Out

Insurance costs have become one of the fastest-growing line items for carriers — and the root cause is litigation, not claims frequency alone. According to FreightWaves and Reliance Partners, verdicts exceeding $1 million have increased 235% since 2012, and commercial auto liability insurance has now been unprofitable for insurers for 14 consecutive years. The Texas Supreme Court reversed a $100 million verdict against Werner Enterprises last June — a rare win — but the broader trend continues upward, per Risk and Insurance reporting that in 2023 alone there were 27 cases awarding over $100 million each. ATRI data shows auto liability premiums have grown nearly 38% per mile over the past decade, with small carriers hardest hit and many forced to raise deductibles, exit lanes, or leave the market entirely. Tort reform efforts are advancing in states like West Virginia (now capping certain trucking damages at $5 million) and Georgia (requiring third-party litigation funder disclosure), but federal reform remains elusive — meaning carriers operating in plaintiff-friendly states face a structurally higher cost floor for the foreseeable future.

Fuel & Cost Pressures

The Hormuz Shock: Diesel Hits $5.37 and Rewrites 2026 Fleet Economics

Every major forecast heading into 2026 called for diesel to average around $3.47 per gallon — a modest year of relief. Instead, the February 28 military action in the Middle East and the subsequent near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz sent crude oil surging past $108 per barrel and pushed the national average retail diesel price to $5.37 per gallon by the week of March 23, per Tradlinx analysis of EIA data. That's a 55% overshoot from projections, adding roughly $0.36 per mile to trucking operating costs almost overnight. Available truck posts on DAT fell to their lowest Week 13 levels in at least 10 years across dry van, reefer, and flatbed as owner-operators parked trucks, cut deadhead miles, and declined unprofitable loads. C.H. Robinson has already revised its 2026 dry van rate forecast upward from +10% to +12%, and with the spot-to-contract gap compressing from $0.39/mile a year ago to just $0.11/mile by March, route guide reliability is deteriorating for shippers who haven't locked in capacity relationships.

Fuel Surcharge Mechanisms Are Breaking Under the Speed of This Spike

Standard EIA-indexed fuel surcharge tables were designed for gradual diesel price movement — not a $1.48-per-gallon swing in three weeks. According to FreightWise analysis, diesel sat at $4.66 as of March 2, a 25.6% increase in just three weeks — and the historical LTL industry average fuel surcharge runs approximately 30% annually across the full year. The surcharge lag creates a dangerous gap: carriers pay today's pump price, but the indexed surcharge may reflect last week's lower EIA average, meaning carriers absorb the spread until contracts reset or they selectively reject loads. Carriers are now increasing base freight rates and fuel surcharge percentages simultaneously — a double hit that is compressing shipper budgets even as total volumes decline. For freight brokerages operating in this environment, the opportunity lies in proactively renegotiating fuel surcharge mechanisms with carrier partners and helping shipper clients understand that today's contract rates were built on a fundamentally different cost environment.

Refinery Margins Widen While CNG Infrastructure Quietly Expands

The Hormuz crisis has exposed a structural vulnerability: U.S. refinery capacity has been contracting through closures and bio-fuel conversions, which means crack spreads — the refinery profit margin per gallon — are expected to widen to $0.84 per gallon in 2026 from $0.52 in 2024, per Fleet Rabbit analysis of EIA data, partially offsetting any crude price relief that would otherwise flow to pump prices. On the alternative fuels front, The Transport Project's Q4 2025 Natural Gas Vehicle Refueling Infrastructure Report confirmed 1,385 CNG and 81 LNG stations now operating across the U.S., with CNG delivering 30–40% fuel cost savings versus diesel for high-utilization fleets. EPA Phase 3 greenhouse gas standards — finalized March 2024 and taking effect for model year 2027 vehicles — will add an estimated $15,000–$20,000 to the purchase price of compliant Class 8 tractors, making the current pre-buy window and alternative fuel evaluation a critical strategic decision for fleet operators through the end of 2026.

Fraud & Security Watch

SAFER Transport Act: Congress Takes Aim at Chameleon Carriers and Freight Crime

On February 26, 2026, Senator Todd Young (R-Ind.) introduced the Securing American Freight, Enforcement, and Reliability in Transport Act — the SAFER Transport Act — backed by ATA, OOIDA, TIA, and six other major industry associations, per Truck News and Land Line Media. The bill would phase out MC numbers entirely in favor of a single USDOT number system, deploy an automated tool to flag suspicious registrations before DOT numbers are issued, mandate monthly state CDL reporting, establish a Freight Fraud and Theft Advisory Committee, and require DOT to refer freight fraud cases to the Department of Justice. The legislation directly targets chameleon carriers — operators that shutter under one DOT number and immediately reopen under a new identity to evade their enforcement history — a practice FMCSA Administrator Derek Barrs has described as an acute public safety threat following a fatal Indiana crash linked to a non-domiciled driver in a chameleon carrier network. For brokers, passage of the SAFER Act would meaningfully change carrier vetting by making prior fraud history harder to obscure across registration restarts.

CDL Mill Crackdown: 7,000+ Schools Purged, Carriers Must Reverify

In one of the most aggressive enforcement actions in trucking history, FMCSA deployed more than 300 investigators across all 50 states in February 2026, conducting over 1,400 on-site sting operations targeting commercial driver's license training schools. The result: 448 schools received formal removal notices, 109 others voluntarily withdrew before investigators arrived, and combined with earlier enforcement waves in December 2025 and January 2026, FMCSA has now purged more than 7,000 training providers from its registry — nearly one in five of the 40,000 listed before the crackdown began, per Overdrive and Jackim Woods reporting. DOT Office of Inspector General investigations conservatively estimated that over 6,000 fraudulent CDLs were issued between 2001 and 2025 to drivers who could not safely operate the vehicles they were licensed to drive. For carriers and brokers onboarding new drivers, this creates an immediate obligation: verify that any recently trained driver's school remains active on FMCSA's Training Provider Registry, as drivers from removed providers may face retesting requirements that delay hiring timelines.

Double-Brokering Enforcement Escalates: $50K Fines and Real-Time Tracking Coming

Double brokering cost carriers an estimated $700 million to $1 billion in 2025 alone, according to the Transportation Intermediaries Association, and FMCSA received over 8,000 related complaints — a four-times increase since 2021. In response, FMCSA finalized three major rules in 2026: the Broker Financial Responsibility rule doubles the minimum surety bond from $75,000 to $150,000; the Double Brokering Prevention rule (effective January 2027) requires load tracking technology that verifies the actual hauling carrier matches the contracted carrier; and enhanced penalties increase fines from $16,000 to $50,000 per violation with mandatory authority revocation for repeat offenders, per Truck Dispatch Experts. FMCSA is also hiring 150 additional fraud investigators — more than tripling its current enforcement team — with bond increases taking effect by July 2026. Cargo theft methods have also evolved to include GPS spoofing to mask unauthorized route changes and tracking portal credential hijacking, per Heavy Duty Trucking, making multi-point carrier verification and closed-network load boards essential risk management tools for brokerages in today's fraud environment.

Technology & Policy

Aurora Driverless Network Triples — 200+ Trucks Targeted by Year-End

Aurora Innovation has moved from a handful of supervised trucks to a rapidly expanding driverless network in less than a year. As of February 2026, Aurora announced it was tripling its driverless route network to five Sun Belt corridors — having surpassed 250,000 driverless miles with zero Aurora Driver-attributed collisions, per the company's official investor press releases. The company's next-generation hardware cuts system cost by half while doubling lidar detection range to 1,000 meters, and Aurora expects to deploy its International LT Series fleet without any ride observer in Q2 2026 — with all commercial capacity already committed through Q3. Aurora targets more than 200 driverless trucks in commercial operation by year-end 2026, with customers including Hirschbach Motor Lines, Schneider, Werner, and energy logistics firm Detmar Logistics, which has contracted 30 Aurora Driver-powered trucks for more than 20 hours of daily utilization hauling frac sand in the Permian Basin. For conventional carriers and brokers, driverless freight remains a middle-mile technology initially limited to Sun Belt long-haul corridors — but the economics are being written at scale in real time.

Truck Parking Gets $200M and a Federal Study — Construction Finally Moves

Truck parking has moved from a chronic nuisance to a funded federal priority. The fiscal year 2026 funding package signed by President Trump on February 3 included $200 million for truck parking projects through the Federal Highway Administration, with states now eligible to tap over $47.4 billion across eight programs for parking capacity projects, per Transport Topics. FMCSA simultaneously launched a new driver survey study — Quantifying the Benefits of Creating New Truck Parking Spaces — targeting 1,000 responses to generate the monetary benefit data needed to persuade state and local governments to accelerate construction funding, per CDLLife. Florida's I-4 corridor, identified as the state's worst truck parking shortage with only 36 public spots along a critical freight lane, is slated for three new facilities with construction beginning this summer. The $200 million in freshly authorized federal funds represents the most direct federal commitment to this HOS compliance and safety problem in years, and the construction pipeline it funds will shape driver routing, HOS exposure, and shipper on-time performance across key freight corridors through 2027 and beyond.

Bottom Line

The trucking industry heading into Q2 2026 is being simultaneously squeezed by a geopolitical fuel shock that no forecast anticipated, a fraud and enforcement environment actively thinning the carrier pool through revocations and CDL disqualifications, and a legal-insurance cost structure that keeps raising the floor on what it costs to safely move a load. For freight brokerages, the operational implication is direct: real, available, insurable, compliant capacity is smaller than FMCSA authority counts suggest — and it is becoming more selective as diesel economics punish marginal operators. Shippers who locked in contract rates before the Hormuz spike and brokers who maintained deep, verified carrier relationships entering Q1 are now best positioned; those dependent on spot-market availability are discovering that surcharge lags, load selectivity, and tender rejection rates above 14% create genuine coverage gaps on key lanes. The next six to twelve months will reward brokers who move fastest on carrier verification and compliance documentation, renegotiate fuel surcharge mechanisms proactively, and treat a vetted, financially stable carrier network as a strategic asset rather than a commodity pool.

title: Weekly Freight Report - March 27, 2026
excerpt: The truckload market enters the final week of March in a sustained carrier-favored cycle, with spot rates posting their seventh consecutive monthly gain. Per DAT data, dry van spot averaged $2.41/mile, reefer $2.88/mile, and flatbed $2.95/mile on the spot board...
content:
Market Pulse

The truckload market enters the final week of March in a sustained carrier-favored cycle, with spot rates posting their seventh consecutive monthly gain. Per DAT Freight & Analytics data released March 17, February averages came in at $2.41/mile for dry van (up $0.09 month-over-month), $2.88/mile for reefer, and $2.72/mile for flatbed. Early March DAT One data pushed flatbed to $2.95/mile. The contract-to-spot gap has compressed from roughly $0.39/mile a year ago to just $0.11/mile, per a joint U.S. Bank and DAT analysis, leaving shippers with far less cushion to absorb volatility. Contract dry van averaged $2.52/mile heading into month-end.

Outbound tender rejections reached a multi-year high of 14.95% in early March, per SONAR data cited by Arrive Logistics — the highest since March 2022. Flatbed open-deck rejections are the standout: Trinity Logistics reported flatbed tender rejections near 40%, extraordinary for a period that historically sees limited open-deck activity. The van load-to-truck ratio stands at 7.73 and reefer at 15.55 per DAT's March 17 Trendlines Report, compared to a 14.07 February reefer average, confirming that produce season is accelerating early in South Texas and the Southeast. According to FreightWaves SONAR, the SONAR Truckload Rejection Index has climbed more than 881 basis points year-over-year.

Regulation & Enforcement

Non-domiciled CDL final rule (effective March 16): FMCSA's new rule restricts non-domiciled CDL eligibility to H-2A, H-2B, and E-2 visa holders only, capping license validity at one year. Several states, including Pennsylvania, have paused issuance. California revoked more than 13,000 improperly issued licenses this month, per Arrive Logistics. Brokers should verify CDL validity in carrier onboarding packets immediately — revocations will tighten capacity in affected regional lanes without warning.

Drug & Alcohol Clearinghouse (DACH-II): Employers and C/TPAs must now report violations within 3 business days, and states are automatically downgrading CDLs upon recorded violations. Civil penalties reach up to $7,500 per occurrence for hiring a driver with an unresolved violation. FMCSA is also rolling out MOTUS — its new USDOT registration platform featuring enhanced identity verification — designed to close the registration loopholes exploited by freight fraudsters.

The 2026 HOS final rule preserves the 11-hour driving limit and 34-hour restart intact while adding an optional 3-hour sleeper berth micro-split and clarified ELD data-transfer standards, per CDL Schools USA. No rollbacks are in play.

Broker Edge

Three operational priorities stand out this week. First, fuel surcharge discipline: the average van FSC climbed to 41 cents/mile in February per DAT — up from 38 cents in January — and the March diesel surge means April FSC schedules will reset higher still. Any shipper contract with FSC caps negotiated before February is already creating friction with carriers. Second, produce season capacity: reefer tender rejections hit 19.37% in mid-February and have stayed elevated per FreightWaves SONAR, running 1,089 basis points above year-ago levels. Brokers on perishable lanes out of the Rio Grande Valley should be securing capacity 5–7 days out. Third, carrier retention: Class 8 tractor counts are down roughly 25,000 units (1.5%) year-over-year per Arrive Logistics, and the narrowing contract-to-spot gap gives carriers real motivation to reject committed lanes. Preferred carrier programs with quick-pay terms will matter more this spring than at any point in the past three years.

Cross-Border Watchlist

The US-Mexico tariff picture has clarified since the Supreme Court's February 20 ruling struck down IEEPA tariffs. The White House replaced them with a 10% Section 122 surcharge on non-USMCA goods, effective February 24 and expiring approximately July 24 unless Congress acts. USMCA-qualifying goods remain tariff-free. USMCA utilization rates have surged from roughly 45% in early 2025 to approximately 85% by January 2026, per Tetakawi analysis. The USTR and Mexico's Secretary of Economy formally launched bilateral USMCA review discussions on March 18 in Washington.

On the ground, Laredo — which handles roughly 46% of the value of US-Mexico truck-transported bilateral trade per C.H. Robinson — is experiencing tighter availability from B1 visa enforcement and network imbalances. A February 22 security operation in Jalisco temporarily closed the Port of Manzanillo and halted customs operations in Guadalajara and Manzanillo, underscoring the need for contingency routing plans on Western Mexico lanes.

Fraud & Security

Cargo theft losses surged 60% to nearly $725 million in 2025, with the average theft value rising 36% to $273,990, per CargoNet's annual analysis. Metals theft climbed 77% and food and beverage thefts spiked 47%. A CCJ Digital report published March 27 noted that cargo theft concerns are up 38% year-over-year per Geotab research, with AI-powered tools enabling fraudsters to convincingly replicate carrier identities — including deepfake voice calls — in minutes.

Senator Todd Young (R-Ind.) introduced the SAFER Transport Act on February 26, backed by ATA, OOIDA, and TIA. The bill would establish a Freight Fraud and Theft Advisory Committee, phase out MC numbers in favor of USDOT numbers to cut identity theft exposure, and mandate automated flagging of suspicious FMCSA registration activity. Double-brokering red flags to enforce now: broker name on rate confirmation differs from the BOL; requests to check in under a different MC number; pickup or delivery location mismatches; and mid-transit calls to change the route.

Equipment, Fuel & Ops

The US-Iran conflict — which began February 28 — triggered the sharpest diesel price spike since 2022. The Strait of Hormuz, carrying roughly 20% of global oil supply, saw vessel traffic collapse from ~138 ships per day to just 20 since late March, per IRU ship-tracking data. The EIA reported the national on-highway diesel average at $5.375/gallon as of March 23 — up $1.81 year-over-year and up $1.57 in one month. California hit $6.87/gallon; even the Gulf Coast averaged $5.13/gallon, per Heavy Duty Trucking. Brent crude closed at $107.81/barrel on March 27 per Fortune — about $34 above year-ago levels. The BTS confirmed March's monthly diesel average at $4.92/gallon, up 37.3% from March 2025. For a typical long-haul fleet, the conflict adds an estimated $0.04–$0.10/mile in additional fuel cost per truck, per OC Trucking analysis.

Class 8 orders remain a bright spot. FTR and ACT Research reported preliminary March orders of 38,200 and 37,200 units respectively — approximately 130% above year-ago levels and the fourth consecutive month of 20%+ year-over-year growth, per Trucks, Parts, Service. The 2026 order season is now up 15% year-over-year since September, confirming an early-stage recovery driven by tighter capacity, EPA 2027 NOx pre-buy activity, and firmer rate expectations.

Action Checklist for Brokers

  • Renegotiate FSC caps immediately. Any shipper contract with fixed or capped fuel surcharges negotiated before February 2026 is eroding carrier relationships. Add variable FSC language before April billing cycles.
  • Audit carrier CDL validity. The March 16 non-domiciled CDL final rule has triggered multi-state revocations. A carrier with a revoked driver is an immediate compliance and coverage risk.
  • Run Clearinghouse pre-employment queries on every carrier driver. DACH-II is live; failure to query exposes your brokerage to up to $7,500 per driver in civil penalties.
  • Implement call-back verification using independently sourced numbers. Before releasing any new load, call the carrier using a number from FMCSA SAFER — not one the carrier provided. AI deepfakes have made incoming voice verification unreliable.
  • Lock in reefer and flatbed capacity for April now. With reefer rejections above 19% and flatbed near 40%, same-day sourcing on produce and construction lanes will be expensive or impossible.
  • Confirm USMCA qualification status with cross-border shippers. USMCA goods are tariff-free; non-qualifying goods face a 10% surcharge. Add 2–3 days of lead time on Laredo tenders given tightening capacity.

title: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup - March 20, 2026
excerpt: Diesel at $5.07/gallon, a Class 8 pre-buy surge at 150% YoY, back-to-back billion-dollar broker M&A deals, and three FMCSA rulemakings in one day — here is what is shaping the next 3–12 months in domestic trucking.
content:
Fleet & Market Trends

Driver Supply Is Shrinking — and the Rules Are Making It Worse

U.S. truck transportation employment plateaued at 1,513,300 jobs in both November and December 2025 — the lowest since July 2021 and a net loss of 21,300 jobs since December 2023, per Entourage Freight Solutions. The National Transportation Institute projects supply will keep leaving the market throughout 2026, with constraints growing "only more intense" as freight volume recovers. Regulatory headwinds are compounding the problem: stricter English-language proficiency rules, enforcement against non-domiciled CDLs, work visa slowdowns, and the shutdown of thousands of CDL training programs are all squeezing supply simultaneously, per C.H. Robinson's 2026 market outlook.

One More Wave of Carrier Failures Is Still on the Table

After roughly 88,000 trucking authorities revoked in 2023 and 1,000–1,500 carrier exits per week in early 2025, ACT Research still characterizes the current phase as an "extended correction cycle" with truckload margins near historic lows. FTR's Avery Vise put it plainly: "Capacity has come down almost as deep as it can without losing a lot of carriers." The missing ingredient is sustained freight demand growth. Insurance premium surges and high-cost 2020–2021 equipment debt remain the most likely triggers for a final shakeout wave, per the IFA Commercial Factor's January 2026 analysis.

Class 8 Pre-Buy Surge Points to a 2027 Cost Cliff

February 2026 Class 8 truck orders hit approximately 47,200 units — up 150–159% year-over-year, the 8th highest single-month total in ACT Research's 44-year tracking history. The surge reflects a pre-buy ahead of EPA 2027 NOx standards, which will add an estimated $8,000–$12,000 per new truck (revised down from initial projections of $20,000–$25,000). OEM build plans for H1 2026 are running at an annualized 220,000 units, and competition for 2026 build slots is intensifying. Fleets waiting on the spring 2026 EPA adjustment before ordering may find capacity already committed.

M&A Is Consolidating Freight Brokerage Around Tech-Enabled Scale

Two major deals in eight weeks are reshaping the broker landscape. Echo Global Logistics agreed to acquire ITS Logistics on January 21, creating a combined entity with pro forma revenue of approximately $5.4 billion, per FreightWaves. On March 3, Thoma Bravo announced the acquisition of WWEX Group — parent of Worldwide Express, GlobalTranz, and Unishippers — to be combined with e-commerce software company Auctane (ShipStation, Stamps.com), per Thoma Bravo's press release. Both deals signal the same thesis: physical freight brokerage is only defensible long-term when paired with proprietary technology platforms.

Insurance Hardening Is Now a Carrier Viability Issue

Trucking insurance rates surged 18.5% through March 2026, per leading actuarial firms. The median nuclear verdict in trucking litigation has reached $36 million, with verdicts exceeding $1 million up 235% since 2012, according to Land Line Media. ATRI ranked insurance costs and availability the #3 concern of motor carriers entering 2026, and FTR's Vise explicitly named premium surges as a potential trigger for the next failure wave. Fleets without dashcams, telematics, and ADAS are finding competitive coverage increasingly difficult to secure.

Fuel & Cost Pressures

The Hormuz Crisis Delivered the Sharpest Diesel Spike in Four Years

Following joint U.S.-Israel military strikes on Iran on February 28, 2026 — including the killing of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei — the Strait of Hormuz was effectively disrupted, with tanker traffic dropping approximately 70%. The diesel price response was immediate: from ~$3.53/gallon in late February, prices reached $5.07/gallon by March 17–19 — a 44% spike in roughly three weeks, per AAA and CNBC. Brent crude peaked near $126/barrel. While the White House reported tankers are "starting to dribble through" as of March 17, Iran's new Supreme Leader has stated the Gulf should remain closed, keeping supply disruption risk elevated through Q2.

Fuel Surcharge Tables Weren't Built for This Speed

Most truckload and LTL contracts use the EIA weekly retail diesel index with tiered surcharge tables built for gradual price movements — not a 44% spike in three weeks. FTR Transportation Intelligence flagged the surge as setting the stage for "the most unfavorable market conditions ever for shippers," per Food Logistics. Carriers are now raising base freight rates and fuel surcharge percentages simultaneously. A federal proposal to cap state fuel taxes at 50 cents per gallon using federal highway fund leverage is gaining attention as a partial offset, per FreightWaves' February 16 report.

Alternative Fuels Are Gaining Traction — But the Tax Credit Gap Stings

Renewable Natural Gas now accounts for 86% of all natural gas used for transportation fuel in the U.S., with 1,385 CNG and 81 LNG stations operating nationwide, per The Transport Project's Q4 2025 report. The renewable diesel market is projected at $26.88 billion in 2026 (CAGR ~9.7%), per Yahoo Finance. The Alternative Fuel Tax Credit — a 50¢/gallon credit for CNG/LNG — expired at end of 2024 and an industry coalition is lobbying Congress for reinstatement. The Hormuz spike has accelerated fleet interest in alternatives, but long-haul BEV remains cost-prohibitive and hydrogen production at $16–18/kg limits near-term scaling.

Fraud & Security Watch

FMCSA Launches Three Rulemakings to Stop Chameleon Carriers

On March 19, 2026, FMCSA launched three formal rulemakings: streamlined suspension and revocation procedures to prevent re-entry via new DOT numbers, new-entrant safety knowledge verification, and broker qualification testing to raise carrier vetting standards, per Overdrive. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy highlighted patterns of hundreds of DOT numbers tied to mailbox addresses. Immediate actions include physical address verification (records available within 48 hours) and unannounced "SafeDRIVE" roadside inspections. The separately ATA-backed SAFE Act would direct FMCSA to automate fraud flagging before suspicious entities receive new USDOT numbers.

NMFTA's SCAC Verified — and the Tech Countermeasure to GPS Spoofing

NMFTA launched SCAC Verified™ on February 26, 2026, transforming the Standard Carrier Alpha Code into an identity-assured credential with biometric matching and address verification at SCAC application. COO Joe Ohr stated the intent: "We're verifying that a real person, at a real, physical address, is tied to every SCAC." GPS spoofing has meanwhile become a routine cargo theft technique, with organized criminal enterprises using AI-assisted phishing to steal dispatcher credentials and generate false location data. Counter-platform GenLogs — operating 1,000+ roadside cameras capturing 15 million commercial vehicle images daily — has recovered over 5,000 trailers since July 2024 and raised $60 million in Series B funding in early 2026, per Forbes.

Technology & Policy

Aurora Is Running Autonomous Trucks Commercially — Right Now

Aurora Innovation has accumulated 250,000 driverless miles with zero Aurora Driver-attributed collisions and expanded to 10 commercial routes as of February 2026, per Aurora IR. Its Fort Worth–Phoenix lane — a 1,000-mile refrigerated route for Hirschbach — is the first autonomous route exceeding Hours of Service limitations. Aurora's March 19 report projects autonomous trucking will deliver $9 billion in annual consumer savings by 2035. The company plans 200+ driverless trucks by year-end 2026, with all current capacity committed through Q3. Gatik also became the first U.S. company to operate fully driverless trucks at scale for commercial middle-mile deliveries in January 2026, reporting $600 million in contracted revenue, per its press release.

IIJA Expires in September — and the Next Transportation Bill Is Coming

The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act expires September 30, 2026, with $360.3 billion obligated (72.6% of $496.1 billion) and $213.7 billion in actual outlays as of January 31, per the DOT status report. Congress is beginning work on the next surface transportation reauthorization — the AMERICA DRIVES Act — which will shape AV policy, freight infrastructure funding, and trucking regulations for the next five-to-six-year cycle. The FY2026 spending bill also includes a historic first: $200 million in dedicated truck parking funding, the first time Congress has ever allocated funds exclusively for that purpose, per the ATA.

Bottom Line

The Hormuz diesel shock is the most immediate operational challenge in Q2 2026 — at $5.07/gallon and still volatile, fuel surcharge tables are structurally broken for this speed of movement, and carriers absorbing the recovery lag are the most financially exposed. But the structural forces underneath are more durable: a driver pool that is aging, over-regulated, and under-compensated; an insurance market where nuclear verdict exposure is systematically pricing out smaller fleets; and a consolidating broker market where two $5 billion-plus deals in eight weeks signal that tech-enabled scale is the only defensible long-term position. The FMCSA's simultaneous launch of three rulemakings, MOTUS deployment, and support for the SAFER Transport Act represent the most concentrated anti-fraud push in years — brokers without real-time carrier vetting are operating behind the curve. Autonomous trucking is running commercial freight today, and its economic model directly targets the cost structure that has kept human-driven long-haul viable.

title: Weekly Freight Report - March 20, 2026
excerpt: Spot rates hit a new cycle high of $2.82/mile, diesel surged to $5.07/gallon on Iran conflict disruptions, the non-domiciled CDL rule took effect March 16, and new broker transparency rules are now in force. Here is what to act on this week.
content:
Market Pulse

Spot rates are at their highest point since late 2022. Per DAT Freight & Analytics, the FreightWaves SONAR National Truckload Index hit $2.82/mile on March 19 — a new cycle high. February dry van spot rates averaged $2.41/mile (the seventh consecutive monthly gain), and mid-March dry van tracked around $2.65/mile nationally, with the Midwest posting $2.77/mile. Flatbed is the real story: the flatbed load-to-truck ratio surged to 73.75 in mid-March — up 29% from February's 57.11 — driven by steel, copper, and aluminum freight tied to manufacturing recovery, data center buildout, and energy infrastructure in the industrial Midwest. Flatbed tender rejections are running 40–42%. Werner CEO Derek Leathers called current conditions "COVID-level type rejection rates."

Contract rates are moving with conviction. DAT data shows dry van contract averaging $2.52/mile in February (+$0.04 vs. January), with the spot-to-contract spread at its narrowest since March 2022. ACT Research reported truckload contracts up mid-single digits in February — a structural shift. The Cass Freight Expenditures Index rose 2.1% year-over-year in February, its first YoY gain in years. On the macro side, the Iran conflict that began February 28 has disrupted Strait of Hormuz oil flows, pushing diesel up roughly 25% since the conflict started (per IRU) and squeezing out marginal carriers — tightening supply even further.

Regulation & Enforcement

FMCSA's "Restoring Integrity" non-domiciled CDL final rule took effect March 16. It limits new non-domiciled CDL eligibility to H-2A, H-2B, and E-2 visa holders; bans EADs as proof of eligibility; requires all renewals in person; and caps validity at one year. Roughly 194,000 current holders will lose renewal eligibility as their licenses expire. Dalilah's Law (H.R. 5688) advanced through the House T&I Committee on March 18 by a 35–26 vote — if enacted, it would mandate English-only CDL testing, ban foreign dispatch services implicated in fraud, and could eventually disqualify an estimated 600,000–614,000 CDL holders nationwide.

ELD enforcement is accelerating hard. FMCSA revoked 14 additional devices on March 4 — 27+ removed in 2026 so far, already outpacing all of 2025. Carriers using Club ELD, DENDRA, Egreen, or any Gorilla Fleet Safety product (Patriot ELD, ClearPath ELD, SimpleX 2 Go, and others) must switch before the May 4 deadline or face OOS citations. New CVSA out-of-service criteria for ELD tampering take effect April 1, and the May 12–14 International Roadcheck will specifically target ELD tampering and cargo securement. FMCSA Administrator Derek Barrs announced approximately nine rulemakings planned for 2026 at the March 17 Chamber of Commerce summit, including a full restart of the entry-level driver training program.

Broker Edge

New FMCSA broker transparency rules took full effect this week under 49 CFR § 371.3. Brokers must provide carriers with an itemized breakdown — shipper payment plus broker margin — within 48 hours of delivery on request. Double-brokering without explicit written consent from all parties renders the transaction void. Penalty: $12,000 per violation, and three NCCDB complaints within 12 months triggers a full financial audit. Any contract clause waiving a carrier's transparency rights is federally unenforceable.

The broker bond rule in effect since January 16 requires $75,000 of readily available security — cash, irrevocable letters of credit, or U.S. Treasury bonds only (loan instruments excluded). A drop below $75,000 not replenished within seven calendar days triggers FMCSA authority suspension. Also watch: the Supreme Court's pending decision in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II (argued March 5) could determine whether federal law preempts state negligent-hiring claims against brokers — a ruling that would significantly affect vetting liability exposure. Thoma Bravo's $12 billion WWEX/Auctane combination and Echo Global's $5.4B ITS Logistics acquisition are both closing Q1–Q2 2026, compressing the large-broker tier and creating service-differentiation opportunity for independents.

Cross-Border Watchlist

Formal USMCA review talks between U.S. and Mexican trade officials began the week of March 16, ahead of the July 1, 2026 mandatory review deadline. Canada remains sidelined — no meaningful negotiations since October 2025, though a joint statement March 13 confirmed renewed contact. At stake: $1.6 trillion in annual trade, with 80% moving by truck. Laredo is under capacity pressure from B1 visa enforcement affecting drayage drivers, and longer lead-time requirements are in effect. Texas approved $58.5 million for a CPKC rail grade separation project at Santa María Boulevard — a long-needed infrastructure investment at the port handling 46% of bilateral US-Mexico truck trade by value.

Current cross-border tariff landscape: USMCA-compliant goods remain duty-free (~85% of Mexico-US trade); steel, aluminum, and copper face 50% tariffs; medium- and heavy-duty trucks face 25% (not USMCA-covered). Mexico's 2026 Customs Law now treats missing Carta Porte documentation as illegal transportation, subject to seizure of goods plus unpaid duty charges. Mexico's domestic trucking sector reported a 25% revenue decline in 2025 (per CANACAR), contributing to northbound-southbound freight imbalances that create southbound capacity opportunities for cross-border operators.

Fraud & Security

Geotab's "2026 Blueprint" report released March 19 puts North American cargo theft losses at $6.6 billion in 2025 — confirmed incidents up 18%, average theft values up 36% to roughly $274,000 per incident. Strategic theft (fraud, identity theft, falsified paperwork) has surged 1,500% since 2021, per CargoNet. FMCSA issued a formal March 19 bulletin warning carriers not to buy, sell, or lease USDOT or MC numbers: discovery triggers immediate authority revocation. Chameleon carriers are 3x more likely to be involved in serious crashes than legitimate new entrants.

A federal indictment announced March 15 charged Talishco LLC broker Khayyam Farajov with collecting over $1 million from USPS freight contracts by fabricating delivery data and laundering proceeds through stock accounts — five wire fraud counts, up to 20 years per count. Fraudulent carrier impersonation is up 213% in 2026 (IDScan/NMFTA). NMFTA's new SCAC Verified™ program (live February 26) now ties each carrier SCAC code to a verified individual, making impersonation at tender significantly harder. Enroll your carrier partners.

Equipment, Fuel & Ops

National average on-highway diesel hit $5.071/gallon the week of March 16, per EIA — up $0.212 week-over-week and up 41.6% year-over-year. Gulf Coast averaged $4.83/gallon; Oklahoma hit $4.28 (cheapest state); California reached $6.49. The EIA's March Short-Term Energy Outlook revised the 2026 annual average diesel forecast to $4.12/gallon (up from $3.43 in February's estimate), with a projected Q3–Q4 pullback if tensions ease. Until then, fuel surcharge accuracy is critical — carriers are already pricing $5+ diesel into spot bids.

Class 8 orders surged to 46,200 units in February, up 156% year-over-year — the 8th-best month in ACT Research's 530-month history. The 2027 EPA pre-buy (expected ~$10,000 premium per compliant truck), rising spot rates, and tariff-frontloading are all driving early orders. Volvo Trucks announced a $2 billion North American investment at TMC 2026 and received a record 400-unit VNL 860 order from TEL. Daimler's 2027 lineup adds six Cummins engines, including the first gasoline option for medium-duty (B6.7 Octane, no DEF/DPF). Maintenance costs continue rising: repair and maintenance CPI climbed 6.9% year-over-year entering 2026, with total annual Class 8 maintenance running $15,000–$25,000 per truck. ATRI pegs total per-mile operating costs at an all-time high of $2.26/mile.

Action Checklist for Brokers

  • Audit your carriers for revoked ELDs immediately. The March 4 revocation list includes Club ELD, DENDRA, Egreen, and all Gorilla Fleet Safety devices. Drivers using these face OOS citations after May 4. Confirm compliance before tendering loads.
  • Verify carrier identity on every load — not just on file. Impersonation is up 213% in 2026. Call back carriers using independently sourced phone numbers. Cross-check USDOT and MC numbers in FMCSA SAFER Web before dispatch.
  • Set up a transparency disclosure process now. The $12,000-per-violation broker transparency rule is live. Document your 48-hour itemized breakdown process for carrier requests and train your team on the "strike three" audit threshold.
  • Update fuel surcharge tables immediately. Diesel is up 41.6% year-over-year. If your fuel surcharge schedule is anchored to an outdated reference price, you're absorbing the difference. Carriers are quoting $5+ diesel into every spot bid.
  • Broaden your flatbed carrier network now. With a 73.75 load-to-truck ratio and 40–42% rejection rates, flatbed capacity is scarce. Build deeper relationships with compliant flatbed carriers in the industrial Midwest corridors before you need them.
  • Confirm Carta Porte compliance on every Mexico cross-border shipment. Mexico's 2026 Customs Law makes missing Carta Porte documentation a seizure-level offense. Verify your carrier partners are issuing compliant CFDIs with the Complemento Carta Porte on all moves.
  • Start building your Q2 carrier network now. Non-domiciled CDL enforcement, CDL mill shutdowns, and the potential passage of Dalilah's Law are all compressing the available driver pool. Secure relationships with compliant carriers before the April–May produce season reefer tightening hits.

title: Weekly Freight Report - March 13, 2026
excerpt: The FreightWaves NTI hit $2.82/mile — a new cycle high. Diesel surged 96¢ in one week to $4.859/gallon on Iran/Hormuz fears. The non-domiciled CDL rule takes effect March 16. Here's what it all means for brokers.
content:
Market Pulse

The FreightWaves National Truckload Index hit $2.82/mile this week — a new cycle high not seen since late 2022. That headline number captures what carriers and brokers are feeling on the ground: spot rates have climbed roughly $0.50/mile net of fuel over the past six months, and load volumes are at multi-year peaks. The market is no longer quietly recovering — it is tightening.

Per DAT data for the week of March 1–7 (the closest published weekly dataset), van linehaul spot averaged $2.00/mile (down 2¢ week-over-week, fuel-excluded) on a van load-to-truck ratio of 8.1. Reefer linehaul came in at $2.38/mile with an L/T ratio of 14.9. Flatbed was the standout: $2.33/mile linehaul with a load-to-truck ratio of 70.3 — up from 68.9 the prior week and the 13th gain in 14 consecutive weeks. All-in spot rates including fuel surcharges are running substantially higher: per Scale Funding's mid-March DAT data, national all-in van spot reached $2.65/mile, reefer $2.84/mile, and flatbed $2.94/mile — with Midwest flatbed averaging $3.14/mile.

DAT's February 2026 monthly report, published March 17, confirms the trend: spot van averaged $2.41/mile for the month, the seventh consecutive monthly gain. The spread between spot and contract van rates narrowed to its smallest gap since March 2022 — a signal that the market is approaching equilibrium after years of contract premiums over spot.

Tender rejection rates underscore the tightness. According to Trinity Logistics, overall rejection rates are running near 14%, with Midwest rejections sustaining above 18% for the past month — the highest level since March 2022 per FreightWaves. Open-deck rejections hit an extraordinary ~40%, driven by data center construction, infrastructure projects, and steel demand. Werner Enterprises CEO Derek Leathers called the current flatbed environment "COVID-level type rejection rates."

The macro backdrop supports continued tightening. ISM Manufacturing PMI came in at 52.4% for February — the second straight month of expansion and only the third time in 40 months the index has been above 50. New Orders reached 55.8%. The Prices Index surged to 70.5%, the highest since June 2022, reflecting tariff-driven input cost pressures that are feeding directly into shipper freight budgets.

M&A activity continued reshaping the broker landscape. The Echo Global Logistics + ITS Logistics deal (announced January 21) will create a $5.4 billion combined 3PL expected to close in the first half of 2026. Thoma Bravo's acquisition of WWEX Group — which includes Worldwide Express, GlobalTranz, Unishippers, JEAR Logistics, and BLX Logistics — was announced March 3 and creates a combined platform serving 130,000+ customers across 70 million+ shipments annually. On March 10, AI-powered brokerage Fura announced its fifth acquisition, adding Texas-based Barton Logistics to its portfolio. Consolidation at the top is accelerating.

Regulation & Enforcement

Three days from now — March 16 — FMCSA's non-domiciled CDL final rule takes effect. This is the most consequential near-term compliance event in the industry. The rule (published in the Federal Register February 13 at 91 FR 7044) limits non-domiciled CDL eligibility to three visa categories only: H-2A, H-2B, and E-2. Employment Authorization Documents are no longer accepted. DACA recipients and citizens of Mexico or Canada are ineligible for non-domiciled CDLs. States that cannot comply must immediately pause issuance. FMCSA has strongly encouraged states to revoke all unexpired non-compliant credentials. Per the Los Angeles Times, the rule affects nearly 200,000 nondomiciled commercial drivers nationwide — California alone was ordered to cancel approximately 13,000 non-domiciled CDLs.

On the same day this article publishes — March 13 — FMCSA issued a formal bulletin with a blunt headline: "DO NOT Sell, Purchase, or Lease a USDOT Number or Operating Authority (MC Number) online or elsewhere from an unknown person or outside of a legitimate corporate transaction." Per FreightWaves, FMCSA will inactivate USDOT numbers and revoke all related registrations upon discovering improper transfers. The bulletin is tied to the broader crackdown on chameleon carriers — companies shut down for safety violations that reconstitute under new identities — and to the rollout of MOTUS, FMCSA's new registration platform with enhanced identity verification capabilities.

ELD enforcement deadlines are also approaching. FMCSA's second round of ELD revocations — 14 additional devices removed from the registered list on March 4 — carries a compliance deadline of May 4, 2026. After that date, carriers still operating those devices face out-of-service citations under 395.8(a)(1). A prior round (February 12) covering 9 devices has a deadline of April 14, 2026.

On the legislative side, the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee approved Dalilah's Law on March 18 by a 35–26 vote. The bill would require all CDL holders to demonstrate English comprehension, place non-compliant drivers out of service immediately, and strip federal highway funds from states issuing CDLs to illegal immigrants. It also targets foreign dispatch services linked to freight fraud. ATA, TCA, and multiple state trucking associations have issued joint support statements.

FMCSA is also recruiting 18 drivers for a pre-testing phase of two HOS flexibility pilot programs — a Flexible Sleeper Berth program (adding 6/4 and 5/5 split options) and a Split Duty Period program (allowing a 3-hour pause in the 14-hour driving window). Full pilot programs covering 256 drivers each are expected to follow.

Broker Edge

The non-domiciled CDL rule effective March 16 is not an abstract compliance issue — it is a capacity event. Per Marketplace, analysts expect the new restrictions to further tighten trucking capacity precisely as rates are already climbing and diesel is squeezing out marginal operators. As a broker, any carrier in your network operating with non-domiciled CDL holders needs to be verified now. An out-of-service driver mid-haul is your problem too.

The consolidation wave has a direct implication for independent brokers: the entities being built — a $5.4B Echo/ITS platform, a $5B+ Thoma Bravo/WWEX mega-3PL — are making scale plays that will increase their negotiating leverage with both shippers and carriers. Your advantage is speed, relationships, and specialization. Double down on lanes and commodity verticals where large platforms are slow or indifferent.

Fuel surcharge management is critical right now. The EIA's March 9 reading of $4.859/gallon — a record single-week jump of 96¢/gallon — means FSCs negotiated on February averages (41¢/mile per DAT) are already inadequate. Carriers are watching this carefully, and contract freight holders who don't adjust will see rejection rates climb further. Review your FSC tables and carrier agreements this week.

The Midwest is the tightest capacity zone in the country. Flatbed rejections above 40%, van rejections above 18%, and a tornado outbreak on March 10–11 (85 reported tornadoes across Illinois, Indiana, Mississippi, and the Southeast) that disrupted freight corridors compound seasonal tightness. If you're moving flatbed or van freight through the Midwest, build in extra lead time and wider rate brackets on spot coverage.

For South Texas border lanes: the Rio Grande Valley produce season is ramping with Mexico imports up 32% in a single week in late February, per Keynnect Logistics. Laredo-to-Houston reefer lanes are running around $3.00/mile with load posts up nearly 30%. Long-haul loads from McAllen, Pharr, and Laredo to the Northeast are clearing at $6,000–$7,400/load. These lanes have genuine volume if you have reefer capacity relationships in the Valley.

Cross-Border Watchlist

The Laredo corridor remains the backbone of US-Mexico freight. Port-Laredo reported $353.94 billion in international trade volume for 2025 — an increase of $14.94 billion over 2024 — and announced its inaugural Global Trade Summit on March 10, 2026, with USMCA updates as a featured agenda item.
