The USMCA six-year review is the overriding cross-border policy story of 2026. By July 1, 2026, the US, Mexico, and Canada must agree to extend the agreement for 16 years, approve a revised deal, or enter annual reviews leading to expiration in 2036. The Trump administration is expected to push for concessions on auto content rules, minimum wage thresholds, and restrictions on Chinese supply chain involvement. Mexico continues to face 25% IEEPA tariffs on non-USMCA-compliant goods (justified under the fentanyl/migration national emergency declaration) plus 25% Section 232 tariffs on steel and aluminum. Multiple additional Section 232 investigations are active in sectors directly relevant to trucking: timber, copper, medium/heavy trucks, and pharmaceuticals.

Despite the tariff headwinds, nearshoring activity is accelerating. US-Mexico trade is projected to hit $872.8 billion in 2025 as manufacturers continue relocating production from Asia to northern Mexico to reduce supply chain exposure. This creates sustained long-haul freight demand on I-35 and parallel US-Mexico corridors. The flip side: per MexicoBusiness News, Mexico's heavy truck output and exports fell over 50% after the 25% US tariff on trucks, limiting domestic fleet growth south of the border.

On the US-Canada side, Canada has largely aligned with US trade policy on Chinese goods — a relative stabilizer — but cross-border freight operators should monitor USMCA review developments monthly as the July deadline approaches.

Fraud & Security

The NMFTA launched its Freight Fraud Prevention Hub on March 5, 2026 at freightfraudhub.com. The platform offers best practices, fraud basics content, expert webinars, and industry insights tied to NMFTA's SCAC Verified™ carrier identity program. The launch was timed against a staggering backdrop: per ATRI data cited by NMFTA, freight fraud costs the US transportation industry $6.6 billion annually.

The scale of the problem is worsening. CargoNet's 2025 annual report (published January 21) put estimated cargo theft losses at nearly $725 million — a 60% increase from 2024 — with average theft value per incident jumping 36% to $273,990. The Geotab 2026 Blueprint Report, released this week, warns that cargo theft has entered a "new phase" dominated by cybercrime tactics: GPS spoofing, stolen credentials, and AI-powered social engineering. Nearly a quarter of fleet professionals now identify strategic theft — fraud, identity theft, and falsified paperwork — as their greatest threat. Double-brokering-based strategic theft has surged 1,500% since 2021 per CargoNet.

On the FMCSA March 13 USDOT number bulletin: this is directly connected to the chameleon carrier fraud problem. Carriers buying or "inheriting" a DOT number from another entity are acquiring the compliance history, safety rating, and insurance record attached to that number — often fraudulently. As a broker, you are legally exposed if you tender freight to a carrier operating under a fraudulently transferred authority. Verify carrier identity through SAFER, check for recent authority grants (less than 6 months old is a risk flag), and cross-check the carrier's MC number against the USDOT number in FMCSA records before every new carrier relationship.

Legislative momentum is building. Sen. Todd Young's SAFER Transport Act (introduced February 26) would create a Freight Fraud and Theft Advisory Committee under DOT, require FMCSA to flag suspicious registration activity automatically, phase out standalone MC numbers, and increase oversight of foreign dispatch services. The bill has broad industry support from ATA, TCA, OOIDA, and TIA. Michigan's House also passed cargo theft legislation this week that would classify theft as a Class D felony with a 10-year maximum sentence, responding to organized international gang activity in the Detroit area.

Equipment, Fuel & Ops

Diesel crossed $4.859/gallon on the EIA's March 9 weekly reading — a 96¢ single-week jump, the largest on record per the Wall Street Journal. This surge is direct fallout from Iran's threats to tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz following the US-Israeli Operation Epic Fury launched February 28. Crude oil peaked above $120/barrel around March 9 before settling near $100/barrel by March 13, per IRU. Crude tanker transits through the Strait fell to 4 vessels per day from a normal 24/day average, with approximately 200 tankers stranded in the Gulf. IEA members have released 400 million barrels from strategic reserves — enough to offset roughly 20 days of a full blockade.

By the time this article publishes, diesel is approaching $5.00/gallon nationally and has already crossed that threshold in several regions. California is at $6.43/gallon; New England at $5.24; West Coast at $5.55. The EIA has revised its 2026 full-year diesel forecast upward by 20.1% to $4.12/gallon — a forecast that may already be conservative. Pennsylvania carriers told local media their costs are "almost a dollar higher than prior to the onset of the Iran War."

Class 8 truck orders surged in February to 47,200 units — a 47% jump from January and a 159% year-over-year increase, the highest monthly total since late 2022, per FTR. ACT Research attributes the surge to stronger freight rates, improved EPA 2027 regulatory clarity, and an aging tractor population. However, OEM build rates for the first half of 2026 are trimmed to an annualized rate of approximately 220,000 units — production discipline remains the defining theme. Capacity relief from new iron is 12–18 months away at minimum.

Kenworth unveiled the C580 extreme-duty vocational truck at ConExpo (March 3–7 in Las Vegas), replacing the iconic C500 after 50+ years of production. Production begins January 2027. The C580 handles GCW up to 1 million pounds, powered by a Cummins X15 at up to 605 hp/2,050 lb-ft torque — relevant for construction and energy haulers in a flatbed market this tight.

On driver parking: the Trump administration began distributing nearly $500 million in federal grants for truck parking expansion (announced March 4), combining the FY2026 spending bill's historic $200 million dedicated truck parking appropriation with prior funding. Florida, Ohio, and Tennessee are early recipients. The average driver spends 56 minutes daily seeking safe parking — a productivity drag that these funds are beginning to address.

Action Checklist for Brokers

  • Audit your carrier network for non-domiciled CDL exposure before March 16. The FMCSA rule takes effect Sunday. Contact carriers with drivers holding non-domiciled CDLs to confirm compliance status. An OOS driver discovered mid-load is your liability exposure as well as theirs.
  • Rebuild your fuel surcharge tables this week. February's national average diesel was $3.71/gallon. The March 9 EIA reading was $4.859 and climbing. FSCs negotiated on February averages are leaving carriers underwater. Update your tables using current EIA data and communicate changes to shippers proactively — before carriers start refusing loads.
  • Verify every new carrier authority through FMCSA SAFER before tendering. The March 13 USDOT number bulletin is a direct warning about chameleon carriers. Flag any carrier whose authority was granted in the past 6 months. Cross-check MC numbers against USDOT records. Register for alerts on the Freight Fraud Prevention Hub at freightfraudhub.com.
  • Book Midwest flatbed capacity now — don't wait for shipper confirmation. With flatbed rejections near 40% and Midwest L/T ratios above 73, spot coverage on short notice is expensive and often unavailable. Pre-position relationships with flatbed carriers in Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio for April loads.
  • Develop South Texas reefer lane coverage for the spring produce surge. Mexico import volumes through the Rio Grande Valley are up 32% and growing. Laredo-to-Houston is running $3.00/mile. Long-haul Northeast loads are clearing $6,000–$7,400. If you don't have carrier relationships in McAllen, Pharr, or Laredo, now is the time to build them.
  • Check your ELD compliance calendar. April 14 deadline for the 9 ELDs revoked February 12; May 4 deadline for the 14 revoked March 4. Ask your carriers directly — carriers operating on revoked devices after those dates face out-of-service citations and will be off the road with your freight on board.
  • Monitor Strait of Hormuz developments daily. Brent crude at $100/barrel is a moving target. The IEA's 400-million-barrel reserve release buys time but doesn't resolve the supply disruption. Any escalation in tanker traffic restrictions will push diesel toward $5.50+ and force another round of FSC renegotiations. Set up price alerts and have your rate update process ready to execute within 48 hours.

title: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup - March 13, 2026
excerpt: Three M&A deals in 90 days, $5 diesel from the Hormuz crisis, 194,000 drivers exiting under the new non-domiciled CDL rule, and a wave of fraud enforcement actions. Here is what is shaping trucking over the next 3-12 months.
content:
Fleet & Market Trends

Three Deals, One Direction: Brokerage Consolidation Accelerates

Three Q1 2026 acquisitions define where the brokerage market is heading. Echo Global Logistics is acquiring ITS Logistics to build a combined platform with ~$5.4 billion in pro forma 2025 revenue. Thoma Bravo is acquiring WWEX Group (Worldwide Express, GlobalTranz, Unishippers) and merging it with Auctane (ShipStation, Stamps.com) into an AI-enabled end-to-end logistics stack. AI-powered FTL brokerage Fura completed its fifth acquisition, absorbing Barton Logistics. Lincoln International estimates $4 trillion in PE dry powder is targeting fragmented markets — freight brokerage is squarely in range.

What This Means for Independent Brokers

Tech-platform acquirers are absorbing independents — trading AI tools and carrier networks for existing shipper relationships. Logisyn CEO Ron Lentz noted that brokerages now require 8x–10x EBITDA multiples to attract qualified buyers, and that AI is compressing mid-market margins. RSM US projects an uptick in carrier bankruptcies among smaller fleets in 2026. Independents without technology infrastructure are running out of time to invest on their own terms.

Wabash Plant Closures: No Fast Fleet Expansion Ahead

Wabash National announced closures at four plants — Goshen, IN; Little Falls, MN; Perris, CA; Moreno Valley, CA — affecting 300+ workers after reporting revenues down 20% in 2025. Trailer manufacturers are a leading indicator of fleet investment cycles; when new trailer orders collapsed from 2023 through 2025, OEMs rightsized. These closures confirm that no rapid fleet expansion cycle is expected near-term. Source: Trucks, Parts, Service.

Non-Domiciled CDL Rule: 194,000 Drivers Exiting

FMCSA's final rule on non-domiciled CDLs took effect March 16, eliminating Employment Authorization Documents as a CDL eligibility basis. FMCSA projects ~194,000 current CDL holders will exit the freight market as licenses expire and cannot be renewed. The phase-out takes roughly two years, but spot rates are already reflecting anticipated capacity withdrawal. Insurance companies are reportedly refusing to cover carriers with affected drivers, accelerating exits beyond the license-expiration timeline. This structural driver supply reduction will pressurize contract rates in the next bid cycle. Source: FMCSA, TruckSmarter.

Fuel & Cost Pressures

Two Weeks Into the Hormuz Crisis

U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iranian targets in late February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz to oil tanker traffic, forcing production shut-ins in Iraq and Kuwait. By March 9, Brent crude hit $103.47/barrel (+11.6%), with intraday peaks near $119.50; diesel crossed $5 per gallon nationally for the first time since 2022. The EIA's March 10 Short-Term Energy Outlook revised its 2026 average diesel forecast up 20% to $4.12/gallon. The Trump administration authorized 172 million barrels from the SPR; the IEA committed 400 million barrels from member nations. Analysts see prices falling to the $80s if the strait reopens, or $135 Brent if disruption extends. Source: CNBC, EIA.

Carrier Margin Math at $5 Diesel

At 6 mpg, moving from $4.60 to $5.00 diesel adds 6–8 cents per mile against an ATRI all-in benchmark of ~$2.27/mile — eliminating margins on already-thin freight. Fuel is paid at the pump today; revenue arrives 30–45 days later without factoring. A carrier running five loads per week faces $1,500–$2,000 in incremental weekly fuel outlay before any revenue returns. FreightWaves noted that a recovery had appeared within reach before the Hormuz crisis re-opened the margin gap. Source: FreightWaves.

Volvo's $2B North America Commitment; Electric Ramp Continues

Volvo Trucks announced a $2 billion-plus product investment program at TMC 2026 — its largest in North American history — including a $400M upgrade to its Dublin, VA plant and a new $700M Monterrey, Mexico factory starting production in summer 2026. The new VNL platform delivers 10% better fuel efficiency. Tesla, meanwhile, confirmed high-volume Semi production begins this year in Reno, with roughly 200 Semis already delivered to PepsiCo and DHL. Commercial ZEV deployments remain concentrated in California drayage — coast-to-coast electrification is years away. Source: FreightWaves, TipRanks.

Fraud & Security Watch

NMFTA Fraud Hub Launches; SCAC Verified Goes Live

NMFTA launched its Freight Fraud Prevention Hub on March 5, centralizing tools and resources to combat freight crime that costs the industry an estimated $6.6 billion annually — $18 million per day. CargoNet's 2025 analysis found the average cargo theft value rose to $273,990, up 36% year-over-year. The hub's launch coincides with NMFTA's SCAC Verified program (live February 26), which adds identity verification to SCAC applications and creates a trust-signal visible to brokers at tendering — intervening before freight moves rather than after a loss. Source: NMFTA.

FMCSA Issues DOT Number Fraud Bulletin

FMCSA issued a direct warning March 13: do not buy, sell, or lease a USDOT or MC number outside of a legitimate corporate transaction. The consequence is not a fine — FMCSA will inactivate the number and revoke all operating authority. The bulletin targets a market for "aged DOT numbers" that lets buyers skip the 90-day new-carrier waiting period. FMCSA Administrator Derek Barrs cited a carrier network using hundreds of DOT numbers tied to mailbox addresses as the catalyst, and intent is not a defense. The crackdown also includes MOTUS (FMCSA's new registration system) and the purging of 42 non-compliant ELDs from the approved list. Source: FreightWaves.

GenLogs Raises $60M; FreightWaves Fraud Symposium Announced

GenLogs closed a $60 million Series B on February 2, expanding its roadside camera network that captures ~15 million commercial vehicle images per day and monitors 93% of active motor carriers — reading USDOT numbers and trailer logos in real time, recovering 5,000+ stolen loads since July 2024. Because it operates independently of ELD and telematics data, bad actors cannot spoof it. FreightWaves also announced the Freight Fraud Symposium 2026 for May 20 in Cleveland, covering AI deepfakes, zero-trust onboarding, and chameleon carrier identification. Source: FreightWaves, Symposium page.

Technology & Policy

Aurora at 250,000 Driverless Miles; Gatik Achieves Commercial Scale

Aurora Innovation has accumulated 250,000 driverless miles with zero Aurora Driver-attributed collisions across 10 Sun Belt routes, including a Fort Worth–Phoenix lane that exceeds Hours of Service limits. All commercial capacity is committed through Q3 2026; Aurora targets 200+ trucks by year-end. Gatik became the first U.S. company to operate fully driverless trucks at commercial scale — no driver, no observer — under $600 million in contracted revenue. Industry consensus, per the New York Times, is that fully autonomous Class 8 trucking on major highways arrives in 2027. Source: Aurora, Gatik.

Dalilah's Law Passes Committee; FMCSA Opens HOS Pilots

The House T&I Committee passed Dalilah's Law on March 18. Key provisions: English Language Proficiency requirements with immediate out-of-service enforcement; a ban on dispatch services outside North America with a $50,000 minimum civil penalty per incident; state CDL verification mandates backed by federal highway funding penalties up to 12%; and a CDL mill crackdown ending self-certification of training schools. The foreign dispatch ban directly targets the operational structure behind many double-brokering schemes. FMCSA also opened enrollment for HOS pilot programs testing a 3-hour pause on the 14-hour window and flexible sleeper berth splits. Source: FreightWaves, FMCSA.

EPA 2027 Engines, IIJA Cliff, and First-Ever Truck Parking Funding

Daimler's Gen 6 DD13 and DD15 engines, available January 2027, meet EPA 2027 standards via dual-stage SCR — an 82–90% NOx reduction, the most stringent diesel standard in U.S. history; plan for higher 2027 model-year acquisition costs. The IIJA expires September 30, 2026; Congress must pass a new surface transportation bill before that date or risk a $350 billion highway funding cliff. The FY26 appropriations bill included a first-ever $200 million dedicated truck parking appropriation, with Love's Travel Stops adding 1,500 spaces in 2026 — addressing a problem ATRI estimates costs drivers 56 minutes of daily drive time just to find safe parking. Source: DieselNet, ATA.

Bottom Line

Two structural pressures are converging in March 2026: a fuel spike that has erased the margin cushion small carriers were just beginning to rely on, and a regulatory-driven capacity reduction that will take two years to fully register in rates. Three major M&A deals in 90 days confirm that the technology-backed scale race in brokerage is no longer theoretical — independents without automation infrastructure are increasingly acquisition targets rather than competitors. The concentration of fraud and compliance activity — FMCSA's DOT number bulletin, NMFTA's fraud hub, MOTUS, Dalilah's Law — signals that verification standards that were optional a year ago are becoming structural requirements for doing business. The underlying freight market remains positioned for a rate recovery; the question is whether most operators can protect cash long enough to reach it.

title: Weekly Freight Report - March 6, 2026
excerpt: Spot rates hit a 7-month high as tender rejections reach 14.3%—COVID-era levels. Then Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz on Feb. 28, sending diesel above $4.86/gallon in a week. Here’s what brokers need to know.
content:
Market Pulse

The number that defined this week: 14.3%. That is where national tender rejection rates sat in early February — described by Werner Enterprises CEO Derek Leathers as "COVID-level type rejection rates." Two years ago, that number was 5%.

Per DAT data, truckload spot rates posted their seventh consecutive monthly gain in February 2026, extending a streak that began in August 2025. Dry van spot hit $2.41/mile (+$0.09 month-over-month), reefer reached $2.88/mile, and flatbed surged to $2.72/mile (+$0.14). Van rates have climbed 19% since the August 2025 low of $2.03/mile. The spot-to-contract spread has narrowed to its tightest since March 2022. According to ACT Research, spot rates were running more than 20% higher year-over-year in early February, with reefer at roughly 25% YoY gains. Cass Freight Index data implies freight rates improved approximately 9.2% from a year ago. ACT Research is clear this is supply-driven tightening, not demand recovery — structurally leaner capacity after prolonged carrier attrition.

Three named winter storms — Fern, Gianna, and Ezra — drove a 40% surge in spot load postings week-over-week and pushed dry van spot rates up 11 cents in seven days, the steepest weekly move since early 2021, per DAT. Reefer load-to-truck ratio hit 26.8:1 per C.H. Robinson. Midwest tender rejections exceeded 18%, highest since March 2022 per FreightWaves.

Then came Iran. On February 28, joint US-Israeli strikes triggered an IRGC declaration closing the Strait of Hormuz — a passage carrying roughly one-fifth of the world's daily oil supply. By March 9, Brent crude settled at $94/barrel. National average retail diesel hit $4.859/gallon, the largest single-week increase in recorded history per EIA. Diesel topped $5/gallon shortly after — the first time since 2022. FTR's Avery Vise put the carrier cost impact at nearly 14 cents per mile in a single week, pushing fuel cost-per-mile above 69 cents. Unlike 2022, FTR expects this spike to be inflationary for rates rather than a market collapse trigger, given recovering fundamentals.

Regulation & Enforcement

FMCSA moved on multiple fronts this week. The non-domiciled CDL final rule — published February 13, effective March 16 — restricts non-domiciled CDL eligibility to three visa categories (H-2A, H-2B, E-2), eliminating asylum seekers, TPS holders, DACA recipients, EAD holders, and Mexican and Canadian citizens. FMCSA estimates 194,000 current holders will lose renewal eligibility over five years, with future annual issuance collapsing from roughly 200,000 to approximately 6,000 per year. This is a deliberate supply constraint on the driver pool.

On March 4, FMCSA removed 14 ELDs from its registered list — the second wave following 9 revocations on February 12. Replacement deadlines are April 14 (Wave 1) and May 4 (Wave 2). After those dates, drivers on revoked devices get cited and placed out-of-service. Starting April 1, CVSA's updated out-of-service criteria add a dedicated ELD tampering category with a mandatory 10-hour OOS order when rest periods cannot be determined. The 2026 International Roadcheck (May 12–14) will specifically target ELD tampering.

FMCSA's February CDL school sweep — 300+ investigators, 1,426 on-site investigations — resulted in 448 formal notices of proposed removal and 109 voluntary withdrawals. Combined with December 2025 and January 2026 waves, FMCSA has removed more than 7,000 CDL schools, nearly one in five previously listed. The chameleon carrier crackdown, announced February 20 by Secretary Duffy, added physical address verification and 48-hour records availability requirements. At the US Chamber of Commerce's Keep America Moving Summit, FMCSA Administrator Barrs announced nine rulemakings planned for 2026, including broker qualification testing and a full rebuild of CDL school certification.

Broker Edge

The spot-to-contract van spread narrowing to a four-year low means carriers no longer need to discount to the open market. Any contract negotiated before Q4 2025 deserves a review — particularly fuel surcharge provisions. The van FSC averaged 41 cents/mile in February, up from 38 cents in January. That was before the Iran spike. Recalculate FSC tables now, document against EIA data, and notify shippers proactively rather than absorbing the difference.

FMCSA's announced broker qualification testing rulemaking is a direct signal: compliance infrastructure is no longer optional. The SAFER Transport Act (introduced February 26 by Sen. Todd Young) would phase out MC numbers, mandate reporting of ownership changes, and automate fraud flagging in the FMCSA registry. Brokers with documented carrier vetting processes and audit trails will have an easier path to compliance when these rules land.

The Midwest remains the tightest operating region — rejection rates 18%+ versus roughly 5% on the West Coast, per FreightWaves. ISM Manufacturing PMI hit 52.4% in February with New Orders at 55.8% and Backlogs at the highest since May 2022. Interior US freight demand is structural, not seasonal. Build Midwest carrier relationships before you need them.

Cross-Border Watchlist

US-Mexico bilateral trade talks opened the week of March 16 ahead of the USMCA six-year review. Two-way US-Mexico trade hit $872.83 billion in 2025 — making Mexico the US's largest trading partner — with Port Laredo handling roughly $354 billion of that. 80% of USMCA trade moves by truck. The Trump administration has signaled willingness to exit or restructure the agreement, and CSIS has flagged active Section 232 investigations covering medium and heavy-duty trucks, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, copper, and lumber.

Nearshoring continues to accelerate as brands shift production from Asia to Mexico to cut transit times from weeks to days. IRU's North American trucking leadership dialogue in Mexico City on February 24 flagged insufficient border infrastructure as the primary constraint on nearshoring-driven freight growth. Brokers building presence in the Laredo, El Paso, and Nogales corridors are positioning ahead of a structural volume increase that USMCA uncertainty does not eliminate — it just complicates.

On the US-Canada side, Canada's 25% retaliatory tariffs on C$30 billion-plus in US goods remain in force. A 25% tariff on imported medium- and heavy-duty trucks is already in effect under Section 232. More than 85% of Canada-US trade remains duty-free under USMCA exemptions, but the exposed commodity lanes create real pricing volatility for cross-border carriers and brokers.

Fraud & Security

North American cargo theft losses hit an estimated $6.6 billion in 2025, according to Geotab's 2026 Blueprint Report. Confirmed incidents rose 18% year-over-year; average theft value climbed 36% to approximately $274,000 per incident. CargoNet data puts verified 2025 losses at $725 million — up 60% from 2024 — with food and beverage thefts spiking 47% and California accounting for 1,218 of 2,646 incidents.

Geotab flags a qualitative shift: criminals are using GPS spoofing, stolen fleet portal credentials, and AI-powered phishing at scale. WTW identifies the primary 2026 targets for fictitious pickup and double-brokering: electronics, pharmaceuticals, food and beverage, and luxury goods. Nearly a quarter of fleet professionals surveyed identified strategic theft — fraud, identity fraud, falsified paperwork — as their top threat.

The SAFER Transport Act (February 26) and Dalilah's Law (cleared committee March 18) both include freight fraud provisions, with double-brokering enforcement legislation simultaneously hitting the Senate floor. A specific carrier fraud risk this week: CargoNet warned that the non-domiciled CDL enforcement push will expand the pool of distressed, at-risk carriers — creating new acquisition targets for criminal enterprises seeking to absorb FMCSA-registered operating authority. Run full authority verification on every new carrier you add, regardless of how the load was sourced.

Equipment, Fuel & Ops

Diesel is in price shock. The February national average was $3.71–$3.72/gallon per BTS. By March 9, it hit $4.859/gallon nationally; Southern California reached $5.808/gallon. The EIA revised its 2026 annual diesel forecast to $4.12/gallon — a 20% upward revision from its pre-conflict estimate of $3.43. Any fuel surcharge table built before February 28 needs to be updated immediately.

Class 8 truck orders were the equipment story of the month. February came in at 47,200 units per FTR — up 47% month-over-month and 159% year-over-year, the highest single month since September 2022. ACT Research calls it the 8th highest in their 44-year history. The surge reflects EPA 2027 regulatory clarity, sustained rate recovery, and a national fleet past its replacement tipping point. OEMs have pivoted hard away from EV programs — McKinsey reports 42% of BEV programs planned for 2025–2030 were cancelled — with ICE fleets getting extended production timelines.

Driver pay: average OTR rates run $0.62–$0.75/mile, with sign-on bonuses recovering to $5,000–$12,000 for clean-MVR drivers per Drivers 1st. The CDL school purge and non-domiciled CDL restrictions will further tighten the qualified driver pool over the next 12–18 months, supporting continued upward pressure on carrier rates.

Action Checklist for Brokers

  • Audit carrier ELD compliance now. FMCSA revoked 14 more ELDs on March 4, bringing the total removed this quarter to 23. Carriers on revoked devices face out-of-service citations after April 14 and May 4 deadlines. Verify every active carrier against the current FMCSA-registered ELD list before your next tender.
  • Update fuel surcharge schedules. Diesel jumped from a February average of $3.71 to nearly $4.86/gallon by March 9. Recalculate your FSC tables against current EIA pricing and notify shippers in writing with the data behind the change.
  • Tighten new carrier vetting for fraud and CDL risk. CargoNet explicitly warned that distressed carriers losing non-domiciled CDL eligibility are becoming targets for criminal takeover. Run authority age, insurance, and SMS checks on every new carrier. Do not rely on a clean record from six months ago.
  • Build Midwest carrier relationships before Q2 peak. With rejection rates above 18% and ISM manufacturing New Orders at 55.8%, interior US capacity is structurally tight. Identify and lock in reliable carriers in Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, and Michigan now — not when you need them for a load.
  • Review contract rate structures and fuel provisions. The spot-contract spread is the narrowest since March 2022. Contracts locked in before Q4 2025 may have stale rate floors and FSC assumptions. Revisit rate floors, fuel escalators, and fuel basis definitions before the next negotiation cycle.
  • Monitor USMCA developments for cross-border lane exposure. US-Mexico talks are underway with an uncertain outcome. If you have consistent southbound or cross-border volume in automotive, electronics, or industrial goods, identify domestic sourcing alternatives or rerouting options shippers could activate if tariff structures change materially.
  • Document your compliance infrastructure now. FMCSA has announced broker qualification testing as a 2026 rulemaking priority. Start documenting your carrier vetting process, dispute resolution procedures, and bond compliance records. Brokers who already operate to a defined standard will have a much easier path when the rule is finalized.

title: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup - March 6, 2026
excerpt: The Hormuz fuel shock, carrier attrition, nuclear verdict crisis, $6.6B in cargo theft, and the FedEx Freight spinoff are reshaping freight economics. Here's what brokers and carriers need to watch over the next 3-12 months.
content:
Fleet & Market Trends

Driver Shortage Deepens as the CDL Pipeline Narrows

ATA projects a shortage of up to 80,000 drivers by end of 2026, with some analyses reaching 174,000+ once retirement attrition is factored in. Trump administration English Language Proficiency enforcement is generating over 2,000 out-of-service orders per month and could remove nearly 200,000 CDL holders from the active pool, per Bobtail. FMCSA's Safe Driver Apprenticeship Pilot lowers the interstate driving age to 18, but the supply math doesn't work heading into 2027.

Carrier Attrition: Still Contracting, Still Oversupplied

More than 50,000 carrier authorities have exited the market since early 2023, including STG Logistics (Chapter 11, $1B+ in liabilities), 10 Roads Express (2,462 units pulled January 30), and Texas International Enterprises (1,700+ trucks). Despite the purge, the for-hire carrier population still sits 33% above pre-pandemic levels, per Trucking Dive. The Outbound Tender Rejection Index crossed 13% in early February — FreightWaves' threshold for "serious capacity problems" — while truck posts fell 14% year-over-year. ACT Research calls it an "extended correction cycle": contraction is over; profitability recovery remains slow.

FedEx Freight Spinoff Sets a June 1 Launch Date

FedEx filed its Form 10 with the SEC on January 16, targeting a June 1, 2026 spin-off under NYSE ticker "FDXF," per the FedEx Newsroom. The standalone company will be the largest North American LTL carrier — roughly 30,000 vehicles, 39,000 employees, 355 service centers. Independence gives FedEx Freight commercial flexibility but full execution accountability. Brokers with multi-year contracts should expect pricing strategy to shift as the new entity sets its own direction.

Nuclear Verdicts vs. a $750K Federal Minimum — The Math Doesn't Work

FMCSA's 2026 report to Congress put the median nuclear verdict at $51 million — up from $21 million four years ago — while the federal minimum financial responsibility has been $750,000 since 1985, covering less than 1.5% of the median award, per FreightWaves. When carriers price in that risk, capacity exits faster than cycle models predict. A new FMCSA rule (effective January 16, 2026) requires broker security to consist of available assets — cash, letters of credit, or Treasuries — with authority suspension possible within days of a shortfall.

Class 8 Pre-Buy: The 2027 Cost Gap Is Locked In

The EPA 2027 NOx rule — an ~82% reduction to 0.035 g/bhp-hr — survived the Trump GHG rollback and remains binding for model year 2027. Compliant trucks are projected to cost $8,000–$15,000 more per unit; the Section 232 heavy-vehicle tariff adds another ~$9,500, per Overdrive. Fleet Advantage estimates a 100-truck order placed now saves at least $900,000 versus waiting. Late 2026 build slots are already tightening, per ACT Research.

Fuel & Cost Pressures

Strait of Hormuz Shock: The Fastest Diesel Spike on Record

U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iran on February 28, 2026 triggered Iranian targeting of vessels in the Strait of Hormuz — carrying roughly 20% of global oil supply. National average diesel was $3.72/gallon in February, hit $4.66 by March 2, and reached $4.859 for the week ending March 9 — the highest weekly increase on record since federal tracking began in 1994, per FTR's Avery Vise via the Wall Street Journal. Vise: "There will certainly be a lot of small trucking companies that aren't going to survive this surge." How long Hormuz stays disrupted is the key variable for carrier viability over the next 3–6 months.

Refinery Closures Are Making the Fuel Problem Structural

The Iran shock landed on an already stressed supply picture: the EIA projected U.S. distillate inventories would end 2026 at 375 million barrels — the lowest since 2000. LyondellBasell's Houston refinery shut in early 2025; two California refineries totaling 284,000 barrels/day are closing; Valero's Benicia plant idles by April 2026, per BIC Magazine. In 1H 2025, renewable diesel consumption dropped 35%, drawing down petroleum distillate stocks. Diesel could stay elevated through year-end.

Fuel Surcharge Contracts Are Breaking Under the Spike

Carriers are raising both base rates and surcharge percentages simultaneously, compounding shipper costs as volumes decline. Owner-operators absorb the most direct exposure because slow contract repricing cycles mean they eat the spike before passing it through. A bill introduced in March would mandate a fuel surcharge line-item in small carrier contracts guaranteeing direct pass-through, per Heavy Duty Trucking. Any broker contract written before February 28 is likely already out of market.

Fraud & Security Watch

$6.6B in Annual Cargo Losses — and the Threat Is Shifting Online

ATRI estimates cargo theft costs the industry over $18 million per day (~$6.6 billion annualized), per the ATA. CargoNet's 2025 analysis found losses surged to nearly $725 million — a 60% jump from 2024 — with average incident value up 36% to $273,990. Strategic theft — cyber fraud to divert freight — surged 1,475% between Q1 2022 and Q4 2024. AI tools generate convincing fake broker websites; GPS spoofing masks route diversions; phishing harvests load-board credentials. Fuel-stressed environments historically accelerate all of this.

SAFER Transport Act Takes Aim at the Enforcement Gap

Sen. Todd Young (R-IN) introduced the SAFER Transport Act on February 26, 2026, with ATA, OOIDA, and TIA support, per Transport Topics. Key provisions: a mandatory DOT-DOJ fraud referral pipeline, a five-year phase-out of MC numbers in favor of USDOT numbers, a felony bar blocking fraud convicts from operating authority, and automated FMCSA fraud-flagging systems. Nearly one in four brokers reports losing $200,000 to fraud in the last six months, per Truckstop.com — reflecting the enforcement gap the bill targets.

FMCSA Purges 7,000+ CDL Mills; GenLogs and NMFTA Deploy Verification Tools

FMCSA has removed more than 7,000 CDL training providers from the Registry since late 2025, with 448 removals from 1,426 on-site sting operations in a single week, per Commercial Carrier Journal. In parallel, 42 ELDs were delisted and 238 blocked from self-certifying. GenLogs ($60 million Series B, February 2026) monitors 93% of active motor carriers via 1,000+ corridor cameras, recovering over 5,000 stolen loads since July 2024. NMFTA's SCAC Verified ties each SCAC to a verified identity — turning a static code into a fraud-resistant credential.

Technology & Policy

Aurora, Kodiak, and Gatik Are Past the Pilot Stage

Aurora tripled its driverless network to 10 Sun Belt routes on February 11, 2026, logging 250,000+ miles with zero Aurora Driver-attributed collisions, per its press release. Its Fort Worth–Phoenix lane exceeds Hours of Service limits, enabling roughly 50% faster delivery than a single-driver fleet; commercial capacity is committed through Q3 2026. Kodiak AI ended 2025 with 20 driverless trucks generating 10,700+ revenue hours; Gatik has completed 60,000 driverless Walmart orders. NHTSA is building a regulatory framework for vehicles already running commercially.

ConExpo Debuts: Mack Keystone and Kenworth C580

ConExpo (March 3–7, Las Vegas) brought two equipment reveals. Mack unveiled the Keystone — a Class 8 vocational tractor with the MP13 engine (540 hp / 1,950 lb-ft torque) and up to 6% better fuel efficiency than the Pinnacle, taking orders late Q3 2026, per Mack Trucks. Kenworth replaced the C500 (in production since 1972) with the C580 — rated for gross combination weights up to 1 million pounds, with the Eaton Endurant XD Pro automated transmission entering extreme-duty applications for the first time, production January 2027, per Kenworth.

FMCSA MOTUS Launches; Congress Approves First-Ever Truck Parking Funds

FMCSA is rolling out MOTUS — a unified USDOT Registration System — to all carriers, brokers, and freight forwarders in 2026, replacing the legacy process with a single mobile-friendly dashboard featuring Login.gov authentication and identity verification, per FMCSA.dot.gov. The FY2026 appropriations package includes $200 million dedicated exclusively to truck parking — the first-ever standalone federal truck parking funding after years of ATA advocacy. How funds are allocated across corridors will matter for OTR carriers.

Bottom Line

The next 3–12 months are defined by compounding pressure on every front. The Hormuz-driven fuel spike is the most immediate threat — diesel above $4.85/gallon accelerates carrier failures set up by three years of margin compression, with small carriers and owner-operators bearing the most direct exposure. The capacity story was already tightening: driver supply erosion and 50,000+ exits had created conditions for rate recovery; the fuel shock compresses that timeline. The SAFER Act, CDL mill purge, and identity verification tools represent the most coordinated anti-fraud push in years — but criminal sophistication is keeping pace. Operators who navigate Q1–Q2 intact will find the second half of 2026 materially different: capacity tighter, autonomous milestones real, and federal infrastructure being modernized for the first time in decades.

title: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup - February 27, 2026
excerpt: Heading into spring 2026, the domestic trucking market looked less like a clean “rebound” and more like a system with reduced slack: capacity attrition, selective hiring, and equipment aging mean volatility can return quickly when demand or enforcement shifts.
content:
Fleet & Market Trends

Driver recruiting costs climbed even as freight stayed choppy

Carrier recruiting teams headed into 2026 facing a tighter “qualified” driver pool, not just a headcount issue, as enforcement actions and higher hiring standards raised friction in onboarding. According to Transport Topics, Q4 cost-per-hire rose 24% year over year, while equipment issues (32.1%) ranked as the leading retention driver—signaling that fleets that can keep trucks reliable and reduce driver downtime will win seats faster than fleets that only raise pay. Over the next 3–12 months, expect more selective hiring and greater use of recruiting automation, especially in segments where a single safety event can trigger insurance and customer fallout. Key data point: Cost-per-hire increased 24% year over year in Q4 2025.

Capacity attrition set the stage for a faster flip from “loose” to “tight”

Carrier exits and delayed equipment replacement continued to quietly remove slack from the market, increasing sensitivity to any demand pop, weather disruption, or regulatory enforcement wave. FreightWaves argued that the market’s starting point was so saturated that weekly rate charts masked a slow erosion of usable capacity, but that the replacement pipeline is now thin enough that disruptions will hit harder when they arrive. The near-term implication for brokers: plan for more selective carrier acceptance, especially on secondary lanes and weekend coverage, as smaller fleets protect cash flow and reduce unprofitable miles. Key data point: Capacity tightening is being driven by “parked equipment” and delayed replacement cycles, not a single demand surge. (FreightWaves)

For-hire tonnage improved, but the story was “more freight with fewer trucks”

Early 2026 freight metrics suggested modest recovery pockets—particularly industrial and construction-linked freight—while overall market confidence remained cautious. In reporting on ATA’s February results, Transport Topics highlighted that sequential volume gains were likely magnified by lower industry capacity, implying that even modest demand increases can create outsized service variability when carrier networks are lean. For the next 3–12 months, expect better routing discipline from carriers and more shipper pressure to secure committed capacity for predictable lanes. Key data point: ATA’s truck tonnage index reached 116.2 in February. (Transport Topics)

Truck replacement decisions stayed constrained by uncertainty and financing pressure

Equipment cycles remained a strategic lever: fleets that kept delaying replacements risked higher maintenance-related service failures, while buying into uncertainty risked overcapacity. Transport Topics noted that weak early-year Class 8 sales reflected fleets working through tariff and regulatory uncertainty from 2025, even as order activity strengthened into early 2026. This sets up a 3–12 month window where any sustained rate lift could translate into a faster-than-expected equipment and used-truck market shift, but only for well-capitalized operators. Key data point: February Class 8 sales fell 17.4% year over year to 12,992 units. (Transport Topics)

Fuel & Cost Pressures

Diesel economics remained a margin stress-test for small carriers

Fuel stayed a primary volatility channel for both spot pricing and carrier survivability, particularly for small fleets without hedging or bulk-buy leverage. The U.S. Bureau of Transportation Statistics reported February 2026 diesel averaged $3.72/gal, up 5.6% month over month, reinforcing that even “normal” price moves can reprice lanes quickly when capacity is thin. Over the next 3–12 months, expect tighter alignment between fuel indices, surcharge schedules, and carrier willingness to honor contracts on fuel-sensitive lanes (long haul, deadhead-heavy backhauls). Key data point: February 2026 diesel averaged $3.72/gal (+5.6% MoM). (Bureau of Transportation Statistics)

Refinery constraints kept distillate risk elevated into 2026

Refinery closures and constrained distillate supply fundamentals continued to raise the floor under diesel risk, even if demand stayed uneven. The EIA noted that refinery closures contributed to forecasts of low distillate inventories through 2026, with renewable diesel growth only partially offsetting declines in distillate production. For brokers, that means fuel cost shocks can reappear quickly and disproportionately impact regional markets already short on capacity (notably the Gulf and West Coast). Key data point: EIA expects low distillate inventories to persist through 2026. (U.S. Energy Information Administration)

Nuclear verdict exposure continued to drive insurance pricing and underwriting strictness

Insurance remained a structural cost problem rather than a cyclical one, and it directly influences carrier availability for brokers through higher minimum premiums, stricter underwriting, and tighter safety requirements. Land Line summarized ATRI findings that from 2013 to 2022, nuclear verdicts increased in both frequency and median size, with a median verdict of $36 million and a 6% increase in verdicts exceeding $50 million. Over the next 3–12 months, expect carriers to further prioritize “clean freight” customers (predictable appointments, lower claims risk), and expect more carriers to demand stronger contract language around indemnity and claims handling. Key data point: ATRI cited a $36 million median nuclear verdict and a 6% rise in verdicts over $50 million (2013–2022). (Land Line)

Fuel surcharge friction pushed more shippers to re-check index mechanics

As fuel costs stayed volatile, shippers and carriers continued to debate whether standard surcharge tables keep up with real-world pump prices—especially when price swings happen quickly. The practical implication is less about “who’s right” and more about how disputes affect tender acceptance: if carriers perceive surcharge lag, they become more selective or push base-rate resets earlier in bid cycles. For the next 3–12 months, expect more negotiations around surcharge trigger points, regional differentials, and transparency in how FSC is calculated and audited. Key data point: The diesel index is a weekly-moving benchmark, but contractual surcharge tables often lag rapid price moves. (Bureau of Transportation Statistics)

Fraud & Security Watch

SAFER Transport Act elevated freight fraud to a national enforcement priority

Freight fraud and cargo theft shifted from being treated as an operational nuisance to a legislative agenda item as organized schemes expanded (fictitious pickups, double-brokering scams, hostage loads). Truck News reported that Sen. Todd Young introduced the SAFER Transport Act to strengthen federal prevention, detection, and penalties, including tighter CDL issuance and improved oversight of CDL training providers. Over the next 3–12 months, expect more pressure on brokers to prove they have robust carrier identity controls and stronger documentation practices at pickup and delivery. Key data point: The SAFER Transport Act targets freight fraud and cargo theft with enhanced federal oversight tools. (Truck News)

DOT signaled it will use AI and analytics to expand fraud enforcement capacity

Enforcement agencies publicly leaned into AI as a force multiplier for fraud detection and registration integrity, a notable shift given long-standing investigator resource constraints. Overdrive reported DOT leadership plans to use AI and advanced analytics to improve enforcement effectiveness, including identifying trucking fraud and instances of illegal foreign drivers, and highlighted the opportunity to use analytics for faster action on high-risk carriers. For brokers, this suggests the next year will bring more data-driven enforcement actions and faster deactivations of suspicious authorities—raising the value of continuous monitoring rather than one-time onboarding checks. Key data point: DOT described AI as a way to improve fraud enforcement effectiveness and speed. (Overdrive)

“Proof-of-physical-reality” tools emerged as a new anti-theft layer

Technology vendors pushed beyond document checks toward independent verification of trucks, trailers, and locations—important as fraudsters improve impersonation and synthetic identity tactics. Forbes highlighted GenLogs’ approach of using a large camera network and visual recognition to identify trailers and read USDOT numbers, and reported the platform had helped recover more than 5,000 trailers and stolen loads since July 2024. Over the next 3–12 months, these solutions will likely be adopted first for high-theft commodities and high-risk lanes, then broaden as the ROI becomes clearer. Key data point: GenLogs has assisted in recovering 5,000+ trailers and stolen loads since July 2024. (Forbes)

Carrier verification became an “always-on” workflow, not a setup checklist

Double-brokering and identity fraud increasingly exploited gaps between company-level legitimacy and contact-level legitimacy (email, phone, dispatch identity), forcing brokers to harden day-of-load controls. Truckstop emphasized multi-point verification, ongoing behavior monitoring, and stronger onboarding standards as the direction of travel as regulators and industry groups increase pressure. For the next 3–12 months, expect more broker adoption of closed-network load boards, MFA-protected portals, and automated anomaly detection (unexpected reassignments, last-minute contact changes, geofence mismatches). Key data point: Fraud losses are large enough to justify continuous carrier monitoring and stricter onboarding controls. (Truckstop)

Technology & Policy

A federal autonomous trucking framework moved closer to reality

Autonomous freight shifted from a patchwork of state-by-state constraints toward a potential national pathway as Congress explored a new federal framework. FreightWaves reported that the 2026 draft SELF DRIVE Act would authorize limited commercial operations during pilots and create a National Automated Vehicle Safety Data Repository with covered-crash reporting and quarterly revenue-mile reporting. Over the next 3–12 months, the biggest operational impact is likely to be in lane-level pilots (Sun Belt corridors) and in how brokers and shippers structure insurance, reporting, and service-level expectations for mixed human/ADS capacity. Key data point: The draft bill contemplates quarterly reporting of “total miles traveled in revenue service during commercial operations.” (FreightWaves)

FMCSA modernization funding signaled more digital compliance and identity controls

Regulatory agencies continued shifting from paper and legacy systems toward digitally enforced compliance, which raises the importance of data accuracy and system integrations. FMCSA’s FY 2026 budget request emphasized modernization of IT systems, including replacing legacy platforms and improving security and service delivery. Over the next 3–12 months, expect more “system-enforced” compliance (fewer manual workarounds), more focus on registration integrity, and more opportunities for brokers to integrate directly into authoritative data sources for verification and monitoring. Key data point: FMCSA’s budget narrative prioritizes modernizing technology systems and replacing decades-old legacy IT. (U.S. Department of Transportation)

EPA and engine policy uncertainty kept equipment planning complicated

Emissions policy uncertainty remained a planning risk for fleets deciding whether to buy new trucks, hold equipment longer, or invest in alternative fuels. Mansfield Energy reported that EPA rescinded the 2009 endangerment finding (a legal foundation for greenhouse gas vehicle regulation), while noting other rules (including 2027 NOx standards) remained in place. For the next 3–12 months, this mixed signal likely keeps fleets cautious: some will delay purchases awaiting clarity, while others will accelerate replacements to avoid future compliance surprises. Key data point: 2027 NOx emissions standards were described as remaining in place. (Mansfield Energy)

Truck parking pressure stayed a safety and utilization constraint—especially in Texas

Parking scarcity continues to erode driver productivity and raises safety exposure through off-network parking choices, which directly affects on-time performance and hours-of-service planning. A 2026 state-by-state analysis ranked Texas as the worst state for truck parking and cited 1,409 public spaces and 7.6 public spaces per 100 National Highway System miles of roadway. Over the next 3–12 months, expect more shipper and broker scrutiny of appointment windows and detention policies, and more demand for facilities that can support predictable staging and safe parking options. Key data point: Texas was cited at 7.6 public truck parking spaces per 100 NHS miles. (Best Truck Parking)

Bottom Line

Heading into spring 2026, the domestic trucking market looked less like a clean “rebound” and more like a system with reduced slack: capacity attrition, selective hiring, and equipment aging mean volatility can return quickly when demand or enforcement shifts. Cost pressure remained multi-front—diesel moved up month over month, distillate supply risk stayed elevated, and litigation-driven insurance costs continued to shape underwriting and carrier behavior. Fraud moved up the agenda, with legislative momentum (SAFER Transport Act) and federal signals that AI-enabled enforcement is coming, pushing brokers toward always-on verification and anomaly detection. Meanwhile, technology and policy changes—from autonomous pilot frameworks to FMCSA modernization—reinforced a clear theme for the next 3–12 months: data quality and operational discipline will increasingly determine who gets trucks first and who absorbs the most disruption.

title: Weekly Freight Report - February 27, 2026
excerpt: Spot rates eased late February, but capacity stayed tight as load-to-truck ratios rose and truck posts hit a 10-year low for Week 9. For the week of Feb. 22–28, DAT reported $2.39/mi dry van, $2.78 reefer, and $2.66 flatbed.
content:
Market Pulse — spot/contract rates, load-to-truck ratios, capacity

Spot market rates softened at the end of February, but capacity remained tight (especially in flatbed) as load posts rebounded and truck posts hit a multi-year low. For the week of Feb. 22–28 (closest weekly dataset covering Feb. 20–27), DAT’s broker-to-carrier 7‑day average spot rates were $2.39/mi dry van (‑$0.01 WoW), $2.78/mi reefer (‑$0.05), and $2.66/mi flatbed (+$0.03). (The Trucker)

Under the hood, linehaul (excluding fuel) showed the same pattern: $2.04/mi van (‑$0.02), $2.46/mi reefer (‑$0.07), and $2.26/mi flatbed (+$0.02). (The Trucker)

Load-to-truck ratios (LTRs) increased across all three equipment types, signaling demand outpacing posted capacity. DAT reported LTRs of 8.6 (van) (up from 8.4), 15.8 (reefer) (up from 14.1), and 70.3 (flatbed) (up from 57.5). (The Trucker)

Volume and capacity indicators were equally telling: total loads posted to the DAT One marketplace rose to 3.4 million (+6% WoW), while total truck posts fell to 218,916, which DAT described as a 10‑year low for Week 9. (The Trucker)

At the monthly level, February’s pricing trend was still constructive: DAT reported national average February spot rates of $2.41/mi van (+$0.09 MoM), $2.88/mi reefer (+$0.07), and $2.72/mi flatbed (+$0.14). (Yahoo Finance)

Contract pricing firmed modestly in February as well, with DAT citing national average contract rates of $2.52/mi van (+$0.04 MoM), $2.89/mi reefer (+$0.08), and $3.13/mi flatbed (+$0.12). (Yahoo Finance)

Regulation & Enforcement — FMCSA/DOT rules, ELD, CDL, state regs

The biggest regulatory headline around this week’s window was FMCSA’s move to lock in stricter non-domiciled CDL restrictions. FMCSA finalized the rule and indicated it would be published Feb. 13, 2026, with an effective date 30 days after publication, restricting eligibility to certain visa categories (H‑2A, H‑2B, E‑2). (Scopelitis)

From a brokerage perspective, the immediate issue isn’t just compliance—it’s capacity risk. If states tighten issuance practices or revoke improperly issued credentials during audits, some carriers may sideline drivers, especially in high-turnover, spot-heavy networks. (FMCSA regulations page)

FMCSA also continued publishing rulemaking status updates through February 2026, reinforcing that multiple safety and registration modernization initiatives remained in flight. (FMCSA)

Broker Edge — what brokers need to know, competitive positioning

1) Don’t mistake a small WoW rate dip for loosening capacity. Even as van and reefer spot rates edged down late month, LTRs rose and truck posts fell to a decade-low Week 9 level—classic “tight but choppy” spot conditions that punish slow tendering and weak carrier coverage. (The Trucker)

2) Flatbed remained the standout. DAT noted flatbed load posts +10% WoW and equipment posts ‑10% WoW, pushing the flatbed LTR to 70.3. That imbalance is a broker opportunity: win by bundling reliable capacity (not by winning on price) for industrial, construction-adjacent, and project freight. (The Trucker)

3) Use the contract/spot spread to position mid-quarter bids. With February contract van at $2.52/mi vs. spot van at $2.41/mi, the inversion narrowed versus prior years and suggested upward pressure building. For shippers, that’s a reason to secure core carriers; for brokers, it’s a reason to protect margin by tightening accessorial discipline and reducing empty miles. (Yahoo Finance)

4) Operationally, fuel volatility was a near-term risk. DAT flagged that crude price moves typically show up at the pump within 1–2 weeks—meaning March surcharges and all-in rates could move quickly. (The Trucker)

Cross-Border Watchlist — US-Mexico, US-Canada, USMCA, tariffs

Cross-border demand signals remained structurally strong, especially on U.S.-Mexico lanes. February 2026 goods trade between the U.S. and Mexico totaled $73.2B, up 7.1% year over year, according to an analysis citing U.S. Census figures. (T21)

Meanwhile, USMCA’s 2026 review clause became a bigger planning factor for shippers and brokers heading into spring. CSIS highlighted that the governments must decide by July 1, 2026 whether to extend the agreement for another 16 years, and that uncertainty scenarios (including serial annual reviews) could chill investment decisions. (CSIS)

Broker implication: if customers are exposed to Mexico/Canada sourcing, build contingency routing and customs-broker relationships now; if USMCA uncertainty increases, shippers may front-load cross-border moves (helpful for volumes, harder for capacity planning). (CSIS)

Fraud & Security — cargo theft, double-brokering, CDL fraud

Cargo theft and brokerage fraud remained a primary operational risk. In Southern California, law enforcement reported that an investigation spanning December 2025 through February 2026 resulted in recovery of approximately $7 million in stolen cargo and $1 million in currency, with nine arrests. (LASD (Instagram))

Double-brokering and identity-based cargo theft also remained active nationally. In one federal case, a defendant was charged in connection with a double-brokering cargo theft scheme involving items such as 33,750 pounds of frozen snow crabs valued at about $325,000 and other high-value consumer goods. (Overdrive)

Broker takeaway: as enforcement attention rises on non-domiciled CDLs and “bad actor” networks, brokers should assume fraud attempts will concentrate on (a) high-value loads, (b) short-notice recoveries, and (c) lanes with limited carrier density where shippers relax vetting under time pressure. (Scopelitis)

Equipment, Fuel & Ops — diesel prices, truck orders, driver pay

Fuel was trending up into late February. DAT cited a national average on-highway diesel price of $3.81/gal, up 18 cents since the week ending Jan. 27. (The Trucker)

On a monthly basis, the U.S. DOT’s BTS reported the average price for diesel No. 2 was $3.72/gal in February 2026, up 5.6% from January. (BTS (USDOT))

Equipment signals turned sharply positive: North American Class 8 net orders surged in February to roughly 46,200 units (+156% YoY), per ACT Research figures reported by Transport Topics. (Transport Topics)

Operational interpretation: strong orders can be read two ways. In the near term, it suggests big fleets see improving freight fundamentals and want to refresh aging equipment; over a longer horizon, it raises the risk that capacity could rebuild later in 2026 if those orders convert to deliveries quickly. (Transport Topics)

Action Checklist for Brokers — 5-7 bullet points

  • Price the week, not the month: use late-February weekly spot rates (van $2.39, reefer $2.78, flatbed $2.66) plus rising LTRs to avoid under-quoting on tight lanes. (The Trucker)
  • Build a flatbed coverage plan: prioritize core carriers and faster check-calls on flatbed where the LTR hit 70.3. (The Trucker)
  • Re-tighten carrier onboarding: reinforce identity verification and document checks given active double-brokering cases and high-value cargo targeting. (Overdrive)
  • Update theft playbooks for CA hubs: review high-risk facility lists and after-hours protocols in the LA/Inland Empire ecosystem, where authorities reported major recoveries tied to Dec–Feb theft activity. (LASD (Instagram))
  • Audit cross-border exposure: identify customers sensitive to USMCA review uncertainty and prepare alternate routings and customs partners ahead of July 1 decision timing. (CSIS)
  • Watch fuel pass-through timing: incorporate diesel trend signals (DAT’s $3.81/gal late-Feb read; BTS February avg $3.72/gal) into surcharge language and quote validity windows. (The Trucker) (BTS (USDOT))

title: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup - February 20, 2026
excerpt: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup — February 20, 2026: Capacity kept leaking out even as demand stabilized, while diesel and insurance remained the biggest cost multipliers. Fraud enforcement accelerated with the SAFER Transport Act and DOT signals of AI-driven enforcement…
content:
Fleet & Market Trends

Capacity kept leaking out even as demand stabilized

February data continued to point to a slow-burn rebalancing: shipment volumes weren’t surging, but the supply side kept shrinking as marginal fleets exited. Spot Freight’s February market update framed capacity contraction as the “dominant story,” with tender rejections elevated as carriers turned down lower-paying freight. Key data point: trucking employment was down 125,000 jobs (-7.9%) from the 2022 peak, which matters for brokers because fewer available drivers and trucks can tighten coverage quickly once demand improves.

According to Spot Freight, tender rejections were roughly in the low-teens, suggesting carriers were already becoming more selective about freight even before a true recovery.

Carrier failures were no longer “just small fleets”

By early 2026, the attrition narrative expanded beyond single-truck operators: bankruptcy headlines increasingly included mid-sized or diversified logistics names. This matters for routing guides because failures can trigger sudden service disruptions, unpaid invoices, and tighter credit terms across the carrier base. Key data point: multiple notable 2026 filings included STG Logistics and Bulmaks, a reminder that prolonged weak rates plus higher operating costs can break larger operators too.

AltLINE’s running tracker emphasizes that the freight recession and tight credit conditions continued to pressure carriers into 2026 (altLINE).

Workforce demographics kept reinforcing a “replacement” problem

Even when freight is soft, trucking’s labor challenge remains structural: retirements and lifestyle preferences keep the replacement pipeline thin. ATRI highlighted an aging workforce and persistently low female participation as key constraints on long-run driver supply. Key data point: women comprised just 4.1% of truck drivers, underscoring why recruiting strategies are shifting toward under-tapped talent pools.

ATRI’s demographic research points fleets toward more targeted recruiting and retention programs rather than relying on cyclical hiring swings (American Transportation Research Institute).

LTL consolidation continued to reshape pricing power and network options

Shippers and brokers kept dealing with a more concentrated LTL market, where network density and terminal coverage increasingly favor larger platforms. Consolidation can improve service consistency in some lanes, but it can also reduce optionality on bid events—especially for “in-between” volumes that don’t fit core networks. Key data point: consolidation was widely cited as redefining regional capacity and pricing models in 2026, pushing more buyers to revisit mode mix and shipment profiles.

Industry commentary continued to highlight consolidation-driven shifts in competitiveness and rate discipline (GoTrucking.news on LinkedIn).

Fuel & Cost Pressures

Diesel moved up month-over-month, pressuring small fleets first

Fuel remained one of the fastest-moving inputs for trucking economics, with month-to-month changes quickly showing up in carrier acceptance behavior and surcharge discussions. The Bureau of Transportation Statistics reported diesel rising in February versus January. Key data point: average diesel No. 2 was $3.72/gallon in February 2026 (+5.6% vs. January), a move large enough to matter for spot-market decisions on thin-margin lanes.

According to USDOT BTS, diesel was also modestly higher year-over-year, keeping upward pressure on all-in transportation budgets.

Insurance inflation stayed tied to “nuclear verdict” risk

Insurance remained a compounding cost driver because it hits carriers regardless of utilization. Litigation severity and jury awards continue to influence underwriting, deductibles, and whether smaller operators can afford to keep authority active. Key data point: ATRI reported the median nuclear verdict in trucking reached $36 million (2022), a figure that has become a shorthand for why premiums keep climbing.

Industry analysis connecting verdict severity to capacity exits highlights why brokers should expect stricter carrier qualification and more frequent changes in insurance documentation (CXTMS).

Premium pressure persisted even as fleets added safety tech

Even carriers investing in cameras and ADAS are still operating in a hard market for auto liability, where loss trends and verdict risk dominate pricing. Reliance Partners noted that commercial auto liability has been pressured for years and tied part of the rate trajectory to nuclear verdict growth. Key data point: verdicts exceeding $1 million have risen more than 235% since 2012, raising the bar for documentation and safety programs.

Reliance Partners’ FreightWaves-hosted analysis highlights why underwriters increasingly treat safety management as a requirement rather than an option (Reliance Partners).

Fraud & Security Watch

SAFER Transport Act put freight fraud on a legislative fast track

Freight fraud and cargo theft continued shifting from “operations headache” to policy priority, with lawmakers targeting registration loopholes and enforcement coordination. Overdrive reported that Sen. Todd Young introduced the SAFER Transport Act to strengthen prevention, detection, and penalties across the ecosystem. Key data point: the bill would phase out MC numbers within 5 years and transition to USDOT numbers, aiming to reduce identity-based abuse in registration workflows.

Overdrive also noted the proposal would require FMCSA to develop automated systems to flag suspicious activity in registration and operations (Overdrive).

DOT signaled heavier use of AI and analytics to identify fraud patterns

Federal enforcement leaders increasingly described fraud as a data problem—one that can be addressed with pattern recognition, network analysis, and faster rulemaking workflows. CDLLife reported comments from the U.S. DOT Deputy Secretary about using AI to improve enforcement effectiveness, including identifying fraud and illegal driver activity. Key data point: DOT said it plans to use “advanced data analytics” to improve enforcement and identify trucking fraud, foreshadowing more automated screening and investigations.

That posture supports tighter carrier onboarding practices and more aggressive back-end audits over the next 3–12 months (CDLLife).

Bond and penalty proposals kept rising in response to double-brokering losses

While enforcement timelines vary, the direction of travel is clear: larger financial responsibility requirements and bigger penalties are becoming central deterrents. Industry summaries of FMCSA-related proposals emphasized higher bonds and stronger punishment for repeat offenders. Key data point: proposals highlighted increasing broker bond requirements to $150,000 and penalties up to $50,000 per violation, raising the cost of fraud and potentially shrinking the long tail of undercapitalized intermediaries.

One example overview outlining those potential changes is provided by Truck Dispatch Experts.

Technology & Policy

FMCSA’s TechCelerate Now kept pushing ADAS adoption and standards

Safety technology adoption is increasingly tied to both insurance survivability and shipper expectations, especially as verdict risk stays elevated. Transport Topics reported that FMCSA’s TechCelerate Now (renewed for a multi-year second phase) is examining a broader set of technologies beyond core braking and lane systems—including cameras and mirror-replacement vision systems. Key data point: FMCSA renewed TechCelerate Now in 2024 with a four-year Phase 2, suggesting sustained federal focus on tech-enabled safety outcomes through at least 2028.

Transport Topics also noted TMC work on recommended practices around calibration, cybersecurity, and training—areas that can turn tech purchases into measurable safety results (Transport Topics).

Autonomous trucking pilots were expanding on major freight corridors

Autonomous programs continued moving from closed tests into supervised real-freight operations on repeatable lanes, which is where brokers may see capacity “pockets” emerge first. Truck News reported International Motors and Ryder launched an autonomous pilot on a daily 600-mile I-35 corridor route between Laredo and Temple, Texas. Key data point: early pilot findings cited 92% autonomous route coverage, with human safety supervision still in place.

For Texas brokers, I-35 pilots matter because they align with high-volume cross-border and domestic distribution flows (Truck News).

EPA policy volatility added uncertainty, but NOx timelines still mattered

Emissions policy risk remained a planning factor for fleet capex and equipment availability, especially for carriers weighing pre-buy decisions versus waiting for newer engine platforms. Mansfield Energy reported EPA rescinded a key policy underpinning greenhouse gas regulation authority, altering the outlook for certain federal mandates. Key data point: Mansfield reported the 2027 NOx emissions standards remain in place, meaning engine and aftertreatment changes are still a near-term operational reality.

Even with shifting policy, fleets and brokers should expect equipment strategies to stay cautious as manufacturers and carriers manage compliance cost and residual values (Mansfield Energy).

Truck parking funding and shortages stayed a safety-and-productivity constraint

Parking constraints continue to reduce effective capacity by forcing earlier shut-down decisions, increasing HOS stress, and raising crash and cargo-theft exposure. Industry reporting has repeatedly cited a severe mismatch between trucks on the road and legal overnight spaces. Key data point: ATA has estimated roughly one truck parking space for every 11 trucks, a structural bottleneck that won’t resolve quickly even with new grants and private capacity coming online.

One example discussion of the shortage and its safety implications cites that “one space for every 11 trucks” estimate (Keynnect Logistics).

Bottom Line

The February 2026 trucking outlook was defined by a slow tightening of supply rather than a surge in demand, which sets up more volatility once freight volumes improve. Diesel and insurance remained the two cost levers most likely to force small-carrier exits or push rate resets over the next several bid cycles. Fraud risk is moving from “best practice” to “policy priority,” with legislation and AI-driven enforcement pointing toward stricter registration controls and more automated carrier screening. For brokers, the next 3–12 months reward disciplined carrier verification, flexible mode strategy (especially in LTL), and tighter cost-to-serve management as capacity availability becomes less forgiving.

title: Weekly Freight Report - February 20, 2026
excerpt: Market Pulse stayed elevated but choppy during Feb 13–20, 2026 as winter disruption eased while capacity tightened. SONAR’s Pricing Power Index held at 60, and tender rejection rates were rising versus the 2023–2025 baseline.
content:
Market Pulse — spot/contract rates, load-to-truck ratios, capacity

Spot market pricing stayed elevated but increasingly choppy during the week of Feb. 13–20 as winter disruption eased in some lanes while capacity remained structurally tighter than 2025. FreightWaves’ SONAR Pricing Power Index (PPI) commentary in mid-February continued to frame the market as shifting toward carriers (PPI held at 60 in early/mid-February) (SONAR Pricing Power Index archive).

DAT’s winter-period reporting (early-to-mid February) showed national broker-to-carrier spot benchmarks still well above prior-year levels, with dry van in the mid-$2.40s/mile and reefer near the high-$2.80s to low-$2.90s/mile during the early-February storm window (Blue Book (citing DAT Trendlines)). As conditions normalized into mid-February, third-party summaries referencing DAT linehaul averages indicated van linehaul around $2.06/mile, reefer linehaul around $2.53/mile, and flatbed linehaul around $2.24/mile (all excluding fuel) (TruckersReport summary (citing DAT/FTR)).

Load-to-truck ratios remained the clearest signal of tightness. In the late-February DAT week that followed, DAT cited a van load-to-truck ratio of 8.6, a reefer load-to-truck ratio of 15.8, and a flatbed load-to-truck ratio of 70.3—levels consistent with a market that was already tightening coming out of the Feb. 13–20 week (The Trucker (citing DAT)).

On the contract side, January-to-February commentary from industry advisors showed contract pricing stabilizing modestly higher, with cited all-in contract levels around $2.48/mile (dry van), $2.81/mile (reefer), and $3.04/mile (flatbed) (Spot Freight market update).

  • Capacity: Tender rejection rates were no longer “dead-flat.” A SONAR/Ryder report referenced by Trucking Dive noted tender rejection rates rising to ~14.3% in early February and remaining elevated versus the ~5% levels common across 2023–2025 (Trucking Dive).
  • Mode notes: Flatbed continued to act “tighter” than van/reefer, consistent with SONAR flatbed rejection and spot strength later in February (SONAR Pricing Power Index archive).

Regulation & Enforcement — FMCSA/DOT rules, ELD, CDL, state regs

The most consequential regulatory development for the Feb. 13–20 week was FMCSA’s non-domiciled CDL action. FMCSA published its final rule on Feb. 13, 2026, tightening eligibility and standardizing issuance; the agency’s guidance emphasizes that states must pause issuance if they cannot comply (FMCSA Non-Domiciled CDL Final Rule FAQs). The rule was set to take effect March 16, 2026, creating near-term uncertainty for fleets that rely on non-domiciled drivers (FMCSA).

For brokers, the compliance takeaway was straightforward: verify carrier eligibility and credentials more rigorously—especially for cross-border and high-fraud lanes—because capacity and onboarding friction can tighten quickly when licensing rules shift (Land Line Media).

  • FMCSA pipeline: FMCSA leadership signaled a busy 2026 rulemaking calendar and broader enforcement focus on unsafe carriers, CDL mills, and fraud-related items (Land Line Media).
  • State impacts: Cross-border operators also watched provincial changes, including Quebec’s mandatory Class 1 driver training program that began in early 2026, which could constrain capacity into spring (C.H. Robinson cross-border update (Feb 2026)).

Broker Edge — what brokers need to know, competitive positioning

The Feb. 13–20 week sat in an “inflection zone”: rates were still elevated from winter volatility, but SONAR tender rejection data and broker anecdotes increasingly pointed to a carrier-favoring shift rather than a short-lived weather spike (SONAR PPI archive; Trucking Dive).

For American Lady Transportation, the competitive edge in that environment was less about blasting cheap capacity and more about execution reliability:

  • Reprice faster than weekly: Use mini-bids (2–4 weeks) in regions where rejections rise fastest (Midwest winter lanes were cited as exceptionally tight earlier in February) (Trucking Dive).
  • Separate linehaul from fuel: EIA diesel moved up through February (see fuel section), so keep surcharge language explicit and current (EIA weekly diesel series).
  • Lean into flatbed specialization: Flatbed ratios in the 50–70 range around this period implied meaningful tightness versus vans (~8–9) (The Trucker (citing DAT)).

Cross-Border Watchlist — US-Mexico, US-Canada, USMCA, tariffs

U.S.–Mexico: Early-2026 cross-border indicators remained constructive, with C.H. Robinson noting that Mexico finished 2025 strong and that non-automotive manufacturing exports (electronics/machinery) were driving growth into 2026 (C.H. Robinson cross-border update (Feb 2026)). This mix matters for brokers because electronics-heavy supply chains typically demand tighter appointment compliance and higher security protocols.

U.S.–Canada: Canada’s official February trade release showed a sharp increase in activity: imports +8.4% and exports +6.4% month over month, with motor vehicles and parts rebounding strongly in exports (Statistics Canada (Feb 2026 trade)). Imports from the United States rose 13.6% while exports to the United States rose 4.4%, narrowing Canada’s trade surplus with the U.S. to $1.7B (Statistics Canada).

USMCA: Businesses were increasingly focused on the 2026 review window and the uncertainty it can create for capital spending and sourcing decisions, with cross-border commentators flagging “wait and see” behavior on some investment categories (C.H. Robinson cross-border update (Feb 2026); Talking Logistics).

Fraud & Security — cargo theft, double-brokering, CDL fraud

Freight fraud and cargo theft remained a front-burner operational risk. An industry legal briefing cited American Transportation Research Institute estimates that cargo theft represented ~$6.6B annually in 2025 (about $18M/day), and that “strategic theft” (identity/cyber-enabled diversion) was up 1,500% since 2021 (Amundsen Davis (citing ATRI)).

Double-brokering schemes continued to surface in federal actions; Overdrive later detailed an alleged double-brokering cargo theft conspiracy involving high-value goods (including frozen seafood and designer products), illustrating how email impersonation and identity spoofing remain common tactics (Overdrive).

  • Fraud posture for the week: Treat “tight market” signals as fraud accelerants—when capacity tightens, criminals exploit urgency and rate pressure to bypass vetting.
