  • Operational control: Require a second-channel identity confirmation (carrier phone + insurance cert + FMCSA profile cross-check) on any first-time carrier, especially for reefer and electronics loads (Amundsen Davis (citing ATRI)).

Equipment, Fuel & Ops — diesel prices, truck orders, driver pay

Diesel moved higher through the heart of February. EIA’s weekly U.S. on-highway diesel series shows $3.688/gal (Feb. 9), $3.711/gal (Feb. 16), and $3.809/gal (Feb. 23), implying rising fuel surcharge pressure through and immediately after the Feb. 13–20 week (EIA weekly diesel series).

Equipment demand accelerated. ACT and FTR-based reporting showed February Class 8 orders surging to roughly 46,200–47,200 units, up roughly ~156–159% year over year—an indicator fleets believed rate improvement might persist and that some pre-buy behavior was forming ahead of future regulatory cost steps (ACT Research Class 8 blog; Trucks, Parts, Service).

Ops implication: Higher diesel plus rising orders often translate into tougher carrier rate conversations (carriers seek to protect margins while also funding replacement cycles). Brokers should assume faster cost pass-through in March than they saw in 2025.

Action Checklist for Brokers — 5-7 bullet points

  • Re-benchmark weekly: Track van/reefer/flatbed spot and linehaul separately; don’t assume storm-era pricing holds once networks normalize (The Trucker (citing DAT)).
  • Watch rejection velocity: If tenders stay in the low-to-mid teens nationally, treat it as a “real” tightening cycle, not noise (Trucking Dive).
  • Fuel-surcharge discipline: Update FSC tables weekly; EIA diesel rose from $3.688 to $3.711 during the week’s window (EIA weekly diesel series).
  • Prepare for CDL-related friction: Audit carrier onboarding steps for non-domiciled CDL compliance risk ahead of the March 16 effective date (FMCSA).
  • Raise security on high-value freight: Apply multi-factor carrier verification; strategic theft is up 1,500% since 2021 per ATRI estimates (Amundsen Davis (citing ATRI)).
  • Cross-border lane planning: Expect volatility tied to Canada winter conditions and Mexico’s shifting export mix toward electronics/machinery (C.H. Robinson cross-border update (Feb 2026)).

title: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup - February 13, 2026
excerpt: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup — February 13, 2026: Carrier attrition is tightening capacity, but demand is still the trigger for a sustained rate recovery. Diesel rose in February, refinery and distillate dynamics keep volatility risk al
content:
Fleet & Market Trends

Carrier attrition keeps tightening capacity — but demand is the missing spark

Across 2025 into early 2026, the U.S. for-hire market continued to shed carriers, pushing the industry closer to a “floor” in available capacity — a setup that can reprice quickly if freight demand improves later in 2026. Analysts have framed the next 3–12 months as a balancing act: capacity has already thinned materially, yet sustained rate recovery still depends on volumes turning up. Key data point: FMCSA-authority counts for property carriers were reported as down more than 11% from December 2022 to December 2025, highlighting how long the shakeout has run ([TruckersReport](https://www.thetruckersreport.com/news/trucking-capacity-bottomed-2026-hinges-freight-demand/)).

Fleet failures are no longer “small-carrier only” as credit stays tight

Industry commentary entering 2026 continued to emphasize that elevated financing costs and stubborn operating expenses can push even mid-sized fleets into restructuring, not just single-truck operators. For brokers, this translates into more abrupt service disruptions and a greater need for multi-carrier backup coverage on contracted lanes. Key data point: industry analysts have estimated 5,000–8,000 trucking companies effectively exited in 2025 (definition-dependent), underscoring how deep the shakeout has been ([Luna Logistics](https://lunalogistics.net/carrier-bankruptcies-freight-capacity-crisis-2025/)).

LTL network reshaping continues as former Yellow terminals get redeployed

The LTL sector’s post-Yellow recalibration remained a live issue heading into 2026, with large carriers and real-estate buyers taking pieces of the former terminal footprint — a trend that can change linehaul density, service maps, and LTL pricing discipline over the next year. For shippers, the practical takeaway is that service coverage and accessorial practices can change as networks rebalance. Key data point: Yellow operated 169 terminals (and leased 142) at the time it shut down in July 2023, making its footprint meaningful enough that its breakup still matters for market structure ([Transport Topics](https://www.ttnews.com/articles/yellow-terminals-sale-court)).

Workforce demographics: the “replacement pipeline” problem is getting harder to ignore

ATRI research has continued to spotlight a demographic shift: an aging driver population alongside low representation of women, pushing fleets to rethink recruiting and retention programs. Over the next 3–12 months, expect more targeted outreach (nontraditional candidates, new training pathways) as fleets compete for fewer experienced applicants. Key data point: ATRI noted women comprise about 4.1% of truck drivers, reinforcing how much labor supply is still “untapped” ([ATRI](https://truckingresearch.org/2025/07/new-atri-research-highlights-evolving-truck-driver-demographics/)).

Fuel & Cost Pressures

Diesel economics: a winter uptick is a reminder budgets can swing fast

Diesel moved higher early in 2026, a reminder that even modest month-to-month changes can ripple through linehaul pricing, fuel surcharge tables, and carrier cash flow. For the next 3–12 months, the planning challenge is volatility: spot fuel spikes can quickly stress smaller fleets and create mid-contract pricing disputes. Key data point: average No. 2 diesel was $3.72 in February 2026, up 5.6% from January 2026 ([Bureau of Transportation Statistics](https://www.bts.gov/newsroom/motor-fuel-prices-february-2026-0)).

Refinery capacity and distillate inventories: structural tightness is the quiet risk

U.S. distillate supply remains a strategic watch item for trucking because refinery closures and inventory dynamics can keep diesel markets sensitive to disruptions. Even if pump prices stabilize, the next year’s risk profile still includes higher “tail risk” volatility during outages or demand surges. Key data point: EIA has pointed to refinery closures as a factor behind low distillate inventories through 2026 ([EIA Today in Energy](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=66124)).

Alternative fuels: renewable diesel growth helps, but the buildout is uneven

Renewable diesel capacity expansion continues, but updated projections have suggested the near-term ramp may be slower than earlier expectations — which matters for fleets hoping RD displaces meaningful diesel volume quickly. Over the next 3–12 months, availability by region and price spreads (plus RIN economics) will likely determine adoption more than intent. Key data point: updated estimates projected 22 renewable diesel plants in operation by the end of 2026 ([farmdoc daily](https://farmdocdaily.illinois.edu/2024/11/updated-estimates-of-the-production-capacity-of-u-s-renewable-diesel-plants-through-2026.html)).

Insurance and “nuclear verdict” exposure keeps pressure on small fleets’ operating costs

Liability severity remains a major cost driver in trucking, feeding into premium increases and stricter underwriting — and, indirectly, into the carrier exits brokers have been managing through the freight downturn. The next year’s practical impact: tighter carrier qualification filters (experience, safety programs, camera/telematics adoption) and higher all-in rates on riskier freight. Key data point: FreightWaves highlighted FMCSA’s focus on the gap between legacy insurance minimums and modern liability realities, underscoring why the topic won’t fade quickly ([FreightWaves](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/fmcsa-spotlights-truckings-multi-million-dollar-insurance-gap)).

Fraud & Security Watch

Washington turns up the heat: SAFER Transport Act puts freight fraud on the policy agenda

Freight fraud and cargo theft have become visible enough that federal lawmakers are proposing broader enforcement and tighter registration/credential controls, signaling more compliance scrutiny in 2026. For brokers, the most important effect over the next 3–12 months may be behavioral: more shipper questions about verification controls and more carrier skepticism about counterparties. Key data point: the SAFER Transport Act was introduced Feb. 26, 2026 ([Sen. Todd Young press release](https://www.young.senate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/young-introduces-bill-to-protect-american-roads-and-supply-chains/)).

Double-brokering prevention shifts from “best practice” to a compliance expectation

Industry guidance around double-brokering prevention increasingly emphasizes faster access to transaction records and stricter financial responsibility checks — tools meant to reduce nonpayment events and hidden rebrokering. In the next 3–12 months, expect carriers to request clearer documentation and faster confirmations, and expect shippers to ask brokers how they validate “who is actually hauling.” Key data point: updated rules discussed in industry guidance highlight a 48-hour requirement for brokers to provide electronic transaction records upon request ([Truckstop](https://truckstop.com/blog/double-brokering-prevention-strategies-under-new-fmcsa-rules/)).

Carrier identity and verification platforms move to the center of brokerage risk controls

Verification tools are evolving from static compliance checks into ongoing monitoring (authority status, ownership structure flags, and identity signals) that help reduce impostor-carrier risk. Over the next year, brokers that operationalize “verify at tender + verify at pickup” workflows will be better positioned as enforcement and shipper expectations rise. Key data point: Central Dispatch’s carrier scorecard highlights warnings/flags like inactive status and outdated filings inside the dispatch workflow ([Cox Automotive](https://www.coxautoinc.com/insights-hub/central-dispatch-takes-carrier-verification-to-next-level-with-launch-of-carrier-scorecard-boosting-vehicle-shipping-security-and-transparency/)).

AI fraud detection becomes practical: automate screening, alerting, and faster blocks

As fraud tactics scale, broker operations are increasingly pairing carrier vetting databases with automated document checks and anomaly alerts to reduce manual workload and shorten response time. In the next 3–12 months, expect wider adoption of automated “carrier packet + identity confidence” tooling, especially for spot-market coverage. Key data point: Highway described workflows where automated carrier screening and real-time alerts reduce manual effort and speed fraud response ([Highway](https://highway.com/posts/how-fleetworks-ai-powered-solution-is-combating-freight-fraud-with-highway)).

Technology & Policy

Autonomous trucking: Texas pilots set up 2026 as a scale year on select lanes

Autonomous linehaul remains corridor-specific, but 2026 is shaping up as a transition year from limited demonstrations toward broader commercial operations in the Sun Belt. For brokerages, the near-term relevance is lane strategy: consistent, repeatable freight flows on AV-friendly highways may begin to see new capacity options and new shipper questions about safety, liability, and service-level design. Key data point: industry commentary has described Aurora’s plan to field “hundreds” of driverless trucks by the end of 2026 ([LinkedIn analysis](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/hundreds-driverless-trucks-2026-what-auroras-plan-really-ycymc)).

FMCSA tech modernization: TechCelerate Now pushes safer adoption of ADAS and connected systems

FMCSA’s TechCelerate Now program is influencing how fleets evaluate and deploy safety technology, including collision warning and camera system standards and related cybersecurity considerations. Over the next 3–12 months, brokers may see more carriers using ADAS-driven safety narratives to compete for freight and insurance terms. Key data point: Transport Topics noted TechCelerate Now was renewed in 2024 for a four-year second phase ([Transport Topics](https://www.ttnews.com/articles/tmc-pushes-techcelerate-now)).

Truck parking: capacity is still far behind demand, increasing service risk and compliance friction

The ongoing shortage of safe truck parking remains a service reliability issue: drivers lose time searching for parking, and parking scarcity can amplify detention, hours-of-service constraints, and safety risk. Over the next year, shippers and brokers should expect more location-specific problems (metro areas, corridors) and more emphasis on appointment discipline. Key data point: national inventories cited about 313,000 truck parking spaces — roughly one space per 11 truck drivers ([Parking & Mobility Magazine](https://parking-mobility-magazine.org/online-exclusive/bridging-the-truck-parking-gap/)).

Bottom Line

The February 2026 picture is a market that has already “bled off” a lot of excess capacity, but where a durable upcycle still hinges on freight demand improving later in 2026. Diesel and insurance remain the two cost levers most likely to force additional fleet exits or harder underwriting, which can tighten capacity faster than shippers expect. Meanwhile, freight fraud has become a board-level risk topic, pushing verification, transaction transparency, and AI-enabled screening from optional to expected. The operational winners over the next 3–12 months will be brokerages that combine disciplined carrier sourcing with modern identity controls and tighter fuel/contract playbooks.

title: Weekly Freight Report - February 13, 2026
excerpt: Spot rates stayed elevated into early February as winter disruptions tightened capacity. In DAT’s week covering Feb. 1–7, broker-to-carrier national average spot rates were $2.45/mi dry van, $2.94/mi reefer, and $2.58/mi flatbed.
content:
Market Pulse — spot/contract rates, load-to-truck ratios, capacity

Spot rates stayed elevated into early February as winter disruptions tightened capacity. In DAT’s week covering Feb. 1–7, broker-to-carrier national average spot rates were $2.45/mi dry van, $2.94/mi reefer, and $2.58/mi flatbed, with linehaul (excluding fuel) at $2.08/mi van, $2.57/mi reefer, and $2.21/mi flatbed ([Blue Book](https://www.bluebookservices.com/dat-spot-truckload-rates-continued-to-strengthen/)).

Volume remained strong on load boards even with normal seasonal churn: DAT reported 3.7 million total loads posted for that same week (down 1% w/w), while truck posts were 217,734 (up 2% w/w, but 14% lower y/y), signaling a tighter carrier side of the marketplace ([Blue Book](https://www.bluebookservices.com/dat-spot-truckload-rates-continued-to-strengthen/)).

Under the hood, equipment-specific activity showed mixed signals: van loads were 1.65 million (-3% w/w) vs. 154,611 van equipment posts (+2% w/w); reefer loads were 942,472 (-10% w/w) vs. 36,670 reefer equipment posts (+3% w/w); and flatbed loads were 1.1 million (+10% w/w) vs. 22,434 flatbed equipment posts (+2% w/w) ([Blue Book](https://www.bluebookservices.com/dat-spot-truckload-rates-continued-to-strengthen/)).

Lane-level tightness mattered more than the national average. DAT noted the average spot van rate across its top 50 lanes by volume was $2.32/mi and that the Midwest (13 states representing ~45% of national load volume) averaged $2.58/mi after a 19-cent week-over-week jump ([Blue Book](https://www.bluebookservices.com/dat-spot-truckload-rates-continued-to-strengthen/)).

Reefer markets began to show early “Valentine’s Day” behavior. DAT highlighted capacity shortages in California produce regions, with reported spot prices to East Coast markets averaging $8,300–$9,000 per load (roughly $2.65–$2.88/mi on ~3,100-mile runs), consistent with seasonal produce pressure and fewer available trucks in the West ([Blue Book](https://www.bluebookservices.com/dat-spot-truckload-rates-continued-to-strengthen/)).

On contract dynamics, early-2026 reporting pointed to a narrowing spread between spot and contract pricing, a classic sign of rebalancing. In DAT’s February 2026 monthly view (released later), national average rates were reported at $2.41/mi spot van vs. $2.52/mi contract van, and $2.88/mi spot reefer vs. $2.89/mi contract reefer, with the spot-to-contract van gap described as the smallest since March 2022 ([Blue Book](https://www.bluebookservices.com/dat-truckload-spot-rates-post-seventh-straight-monthly-gain-in-february/)).

Capacity indicator to watch: FreightWaves’ SONAR data later showed the Truckload Rejection Index (STRI) peaking at 14.27% on Feb. 5 and remaining historically elevated into February, indicating that contract compliance was still stressed and spot opportunities would persist on disrupted lanes ([FreightWaves](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/truckloads-tightness-persists-into-spring)).

Regulation & Enforcement — FMCSA/DOT rules, ELD, CDL, state regs

The regulatory backdrop for this week was less about brand-new rules and more about enforcement momentum and near-term compliance changes that would affect carrier availability and onboarding.

Non-domiciled CDL tightening was moving toward implementation. FMCSA later published detailed FAQs tied to a February 13, 2026 final rule with a March 16, 2026 effective date, emphasizing that States not ready to comply should pause issuance of non-domiciled CLPs/CDLs until they can meet the clarified standards ([FMCSA](https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/regulations/non-domiciled-cdl-2026-final-rule-faqs)).

ELD enforcement risk was rising. FMCSA’s ELD News and Events page documented removals from the registered ELD list on Jan. 13, 2026 and continued device enforcement actions into 2026, reinforcing the need for carriers to confirm device status and avoid hours-of-service exposure ([FMCSA ELD](https://eld.fmcsa.dot.gov/support/newsandevents)).

Broker takeaway: As enforcement tightens around credentials and electronic compliance, expect more carriers to be “temporarily sidelined” during audits, upgrades, or state-level processing delays—especially smaller fleets that run older technology or weaker documentation processes.

Broker Edge — what brokers need to know, competitive positioning

1) Price volatility was being driven by supply constraints, not a demand boom. The week’s DAT data showed strong load posting and comparatively low truck posting—an environment where daily market swings can be sharp when weather or produce surges hit ([Blue Book](https://www.bluebookservices.com/dat-spot-truckload-rates-continued-to-strengthen/)).

2) Protect margin with lane-level discipline. National averages hid meaningful dispersion: Midwest dry van pricing and California produce outbound moves were materially higher than baseline lanes, so quoting “national” benchmarks risked underpricing in tight pockets ([Blue Book](https://www.bluebookservices.com/dat-spot-truckload-rates-continued-to-strengthen/)).

3) Watch the spot-to-contract spread. When spot pricing rises toward contract (as DAT later described for February), shippers become more sensitive to service failures and tend to accept tighter contractual terms—creating opportunities for brokers who can quantify performance and secure committed capacity ([Blue Book](https://www.bluebookservices.com/dat-truckload-spot-rates-post-seventh-straight-monthly-gain-in-february/)).

4) Use “capacity narrative” in shipper conversations. SONAR tender rejections staying elevated after the Feb. 5 peak signaled that carriers still had leverage on imperfectly balanced lanes, and that rapid coverage (not just low rate) was the differentiator for brokers ([FreightWaves](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/truckloads-tightness-persists-into-spring)).

Cross-Border Watchlist — US-Mexico, US-Canada, USMCA, tariffs

Cross-border freight remained a bright spot for surface transportation strategy, but policy and compliance risk was increasing.

Mexico remained the top U.S. trading partner in February 2026: total two-way goods trade was reported at $73.2B, up 7.1% year over year, with Canada down 8.9% at $57.5B in the same period (using U.S. Census Bureau data summarized by T21) ([T21](https://t21.us/mexico-maintains-its-trade-advantage-over-the-us-in-february/)).

USMCA process and tariff noise were back in the headlines. A trade-law update noted the Senate Finance Committee scheduled a public hearing on the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement for Feb. 12, 2026, reinforcing that North American trade policy was again an active variable for shippers with cross-border exposure ([Sandler, Travis & Rosenberg](https://www.strtrade.com/trade-news-resources/str-trade-report/trade-report/february/legislative-update-tariffs-preference-programs-usmca-duty-refunds-imports)).

Operational implication for brokers: Treat border freight as a compliance product—tight carrier vetting, document discipline, and contingency routing—because policy uncertainty tends to increase inspection intensity and documentation errors.

Fraud & Security — cargo theft, double-brokering, CDL fraud

Freight fraud and cargo theft stayed a top risk theme for 2026, and brokers should assume bad actors will target periods of tight capacity and fast-moving spot volume.

A February 2026 legal alert cited ATRI research estimating cargo theft losses at $6.6B annually in 2025 (about $18M/day) and noted “strategic theft” (blending cyber and identity methods) was up 1,500% since 2021 ([Amundsen Davis](https://www.amundsendavislaw.com/alert-combatting-cargo-theft-and-organized-crime-strategies-for-trucking-and-logistics-companies)).

In Congress, Senator Todd Young introduced the SAFER Transport Act on Feb. 26, 2026, describing provisions aimed at freight fraud tactics such as fictitious pickups and double brokering, plus changes to registration controls and CDL-related oversight ([CDLLife](https://cdllife.com/2026/bill-seeks-to-fight-freight-fraud-tactics-including-double-brokering-and-hostage-loads-within-trucking-industry/)).

Broker posture for this week: assume identity-based fraud attempts rise as spot rates rise, and ensure every “new carrier” onboarding step is auditable (authority verification, insurance confirmation directly with agent, and in-network behavioral flags).

Equipment, Fuel & Ops — diesel prices, truck orders, driver pay

Fuel: Diesel prices were climbing through early February. EIA’s weekly U.S. on-highway diesel series shows $3.681/gal for the week of Feb. 2, 2026 and $3.688/gal for the week of Feb. 9, 2026 ([EIA](https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/LeafHandler.ashx?n=pet&s=emd_epd2d_pte_nus_dpg&f=w)).

Because spot rates are typically quoted “all-in,” rising diesel tends to flow rapidly into total linehaul+fuel pricing and can narrow broker margin if contract surcharges lag or if customers resist mid-cycle accessorial updates.

Equipment: While outside the exact Feb. 6–13 week window, equipment demand signals strengthened around the same period. Industry reporting on preliminary February results put North American Class 8 net orders at roughly 47,200 units (FTR estimate) and 46,200 units (ACT estimate), up roughly ~150% y/y, reflecting replacement demand and expectations of higher regulatory-related equipment costs ahead ([Trucks, Parts, Service](https://www.truckpartsandservice.com/trucks-trailers/class-7-8/article/15818707/class-8-commercial-truck-orders-exceed-47k-units-february-2026), [Truckinginfo.com](https://www.truckinginfo.com/news/ftr-reports-class-8-truck-orders-surged-in-february)).

Macro demand: The Cass Freight Index for February 2026 reported shipments down 7.2% y/y but up 10.4% m/m, while expenditures were up 2.1% y/y, indicating that even with softer volumes, higher rates and fuel were pushing spend upward ([Cass Information Systems](https://www.cassinfo.com/freight-audit-payment/cass-transportation-indexes/february-2026)).

Action Checklist for Brokers

  • Quote with lane context: validate Midwest and produce outbound pricing vs. “national averages” before committing to fixed quotes ([Blue Book](https://www.bluebookservices.com/dat-spot-truckload-rates-continued-to-strengthen/)).
  • Reconfirm capacity daily on weather-sensitive lanes when tender rejections remain elevated after early-Feb peaks ([FreightWaves](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/truckloads-tightness-persists-into-spring)).
  • Audit fuel surcharge logic against EIA weekly diesel movements (Feb. 2: $3.681; Feb. 9: $3.688) to prevent margin leakage ([EIA](https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/LeafHandler.ashx?n=pet&s=emd_epd2d_pte_nus_dpg&f=w)).
  • Harden fraud controls: treat new-carrier onboarding as a security workflow; prioritize direct insurance verification and pickup identity checks ([Amundsen Davis](https://www.amundsendavislaw.com/alert-combatting-cargo-theft-and-organized-crime-strategies-for-trucking-and-logistics-companies)).
  • Cross-border playbook refresh: ensure USMCA documentation and shipper instructions are current ahead of policy hearings and potential enforcement shifts ([Sandler, Travis & Rosenberg](https://www.strtrade.com/trade-news-resources/str-trade-report/trade-report/february/legislative-update-tariffs-preference-programs-usmca-duty-refunds-imports)).
  • Carrier compliance screening: confirm ELD status and watch for credential changes that could sideline drivers as FMCSA guidance evolves ([FMCSA ELD](https://eld.fmcsa.dot.gov/support/newsandevents), [FMCSA](https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/regulations/non-domiciled-cdl-2026-final-rule-faqs)).

title: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup - February 6, 2026
excerpt: Going into early 2026, trucking’s most strategic theme is that capacity is tightening from the supply side—through driver qualification pressure, carrier exits, and higher operating costs—rather than from a demand boom. Diesel volatility and insurance/litigation exposure continue to raise the floor
content:
Fleet & Market Trends

Driver recruiting tightens as carriers fight for “qualified supply”

Driver availability showed signs of tightening into early 2026 as enforcement actions and tougher CDL oversight reduced the pool of qualified applicants, even while freight demand remained uneven. Carriers that kept recruiting pipelines active (and improved their speed-to-contact) were positioned to seat trucks faster if volumes improved, according to Transport Topics. Expect the next 3–12 months to reward fleets and brokers that can validate safety/qualification quickly and keep backup capacity warm.

Key data point: Cost-per-hire rose 24% year over year in Q4 2025, a sign that “cheap capacity” was becoming harder to source even before peak season shifts (Transport Topics).

Workforce demographics: aging and underrepresented groups stay central to capacity planning

Longer-term labor constraints remained the backdrop for 2026 network planning, with fleets increasingly focused on retention, training pipelines, and widening the recruitment funnel. ATRI’s demographic work pointed to an aging workforce and extremely low female participation, reinforcing why carriers are investing in lifestyle improvements and targeted pathways into trucking for underrepresented populations (ATRI). For brokers, this matters because carrier service consistency and surge coverage depend on who can hire (and keep) drivers, not just who has trucks.

Key data point: Women comprise 4.1% of truck drivers, underscoring the size of the untapped labor pool (ATRI).

Carrier attrition looks deeper than previously reported as revised employment data lands

Revised federal employment data suggested the post-2022 “purge” of drivers was larger than earlier estimates, which could translate into more rate sensitivity during weather or regional disruptions. Land Line reported that revised figures showed a larger cumulative decline from the 2022 peak than previously believed, supporting the view that capacity was slowly resetting after a prolonged downcycle (Land Line). Over the next 3–12 months, tighter effective capacity raises the stakes for routing-guide depth, contingency carriers, and fast carrier onboarding.

Key data point: Revised data indicated about 122,000 fewer truck drivers since the 2022 peak than earlier reports suggested (Land Line).

LTL reshapes: FedEx Freight spinoff puts pricing and network strategy in motion

The LTL sector kept moving toward structural change as FedEx set a June 2026 timeline to separate FedEx Freight, a shift that could influence pricing discipline, sales strategy, and shipper contracting behavior into the second half of 2026. FreightWaves noted the spinoff timing and the operational pressure FedEx Freight faced from weaker tonnage and margin headwinds, even as it built out a large dedicated sales team (FreightWaves). For brokers, the takeaway is to anticipate more active bid events and carrier mix changes as networks reposition.

Key data point: FedEx Freight revenue fell 1.7% year over year in its fiscal Q2 ended Nov. 30, reflecting a still-choppy demand backdrop (FreightWaves).

Freight volumes tick up while capacity exits amplify spot-rate responsiveness

Even modest improvements in freight volumes can move pricing when the carrier base is leaner. Transport Topics reported the ATA For-Hire Truck Tonnage Index hit a three-year high in February, with ATA’s economist explicitly tying the gain to lower industry capacity (Transport Topics). The next 3–12 months likely bring more volatility around seasonal demand and disruptions, with shippers needing better execution to avoid fall-offs to spot.

Key data point: The ATA For-Hire Truck Tonnage Index rose 2.6% sequentially to 116.2 in February (Transport Topics).

Fuel & Cost Pressures

Diesel economics stay a swing factor for small fleets and spot market behavior

Fuel remained a major variable for carrier survival and lane pricing, especially for small fleets without strong surcharge protection. As diesel rose sharply in early 2026, Heavy Duty Trucking reported the national average retail diesel price reached $5.643 per gallon in early April, with extreme regional spikes (notably California) that can distort network costs and repositioning decisions (Heavy Duty Trucking). Over the next few quarters, diesel volatility increases the likelihood of abrupt capacity withdrawals from marginal carriers and more aggressive accessorial negotiations.

Key data point: U.S. average diesel hit $5.643 per gallon (week of April 6) (Heavy Duty Trucking).

Fuel surcharge friction grows as price moves outrun weekly index mechanisms

Fuel surcharge (FSC) mechanisms, often tied to weekly DOE/EIA benchmarks, can lag rapid price moves—creating near-term margin squeezes and tense renegotiations. Brokers and shippers should expect more disputes about baseline MPG assumptions, reefer adders, and “emergency” adjustments when diesel moves quickly. This becomes a strategic issue because FSC disagreements can directly affect tender acceptance and service reliability.

Key data point: Typical February 2026 FSC ranges of about $0.38–$0.50 per mile were cited for DOE diesel in the mid-$3 range (O Trucking).

Insurance inflation and nuclear verdict risk keep raising the operating floor

Insurance remains a structural cost pressure that doesn’t ease just because freight is soft—particularly as litigation severity continues to influence underwriting. Reliance Partners highlighted how claim severity and large verdicts have pushed insurers to tighten terms and raise premiums, making safety documentation and technology adoption part of basic market access (Reliance Partners). For the next 3–12 months, expect more carriers to reprice lanes, reduce risky freight, or exit entirely if they can’t secure viable insurance renewals.

Key data point: Verdicts exceeding $1 million have increased by more than 235% since 2012, a major driver of insurer behavior (Reliance Partners).

Fraud & Security Watch

SAFER Transport Act targets double-brokering, fictitious pickups, and registration vulnerabilities

Freight fraud moved from an operational headache to a legislative priority in early 2026. The American Trucking Associations backed Sen. Todd Young’s SAFER Transport Act, which aims to modernize FMCSA registration controls, phase out MC numbers in favor of USDOT identifiers, and strengthen enforcement tools and penalties (American Trucking Associations). Over the next year, brokers should anticipate tighter identity verification expectations and more scrutiny of onboarding workflows.

Key data point: ATRI estimates cargo theft costs the trucking industry more than $18 million per day (American Trucking Associations).

Strategic theft via identity manipulation keeps surging, forcing stronger verification

High-tech “strategic theft” has grown fast enough to change the default operating posture for brokers, carriers, and shippers. ATA cited CargoNet data showing strategic theft has surged dramatically since 2021, often exploiting weaknesses in carrier identity and registration systems (American Trucking Associations). In the coming quarters, expect more brokers to require multi-factor verification, validated contact callbacks, and tighter tender controls to reduce exposure.

Key data point: Strategic theft has surged by 1,500% since 2021, according to CargoNet via ATA (American Trucking Associations).

DOT leans on AI and analytics to spot fraud patterns and improve enforcement targeting

Federal enforcement leaders signaled a shift toward more advanced data approaches to detect fraud and suspicious activity at scale. CDLLife reported DOT leadership discussing the use of AI and advanced analytics to improve enforcement effectiveness and identify fraud in the trucking industry (CDLLife). For brokers, the practical implication is that digital footprints (addresses, identity mismatches, repeated reinstatements) are more likely to trigger enforcement attention, increasing the value of clean, documented onboarding.

Key data point: DOT leadership said it plans to use AI to improve enforcement accuracy, including fraud identification (CDLLife).

Technology & Policy

FMCSA TechCelerate Now keeps pushing ADAS adoption and ROI tools

Safety technology adoption—especially ADAS and camera systems—continued to move from “optional” to “expected,” driven by both safety outcomes and insurance requirements. Transport Topics covered how TMC highlighted progress supporting FMCSA’s TechCelerate Now program, including updated ROI tools and expanded scope beyond core braking/lane systems to cameras and mirror-replacement vision tech (Transport Topics). Over the next 3–12 months, brokers may see greater differentiation between carriers that can document safety tech and those that cannot.

Key data point: TechCelerate Now was renewed in 2024 for a four-year second phase, keeping federal focus on deployment and best practices (Transport Topics).

Autonomous trucking policy: new federal framework proposal aims to scale pilots

Autonomous trucking moved closer to a structured national approach with a 2026 discussion draft proposing a federal framework for commercial freight pilots and safety reporting. FreightWaves reported the SELF DRIVE Act of 2026 would require reporting for certain crashes and quarterly mileage disclosures in revenue service to build a comparable safety record against human-driven operations (FreightWaves). For the next year, expect more pilot activity and more shipper questions about where autonomous capacity will first become commercially relevant (often in predictable, long-haul corridors).

Key data point: The proposal includes quarterly reporting of total miles traveled in revenue service during commercial operations (FreightWaves).

Truck parking gets funding attention as capacity tightens and compliance remains strict

Truck parking remained a safety-and-productivity bottleneck with real downstream effects on HOS compliance, detention risk, and driver retention. Transport Topics reported a House legislative version of FY 2026 transportation funding included a dedicated allocation for expanding truck parking operations nationwide (Transport Topics). Over the next 3–12 months, more public investment may help at the margin, but near-term constraints keep making parking strategy (route planning, appointment discipline) a competitive factor.

Key data point: $200 million was proposed specifically for expanding truck parking operations nationwide (Transport Topics).

Bottom Line

Going into early 2026, trucking’s most strategic theme is that capacity is tightening from the supply side—through driver qualification pressure, carrier exits, and higher operating costs—rather than from a demand boom. Diesel volatility and insurance/litigation exposure continue to raise the floor for small fleets, which can accelerate attrition and increase spot-market sensitivity. Meanwhile, fraud prevention is moving toward tougher identity controls and more enforcement, making carrier verification and clean onboarding processes core brokerage capabilities. Technology initiatives—from ADAS adoption frameworks to autonomous pilot policy—are steadily shaping how safety, compliance, and capacity will be measured over the next year.

title: Weekly Freight Report - February 6, 2026
excerpt: Spot rates strengthened as winter disruptions tightened networks: DAT’s Feb. 1–7 reading showed $2.45/mi dry van (+7¢ WoW), $2.94/mi reefer (+9¢), and $2.58/mi flatbed (+5¢). Total load posts were 3.7M.
content:
Market Pulse — spot/contract rates, load-to-truck ratios, capacity

Spot rates moved higher as winter weather disruptions tightened networks across the eastern half of the U.S. and typical early-February restocking activity lifted demand for capacity, per DAT spot market data for Feb. 1–7 (covering most of the Jan. 30–Feb. 6 window). According to Blue Book’s summary of DAT iQ, the broker-to-carrier 7-day national average spot rates were $2.45/mi dry van (+$0.07 WoW), $2.94/mi reefer (+$0.09), and $2.58/mi flatbed (+$0.05).

On the volume side, DAT reported 3.7 million total loads posted (down 1% WoW) and 217,734 truck posts (up 2% WoW) for the same week, with truck posts down 14% YoY, signaling a shrinking “extra” carrier pool despite only modest weekly changes (Blue Book/DAT iQ).

By equipment type (DAT, Feb. 1–7):

  • Dry van: 1.65M loads (−3% WoW) vs. 154,611 equipment posts (+2% WoW), with linehaul at $2.08/mi (+$0.07) (Blue Book/DAT iQ).
  • Reefer: 942,472 loads (−10% WoW) vs. 36,670 equipment posts (+3% WoW), with linehaul at $2.57/mi (+$0.08) and noted as $0.59/mi higher YoY (Blue Book/DAT iQ).
  • Flatbed: 1.1M loads (+10% WoW) vs. 22,434 equipment posts (+2% WoW), with linehaul at $2.21/mi (+$0.05) (Blue Book/DAT iQ).

Load-to-truck ratios: DAT’s week summary above did not publish the standard load-to-truck ratios in the same write-up (Blue Book/DAT iQ). As a directional proxy, dividing load posts by equipment posts for the week implies elevated demand relative to available postings (e.g., roughly 10.7 van loads per van equipment post; ~25.7 reefer loads per reefer equipment post; ~49.0 flatbed loads per flatbed equipment post), but these are not the official DAT ratios and should be treated as indicative rather than directly comparable to DAT’s published LTR methodology.

Regional pricing signal: The Midwest continued to show premium conditions: DAT reported the 13 Midwest states (about 45% of national load volume) averaged $2.58/mi for spot van freight, $0.50/mi above the national average, after a $0.19/mi WoW increase (Blue Book/DAT iQ). DAT also noted its top 50 van lanes averaged $2.32/mi (Blue Book/DAT iQ), highlighting that the national average can mask tighter “high-volume” corridors.

Contract rate direction: While weekly contract rate prints vary by shipper and bid cycle timing, the broader early-2026 theme is that spot has been closing the gap with contract. A later Q1 analysis of U.S. Bank’s freight payments data (produced with DAT) described contract pricing around $2.12/mi in February 2026 and spot around $2.01/mi, putting the spread near $0.11/mi by March (Trucking Dive). For brokers, the implication is simple: when spot rises toward contract, shippers become more open to mini-bids and mid-cycle adjustments, but they also expect better service execution and fewer fall-offs.

Regulation & Enforcement — FMCSA/DOT rules, ELD, CDL, state regs

ELD enforcement stayed aggressive entering 2026. FMCSA continued removing devices from the registered ELD list after a sharp increase in revocations during 2025, and carriers using revoked devices were required to revert to paper logs and replace units within the allowed window, per FreightWaves. The practical brokerage impact is higher “day-of” risk for small carriers who fail inspections or get placed out of service due to ELD noncompliance—especially on time-sensitive freight.

Broker financial responsibility enforcement date was nearing. FMCSA’s “Broker and Freight Forwarder Financial Responsibility” final rule required compliance as of Jan. 16, 2026, according to FMCSA’s February 2026 Report to Congress (FMCSA (PDF)). Brokers should assume carriers and shipper risk teams will increasingly check bond/trust standing and payment behavior as part of qualification.

CDL/medical credential digitization and tighter driver qualification enforcement remained a theme. Industry compliance summaries highlighted the shift to electronic medical certification workflows (NRII) and increased scrutiny around driver eligibility (including non-domiciled CDLs and English-language proficiency), emphasizing that data accuracy and real-time verification are becoming more important than paper documentation (Compliance Navigation Specialists).

Broker Edge — what brokers need to know, competitive positioning

What changed this week: the spot market gained momentum, with dry van, reefer, and flatbed all moving higher WoW in DAT’s Feb. 1–7 reading (Blue Book/DAT iQ). That combination—firming rates and lower YoY truck posts—typically produces two brokerage realities: (1) faster carrier selectivity and (2) higher exposure to service failures from “thin margin” carriers.

Where brokers can win:

  • Lean into regional heat maps: The Midwest’s $2.58/mi spot van average vs. $2.45/mi national signals where carriers will demand premium and where shippers should pre-plan (Blue Book/DAT iQ).
  • Use linehaul moves to guide quotes: The week’s linehaul changes were meaningful: van linehaul $2.08/mi (+$0.07), reefer linehaul $2.57/mi (+$0.08), flatbed linehaul $2.21/mi (+$0.05) (Blue Book/DAT iQ).
  • Protect margins with “carrier-ready” tenders: When weather tightens capacity, the best defense is operational excellence: accurate pickup numbers, staged appointments, and detention clarity. This matters more as spot approaches contract and shippers compare “spot” execution to their primary carriers.
  • Audit your carrier bench for compliance: With ELD revocations and heightened enforcement continuing (FreightWaves), brokers that pre-screen for compliant devices, clean inspection history, and stable authority reduce costly recoveries.

Cross-Border Watchlist — US-Mexico, US-Canada, USMCA, tariffs

USMCA review pressure was building. Cross-border stakeholders were watching the 2026 USMCA review cycle closely, with reporting emphasizing that uncertainty around tariffs and the review process can influence investment and freight planning (Land Line).

Tariff complexity remained a trucking factor. Land Line noted that a 25% tariff on heavy-duty trucks was in effect, while some USMCA-qualifying parts could be exempt depending on qualification and documentation (Land Line). For brokers supporting automotive and equipment supply chains, tariff exposure shows up as (a) lane volatility, (b) different shipper routing decisions, and (c) surges ahead of rule changes.

Mexico-focused takeaway for brokers in Texas: Laredo is structurally positioned as the primary truck gateway, and cross-border mix shifts (electronics/computers vs. finished vehicles) can change trailer type demand and appointment patterns. A later cross-border market note highlighted strong Mexico export growth early in 2026 and Mexico’s large share of total U.S. imports (C.H. Robinson), reinforcing the strategic importance of northbound reliability even when domestic demand is uneven.

Fraud & Security — cargo theft, double-brokering, CDL fraud

Cargo theft remained elevated and increasingly organized. Overhaul’s 2025 U.S. Cargo Theft Report (as covered by Land Line) recorded 2,576 theft incidents in 2025 (up 16% YoY), with California accounting for 38% of reported thefts and Texas 20%—high relevance for a Willis, TX brokerage managing Houston-area freight flows.

What thieves targeted: Land Line’s summary of Overhaul data said electronics were 22% of thefts, with food/drink at 15% and home/garden and apparel/shoes each at 11% (Land Line). For brokers, these categories should trigger “enhanced handling” playbooks (identity verification, check-calls, no reconsignment without shipper callback, etc.).

Real enforcement example: The Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department reported a Dec. 2025–Feb. 2026 operation that led to nine arrests and recovery of approximately $7 million in stolen cargo freight plus $1 million in currency (LASD). Even though this is outside Texas, it underscores the scale and professionalism of cargo theft rings affecting national networks.

Fraud beyond theft: FMCSA officials discussed ongoing investigations tied to identity theft, registration issues, fraudulent ELDs, and driver training fraud, and emphasized reporting via the National Consumer Complaint Database, per Overdrive. That matters for brokers because the “best price” carrier in a tight week can be the highest risk if identity is compromised.

Equipment, Fuel & Ops — diesel prices, truck orders, driver pay

Diesel ticked up into early February. EIA’s weekly retail diesel series (republished by YCharts) showed $3.624/gal for the week of Jan. 26, 2026, rising to $3.681/gal for the week of Feb. 2 and $3.688/gal for the week of Feb. 9 (YCharts (EIA series)). For brokers, higher diesel translates quickly into (1) higher fuel surcharges on contract freight and (2) higher spot “all-in” quotes from smaller fleets when deadhead increases due to weather disruption.

Class 8 order activity was improving—signaling cautious carrier confidence. FTR reported 32,500 North American Class 8 net orders in January 2026 (down 24% from December but up 27% YoY), while ACT’s preliminary estimate was 30,800 (up 20% YoY), according to Trucks, Parts, Service. For operations, rising orders don’t add trucks immediately, but they can mark the point where large fleets begin planning for replacement—and where capacity tightening becomes more “real” over the next 6–18 months.

Operational note for the week: Winter disruptions that lift spot rates often also increase dwell and rescheduling risk. Make sure appointment windows, lumper expectations, and detention terms are confirmed in writing before dispatch—especially on reefer and Midwest lanes where DAT signaled stronger pricing and tighter conditions (Blue Book/DAT iQ).

Action Checklist for Brokers — 5-7 bullet points

  • Reprice Midwest van freight weekly (not monthly) while the region holds a $0.50/mi premium vs. national in DAT spot data (Blue Book/DAT iQ).
  • Update your spot quoting logic using linehaul moves (van linehaul $2.08/mi, reefer $2.57/mi, flatbed $2.21/mi for Feb. 1–7) to avoid under-quoting in tightening weeks (Blue Book/DAT iQ).
  • Expand carrier verification steps on high-theft commodities (electronics, food/drink, apparel) given Overhaul’s 2025 theft mix and hotspot concentration in CA/TX (Land Line).
  • Proactively screen ELD compliance (and have a backup plan) because FMCSA continued device removals entering 2026 (FreightWaves).
  • Double-check broker bond/trust standing internally and be prepared for more counterparties to verify it as FMCSA’s financial responsibility compliance date passed Jan. 16, 2026 (FMCSA (PDF)).
  • For cross-border moves, add buffer lead time and closely manage documentation as USMCA review uncertainty and tariff complexity persist (Land Line).
  • Build a weather playbook (pre-book capacity, communicate re-delivery terms, confirm detention) because winter systems can flip a loose market to tight quickly, as reflected in DAT’s Feb. 1–7 rate jump (Blue Book/DAT iQ).

title: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup - January 30, 2026
excerpt: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup — January 30, 2026. Analysts entering 2026 framed the market as “leaner,” with carrier exits tightening capacity, but pricing power still depends on demand. Fuel volatility, workforce demographics, and fraud
content:
Fleet & Market Trends

Capacity has tightened, but pricing power still hinges on demand

Analysts heading into 2026 framed the market as “leaner,” with multi-year carrier exits shrinking for-hire capacity enough that it’s close to a practical floor. That sets up a more volatile 3–12 month window: if demand firms even modestly, carriers regain leverage faster than shippers expect; if demand stays soft, the industry risks another wave of failures rather than a clean recovery. FMCSA data showed property carrier authority down more than 11% from Dec. 2022 to Dec. 2025. (per FleetOwner)

Fleet failures shift from “new entrants” to more established operators

Industry commentary on the freight downturn noted that exits were no longer limited to brand-new “truck-for-a-year” carriers; more mature fleets were increasingly among those leaving the market. That matters for 2026 because the remaining capacity mix may be higher quality but also less flexible—raising the odds of spot-market spikes when lanes tighten. In 2024, about half of exits involved carriers older than three years (up from 37% in 2023). (per International Factoring Association’s Factorings magazine)

Driver workforce demographics remain a structural constraint (even in a soft market)

Workforce pressures didn’t disappear with softer freight: demographic trends continued to point to a smaller pipeline of new entrants relative to retirements. ATRI highlighted the need for carriers to broaden recruiting into younger and more diverse pools and improve retention strategies. Women comprised just 4.1% of truck drivers in ATRI’s demographic research. (per ATRI)

LTL networks stay disciplined on yield, setting up tougher renewals

Large network carriers typically protect pricing even when volume is flat, and that discipline can be an early indicator of leverage returning before truckload turns. For brokers and shippers, the near-term play is to assume tougher accessorial enforcement and fewer “discount outs” at renewal if carriers keep freight selection tight. C.H. Robinson expected mid-single-digit LTL rate increases and a still-limited pool of LTL carriers. (per C.H. Robinson)

Fuel & Cost Pressures

Diesel volatility raises the risk of another attrition wave

Even before any demand recovery, fuel is a swing factor that can quickly push marginal fleets into the red, especially those living on spot freight without strong surcharge protection. The strategic impact for the next 3–12 months is higher tender risk when prices spike (more “no trucks”) and more aggressive surcharge negotiations. At elevated levels, fuel can account for 30%+ of total operating costs for carriers. (per The Truckers’ Wall of Shame post summarizing analyst commentary)

Refinery output assumptions matter more than shippers think

Fuel outlooks going into 2026 were sensitive to refinery utilization and inventory swings, because even small per-gallon changes cascade into cents-per-mile cost. For procurement teams, that means budgeting for volatility and tightening surcharge language to avoid disputes when diesel moves faster than contract reset schedules. EIA’s December 2025 outlook projected a 2026 on-highway diesel average around $3.50/gal. (per Fleet Rabbit citing EIA STEO)

Fuel surcharge fights intensify as base rates rise

Shippers have pushed back on surcharges that feel like “double dipping” when base rates increase—while carriers argue surcharge mechanics don’t fully cover real-world fuel exposure (deadhead, idling, regional differentials). The next 3–12 months will likely bring more lane-by-lane surcharge negotiations and more all-in rate bids to reduce friction. Typical fuel surcharge tables in early 2026 implied roughly $0.38–$0.50 per mile in FSC. (per OTrucking)

Alternative fuels and renewable diesel expand, but won’t be a “single-solution” reset

OEM messaging emphasized that decarbonization will be multi-path: battery electric for some duty cycles, and renewable fuels/hydrogen pathways for others. In the near term, brokers should expect limited availability and regional variability—especially as more fleets experiment with renewable diesel (HVO) where supply exists. Volvo highlighted HVO/renewable diesel, biodiesel, battery-electric, and hydrogen as parallel pathways rather than a single winner. (per Volvo Trucks)

Fraud & Security Watch

SAFER Transport Act targets double-brokering, fictitious pickups, and “hostage loads”

Federal lawmakers proposed a broad package aimed at making freight fraud harder to execute and easier to prosecute, including registration reforms and more interagency coordination. For the next 3–12 months, the practical takeaway is that brokers should document verification steps, keep tighter carrier onboarding rules, and expect increased scrutiny of registration changes and ownership links. The bill proposed phasing out MC numbers in favor of USDOT numbers and adding an automated tool to flag suspicious registration activity. (per CDLLife)

Legislation also moves to restore faster civil penalties for unauthorized brokerage

Separate efforts tied to household goods fraud were positioned to restore and formalize FMCSA’s ability to impose civil penalties for unauthorized brokerage—an enforcement lever the industry has argued is needed for timely action. Even if originally framed around household goods, the broader direction is clear: more verification requirements (like physical addresses) and more tools for regulators to act without long DOJ timelines. The bill would require applicants to provide a legitimate physical business address (not just a P.O. box) before authority is granted. (per Yahoo News)

Carrier identity “scorecards” and verification UX move into the booking workflow

Platforms are pushing verification upstream—surfacing risk signals at dispatch rather than after a loss event. This is strategically important for 2026 because fraudsters exploit speed and volume; moving checks into the workflow reduces reliance on ad-hoc manual vetting. Central Dispatch’s carrier scorecard displays FMCSA-sourced details plus warnings/flags inside the dispatch flow. (per Cox Automotive)

AI-driven carrier screening becomes a practical defense (not a buzzword)

AI-assisted vetting is being used to automate checks and trigger real-time alerts when identity signals don’t match, helping broker teams keep pace with load volume without loosening controls. Over the next year, expect this to become table stakes for broker compliance programs, especially as regulators focus on registration integrity. Highway described AI-enabled automation for carrier screening and real-time alerts as part of fraud prevention workflows. (per Highway)

Technology & Policy

FMCSA’s TechCelerate Now pushes faster adoption of ADAS and camera systems

Safety technology adoption is increasingly treated as an operational ROI decision, not just compliance. TechCelerate Now’s updated ROI tools and recommended practices (e.g., calibration standards) aim to reduce friction in deploying ADAS, cameras, and related cybersecurity and training practices. FMCSA launched TechCelerate Now in 2020 and renewed it in 2024 for a four-year second phase. (per Transport Topics)

Autonomous trucking pilots in Texas shift from demos to daily linehaul routes

Autonomy programs increasingly emphasize repeatable freight lanes with measurable service metrics, which is what brokers need to evaluate reliability and operational fit. If these pilots hold, the next 12 months could bring more “autonomy-ready” contract proposals on select corridors rather than broad national rollout. International and Ryder launched a daily ~600-mile I-35 corridor pilot between Laredo and Temple, Texas. (per Truck News)

Infrastructure and truck weight policy debate heats up ahead of reauthorization

As Congress approaches the next surface transportation reauthorization window, the policy fight over heavier trucks is resurfacing, with bridge wear and replacement cost the central argument. For brokers, any weight-limit changes would alter payload economics, equipment utilization, and lane constraints—but could also trigger new local restrictions if bridges are stressed. A study cited by local government groups warned 65,157–82,457 local bridges could be put at risk under heavier truck proposals. (per The River Reporter)

Truck parking funding remains a live issue as policymakers tee up the next bill

Parking constraints remain a safety and productivity drag (hours lost hunting for spaces, compliance pressure at the end of HOS windows). Industry groups signaled optimism that dedicated funding could expand, which would matter for detention, appointment planning, and driver retention over the next year. Industry advocates pointed to $200 million set aside in appropriations for truck parking as a key win that still needed to “cross the finish line.” (per The Trucker)

EPA emissions policy uncertainty complicates 2026–2027 equipment planning

Regulatory swings can change the timing of fleet trade cycles, emissions-system maintenance risk, and residual values—especially when requirements differ by state. The near-term effect is planning complexity: fleets may delay purchases or extend trade cycles while watching how federal and California rules evolve. Land Line noted that a 2022 heavy-duty NOx rule set new requirements for model year 2027 and newer trucks, even as early-2026 policy moves targeted other emissions rules. (per Land Line)

Bottom Line

Heading into late Q1 2026, the domestic trucking story is less about a clean “rebound” and more about a fragile equilibrium: capacity has been purged, but demand still dictates when pricing power returns. Fuel volatility, insurance and compliance costs, and continued carrier attrition are the biggest near-term catalysts that can tighten markets quickly. Meanwhile, fraud and identity-based schemes are accelerating investment in carrier verification and AI-driven screening, alongside policy pushes like the SAFER Transport Act. Over the next 3–12 months, brokers that formalize verification, tighten surcharge language, and diversify capacity (including disciplined LTL partners) will be best positioned for a choppier operating environment.

title: Weekly Freight Report - January 30, 2026
excerpt: January closed with a spot market that stayed firmer than normal for a post-holiday period as weather-related disruption and a thinning carrier base tightened effective capacity. DAT’s January benchmarks showed national average spot rates at $2.32/mile
content:
Market Pulse — spot/contract rates, load-to-truck ratios, capacity

January closed with a spot market that stayed firmer than normal for a post-holiday period as weather-related disruption and a thinning carrier base tightened effective capacity. DAT’s January benchmarks showed national average spot rates (incl. fuel) at $2.32/mile dry van, $2.81/mile reefer, and $2.85/mile flatbed, with reefer and flatbed posting the largest month-over-month gains (+12¢ and +22¢, respectively) ([DAT](https://www.dat.com/company/news-events/news-releases/dat-january-truckload-freight-rates-show-resilience-amid-winter-disruptions)).

On the contract side, pricing stayed relatively stable: $2.48/mile contract van, $2.81/mile contract reefer, and $3.04/mile contract flatbed (flatbed down 1¢ m/m) ([DAT](https://www.dat.com/company/news-events/news-releases/dat-january-truckload-freight-rates-show-resilience-amid-winter-disruptions)). For brokers, the most important story this week is the narrowing spread: spot is rising faster than contract in early 2026, compressing the traditional contract premium and increasing shipper sensitivity to routing-guide failures.

Volume signals were mixed. DAT’s Truckload Volume Index (TVI) for January came in at 219 for van (-4% m/m), 184 for reefer (-4%), and 257 for flatbed (+2%), consistent with a post-holiday slowdown plus comparatively better industrial/open-deck demand ([DAT](https://www.dat.com/company/news-events/news-releases/dat-january-truckload-freight-rates-show-resilience-amid-winter-disruptions)). Meanwhile, SONAR-based commentary from FreightWaves earlier in the month highlighted tender rejections near 9.97% (STRI.USA), a level not seen across 2023–2025, supporting the view that capacity—not demand—is doing most of the tightening work ([FreightWaves](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/trucking-market-holds-up-in-january)).

Load-to-truck conditions also tightened through the end of January. C.H. Robinson reported the dry van load-to-truck ratio rising from roughly 27:1 early in the month to about 47:1 by month-end, while reefer climbed to 26.8:1 in the last week of January ([C.H. Robinson](https://www.chrobinson.com/en-us/resources/insights-and-advisories/north-america-freight-insights/feb-2026-freight-market-update/na-truckload/)). The takeaway: even if shippers feel “demand is soft,” brokers should price and cover like it’s a tightening market—because the supply side is still pulling capacity out faster than freight is easing.

Regulation & Enforcement — FMCSA/DOT rules, ELD, CDL, state regs

Compliance risk increased in January as FMCSA continued actively policing the ELD ecosystem. On Jan. 13, 2026, FMCSA removed four electronic logging devices from the registered list (placing them on the revoked list), and carriers using them were given 60 days to replace devices (deadline March 15, 2026) or revert to paper logs in the interim ([FMCSA ELD notice](https://eld.fmcsa.dot.gov/File/OpenKey/Four_ELDs_Removed_from_FMCSA_Registered_Devices_January13_2026/)).

For brokers and shippers, ELD removals matter because they create short-term friction: some small fleets may temporarily switch to paper logs, lose productivity during the transition, or get placed out-of-service if they miss the deadline. This tends to show up first as missed pickup appointments, tighter same/next-day capacity, and higher acceptance prices on short-notice freight.

On enforcement posture, CVSA issued a regulatory update dated Jan. 23, 2026, noting FMCSA activity on documenting burdens tied to CMV marking regulations ([CVSA](https://cvsa.org/regulatory-updates/regulatory-update-january-23-2026/)). While this item was not a market-moving rule change by itself, it reinforces that compliance-related initiatives remain “live,” and brokers should assume continued roadside and administrative enforcement focus into 2026.

Broker Edge — what brokers need to know, competitive positioning

This is a week to shift playbooks from “post-holiday slack” to “weather + compliance + carrier exits” mode. The market is rewarding brokers who can (1) pre-book capacity, (2) run tighter carrier qualification, and (3) communicate proactively when service risk increases.

  • Price discipline matters: With DAT showing spot rising in January while contract stays mostly flat, carriers are more willing to reject low-paying contract freight and chase higher-yield spot opportunities ([DAT](https://www.dat.com/company/news-events/news-releases/dat-january-truckload-freight-rates-show-resilience-amid-winter-disruptions)). Build surge-pricing rules for same-day coverage and for weather-impacted corridors.
  • Segment strategy: Flatbed is the standout: DAT’s January spot flatbed average rose +22¢ m/m to $2.85/mile and was +41¢ y/y, signaling sustained tightness in open-deck and project freight ([DAT](https://www.dat.com/company/news-events/news-releases/dat-january-truckload-freight-rates-show-resilience-amid-winter-disruptions)). If you’re not strong in flatbed, partner up or expand vetted capacity there.
  • Customer messaging: Use a capacity narrative customers can understand: tender rejections near 10% mean contracted carriers are declining roughly 1 in 10 loads, so “contract” is not the same as “guaranteed” ([FreightWaves](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/trucking-market-holds-up-in-january)). Position your brokerage as the insurance policy—fast coverage, verified carriers, and clean documentation.

Cross-Border Watchlist — US-Mexico, US-Canada, USMCA, tariffs

Cross-border freight remains one of the steadier demand anchors as domestic volumes wobble. Mexico retained its position as the U.S. top trading partner in January, with $74.1B in bilateral transactions, up 6.5% y/y ([Mexico Business](https://mexicobusiness.news/trade-and-investment/news/mexico-surplus-hits-17-year-low-us-imports-jump-13)). For brokers in Texas (including the Houston/Willis market), this supports continued opportunities in Laredo/Nuevo Laredo dray + transload + cross-dock moves, especially for automotive, industrial, and consumer goods replenishment.

On the Canada lane, policy uncertainty remained a planning issue in late January amid renewed tariff rhetoric. A widely circulated analysis described a U.S. “100% tariff threat” tied to concerns about transshipment/re-export channels and flagged the upcoming July 2026 USMCA joint review as a key uncertainty milestone ([TimeTrex](https://www.timetrex.com/blog/new-us-100-tariff-threat-against-canada-january-2026)). While outcomes remain uncertain, the operational implication is clear: customs documentation quality and broker-of-record discipline matter more when inspections and compliance checks rise.

Fraud & Security — cargo theft, double-brokering, CDL fraud

Fraud and theft remain a top operational risk as the market tightens. Verisk CargoNet’s year-end analysis showed estimated cargo theft losses of nearly $725 million in 2025 (up 60% from 2024), with confirmed cargo theft incidents rising 18% (from 2,243 to 2,646) and average theft value climbing to $273,990 (+36%) ([Carrier Management/CargoNet](https://www.carriermanagement.com/news/2026/01/22/283728.htm)).

Two broker-relevant patterns to assume are active in late January:

  • Theft-by-deception: CargoNet highlighted a shift toward more strategic theft that starts with deception rather than purely physical theft ([Carrier Management/CargoNet](https://www.carriermanagement.com/news/2026/01/22/283728.htm)). That directly overlaps with double-brokering and identity-based scams.
  • Geographic dispersion: CargoNet noted activity spreading beyond traditional hotspots, with increases in states like New Jersey (+50%), Indiana (+30%), and Pennsylvania (+24%) ([Carrier Management/CargoNet](https://www.carriermanagement.com/news/2026/01/22/283728.htm)). Don’t assume “low-risk” markets are low-risk anymore—treat high-value loads everywhere with the same controls.

Equipment, Fuel & Ops — diesel prices, truck orders, driver pay

Fuel moved higher into the end of the month. EIA reported the U.S. average on-highway diesel price at $3.62/gal (price point published Jan. 27, reflecting that week’s retail average) ([EIA](https://x.com/EIAgov/status/2016255151120568774)). Rising diesel typically widens fuel surcharge components and can push carriers to hold the line on all-in rates, especially on longer hauls where fuel is a bigger share of cost per mile.

Equipment indicators improved: preliminary January Class 8 orders landed around 30,800–32,500 units, up 20–27% y/y (ACT and FTR estimates), though down sequentially from December’s surge ([Trucks, Parts, Service](https://www.truckpartsandservice.com/trucks-trailers/class-7-8/article/15816305/january-2026-class-8-truck-orders-up-20-year-over-year)). This supports the idea that carriers are starting to believe the cycle is turning, but it does not mean near-term capacity relief—new trucks take time to build and staff, and compliance pressure may still sideline marginal operators.

Operationally, the mix of (1) winter disruption, (2) ELD transitions for some fleets, and (3) improving spot yields is a recipe for more “selective service.” Expect higher failure-to-tender acceptance on cheap contracted freight and a higher probability of fall-offs close to pickup unless pricing and communication are strong.

Action Checklist for Brokers — 5-7 bullet points

  • Re-price high-risk lanes using January benchmarks: anchor conversations around $2.32 van, $2.81 reefer, $2.85 flatbed spot averages and highlight that reefer/flatbed rose sharply m/m ([DAT](https://www.dat.com/company/news-events/news-releases/dat-january-truckload-freight-rates-show-resilience-amid-winter-disruptions)).
  • Run an ELD compliance check on small carriers: confirm they are not using revoked devices and document a replacement plan ahead of March 15 enforcement ([FMCSA ELD notice](https://eld.fmcsa.dot.gov/File/OpenKey/Four_ELDs_Removed_from_FMCSA_Registered_Devices_January13_2026/)).
  • Tighten reefer coverage rules: treat end-of-month reefer tightness (load-to-truck up to 26.8:1) as a trigger for earlier booking and fewer “hot reload” assumptions ([C.H. Robinson](https://www.chrobinson.com/en-us/resources/insights-and-advisories/north-america-freight-insights/feb-2026-freight-market-update/na-truckload/)).
  • Elevate security for high-value loads: require photo ID at pickup, track-and-trace, and verify contact changes out-of-band; cargo theft losses were nearly $725M in 2025 with higher average loss severity ([Carrier Management/CargoNet](https://www.carriermanagement.com/news/2026/01/22/283728.htm)).
  • Lean into Mexico lanes: use the $74.1B January U.S.–Mexico trade number as a demand anchor when talking to carriers about consistent cross-border volume opportunities ([Mexico Business](https://mexicobusiness.news/trade-and-investment/news/mexico-surplus-hits-17-year-low-us-imports-jump-13)).
  • Update fuel assumptions weekly: diesel hit $3.62/gal late in the month—refresh FSC tables and watch for rapid changes that can break carrier commitments ([EIA](https://x.com/EIAgov/status/2016255151120568774)).
  • Prepare customers for tighter service: cite tender rejections near 10% as evidence that routing guides are less reliable, and propose a “backup capacity” plan for priority SKUs ([FreightWaves](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/trucking-market-holds-up-in-january)).

title: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup - January 23, 2026
excerpt: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup — January 23, 2026. Carrier attrition, aging driver demographics, and insurance-driven cost pressure are gradually tightening real capacity even when demand is uneven. Fuel volatility is reintroducing cash-flow and pricing friction, increasing the odds of selective coverage and surcharge disputes.
content:
Fleet & Market Trends

Capacity attrition is tightening the “you-call, we-haul” spot market

Carrier exits and tighter underwriting are gradually reducing the pool of truly flexible spot capacity, pushing more freight toward stable, contracted networks over the next two to three quarters. Freight market commentators highlighted that the shift is structural (discipline returning) rather than demand-driven, meaning brokers should expect lane-by-lane tightness even if macro volumes stay uneven. Key data point: persistent net carrier exits are shrinking the available spot-ready carrier pool. Per FreightWaves commentary shared via LinkedIn, this dynamic is already changing how shippers should think about routing guides and backup capacity.

Driver demographics remain a structural constraint, even in a soft market

The near-term hiring pressure may feel muted in certain lanes, but the underlying labor math still points to tighter capacity risk over the next 3–12 months as retirements accumulate. Industry workforce discussions continue to emphasize an aging driver base and the need to replace large cohorts leaving the industry. Key data point: ATA is cited projecting ~82,000-driver shortfall in 2026 and a median driver age of 57. According to a 2026 driver shortage overview citing ATA and BLS context, the replacement pipeline is not keeping pace with retirements.

Fleet failures continue as a “marginless recovery” squeezes small carriers

Forecast commentary heading into 2026 has emphasized slow volume recovery alongside cost pressure (insurance, equipment, and fuel volatility), creating a high-risk environment for undercapitalized fleets. That points to continued churn in the carrier base through 2026, with localized coverage gaps likely in secondary and seasonal lanes. Key data point: FTR commentary suggested contract-rate growth under ~2% is effectively non-viable once inflation and cost inflation are considered. As described in a Commercial Carrier Journal segment featuring FTR’s Avery Vise, this creates a “paradox” where weak rates force capacity out, eventually tightening the market.

LTL consolidation keeps reshaping service options and pricing leverage

Following the Yellow disruption, shippers and brokers are continuing to adapt to an LTL environment where scale and network density matter more, and service variability can rise during peak periods. Over the next few quarters, expect tougher negotiations around accessorials, fuel, and capacity commitments as consolidated networks optimize yield. Key data point: large-scale LTL mergers are described as redefining regional capacity and pricing models. Industry discussion of 2026’s “shifting LTL landscape” has kept consolidation front-and-center.

Fuel & Cost Pressures

Diesel volatility is back on the risk register (and it breaks lagging FSC formulas)

Fuel economics matter most when price moves fast: carriers pay at the pump immediately while revenue often arrives weeks later, creating cash-flow strain that disproportionately hits small fleets. That dynamic increases the probability of parked trucks, selective load acceptance, and renewed pricing pushback during bid events. Key data point: one analysis noted diesel spiking to $5.37/gal versus an EIA forecast of $3.47 for 2026. As described in the Tradlinx analysis, rapid changes can outpace standard fuel surcharge mechanisms, driving disputes and renegotiations.

Refinery capacity and regional supply constraints keep diesel basis risk elevated

Even if national averages normalize, regional refinery changes can create persistent basis spreads that show up in lane-specific carrier behavior (especially West Coast and constrained markets). For brokers, this amplifies the need to monitor regional diesel moves and validate whether FSC tables reflect real operating conditions. Key data point: Industrial Info reported potential for 400,000+ bbl/day of North American capacity additions over five years, alongside meaningful regional shifts. Per Industrial Info Resources, closures and expansion uncertainty can still tighten certain regional markets.

Nuclear verdicts continue pushing insurance premiums higher and filtering out marginal carriers

Insurance remains one of the most destabilizing cost lines because it can rise sharply at renewal, forcing immediate operational changes (lane exits, higher minimum rates, or shutdown). Over the next 3–12 months, expect more carriers to require stricter shipper/broker controls (appointment compliance, detention discipline, clear tender terms) to reduce claim exposure. Key data point: ATRI is cited putting the median nuclear verdict at $36 million (2022), with verdicts over $1 million up 235% since 2012. This dynamic is summarized in insurance-market commentary distributed via Reliance Partners’ FreightWaves channel and related industry analyses.

Fuel surcharge pressure is increasingly an LTL and parcel conversation, not just TL

As networks optimize yield and fuel swings reappear, shippers are paying more attention to how FSC schedules are calculated, when they reset, and whether base-rate moves are effectively “double counting” fuel. The next bid cycle is likely to see more line-item scrutiny and benchmarking of FSC tables across modes. Key data point: rising FSC percentages can materially change total shipment cost even without base-rate changes. Logistics and transportation advisory commentary in early 2026 has highlighted this as a growing budgeting pain point.

Fraud & Security Watch

SAFER Transport Act proposal signals a tougher federal posture on double-brokering and cargo theft

The SAFER Transport Act introduced in late February 2026 aims to modernize registration integrity and enforcement, explicitly targeting fictitious pickups, double-brokering scams, and “hostage load” schemes. If momentum holds, brokers should prepare for identity and ownership-change reporting expectations to tighten, with more interagency coordination (DOT to DOJ) on fraud cases. Key data point: the bill would phase out MC numbers within five years in favor of USDOT numbers, including for brokers and freight forwarders. Per Overdrive’s coverage and additional reporting from CDL Life, the bill also calls for automated tools to flag suspicious registration activity.

DOT and FMCSA plan to use AI and advanced analytics to improve fraud enforcement

At the Transportation Research Board’s annual meeting, DOT leadership said it intends to use AI to accelerate rulemaking and apply advanced analytics to enforcement—specifically calling out trucking fraud and illegal-driver activity. For brokers, the takeaway is that data quality (addresses, phone numbers, affiliations, ownership history) will increasingly determine whether a carrier can stay “clean” in federal systems. Key data point: DOT Deputy Secretary Steven Bradbury said the department wants AI/analytics to identify fraud and illegal foreign driver use. According to Overdrive’s January 16 reporting, FMCSA has also already overhauled parts of its registration system to deter fake carriers using fake addresses.

Carrier identity verification is shifting from “paper packets” to stronger digital signals

As fraud becomes more sophisticated, market pressure is moving toward multi-signal verification: registration history, phone/email integrity, insurance monitoring, affiliation detection, and anomaly flags. The practical 2026 implication is faster onboarding for known-good carriers and tighter friction for new/unknown entities—especially those with mismatched ownership, recycled contact details, or unusual authority patterns. Key data point: industry vetting discussions emphasize detecting ‘chameleon carrier’ affiliations and principal place-of-business abuse. Overdrive’s reporting quoted carrier-vetting tool leader Dale Prax on where AI could sharpen FMCSA enforcement and industry decision-making.

Technology & Policy

Autonomous linehaul is moving from “pilot” to early commercial scaling on Sun Belt lanes

Autonomous trucking developers continue to frame 2026 as a scaling year, focusing on repeatable highway corridors where utilization economics are strongest. Over the next 3–12 months, brokers should track which lanes are becoming “autonomy-ready” and how tendering/insurance standards evolve for those moves.
