Key data point: Aurora has publicly discussed deploying ‘hundreds’ of driverless trucks by the end of 2026. Commentary on Aurora’s roadmap highlights Texas-centered corridors and Sun Belt scaling as the near-term focus.

FMCSA TechCelerate Now (Phase 2) keeps pushing ADAS adoption and ROI tooling

Safety technology adoption is becoming more operationally consequential as insurers and shippers look for demonstrable risk controls (AEB, lane departure, camera systems, and related driver training). For 2026 planning, that means more carriers will request clearer shipper facility policies (yards, speed limits, check-in processes) that align with camera/ADAS workflows and incident documentation. Key data point: TechCelerate Now’s ROI calculator has been updated to include more system types. Transport Topics reported that TMC continues to develop recommended practices on calibration, camera systems, cybersecurity, and driver training in support of FMCSA’s initiative.

First-ever dedicated federal truck parking funding changes the pipeline for new capacity

Parking shortages remain a daily productivity drain and a safety risk, and the new funding should accelerate state projects and technology deployments that help drivers find spaces. The 3–12 month impact is likely to be planning and grant activity, with actual capacity additions ramping over a longer horizon—still, brokers can expect parking constraints to remain a service variable in 2026. Key data point: the 2026 federal spending bill included $200 million specifically for truck parking expansion. Trucking Dive reported the funding and reiterated ATRI findings that drivers spend about 56 minutes per day searching for parking, creating material lost time and wages.

Bottom Line

The 2026 setup looks less like a clean “rebound” and more like a structural reset: carrier attrition, aging labor demographics, and insurance-driven cost pressure are gradually tightening real capacity even when demand growth is uneven. Fuel volatility reintroduces cash-flow and pricing friction, increasing the odds of selective coverage and surcharge disputes. Fraud is escalating from an operational nuisance to a policy priority, with proposed legislation and DOT/FMSCA analytics initiatives pointing to tougher registration integrity and enforcement. For brokers, the next 3–12 months favor disciplined carrier networks, tighter verification playbooks, and proactive cost/technology conversations rather than chasing marginal spot wins.

title: Weekly Freight Report - January 23, 2026
excerpt: Truckload conditions in mid-January remained tighter than many shippers expected for a post-holiday period, with spot pricing supported by thinner capacity and winter disruption risk. DAT’s Trendlines data in late January (a close proxy for the Jan 16–23 window)
content:
Market Pulse — spot/contract rates, load-to-truck ratios, capacity

Truckload conditions in mid-January remained tighter than many shippers expected for a post-holiday period, with spot pricing supported by thinner capacity and winter disruption risk. DAT’s Trendlines data in late January (a close proxy for the Jan 16–23 window) put national average spot van at $2.30/mile, spot reefer at $2.79/mile, and spot flatbed at $2.59/mile. (This “all-in” view typically includes a fuel component and reflects what brokers pay carriers.) ([Scale Funding quoting DAT Trendlines](https://getscalefunding.com/resources/current-freight-rates/))

On the demand-to-capacity side, DAT’s same period read showed load-to-truck ratios near 6.0 for van, 14.42 for reefer, and 37.3 for flatbed, signaling that flatbed capacity was the most constrained of the three (and most sensitive to regional project freight and weather). ([Scale Funding quoting DAT Trendlines](https://getscalefunding.com/resources/current-freight-rates/))

FreightWaves market commentary in mid-January also pointed to a capacity-led tightening narrative: tender rejection metrics were running meaningfully above typical January baselines, indicating carriers were increasingly selective and pushing shippers to the spot market. FreightWaves’ “State of Freight” discussion highlighted rejection readings above 10% in mid-January, despite relatively soft demand—an important signal that the market’s “floor” was being set by supply contraction, not a demand boom. ([FreightWaves State of Freight video transcript](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9qm9_rOokWw))

What it means for brokers: In this environment, pricing discipline matters more than volume. The market is transitioning from “race to the bottom” quoting toward more dynamic replenishment pricing—especially in weather-affected regions and on flatbed-heavy lanes.

Regulation & Enforcement — FMCSA/DOT rules, ELD, CDL, state regs

Regulatory risk remained a core theme for January because enforcement actions and systems changes have second-order effects on capacity (driver availability, out-of-service events, and onboarding friction). FMCSA’s ELD program updates continued to remove noncompliant devices from the registry; FMCSA posted that on January 13, 2026, it removed certain ELDs from the list of registered devices due to failure to meet minimum technical requirements under 49 CFR Part 395, Appendix A. ([FMCSA ELD News & Events](https://eld.fmcsa.dot.gov/support/newsandevents))

Additionally, industry compliance roundups during this period emphasized that early-year registration and safety requirements (including Unified Carrier Registration timing) can create short-term administrative friction for smaller fleets—another subtle contributor to capacity tightness when the spot market is already firm. ([Foley January 2026 compliance overview](https://www.foley.io/articles/january-whats-new-in-safety-dot-compliance))

For brokers, the practical takeaway is that “paper compliance” issues can quickly become “service failures” if a carrier is sidelined by device replacement, credential mismatches, or documentation gaps. Building redundancy in carrier options is a form of risk management—not just a sourcing preference.

Broker Edge — what brokers need to know, competitive positioning

As the market tightens unevenly, the winning brokerage playbook shifts from pure rate shopping to operational trust and lane-specific execution. FreightWaves’ early-2026 outlook positioned the spot market as an intentional procurement lever (not merely a last-resort), with shippers balancing contracted freight and spot agility to manage volatility. ([FreightWaves](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/2026-outlook-spot-market-strategies-for-shippers-carriers-and-brokers))

For American Lady Transportation, competitive positioning in the Jan 16–23 window looked like this:

  • Quote with context: Use load-to-truck ratios and rejection-rate direction to justify pricing moves to customers (especially on flatbed and reefer).
  • Segment by service risk: Not all “cheap trucks” are equal—vet for compliance readiness (ELD status, insurance, authority age, contact validation).
  • Protect margin via routing choices: When capacity is thin, margin often comes from avoiding problem freight (long dwell, high-claim commodities, weak shipper controls), not just from higher buy-sell spreads.

Cross-Border Watchlist — US-Mexico, US-Canada, USMCA, tariffs

Cross-border freight remained a stabilizing demand channel entering 2026, even as domestic indicators were mixed. Market outlook coverage noted that U.S.–Mexico and U.S.–Canada flows were complicated by policy uncertainty and customs friction but generally expected to remain stable into early 2026. ([C.H. Robinson freight market update](https://www.chrobinson.com/en-us/resources/insights-and-advisories/north-america-freight-insights/jan-2026-freight-market-update/))

Strategically, shippers were also looking ahead to the formal USMCA review set to begin in July 2026, which increased sensitivity to compliance, documentation discipline, and potential future border procedures. CSIS summarized that Article 34.7 requires a six-year review starting in July 2026 and noted that Mexico was the top U.S. trading partner in 2024 with nearly $930B in total trade. ([CSIS](https://www.csis.org/analysis/usmca-review-2026))

Broker takeaway for the Texas market: For Willis/Houston-area brokerages, cross-border moves (especially to/from Laredo and South Texas staging points) were a smart place to maintain volume diversity—while tightening carrier vetting and insisting on clear chain-of-custody for handoffs.

Fraud & Security — cargo theft, double-brokering, CDL fraud

Fraud and cargo theft risk continued to evolve from opportunistic “yard theft” toward organized and identity-enabled schemes. A January 16 DOJ announcement described a multi-defendant organized theft ring tied to at least 14 cargo thefts and “millions of dollars” in stolen merchandise, illustrating the scale and professionalism of modern theft operations. ([Amundsen Davis summary referencing DOJ announcement](https://www.amundsendavislaw.com/alert-combatting-cargo-theft-and-organized-crime-strategies-for-trucking-and-logistics-companies))

Industry commentary also underscored that strategic theft—often involving cyber and identity manipulation to divert entire shipments—has grown dramatically in recent years, increasing exposure for brokers that do not rigorously verify counterparties. ([Amundsen Davis](https://www.amundsendavislaw.com/alert-combatting-cargo-theft-and-organized-crime-strategies-for-trucking-and-logistics-companies))

Operational implication: During a tightening market, fraudsters exploit urgency. The Jan 16–23 week was exactly the kind of environment where “need a truck now” becomes an attack surface for double-brokering and carrier impersonation.

Equipment, Fuel & Ops — diesel prices, truck orders, driver pay

Fuel moved higher into late January. The EIA’s diesel fuel update (released Jan 27) showed the national on-highway diesel average rising from $3.459/gal (Jan 12) to $3.530/gal (Jan 19) and $3.624/gal (Jan 26), with the West Coast at $4.301/gal and the Gulf Coast at $3.325/gal as of Jan 26. ([Rigzone summarizing EIA diesel fuel update](https://www.rigzone.com/news/eia_sees_usa_diesel_price_dropping_in_2026-28-jan-2026-182874-article/))

On equipment demand, preliminary order activity suggested fleets were still cautiously replacing equipment, not aggressively expanding. FTR reported 32,500 North American Class 8 orders for January 2026 (down 24% m/m but up 27% y/y), while ACT Research’s preliminary estimate was 30,800 (up 20% y/y). ([Trucks, Parts, Service](https://www.truckpartsandservice.com/trucks-trailers/class-7-8/article/15816305/january-2026-class-8-truck-orders-up-20-year-over-year))

Why it matters: Higher diesel plus cautious equipment ordering reinforces the idea that capacity won’t “flood back” quickly; that supports rate resilience when disruptions hit. For brokers, that means service reliability and carrier relationships remain a moat.

Action Checklist for Brokers — 5-7 bullet points

  • Reprice weekly, not monthly: Use current DAT rate direction and load-to-truck ratios to refresh lane guidance before quoting. ([Scale Funding quoting DAT Trendlines](https://getscalefunding.com/resources/current-freight-rates/))
  • Tighten carrier onboarding: Verify identity, authority, insurance, contact methods, and ELD readiness—especially for “last-minute” coverage. ([FMCSA ELD News & Events](https://eld.fmcsa.dot.gov/support/newsandevents))
  • Build a flatbed playbook: With flatbed ratios elevated, lock down project freight capacity early and pre-negotiate fallbacks. ([Scale Funding quoting DAT Trendlines](https://getscalefunding.com/resources/current-freight-rates/))
  • Fuel-sensitivity audit: Re-check FSC assumptions as diesel moved from $3.459 to $3.624/gal across the Jan 12–26 window. ([Rigzone summarizing EIA diesel fuel update](https://www.rigzone.com/news/eia_sees_usa_diesel_price_dropping_in_2026-28-jan-2026-182874-article/))
  • Cross-border chain-of-custody: For Mexico/Canada moves, document every handoff; require clear appointment windows and staging plans. ([C.H. Robinson freight market update](https://www.chrobinson.com/en-us/resources/insights-and-advisories/north-america-freight-insights/jan-2026-freight-market-update/))
  • Fraud drills: Train ops teams on double-brokering indicators (rate outliers, urgency pressure, mismatched emails/phone numbers) and require verification steps before releasing BOLs. ([Amundsen Davis](https://www.amundsendavislaw.com/alert-combatting-cargo-theft-and-organized-crime-strategies-for-trucking-and-logistics-companies))

title: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup - January 16, 2026
excerpt: Heading into early 2026, domestic trucking was being shaped less by a demand surge and more by a cost-driven capacity reset—insurance, fuel volatility, and credit pressure were still pushing weaker operators out. Fraud risk
content:
Fleet & Market Trends

Capacity shakeout continues into 2026 (and won’t be “fixed” quickly)

Analysts heading into 2026 were increasingly framing the recovery as slow and margin-thin, meaning more fleets could exit before pricing meaningfully improves. In practice, that points to a 3–12 month window where coverage gets less “automatic” on secondary lanes, even if demand stays uneven. FTR signaled contract-rate growth below ~2% through 2026, a level many carriers can’t live on given inflation and cost creep (per Commercial Carrier Journal).

Carrier bankruptcies stay elevated as small fleets run out of runway

Early-2026 filings reinforced that the downturn was still clearing out weaker balance sheets, especially among small interstate operators exposed to spot volatility and rising operating costs. A wave of restructurings tends to tighten reliable capacity faster than load boards show, because surviving carriers get pickier about freight quality and payment terms. Equipment Finance News tallied 21 freight-company bankruptcies in Q3 2025, a trend line that fed into 2026 restructuring headlines (via TheStreet).

Driver “shortage” debate shifts toward a quality-and-replacement problem

Entering 2026, the most useful framing for brokers and shippers was less “there aren’t drivers” and more “there aren’t enough qualified, insurable drivers willing to run the freight you need at the price you want.” That distinction matters because it pushes carriers to tighten hiring filters and raises the value of carriers with strong safety scores and stable rosters. ATRI pegged women at just 4.1% of truck drivers, underscoring how much the industry still relies on a narrow labor pool (per ATRI).

LTL consolidation keeps reshaping service expectations and accessorial pain

Ongoing LTL network rationalization and consolidation continues to change how capacity is allocated: denser networks win, and shippers with weaker freight profiles feel it first through stricter accessorial enforcement and tighter pickup windows. For brokers, that increases the premium on accurate freight classification, dock readiness, and proactive appointment management. Shippers should expect LTL carriers to prioritize network density over marginal volume as consolidation continues (as discussed in industry commentary on LTL consolidation).

Fuel & Cost Pressures

Nuclear verdicts keep pushing insurance up—and underwriting gets stricter

Insurance is increasingly a capacity issue, not just a cost line: higher premiums and tighter underwriting can sideline smaller carriers that can’t meet new requirements. That in turn accelerates attrition and raises the “minimum viable rate” carriers need to accept freight. Verdicts over $1M have increased more than 235% since 2012, a key driver of insurer behavior (per Reliance Partners).

Diesel volatility reopens refinery-capacity and distillate-supply questions

Even when crude prices soften, diesel can stay stubborn due to distillate supply constraints and refinery economics—especially if capacity is offline or converted away from traditional output. That keeps carriers quick to reprice and quick to reject freight that doesn’t recover fuel. EIA’s pre-disruption outlook projected ~ $3.47/gal average diesel in 2026, highlighting how sensitive fleet economics are to forecast misses (per Tradlinx analysis citing EIA outlook).

Fuel surcharge friction rises as shippers push back on lagging formulas

When diesel moves quickly, surcharge mechanisms tied to weekly benchmarks can lag real pump prices, leaving carriers to absorb costs temporarily—or to “self-correct” by declining freight and forcing repricing. Expect more disputes over baselines, regional indexing, and whether surcharges should apply to accessorials. Diesel jumped about 25.6% in roughly three weeks in early March 2026, the kind of move that breaks trust in slow-moving surcharge tables (per FreightWise).

Alternative fuels: fleets test where infrastructure is ready, not where policy wants it

In 2026, most near-term adoption continues to be lane- and duty-cycle-specific: battery electric for return-to-base and urban/regional, renewable diesel/HVO as a “drop-in” decarbonization lever, and hydrogen in early customer-test phases. For brokers, the practical implication is uneven capacity availability by geography and shipper requirements (especially ESG-driven). Volvo said it plans to begin customer tests of hydrogen-powered trucks in 2026 (per Volvo Trucks).

Fraud & Security Watch

SAFER Transport Act spotlights freight fraud as a federal enforcement priority

Strategic cargo theft and fraud (fictitious pickups, hostage loads, identity spoofing) moved from “industry headache” to explicit legislative focus, signaling more interagency coordination and pressure on registration loopholes. If enacted, the bill’s registration reforms and reporting requirements could raise compliance expectations for both carriers and intermediaries. The SAFER Transport Act would phase out MC numbers within five years in favor of USDOT-only identification (per Overdrive).

Double-brokering enforcement shifts toward registration controls and automated flagging

The enforcement playbook is evolving from chasing individual bad transactions to preventing fraudulent entities from registering or rapidly re-registering (“chameleon” behavior). That matters over the next 3–12 months because stronger front-end controls can reduce the total number of bad actors brokers must filter manually. The bill would require FMCSA to develop automated systems to flag suspicious registration activity (per Overdrive).

Carrier verification platforms and AI tools become table stakes for broker risk management

As fraud rings professionalize, brokers are increasingly expected to use layered verification (authority, insurance, device and behavior signals, pickup validation) rather than relying on a single database check. Over the next year, shippers may begin auditing broker processes more aggressively—especially on high-value loads. Overhaul reports its FraudWatch has flagged 104 bad actors and cites $100M in losses avoided (per Overhaul).

Technology & Policy

ADAS adoption gets a push via TechCelerate Now (ROI tools, standards, calibration guidance)

FMCSA’s TechCelerate Now second phase signals continued focus on helping fleets deploy safety tech with clearer ROI models and better implementation guidance. For brokers, that can become a differentiator: carriers with consistent ADAS programs may deliver fewer claims and fewer service disruptions. FMCSA renewed TechCelerate Now in 2024 for a four-year second phase (per Transport Topics).

Autonomous trucking: pilots expand, but the near-term impact is corridor-specific

Autonomous deployments remain concentrated on predictable long-haul corridors, meaning disruption is likely to appear first as “new capacity” on a handful of lanes rather than a broad national reset. The operational implication for the next 6–12 months is more experimentation with dedicated freight, tighter appointment discipline, and new insurance/claims frameworks. Aurora has said it intends to have “hundreds” of driverless trucks on U.S. highways by the end of 2026 (per analysis of Aurora’s public plan).

EPA regulatory whiplash increases equipment-planning uncertainty (NOx still matters)

Policy shifts can change the timing of fleet trade cycles and the pricing of new equipment—effects that feed back into capacity. Even where greenhouse-gas rules face new legal constraints, near-term NOx compliance requirements still shape engine availability and cost. Mansfield Energy reported EPA rescinded the 2009 endangerment finding while noting 2027 NOx standards remain in place (per Mansfield Energy).

Truck parking remains a structural constraint (and a safety/compliance risk)

Parking scarcity directly affects hours-of-service compliance, driver retention, and crash risk, making it a hidden capacity limiter even when trucks and loads are available. Expect more attention on public-private buildouts and on-tech solutions that reserve/price space—especially along high-VMT freight corridors like Texas. One estimate puts the U.S. at fewer than 40,000 public truck-parking spaces for roughly 3.5 million drivers (about 1 space per 87 drivers) (per Best Truck Parking).

Bottom Line

Heading into early 2026, the domestic trucking market’s next 3–12 months were being shaped less by a demand surge and more by a cost-driven capacity reset—insurance, fuel volatility, and credit pressure were still pushing weaker operators out. At the same time, fraud risk was rising fast enough to force process changes, with the SAFER Transport Act signaling momentum toward tighter registration controls and more automated enforcement. Technology adoption (ADAS, verification platforms, and corridor-based autonomy) is advancing, but its near-term impact will be uneven by lane and shipper profile. For brokers, the play is to secure durable carriers, tighten verification and documentation, and treat “total cost to serve” (fuel, claims risk, accessorials, and delay) as the pricing baseline, not the spot quote.

title: Weekly Freight Report - January 16, 2026
excerpt: Spot pricing stayed firm into mid-January, supported by tight capacity signals even as post-holiday volumes normalized. DAT January averages: van $2.32/mi, reefer $2.81/mi, flatbed $2.85/mi, with contract van $2.48/mi.
content:
Market Pulse — spot/contract rates, load-to-truck ratios, capacity

Spot pricing stayed firm into mid-January, supported by tight capacity signals even as post-holiday volumes normalized.

  • DAT January averages (all-in): van $2.32/mi (+$0.03 m/m), reefer $2.81/mi (+$0.12), flatbed $2.85/mi (+$0.22), per DAT.
  • DAT contract January averages: van $2.48/mi (+$0.02), reefer $2.81/mi (+$0.02), flatbed $3.04/mi (-$0.01), per DAT.

For week-level pulse as the market moved through Jan 9–Jan 16, carrier conversations were consistent with load board tightness remaining elevated vs. typical early-January seasonality. One useful directional reference: DAT commentary shared in a late-January Trendlines recap showed national van at $2.30/mi with a national load-to-truck ratio (LTR) around 6.0; reefer $2.79/mi with LTR 14.42; flatbed $2.59/mi with LTR 37.3 (Scale Funding / DAT Trendlines recap).

On the demand side, FreightWaves’ January “State of the Industry” view highlighted a market that tightened sharply after Thanksgiving, with tender rejections 2–3 percentage points higher year over year and spot rates up close to 9% y/y in aggregate (FreightWaves). SONAR commentary during mid-January also pointed to rejection rates sitting just above 10% even without a major winter disruption, reinforcing the “thin-and-getting-thinner” capacity narrative (FreightWaves State of Freight webinar).

Regulation & Enforcement — FMCSA/DOT rules, ELD, CDL, state regs

The most immediate compliance item during the week was ELD enforcement risk tied to device revocations.

  • ELD revocations (Jan 13, 2026): FMCSA removed four ELD products (Premierride Logs, DSGELOGS, State ELOGS, State ELOGS 2) from the registered list and directed carriers to replace them within 60 days to stay compliant (FMCSA ELD notice).
  • Random testing rates for 2026: DOT published that the FMCSA random drug testing rate remains 50% and random alcohol testing remains 10% for 2026 (Overdrive).

Broker takeaway: ELD revocations create service and liability exposure in two ways: (1) a carrier can be placed out of service if running a revoked device past the deadline; (2) short-notice lane coverage gets harder if a meaningful share of small fleets are suddenly forced onto paper logs while they source replacement devices.

Broker Edge — what brokers need to know, competitive positioning

With spot rates elevated and capacity signals tightening, the broker advantage came down to operational credibility and carrier prioritization, not just price discovery.

  • Mind the contract/spot convergence: DAT’s January data showed contract van at $2.48/mi vs. spot van at $2.32/mi, a smaller spread than shippers were used to in 2025 (DAT). Use this to reset shipper expectations: bid cycles will reprice if the spot floor stays higher.
  • Build “compliance-aware” coverage: After the Jan 13 ELD revocations, your carrier selection process should explicitly confirm the ELD provider/device status for any small carrier you onboard or re-activate (FMCSA ELD notice).
  • Capacity is thin even when volumes aren’t booming: FreightWaves’ January analysis framed the environment as supply-driven tightening (rejections 2–3 pts higher y/y) rather than a demand-led boom (FreightWaves).

Positioning for American Lady Transportation: sell shippers on a “protect service first” playbook—multi-carrier routing guides, tighter appointment discipline, and transparent accessorials—because carriers will increasingly choose partners that minimize wasted driver time.

Cross-Border Watchlist — US-Mexico, US-Canada, USMCA, tariffs

Cross-border planning in early January was dominated by tariff-driven uncertainty and the countdown to the USMCA six-year review.

  • USMCA review cycle: C.H. Robinson flagged that 2026 trade policy will be heavily influenced by USMCA review negotiations headed toward a July 2026 decision window (C.H. Robinson).
  • Mexico tariff action (effective Jan 1, 2026): Mexico imposed tariffs reportedly ranging from 5% to 50% on a wide set of goods sourced from non-FTA countries, while goods meeting USMCA rules of origin are generally positioned to remain preferential (C.H. Robinson).

Broker takeaway: Expect more shipper questions on “what changes at the border?” even when nothing operational changed overnight. The broker role is to translate policy into routing and documentation discipline: verify broker/carrier cross-border authority, confirm customs broker-of-record, and pressure-test lead times for inspection variability.

Fraud & Security — cargo theft, double-brokering, CDL fraud

Security risk remained a first-order issue, especially for electronics, branded retail goods, and high-value consumer shipments.

  • Industry legal commentary referenced a DOJ announcement (Jan 16, 2026) tied to an organized theft ring responsible for multiple cargo thefts and multi-million-dollar losses (Amundsen Davis).

Broker controls to tighten this week:

  • Carrier identity verification: verify FMCSA authority, insurance, and phone/email continuity; treat “domain mismatch” as a stop sign.
  • Pickup procedures: enforce pickup numbers, driver photo ID checks, and geofenced check-calls on high-risk loads.
  • Do not re-broker without shipper authorization: double-brokering and “hostage load” tactics thrive when processes are informal and documentation is weak.

Equipment, Fuel & Ops — diesel prices, truck orders, driver pay

Fuel: Diesel began climbing through January, increasing surcharge pressure and raising the “all-in” cost floor for spot moves.

  • EIA weekly retail diesel (as carried by YCharts) rose from $3.459/gal (Jan 12) to $3.530/gal (Jan 19) (YCharts (EIA series)).
  • BTS reported average diesel No. 2 at $3.52/gal in January 2026 (USDOT BTS).

Equipment/orders: New truck orders improved year over year, a sign fleets were cautiously returning to replacement cycles—though not necessarily expanding capacity aggressively.

  • ACT Research preliminary data showed January 2026 Class 8 orders at 30,800 units (+20% y/y), while FTR’s estimate was 32,500 (+27% y/y), according to Transport Topics.

Ops implication: When diesel rises and capacity is thin, carriers get more selective about dwell, deadhead, and payment behavior. Brokers should treat accessorial clarity and fast detention resolution as a capacity tool.

Action Checklist for Brokers — 5-7 bullet points

  • Reset lane guidance using January benchmarks: spot van $2.32/mi, reefer $2.81/mi, flatbed $2.85/mi (DAT January) and explain the contract/spot spread (van contract $2.48/mi) (DAT).
  • Run an ELD compliance check on active carriers; flag any carrier using one of the four FMCSA-revoked devices from Jan 13 (FMCSA ELD notice).
  • Update fuel conversations with customers—diesel was rising (e.g., $3.459 → $3.530/gal from Jan 12 to Jan 19), so expect carrier pushback if FSC lags (YCharts (EIA series)).
  • Prioritize carriers on execution, not just price: fast loading/unloading and clean accessorials matter more when tender rejections are ~10% and capacity is fragile (FreightWaves State of Freight webinar).
  • Increase security for high-value loads with stricter pickup verification and tracking; theft rings remained active and sophisticated (Amundsen Davis).
  • Cross-border: validate documentation for USMCA qualification and watch for tariff-driven lead-time variability ahead of the USMCA review cycle (C.H. Robinson).

title: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup - January 9, 2026
excerpt: Major regulatory changes take effect as 2026 begins, freight markets show post-holiday tightening with elevated spot rates, and winter weather threatens further capacity disruptions across the domestic trucking industry.
content:
Regulatory Overhaul Kicks Off 2026

The new year has brought a wave of regulatory changes that carriers, brokers, and drivers need to navigate carefully. The FMCSA's retirement of MC numbers is now fully in effect — all carriers must use their USDOT number exclusively for registrations, insurance filings, and broker contracts. The move is designed to reduce fraud and eliminate so-called "chameleon carriers" who re-register under new identities after enforcement actions.

Meanwhile, the paper-to-digital transition for CDL and medical certifications reached its January 10 deadline. After that date, all certifications must be submitted electronically to State Driver Licensing Agencies. Carriers who haven't completed the transition face potential compliance issues, per FMCSA guidance. The Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse is also seeing stricter enforcement, with violations now requiring 24-hour reporting and state agencies gaining real-time access to driver records.

Broker Bond Requirements Tighten

Effective January 16, brokers and freight forwarders must maintain a $75,000 bond or trust fund in approved liquid assets under updated FMCSA financial responsibility rules. If financial security falls below that threshold, operating authority can be suspended with just a 30-day compliance window. The rule is intended to reduce non-payment risk and broker defaults — a persistent pain point for small carriers. Industry groups are urging carriers to audit their broker partners ahead of the enforcement date, per FreightWaves reporting.

Post-Holiday Freight Market Tightens

The freight market entered January with notable tightness carried over from the holiday season. According to Arrive Logistics, spot rates surged in December as tender rejections climbed, with dry van rejections peaking near 12% just before Christmas. Reefer spot rates crossed above contract rates for the first time in two years — a significant milestone that reflects real capacity pressure in temperature-controlled freight.

FreightWaves' January State of the Industry report confirmed the pattern: spot rates are up close to 9% year-over-year in aggregate, and rejection rates are running 2-3 percentage points higher than the same period last year. The Cass Freight Index showed shipments down 7.1% year-over-year in January, but the Truckload Linehaul Index rose 3.2% year-over-year, indicating that rates are climbing even as volumes remain soft.

Winter Storm Threatens Capacity Disruption

A major winter storm approaching the central and southern United States is adding uncertainty to an already volatile market. Per Arrive Logistics' January market update, widespread ice and snow threaten meaningful near-term capacity disruption and rate volatility, particularly in regions not typically prepared for severe winter conditions. Pent-up demand from weather-related delays could extend spot rate volatility well beyond normal seasonal patterns.

Carriers operating in the Midwest and Northeast are already dealing with shorter daylight hours, icy roads, and increased transit times. Open-deck and oversized shipments face the greatest disruption risk, with tarping operations becoming especially difficult in freezing conditions.

LTL Sector Faces Headwinds

Early signals suggest the less-than-truckload sector is entering 2026 under pressure. Federal data points to notable job losses in long-distance LTL operations at the start of the year — a trend that bears watching as the sector works to recover from the capacity shock left by Yellow Corp.'s bankruptcy. However, some analysts note that as truckload capacity tightens, heavier shipments above 10,000 pounds are beginning to shift into LTL networks, which has historically signaled the tail end of freight downturns.

Capacity Outlook: Contraction Moderating

The January Logistics Managers' Index came in at 59.6, with Transportation Prices hitting 71.4 — the highest reading since April 2022, per LMI data. Transportation Capacity registered at 47.1, still in contraction territory but a meaningful improvement from December's 36.9. The data suggests the worst of the holiday capacity crunch is fading, but carriers shouldn't expect abundant truck availability anytime soon. LMI respondents predict capacity will continue contracting over the next 12 months, with future readings expected around 42.3.

The Cass analysis noted that the freight economy continues to grow, and the for-hire recovery will begin in earnest when private fleet capacity — which has been in contraction since 2025 — becomes sustainably tight. Even modest 2% contract rate increases feel significant after four years of stagnation or decline.

Insurance Market Tightens for New Entrants

New owner-operators entering the market in 2026 face a notably more challenging insurance environment. Higher down payments, fewer carrier options, and reduced tolerance for early violations mean that setting up authority correctly from day one is critical. On the positive side, the tightening regulatory environment may benefit compliant operators long-term — as unqualified drivers are removed from certain freight segments, capacity stabilizes and insurance companies reward consistent compliance records.

Looking Ahead

The first full week of 2026 has set the tone for what promises to be a transitional year. Regulatory compliance deadlines are stacking up through mid-January, the post-holiday freight market remains tighter than expected, and winter weather adds another layer of unpredictability. For carriers and shippers, the strategic priorities are clear: complete regulatory transitions, audit broker relationships, and build flexibility into capacity planning for a market that's slowly tightening but still far from a full recovery cycle.

title: Weekly Freight Report - January 9, 2026
excerpt: Early January continued the post-holiday pattern: volumes cooled from late-December peak, but capacity stayed tighter than a typical first full week of the year, keeping spot pricing elevated in key lanes. FreightWaves noted spot rates and tender rejections climbed after Thanksgiving and remained firm entering January.
content:
Market Pulse — spot/contract rates, load-to-truck ratios, capacity

Early January continued the post-holiday pattern: volumes cooled from late-December peak, but capacity stayed tighter than a typical first full week of the year, keeping spot pricing elevated in key lanes. FreightWaves noted that spot rates and tender rejections climbed sharply after Thanksgiving and remained firm entering January, driven more by supply contraction than demand growth (FreightWaves January 2026 State of the Industry).

  • Dry van spot: DAT Trendlines commentary later in January referenced national van rates around $2.30/mile (all-in) and a national van load-to-truck ratio around 6.0:1 (with December averaging ~8.56), signaling a post-holiday ease but still workable demand (DAT Trendlines recap (Jan 27, 2026)).
  • Reefer spot: The same DAT recap cited reefer rates around $2.79/mile and a reefer load-to-truck ratio around 14.42:1, consistent with winter-produce and cold-chain variability (DAT Trendlines recap (Jan 27, 2026)).
  • Flatbed spot: DAT’s recap cited flatbed rates around $2.59/mile and a flatbed load-to-truck ratio around 37.3:1, showing structurally tighter capacity than van despite winter seasonality (DAT Trendlines recap (Jan 27, 2026)).

Capacity signals: A January market update highlighted tender rejection rates (a proxy for tightness) around 9.1% for van, 15.3% for reefer and 18.2% for flatbed (Dynamic Logistix January 2026 Market Update). This aligns with FreightWaves’ broader framing that the “flip” was being driven by fewer trucks, not a sudden demand surge (FreightWaves January 2026 State of the Industry).

Contract vs. spot: By early 2026, several market narratives centered on spot closing the gap with contract. Trucking Dive summarized that spot linehaul pricing rose faster than contract pricing over the prior year, narrowing the spread materially (Trucking Dive). For brokers, that backdrop matters: bid season discipline weakens when carriers see spot as a credible alternative.

Regulation & Enforcement — FMCSA/DOT rules, ELD, CDL, state regs

The enforcement tone heading into mid-January was clear: more roadside focus on driver qualification, vehicle condition, and compliance documentation. USDOT/FMCSA’s multi-state campaign “Operation SafeDRIVE” ran Jan. 13–15 (immediately after this report week) and provides a strong leading indicator for how enforcement pressure was building in January.

  • Operation SafeDRIVE results included 8,215 inspections, 704 drivers placed out-of-service and 1,231 vehicles placed out-of-service (CDLLife).
  • Notably, the report stated nearly 500 out-of-service orders were tied to English proficiency violations (CDLLife).

Separate compliance writeups pointed to structural changes slated for January, including transitions around identifiers and documentation. One industry compliance overview noted MC number retirement in favor of USDOT-only identification starting January 2026, and flagged a Jan. 16 effective date for broker financial responsibility compliance expectations (bond/trust) (Fast Forward TMS). While brokers should confirm requirements against FMCSA primary notices, the operational takeaway remains: identity controls and documentation checks were moving to the center of compliance.

Broker Edge — what brokers need to know, competitive positioning

1) Price discovery needs tighter cadence. In a tightening market, “two-week-old” spot assumptions become expensive. The way to protect margin is to update lane intelligence frequently and align offers with actual capacity behavior. FreightWaves’ January view framed the market as tight from supply contraction, meaning a small demand bump can swing pricing quickly (FreightWaves January 2026 State of the Industry).

2) Manage the spot/contract mix deliberately. As spot catches up toward contract, shippers can experience more routing guide failures and “mini tenders” into spot. Trucking Dive described the narrowing contract/spot gap as a structural repricing dynamic (Trucking Dive). Brokers that can offer flexible capacity (power-only, drop, team, weekend coverage) can win share even without being lowest-price.

3) Treat compliance as a service feature. With heightened enforcement (and high out-of-service counts) shippers increasingly value fewer service failures over marginal cost savings. Building “compliance-ready capacity” (clean DQFs, verified ELD, strong inspection history) becomes a differentiator (CDLLife).

Cross-Border Watchlist — US-Mexico, US-Canada, USMCA, tariffs

Cross-border remained one of the steadier demand pools relative to some domestic sectors, but with policy-driven uncertainty around tariffs and uneven end-market strength (especially automotive). FreightWaves reported that executives at Uber Freight viewed U.S.–Mexico freight as a stabilizer, citing exports out of Mexico to the U.S. up roughly 15% in recent months (as discussed in early January) (FreightWaves).

C.H. Robinson’s January cross-border outlook added detail from the latest available Mexican data at the time: Mexican exports were up 7.9% year over year in November (six straight months of export growth), while Mexico’s automotive production contracted 8.4% and vehicle exports fell 3.4% in the same month (C.H. Robinson cross-border update). That divergence matters for brokers covering Laredo and El Paso: expect stronger electronics/industrial flows and more volatility in automotive-heavy corridors.

Tariff and sourcing risk: C.H. Robinson also noted that Mexico implemented new/higher tariffs on certain Asian imports effective Jan. 1, 2026, with tariff ranges cited at 5% to 50% across categories like auto parts, steel, aluminum, plastics, and other goods (C.H. Robinson cross-border update). For U.S. brokers, the key is second-order effects: shifts in Mexico’s inbound supply chain can change northbound export mix and produce imbalanced equipment flows.

Fraud & Security — cargo theft, double-brokering, CDL fraud

Security risk continues to expand from “physical theft” into identity-based and paperwork-based fraud. A 2026 legal alert summarized data from ATRI estimating cargo theft costs of approximately $6.6 billion annually and highlighted that “strategic theft” (blending cyber + identity tactics) was up 1,500% since 2021 (Amundsen Davis).

That same alert pointed to a federal case (Southern District of Indiana) announced Jan. 16, 2026, involving six individuals tied to an organized theft ring responsible for at least 14 cargo thefts stealing millions in merchandise (Amundsen Davis). Even though that announcement fell just after this report week, it reflects the operating reality brokers faced throughout early January: more sophisticated impersonation and more “clean” thefts via reconsignment, fake carrier setups, and document swaps.

Broker takeaways: Tighten carrier onboarding (authority/insurance checks, phone/email domain matching, factoring notices), require in-app tracking for high-theft commodities, and use strict change-control for delivery appointments and consignee edits.

Equipment, Fuel & Ops — diesel prices, truck orders, driver pay

Diesel: EIA weekly retail diesel pricing moved higher through January. The EIA’s weekly series shows U.S. on-highway diesel at $3.477/gal for the week of Jan. 5, 2026 and $3.459/gal for the week of Jan. 12, 2026 (EIA weekly retail prices). Fuel volatility matters even when rates are rising: it changes the speed of carrier repricing and can widen spot bid spreads on short-notice loads.

Class 8 orders: Equipment ordering improved, but with caveats. ACT Research estimated preliminary North American Class 8 net orders of 30,800 units in January 2026, up 20% year over year (Fleet Equipment). FTR’s estimate cited 32,500 units, down sequentially from December but up 27% year over year (Trucks, Parts, Service). The signal for brokers: capacity is not expanding quickly; orders reflect replacement and regulatory-timing behavior more than aggressive fleet growth.

Ops reality: With enforcement tightening and a portion of drivers/tractors being sidelined (even temporarily), carriers price in “compliance friction.” Expect higher premiums for tight pickup windows, high-theft lanes, and weekend/holiday recovery moves.

Action Checklist for Brokers — 5-7 bullet points

  • Reset your weekly lane baselines using current DAT/FreightWaves signals; don’t carry late-December assumptions into early January pricing (FreightWaves January 2026 State of the Industry).
  • Quote with equipment-specific tightness: flatbed remains structurally tighter than van; reefer remains highly seasonal (DAT LTRs and rates support this) (DAT Trendlines recap (Jan 27, 2026)).
  • Pre-qualify capacity for enforcement risk (driver qualification, equipment condition) given the high out-of-service counts seen in mid-January enforcement campaigns (CDLLife).
  • Harden fraud controls: multi-factor carrier verification, strict change-control, and tracking for high-value loads as strategic theft grows (Amundsen Davis).
  • Cross-border: plan around mixed sector strength (stronger non-auto exports, weaker automotive), and bake in extra lead time for border compliance steps (C.H. Robinson cross-border update).
  • Watch fuel weekly; even small diesel moves can swing FSC math and change carrier acceptance behavior (EIA weekly retail prices).
  • Track capacity outlook via truck orders: improving orders suggest replacement demand, not an immediate capacity flood (Fleet Equipment).

title: Domestic Trucking Industry News Roundup - January 2, 2026
excerpt: Domestic trucking entered 2026 with tightening capacity, elevated tender rejections, and growing compliance friction across licensing and broker financial rules. Diesel forecasts looked modestly lower, but volatility, insurance, and fraud enforcement kept risk high.
content:
Fleet & Market Trends

Capacity keeps tightening as spot markets stay elevated after peak season

January did not bring the usual post-holiday slump: tender rejections stayed near double digits and spot pricing remained sticky, signaling that capacity is thinner than headline demand suggests. For shippers and brokers, the next 3–12 months likely look like a “fragile balance” market—where weather, compliance changes, or seasonal surges can cause rapid tightening. Per FreightWaves, rejection rates sat near levels not seen since 2022 and are being supported by supply-side contraction more than a demand boom.

Key data point: National tender rejections were 9.97% and truckload spot rates were $2.62/mile (inclusive of fuel) in mid-January. (Sources: [FreightWaves](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/trucking-market-holds-up-in-january))

Carrier attrition shifts from “headline bankruptcies” to quiet authority expirations

Even without a wave of high-profile collapses, capacity can tighten when small fleets simply stop renewing authority and larger fleets stay in “replacement-only” mode. FreightWaves framed 2026 risk as less about dramatic failures and more about how little slack remains when fleets sideline older equipment, delay new truck purchases, and avoid unseated tractors. For brokers, this implies a higher premium on carrier relationships and shipper operational discipline (fast turn times, clean payments, fewer surprises).

Key data point: FreightWaves warned the market can flip tighter quickly without “mass bankruptcies,” as capacity erodes through parked equipment and delayed replacement cycles. (Sources: [FreightWaves](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/2026-trucking-capacity-why-it-will-tighten-and-who-gets-trucks-first))

Driver workforce integrity becomes a bigger lever than “driver shortage” narratives

Regulators and industry groups continued pushing changes tied to licensing integrity and English-language proficiency, which can affect available capacity even in soft freight cycles. Overdrive highlighted DOT actions around non-domiciled CDLs and the broader debate about whether the U.S. has a true shortage or simply a qualification/compliance bottleneck. Over the next year, broker service quality may increasingly depend on carriers that can keep compliant drivers seated and reduce churn.

Key data point: DOT actions discussed by Overdrive referenced a potential purge affecting “nearly 200,000” non-domiciled CDL holders. (Sources: [Overdrive](https://www.overdriveonline.com/business/article/15768125/dots-move-against-nondomiciled-cdl-holders-and-the-driver-shortage))

CDL training “mills” crackdown signals tighter onboarding pipelines

FMCSA’s tightening of training provider oversight is likely to raise friction in bringing new entrants into the market while improving safety outcomes over time. Overdrive reported thousands of schools removed from the Training Provider Registry as audits expanded, which could reduce near-term training capacity and raise carriers’ costs to source qualified applicants. For the next 3–12 months, expect stronger emphasis on driver quality, verifiable training, and retention as recruiting costs remain elevated.

Key data point: Overdrive reported FMCSA removed nearly 3,000 training providers from the Training Provider Registry as part of a “CDL mill” purge. (Sources: [Overdrive](https://www.overdriveonline.com/regulations/article/15814916/fmcsa-removes-3800-schools-from-training-provider-registry-amid-cdl-mill-purge))

LTL stays “repriced, not broken” as major network changes ripple into 2026

Leadership teams are increasingly treating LTL as structurally firmer on price than broader demand indicators suggest, especially as carriers optimize networks and defend yield. Logistics Management argued that despite “soft” conditions, LTL still feels expensive for many shippers—reflecting repricing dynamics rather than a fully broken market. With FedEx Freight’s planned spinoff and continued focus on sales execution, LTL procurement strategies in 2026 may prioritize network fit and accessorial discipline.

Key data point: Logistics Management characterized 2026 LTL as “repriced, not broken,” with rates remaining firm for many shippers. (Sources: [Logistics Management](https://www.logisticsmgmt.com/article/ltl_freight_in_2026_repriced_not_broken_what_leadership_needs_to_know), [Supply Chain Dive](https://www.supplychaindive.com/news/fedex-freight-forecast-revision-2026/808407/))

Fuel & Cost Pressures

Diesel outlook starts softer—but volatility risk remains a planning constraint

Early-2026 forecasts suggested diesel could average modestly lower versus 2025, which would ease fuel surcharge pressure and improve carrier margin visibility—if demand stays muted. Transport Topics cited EIA expectations for quarterly averages in the mid-$3 range, with crude as the largest component and geopolitical risk acting as a floor. For brokers, this reinforces contract structures that transparently pass fuel swings while keeping linehaul negotiations separate.

Key data point: Transport Topics reported EIA forecasts showing 2026 diesel averaging roughly $3.41–$3.60 by quarter (about $3.50 overall). (Sources: [Transport Topics](https://www.ttnews.com/articles/diesel-price-forecast-2026))

Refining economics support diesel supply, but long-term capacity additions lag demand growth

Even if crude remains abundant, refiners’ ability to sustainably increase distillate output is constrained by investment cycles and capacity decisions. Transport Topics reported refiners’ view that 2026 demand growth could outpace new global refining capacity additions, keeping crack spreads supportive and leaving fleets exposed to periodic spikes. In practice, fuel risk management and surcharge compliance will remain central to shipper-broker-carrier alignment.

Key data point: Transport Topics quoted Phillips 66’s CEO saying 2026 fuel demand growth is expected while refining capacity additions will fall short, supporting stronger crack spreads. (Sources: [Transport Topics](https://www.ttnews.com/articles/crude-big-earnings-us-refiners))

Fuel surcharge debates intensify as shippers scrutinize formulas and baselines

As market power oscillates, disputes often shift from “rate levels” to “rate structure,” including which fuel index to use, what baseline is fair, and how quickly surcharges adjust. FreightWaves’ explainer emphasized common approaches (per-mile vs. percent-of-linehaul) and the importance of using the EIA on-highway benchmark consistently. Over the next year, expect more procurement scrutiny and audits—especially where all-in spot pricing masks fuel recovery gaps.

Key data point: FreightWaves highlighted the common per-mile surcharge formula: (Current fuel price − baseline) ÷ mpg assumption, typically tied to EIA diesel benchmarks. (Sources: [FreightWaves Checkpoint](https://www.freightwaves.com/checkpoint/fuel-surcharge-in-trucking/))

Insurance and “nuclear verdict” exposure continues to reshape carrier operating costs

Carriers face persistent pressure from higher liability premiums, litigation risk, and the need for tighter safety programs—factors that can accelerate attrition among smaller operators. Transport Topics reported industry leaders warning that liability claim escalation is outpacing traditional economic drivers, prompting carriers to rethink coverage structures and invest in mitigation (cameras, coaching, safety culture). For the next 3–12 months, expect carrier selection and compliance posture to matter even more in bid events and shipper onboarding.

Key data point: Transport Topics cited research defining “nuclear verdicts” as $10 million+ and noted that one in four such auto cases involved a commercial trucking company. (Sources: [Transport Topics](https://www.ttnews.com/articles/nuclear-verdicts-get-worse), [Transport Topics](https://www.ttnews.com/articles/trucking-fights-nuclear))

Fraud & Security Watch

FMCSA bond enforcement becomes a real-time compliance risk for brokers

Beginning mid-January 2026, broker financial responsibility rules shift from paperwork to near-real-time enforcement, raising the consequences of claims, chargebacks, and trust-fund structure issues. FreightWaves reported that authority can be suspended if bond/trust availability falls below the minimum and is not replenished quickly, while BMC-85 trusts face stricter liquidity and trustee requirements. This is likely to accelerate broker consolidation and increase shipper preference for financially stable intermediaries.

Key data point: FreightWaves reported the $75,000 bond/trust floor is enforced with a seven-business-day replenishment window starting Jan. 16, 2026. (Sources: [FreightWaves](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/fmcsas-tighter-bond-enforcement-looms-over-freight-brokers-in-2026))

SAFER Transport Act spotlights stronger federal coordination against cargo theft and fraud

Legislative attention to fraud and theft signals that enforcement, data sharing, and penalties are likely to expand—especially around identity abuse and registration loopholes. Overdrive summarized the SAFER Transport Act as requiring DOT-DOJ coordination, creating an advisory committee, and pushing automated flagging systems for suspicious registration activity. Even if timelines shift, brokers should assume higher expectations for carrier verification, audit trails, and rapid reporting.

Key data point: Overdrive reported the SAFER Transport Act proposes phasing out MC numbers within five years and requires automated systems to flag suspicious registration activity. (Sources: [Overdrive](https://www.overdriveonline.com/regulations/article/15818491/safer-transport-act-would-require-prosecution-of-fraudsters-more))

AI-assisted fraud detection moves from private tools to DOT enforcement strategy

Fraud defenses are no longer just a broker tech stack decision—DOT is signaling it will use AI and advanced analytics to target bad actors and improve enforcement throughput. Overdrive reported DOT leadership discussing AI use to identify high-risk carriers, address principal place of business abuse, and surface hidden affiliations (chameleon carriers) faster. In the next year, brokers should expect more data-driven enforcement actions and higher value for systematic vetting workflows.

Key data point: Overdrive reported DOT plans to use AI and advanced analytics to identify trucking fraud and related risks, including chameleon carrier patterns and registration abuse. (Sources: [Overdrive](https://www.overdriveonline.com/regulations/article/15814889/dot-says-it-will-use-ai-to-hunt-down-fraud-illegal-drivers))

Carrier verification platforms expand “multi-layer” checks as fraud tactics evolve

As identity theft, double-brokering, and impersonation schemes grow more sophisticated, verification providers are broadening their signal sets beyond basic authority and insurance snapshots. FreightWaves profiled Verified Carrier’s approach as multi-step third-party verification, reflecting market demand for defensible, repeatable vetting. The next 3–12 months likely bring more “verification at booking” expectations from shippers and more standardized broker workflows (including QR-code or link-based load authentication).

Key data point: FreightWaves reported Verified Carrier uses an eight-step, multilayered verification process including insurance and registration checks. (Sources: [FreightWaves](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/freighttech-friday-verified-carrier-talks-vetting-tech))

Technology & Policy

Autonomous trucking policy takes a step toward a federal pilot framework

The regulatory path for heavy-duty autonomous operations remains uneven, but FreightWaves reported new draft legislation that could preempt conflicting state rules and authorize commercial freight pilots. For the next year, the practical impact is likely concentrated in specific corridors and hub-to-hub lanes, with implications for shipper network design and dedicated capacity strategies. Brokers should monitor which customers and lanes begin experimenting with autonomous-enabled capacity partnerships.

Key data point: FreightWaves reported a 2026 discussion draft of the SELF DRIVE Act would establish a federal framework for autonomous trucking pilots and preempt conflicting state rules. (Sources: [FreightWaves](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/2026-av-bill-a-game-changer-for-heavy-trucking))

FMCSA TechCelerate Now and ADAS adoption support a safety-tech investment cycle

FMCSA’s TechCelerate Now program continues pushing adoption of advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) through ROI tools and recommended practices. Transport Topics reported the program’s renewed multi-year phase and highlighted expanding scope into cameras and mirror-replacement vision systems. Over the next 3–12 months, expect more fleets to justify ADAS spend as an insurance and nuclear-verdict mitigation lever, not just a safety initiative.

Key data point: Transport Topics reported FMCSA renewed TechCelerate Now in 2024 with a four-year second phase, expanding ADAS focus areas and updating ROI tools. (Sources: [Transport Topics](https://www.ttnews.com/articles/tmc-pushes-techcelerate-now))

EPA 2027 engine transition planning starts now (with maintenance and fluid implications)

As 2027-compliant diesel engines approach, fleets and service providers are already preparing for equipment, maintenance, and lubricant changes that can affect operating cost and uptime. FreightWaves emphasized that upcoming EPA regulations drive significant emissions reductions and that operational readiness matters well before model-year turnover. For brokered capacity, this can influence fleet replacement timing and which carriers prioritize newer equipment on premium freight.

Key data point: FreightWaves noted new heavy-duty diesel engines aligned with upcoming EPA requirements arrive for the Jan. 1, 2027 timeframe, implying near-term prep in 2026. (Sources: [FreightWaves](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/new-engine-oil-standards-are-coming-heres-what-truckers-actually-need-to-know))

Truck parking funding and private expansion both point to incremental relief—not a quick fix

Parking remains a safety and productivity constraint, and both public funding proposals and private truck-stop expansion are moving, but slowly relative to need. Transport Topics reported proposed federal funding dedicated to parking expansion along freight corridors, while also noting Love’s plan to add spaces in 2026. For the next year, detention, scheduling, and route planning must still assume constrained parking availability, especially around major metros.

Key data point: Transport Topics reported $200 million proposed for truck parking expansion and Love’s plan to add 1,500 parking spaces in 2026. (Sources: [Transport Topics](https://www.ttnews.com/articles/congress-truck-parking), [Transport Topics](https://www.ttnews.com/articles/loves-1500-parking-spaces))

Bottom Line

The early-2026 trucking picture is defined by supply-side tightening, higher compliance friction, and persistent cost volatility—creating a market that can swing quickly when disruption hits. Diesel may start the year softer on forecasts, but fuel and insurance remain “tail risks” that can accelerate carrier exits and push procurement into surcharge and safety-tech debates. Fraud prevention and broker financial compliance are moving into a more enforcement-driven era, raising the value of repeatable carrier verification and clean operating practices. For American Lady Transportation, the advantage over the next 3–12 months will come from disciplined carrier selection, documented fraud controls, and proactive shipper conversations on fuel, accessorials, and service reliability.

title: Weekly Freight Report - January 2, 2026
excerpt: Market Pulse — spot/contract rates, load-to-truck ratios, capacity Spot rates: year-end peak held into the holiday week. Truckload spot pricing hit a holiday high of $2.76/mile all-in by late December
content:
Market Pulse — spot/contract rates, load-to-truck ratios, capacity

Spot rates: year-end peak held into the holiday week. Truckload spot pricing hit a holiday high of $2.76/mile all-in by late December (National Truckload Index) and tender rejections peaked at 13.24%, signaling a short-lived but meaningful capacity squeeze around Christmas/New Year’s ([FreightWaves](https://www.freightwaves.com/?p=569132)).

In SONAR’s early-January read, the market eased from the extreme but remained firm: the national tender rejection rate was 10.6% (after a peak-season high of 13.2%), with equipment-specific rejection rates of 11.5% (dry van), 18.5% (reefer), and 9.0% (flatbed) ([SONAR Pricing Power Index](https://gosonar.com/pricing-power-index/freight-market-begins-to-normalize-as-capacity-returns)).

Capacity signal: SONAR described the market as roughly in equilibrium at ~10% rejections (still above the typical 7%–8% threshold associated with upward spot-rate pressure), with expectations for further softening as holiday capacity returned ([SONAR Pricing Power Index](https://gosonar.com/pricing-power-index/freight-market-begins-to-normalize-as-capacity-returns)).

Contract-rate proxy (linehaul): The Cass Truckload Linehaul Index (heavily weighted toward contracts) came in at 146.0 for January 2026, up 1.7% m/m and 3.2% y/y—evidence that contract repricing was finally turning positive after a long downcycle ([Cass Information Systems](https://www.cassinfo.com/freight-audit-payment/cass-transportation-indexes/january-2026)).

Broker takeaway on pricing: Spot was elevated versus the late-2025 baseline (seasonal low $2.32/mile on Nov. 15 rising to $2.76/mile by Dec. 28, an 18.9% increase), but early January data indicated normalization rather than collapse—meaning margin management mattered more than “rate chasing” ([FreightWaves](https://www.freightwaves.com/?p=569132); [SONAR Pricing Power Index](https://gosonar.com/pricing-power-index/freight-market-begins-to-normalize-as-capacity-returns)).

Regulation & Enforcement — FMCSA/DOT rules, ELD, CDL, state regs

ELD compliance risk: revoked devices entering enforcement window. FMCSA removed multiple ELDs from the Registered ELD list effective Nov. 20, 2025 and provided a 60-day transition period through Jan. 20, 2026 during which carriers could use paper/backup logs without being cited for “no RODS,” after which noncompliant use can be treated as operating without a compliant ELD ([LS Carlson Law](https://lscarlsonlaw.com/articles/transportation-logistics-regulatory-updates-2026/)).

Broker financial responsibility rule: deadline approaching. FMCSA’s Broker & Freight Forwarder Financial Responsibility final rule had a compliance date of Jan. 16, 2026, tightening how brokers maintain and report the $75,000 security requirement and accelerating notifications when security dips below the threshold ([LS Carlson Law](https://lscarlsonlaw.com/articles/transportation-logistics-regulatory-updates-2026/)).

Operational enforcement note: With holiday capacity disruptions, any carrier-side compliance gaps (ELD transitions, HOS documentation) can translate into missed appointments, higher fall-off risk, and post-load disputes—especially in short holiday weeks when recovery windows are tighter ([LS Carlson Law](https://lscarlsonlaw.com/articles/transportation-logistics-regulatory-updates-2026/)).

Broker Edge — what brokers need to know, competitive positioning

1) Treat the holiday peak like a “stress test” for routing guides. FreightWaves reported tender rejections reached 13.24% and spot peaked around $2.76/mile late December, a combination that can trigger mini routing-guide failures and force last-minute spot coverage ([FreightWaves](https://www.freightwaves.com/?p=569132)).

2) Use rejection-rate stratification to price smarter. SONAR’s early-January snapshot showed reefer rejection rates at 18.5% vs. 11.5% for van, implying that reefer exposure required more aggressive contingency pricing and deeper carrier benches than van during this week ([SONAR Pricing Power Index](https://gosonar.com/pricing-power-index/freight-market-begins-to-normalize-as-capacity-returns)).

3) Tightening isn’t purely demand-led—watch “capacity return.” SONAR framed the early-January market as normalizing as capacity returned from the holidays, suggesting that lane-level volatility (not a broad demand boom) was the right mental model for negotiations and coverage plans ([SONAR Pricing Power Index](https://gosonar.com/pricing-power-index/freight-market-begins-to-normalize-as-capacity-returns)).

4) Contract bids were starting to move. Cass noted increased one-year bid activity alongside its January increase (+1.7% m/m, +3.2% y/y), which matters for brokers positioning as “capacity + compliance” partners rather than pure spot shops ([Cass Information Systems](https://www.cassinfo.com/freight-audit-payment/cass-transportation-indexes/january-2026)).

Cross-Border Watchlist — US-Mexico, US-Canada, USMCA, tariffs

December cross-border demand leaned toward Mexico. Total U.S.-Canada+Mexico transborder freight value in December 2025 was $127.8B (+1.2% y/y), with U.S.-Mexico at $70.5B (+10.5% y/y) while U.S.-Canada was $57.3B (-8.3% y/y) ([Bureau of Transportation Statistics](https://www.bts.gov/newsroom/north-american-transborder-freight-increased-12-december-2025-december-2024)).

Trucks remained the dominant mode. BTS reported truck-moved transborder freight at $81.6B in December (+5.2% y/y) ([Bureau of Transportation Statistics](https://www.bts.gov/newsroom/north-american-transborder-freight-increased-12-december-2025-december-2024)).

What it meant during this holiday week: If you had exposure to Laredo/El Paso/Otay Mesa, the data supported a “Mexico-strong, Canada-soft” posture going into early January replenishment moves, with truck availability and customs timing becoming a larger variable than usual in short weeks ([Bureau of Transportation Statistics](https://www.bts.gov/newsroom/north-american-transborder-freight-increased-12-december-2025-december-2024)).

Fraud & Security — cargo theft, double-brokering, CDL fraud

Cargo theft: higher loss value even with flat incident counts. Verisk CargoNet estimated 2025 cargo theft losses at ~$725M (up 60% y/y), while recording 3,594 supply chain crime events (roughly flat y/y) and 2,646 confirmed cargo thefts (+18% y/y) ([Commercial Carrier Journal](https://www.ccjdigital.com/regulations/article/15815405/cargo-theft-activity-flat-losses-surged-in-2025-cargonet)).

Why it matters in the Dec 26–Jan 2 window: Holiday coverage, shortened operating hours, and increased use of unfamiliar backup carriers raise exposure to “theft by deception” tactics (identity spoofing, fictitious pickups), which CargoNet flagged as a continuing concern into 2026 ([Commercial Carrier Journal](https://www.ccjdigital.com/regulations/article/15815405/cargo-theft-activity-flat-losses-surged-in-2025-cargonet)).

Practical controls for brokers:

  • Authenticate the carrier identity using trusted contact numbers (not the phone/email provided in an inbound request) before tendering high-value loads.
  • Confirm ELD status for carriers that might be in transition from revoked devices ahead of Jan. 20 enforcement exposure ([LS Carlson Law](https://lscarlsonlaw.com/articles/transportation-logistics-regulatory-updates-2026/)).
  • Use strict “no re-brokering” language and confirm who will be on the BOL at pickup—especially in border-adjacent or high-theft metros where deception rings operate.

Equipment, Fuel & Ops — diesel prices, truck orders, driver pay

Diesel: EIA’s weekly on-highway diesel price was $3.50/gal for Dec. 29, 2025 ([EIA on X](https://x.com/EIAgov/status/2006018229957734863)).

Equipment demand snapped back at year-end. Class 8 net orders in December 2025 were reported at 42,200 units by FTR (up 108% m/m and 21% y/y), with ACT at 42,700 units (+16% y/y), a notable shift attributed to improved policy visibility and early positioning ahead of expected 2027 regulatory cost increases ([FreightWaves](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/class-8-truck-orders-roar-back-but-market-recovery-questions-remain)).

Operational implication: Elevated spot rates plus steady (not spiking) diesel in late December created a margin window for well-positioned carriers, but brokers still had to plan for post-holiday “capacity return” and potential spot cooling rather than assume a sustained upcycle ([SONAR Pricing Power Index](https://gosonar.com/pricing-power-index/freight-market-begins-to-normalize-as-capacity-returns); [EIA on X](https://x.com/EIAgov/status/2006018229957734863)).

Action Checklist for Brokers

  • Reprice holiday-week freight by equipment type using rejection-rate spreads (reefer tighter than van) to avoid under-quoting ([SONAR Pricing Power Index](https://gosonar.com/pricing-power-index/freight-market-begins-to-normalize-as-capacity-returns)).
  • Build a Jan. 20 ELD transition filter: require carriers to attest they are not operating on a revoked device, and document backup-log procedures through enforcement date ([LS Carlson Law](https://lscarlsonlaw.com/articles/transportation-logistics-regulatory-updates-2026/)).
  • Run “identity-first” carrier onboarding for any new holiday coverage (callback to SAFER-verified numbers; verify insurance contacts) to reduce theft-by-deception exposure ([Commercial Carrier Journal](https://www.ccjdigital.com/regulations/article/15815405/cargo-theft-activity-flat-losses-surged-in-2025-cargonet)).
  • For cross-border tenders, plan Mexico-strong capacity and pad border appointment windows—December data showed Mexico trade up double digits y/y ([Bureau of Transportation Statistics](https://www.bts.gov/newsroom/north-american-transborder-freight-increased-12-december-2025-december-2024)).
  • Audit broker compliance posture before Jan. 16 (financial responsibility documentation and process readiness) to avoid operational interruptions ([LS Carlson Law](https://lscarlsonlaw.com/articles/transportation-logistics-regulatory-updates-2026/)).
  • Use contracts strategically where possible: Cass indicated contracts were turning positive y/y—lock in service on critical lanes while spot volatility is still elevated ([Cass Information Systems](https://www.cassinfo.com/freight-audit-payment/cass-transportation-indexes/january-2026)).
